artigo.texto: BYD Builds Out European Charging and Storage Networks While Deliveries Slide Published on 10/20/2026 at 05:10 | Editorial boerse-global.de BYD is betting that infrastructure and after-sales muscle can do what a busy product calendar alone has not: revive momentum in a stock that has spent the year under pressure. The Chinese group unveiled a two-pronged expansion on Tuesday, pairing a European fast-charging buildout with a global service network for its battery storage business, even as its sales figures point the other way. On the storage side, the BYD Energy Storage unit announced a worldwide customer service network for its battery systems. The structure takes in nine operations and maintenance centres and leans on more than 200 field engineers, with additional branches slated for South Africa and Bulgaria in 2027. Over 100 research and development specialists are tied into the network, a push aimed at giving commercial clients technical support long after installation and shoring up confidence in the reliability of BYD's storage solutions. Charging, Staffing and a Paris Flagship The vehicle business is moving on a similar scale in Europe. At the Paris Motor Show, BYD presented new models and core technologies alongside its Denza brand, including the seven-seat ATTO 8 flagship SUV and the second generation of its Blade battery. To drive uptake of its own fast-charging technology, the company said it will install 3,000 fast-charging stations across Europe by the end of 2027. Headcount on the continent is set to follow. Deputy chairwoman Stella Li told Bloomberg that the European workforce will soon pass the 10,000 mark, with roughly 40,000 employees planned in the region by 2030. The ATTO 8 itself packs a 115 kilowatt-hour second-generation Blade battery, delivers up to 653 kilometres of WLTP range and comes with fast-charging capability. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying BYD? At home, BYD introduced the Da Han electric flagship sedan, built on a 1,000-volt architecture with up to 1,008 kilometres of CLTC range. The entry-level variant is priced at 235,900 Yuan. The domestic line-up is being refreshed at a brisk clip: the second generation of the compact Seagull EV was due to launch in China on Tuesday, according to media reports, arriving as a larger five-seater with a more powerful electric motor, though official prices were not yet available at launch. Safety Nod and Battery Share International ambitions got a lift from Europe's safety tester. The SHARK DMO plug-in hybrid pickup received the top five-star rating from Euro NCAP in mid-October. In energy storage deployment, data from the China Automotive Battery Innovation Alliance showed BYD installed 18.29 gigawatt-hours of traction batteries in China in September, a market share of 21.09%. Deliveries Retreat as Q3 Looms The product offensive has yet to show through in volumes. BYD delivered 463,561 new-energy vehicles in September, 180,700 of them exported. Over the first nine months of 2026, sales totalled 3,131,576 vehicles, down 3.94% from the same period a year earlier. Investors will get a clearer read on the financial impact shortly. The company has called a board meeting for 29 October 2026 to review unaudited results for the third quarter and the first nine months of the year. The shares have reflected the softer sales momentum. BYD closed yesterday's session at EUR 8.30, leaving the stock just 3.3% above its 52-week low. In today's trading it slipped 0.1% to EUR 8.33, extending its loss since the turn of the year to 22%. The upcoming quarterly report should shed light on how margins and profitability are holding up in an intensifying battle for market share. artigo.texto: PHOENIX (KVOA) -- Federal land managers are reviewing dozens of applications to build massive data centers on public lands across the West, including in Arizona. According to a new interactive map released by the Center for Western Priorities, the Bureau of Land Management is currently considering at least 35 applications tied to data centers and supporting infrastructure. The proposals cover more than 24,000 acres of public land across Arizona, Idaho, Nevada, Oregon, Utah, and Wyoming. The map, which was last updated on Friday, Oct. 16, shows that 17 of these applications are for actual data center campuses, while 13 are for supporting infrastructure like water pipelines and transmission lines. Some of the proposed projects are massive. In Utah, one developer proposed a 9,000-acre project powered by small modular nuclear reactors. Another developer filed 16 proposals across five states, including a 2,520-acre site near Las Vegas. Unlike traditional energy projects, there is currently no established permitting process for building data centers on public land, officials said. On Sept. 24, a group of congressional representatives sent 18 questions to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum demanding answers about public input, with a deadline of Thursday, Oct. 8. "Before even considering putting data centers on public lands, the Trump administration should be obligated to solicit public feedback on this idea," Lauren Bogard, deputy director of the Center for Western Priorities, said. Public opposition to these projects is growing. A Pew Research Center poll found that the share of Americans who believe data centers are bad for the environment rose to 54 percent in September.

artigo.texto: The next decade of battery materials growth is likely to be shaped as much by regulation as by vehicle demand. According to IndexBox, the market for life cycle safe battery production chemicals is expected to keep expanding through 2035, supported by tougher compliance expectations in Europe and by automakers pressing suppliers to clean up their sourcing.The forecast points to a structural shift in how battery inputs are bought, processed and documented. Rather than treating chemicals as a narrow procurement item, cell makers and their upstream suppliers are increasingly being asked to prove that the materials used in production can stand up to scrutiny across the full value chain. That includes traceability, environmental controls and adherence to rules that are becoming more demanding as battery manufacturing scales up.Regulation is now a commercial driverThe most immediate catalyst is the European Union's battery regulatory framework, which has pushed sustainability and disclosure from the margins into the centre of industrial planning. For chemical suppliers, the compliance burden is no longer limited to product quality and pricing. Buyers are now looking for evidence that inputs align with life cycle safety requirements, a trend that is likely to influence sourcing decisions well beyond Europe.IndexBox said the market outlook is being reinforced by automaker supply chain mandates, which are adding another layer of pressure on suppliers. As carmakers seek to de-risk their battery ecosystems, chemical vendors are being pushed to meet tighter standards on safety, documentation and consistency. In practice, that can favour larger suppliers with better process control, audit readiness and the ability to serve multiple geographies from a single compliance framework.Gigafactory expansion is widening the addressable marketAt the same time, the build-out of gigafactories is expanding the volume of chemicals needed for battery production. Every new cell plant adds demand not only for core active materials but also for a range of supporting chemicals used in manufacturing, treatment and quality assurance. As capacity rises, so does the need for suppliers that can deliver at industrial scale without compromising on regulatory standards.This creates a dual effect. On one hand, scale-up increases volumes and opens the door to larger contracts. On the other, it raises the bar for operational discipline, because any compliance lapse can ripple quickly through high-volume battery supply chains. That dynamic is likely to reward producers that can combine capacity, consistency and documentation in a sector where procurement decisions increasingly carry reputational as well as technical risk.What the forecast means for chemical makersFor chemical companies serving the battery industry, the opportunity is not simply about selling more product. The market is moving toward a model in which compliance credentials, product stewardship and supply chain transparency are part of the offer itself. Suppliers that can demonstrate life cycle safety may find themselves better positioned as preferred vendors to battery makers and automakers alike.The wider implication is that battery chemicals are becoming a strategic layer in the energy transition, not just a supporting input. As governments tighten standards and manufacturers expand capacity, the market is likely to favour players that can adapt quickly to documentation-heavy procurement and cross-border regulatory demands.IndexBox's outlook suggests that this is still an early stage of a longer cycle. Through 2035, the combination of battery regulation, automotive sourcing rules and gigafactory investment is expected to keep the market on an upward path, with compliance increasingly tied to commercial competitiveness. For suppliers, the message is clear: growth will depend not only on chemistry, but also on the ability to prove that every step of production is safe, traceable and fit for the next generation of battery manufacturing. - Policy & Regulation - 3 min Read Battery chemical suppliers eye compliance-led growth through 2035 IndexBox expects the market for life cycle safe battery production chemicals to grow through 2035 as EU battery rules and automaker sourcing mandates reshape procurement. Gigafactory expansion is adding demand, but suppliers will need stronger compliance, traceability and documentation to win contracts. - Published On Oct 19, 2026 at 12:46 PM IST

artigo.texto: Pitt County planning staff is scheduled to present an assessment of the county’s existing data center ordinance as the commissioners weigh implementing a moratorium on the facilities. The presentation will take place during the Pitt County Board of Commissioners’ 6 p.m. meeting today at the county office building, 1717 W. Fifth St. Residents have lobbied the commissioners to establish a moratorium in an effort to prevent data centers from locating facilities in the unincorporated areas of the county. In order to adopt a moratorium, the board needs to identify a deficiency in its current regulations that it wants to fix, officials have said during previous discussions. Along with the presentation, planning staff wants input from the commissioners on their concerns, potential impacts or regulatory issues that weren’t addressed in the evaluation. If the board proceeds with the moratorium, it will have to hold a public hearing. Staff is proposing the hearing be held at the board’s Nov. 16 meeting. Zoning amendment The board also is set to hold a public hearing on a request to amend the county’s zoning ordinance so the use “Outdoor Farm and Construction Equipment Auction” can be added as a permitted use. The county planning board in September said it was consistent with the county’s Comprehensive Land Use Plan but recommended it only be allowed as a conditional use in the rural agricultural zoning district. This would require the planning board and board of commissioners to hold public hearings on the request before making a decision. Planning staff recommends it be a permit by right in the rural agricultural zoning district, which only requires staff approval. Other actions State Reps. Gloristine Brown and Tim Reeder will present the commissioners with a $250,000 grant. The commissioners’ agenda did not indicate what grant program made the award or how the money will be used. The board is scheduled to adopt a proclamation recognizing October as Domestic Violence Awareness Month. A representative of Inspire Placemaking Collective, a consultant working with the county to develop a unified development ordinance, is scheduled to provide an overview of the project, which is expected to take 14-18 months to complete.

artigo.texto: Those pushing for a statewide moratorium on data center development worked to amplify their case during a rally on the steps of the courthouse in Leesburg. Organized by the Piedmont Environmental Council, the hour-long event was attended by about 100 supporters who heard comments from residents whose lives have been impacted by data centers and power lines and from state legislators supporting plans to halt work on new projects until new regulations to limit those impacts can be established. The event was held a week after Sen. Russet Perry (D-31) submitted a bill for the upcoming General Assembly session that would impose a three-year state moratorium and just days before a Board of Supervisors vote on plans to slow review of projects in Loudoun County. Jared Mummert is leading the data center reform campaign for the PEC. “For more than 26 years, data centers have been a part of life here in Loudoun, and there is no community that understands and has seen the transition of this industry like us,” he said in kicking off the rally. “We have seen this industry turn from smaller centers closer to office parks … and they have transitioned into energy-guzzling, grid-destabilizing, water-consuming, ear-ringing, air-polluting, skyrocketing electric bill giants that they are today. And they're ugly, absolutely.” “Loudoun has 233 data centers, with 100 more on the way, and there are hundreds of others across the state. Today, from the data center capital of the world, we say enough is enough,” Mummert said. Speakers included Ashley Warmerling, a Lovettsville area resident leading the fight against the Valley North transmission line; Victor Block, the HOA president working to limit the impact of new transmission lines on his Loudoun Valley Estates neighborhood; Gregory Pirio, a Sterling resident who raised concerns about the health impacts of a natural gas power plant feeding a data center in his community; Sarina Virmani, a Riverside High School student working to help young people have a greater voice in community issues; and attorney Phillip Thompson, a member of the Loudoun NAACP who said a moratorium is needed to protect the public’s health and safety. Perry and Del. John McAuliff (D-30) said they will continue to make better regulations of data centers a top priority. “When I first ran for office last year, I channeled, or I tried to channel the best I could, that anger and that frustration into the first race ever fully focused on data centers, and we won—with your help, we won,” McAuliff said. “This year, you've shown up at public hearings, raised your concerns, and asked whether anybody is listening while project after project continues to move forward. No more. Because of your voice, our leaders in Richmond, governors, senators, congressmen from around the country are all racing to show how much they're going to do about data centers because of the work that you all have done.” McAuliff said history was made last year when the General Assembly imposed the first restrictions on dirty diesel generators and the first zoning rules on data centers. “No one had ever done that before until you spoke up,” he said. McAuliff laid out a five-point plan for additional work to better protect the region. That includes ending the use of dirty diesel generators for all existing data centers, banning data centers in low groundwater areas and on farmland, making existing data centers pay for “every dime” of their energy and infrastructure need, protecting homes and farms from transmission lines and fully compensate those impacted, and imposing a moratorium on new data center development across the commonwealth. “You have done your part by showing up today, making your voices heard time and time again. It is now our responsibility to take those concerns and turn them into actions,” McAuliff said. “Don't stop speaking up. Don't stop organizing. … We have already sent an unmistakable message, which is that we demand better and we will win.” Perry said that when she first went to Richmond three years ago, the state senators who were concerned about the impacts of data centers could fit inside a Honda Civic. But that has changed. “[There were] three of us, three of 40. It was worse than apathy,” she said. “Just last year, Governor Youngkin stood before the General Assembly and delivered his State of the Commonwealth address. And what he said was he wanted Virginia to be the data center capital of the world, and the room jumped to its feet, including people who represent Loudoun County. Rest assured, I was not clapping, and I certainly was not standing. But things have changed, and you all are all the reasons.” State leaders are increasingly raising concerns about higher electric bills, groundwater depletion, the loss of farmland and community impacts of data centers and transmission lines. “Legislators from across the commonwealth are slowly, too slowly, but starting to join and see what you all have been saying for so long,” Perry said. “Virginia does not exist to be a pass-through state for corporate greed. We do not exist to swallow massive high-voltage lines and bail out bad corporate math. And we will not be quieted. We will not sit down, and we will not let anyone sacrifice our quality of life for their bottom line.” Perry said her bill, SB 843, would create a three-year pause that would give state leaders time to develop better rules for the scale, design and location of data centers. “That's three years to stop and think, three years to build a real statewide plan for where these facilities go, how they're powered, and who pays for them. artigo.texto: SHENZHEN, China, Oct. 19, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- BYD Energy Storage has built a comprehensive after-sales service network in a multi‑tier framework: station O&M, project centers, regional centers and global headquarters. BYD Energy Storage operates nine O&M centers globally, each spanning 2,500 square meters. Its after-sales service network covers China, Chile, South Africa, the UK, the US, Australia, Japan, Poland, and the Middle East. New service centers will open in South Africa and Bulgaria in 2027 to further expand its global service footprint. The centers deliver core functions including spare parts storage and management, batteries repair and maintenance, regional spare parts allocation, batteries recycling, and training for locally hired engineers. BYD Energy Storage’s regional centers fully comply with local regulatory requirements, deliver structured workforce training and enable rapid on-site response. The professional service team comprises over 200 field engineers and more than 100 R&D specialists. The company enforces standardized service SLAs: response within 24 hours, on-site arrival within 48 hours, and fault troubleshooting within 7 days. The company's global service network has achieved widespread coverage. It forms a multi-point supply network that ensures rapid spare parts delivery worldwide. Furthermore, leveraging localized production lines, its O&M teams integrate regional resources to deliver local battery repair services, providing global customers with fast, convenient, and localized after-sales support. "Our global service footprint is tailored to our fast‑growing BESS deployments. Trustworthy after‑sales support underpins the long‑term stable operation of energy storage assets,” commented Mr. He Dehong, Head of Global After-sales Service at BYD Energy Storage. Guided by its vision, empower global energy storage industry with digital and intelligent service, BYD Energy Storage’s mature global O&M system strongly supports its expanding battery energy storage footprint. Uma pesquisa da Gallup realizada em março constatou que 71% dos americanos se opõem à construção de um data center em sua região. Entre as principais preocupações está o consumo de energia. Metade dos americanos entrevistados pelo Pew Research Center em julho e agosto afirmou que os data centers seriam predominantemente prejudiciais ao meio ambiente e aos custos de energia das famílias. Agora, o Google aposta que um enorme data center voltado à inteligência artificial pode ajudar a financiar uma rede elétrica mais limpa e confiável. O acordo proposto com a Xcel Energy acrescentaria uma capacidade de geração de energia e armazenamento em baterias superior à que o data center deverá consumir. Pelo acordo, o Google ajudaria a pagar pela capacidade adicional e continuaria arcando com os custos mesmo que não utilizasse toda a energia disponível. Leia também: Google terá uma nova fonte de energia; conheça o projeto de US$ 4 bilhões Pine Island, em Minnesota, é uma pequena cidade com cerca de 4 mil habitantes, localizada a uma hora a sudeste de Minneapolis. O Google espera que seu projeto de data center de 780 megawatts fortaleça o relacionamento com a comunidade local e ajude a empresa a cumprir a meta de operar com energia livre de carbono 24 horas por dia, sete dias por semana, até 2030. O Google, cuja divisão de computação em nuvem sustenta sua própria inteligência artificial Gemini e gerou quase US$ 25 bilhões em receita no segundo trimestre, alta de 82% em relação ao mesmo período do ano anterior, afirma ter encontrado um modelo para desenvolver esse tipo de projeto de maneira adequada. A empresa planeja financiar a adição de 1.400 megawatts de energia eólica, 200 megawatts de energia solar e 300 megawatts de armazenamento em baterias à rede da Xcel. Essa capacidade adicional supera a potência do próprio data center. Segundo o Google, isso ocorre porque as fontes eólica e solar não geram energia continuamente. A Xcel Energy afirmou que a nova eletricidade atenderá a todos os consumidores da região, e não apenas ao Google. A concessionária também disse que as melhorias contribuirão para ampliar o fornecimento de energia livre de carbono na rede local. O acordo proposto entre Google e Xcel inclui cobranças mínimas por demanda e taxas de saída. Segundo o Google, essas cláusulas manterão a empresa responsável pelos custos da infraestrutura construída para atendê-la, mesmo que o crescimento da inteligência artificial perca força. O Google pagará por pelo menos 75% da capacidade contratada, mesmo que utilize menos energia. Caso encerre o contrato antecipadamente, poderá ter de pagar o equivalente a até oito anos dessas cobranças mínimas por demanda. “Ninguém quer realizar uma grande expansão e depois não ter para onde direcionar essa energia nem quem pague por ela”, afirmou Amanda Rome, vice-presidente executiva e diretora de relacionamento com clientes da Xcel Energy. “É para isso que servem essas proteções.” O acordo entre Google e Xcel Energy ainda depende da aprovação da Comissão de Serviços Públicos de Minnesota. Leia também: Chefe do Google DeepMind alerta para novos riscos de segurança envolvendo I.A. Novos data centers responderão pela maior parte do aumento projetado da demanda por eletricidade na próxima década, segundo a North American Electric Reliability Corporation, organização reguladora sem fins lucrativos. O Departamento de Energia dos Estados Unidos, durante o governo do presidente Joe Biden, informou que mais de 70% das linhas de transmissão e dos transformadores elétricos do país tinham pelo menos 25 anos. O órgão também concluiu que as alternativas mais baratas para atender à demanda futura exigiriam mais que dobrar a capacidade do sistema nacional de transmissão até 2050. Siga o Times | CNBC As grandes empresas de tecnologia que operam serviços de computação em nuvem, conhecidas como hyperscalers, argumentam que podem financiar melhorias necessárias à rede elétrica e, ao mesmo tempo, torná-la mais limpa e confiável. “O momento desta revolução industrial não poderia ser mais perfeito”, afirmou Amanda Peterson Corio, chefe global de energia e eletricidade do Google. “Isso acontece justamente quando precisamos de capital para consertar a infraestrutura envelhecida dos Estados Unidos.” Leia também: Como funciona a ferramenta do Google para identificar conteúdos feitos por IA Jigar Shah, sócio da Multiplier, consultoria que ajuda startups de energia limpa a abrir capital, afirmou que as operadoras de data centers poderiam construir instalações menores em locais onde a rede elétrica já possui capacidade ociosa. Isso reduziria a necessidade de construir – e financiar – novos equipamentos de geração e transmissão. “Se o crescimento da carga elétrica desejado pelos data centers fosse acomodado na rede existente, as tarifas de todos cairiam bastante”, disse Shah. Isso ocorre porque a rede elétrica existente tem custos fixos elevados, relacionados à infraestrutura já instalada, como usinas, linhas de transmissão e subestações. artigo.texto: MELBOURNE, Australia, Oct. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Fox ESS, a global leader in renewable energy solutions, has introduced Power Cube, an all-in-one residential energy storage system combining the inverter and batteries in a sleek, stackable design. Engineered for simpler, faster installation, it helps Australian households manage their energy needs today while allowing flexibility for the future. The launch follows SunWiz's announcement that Fox ESS ranked No. 1 in Australia for installed energy storage capacity in H1 2026, reinforcing the company's strong position in the market. By integrating essential components into one compact system, Power Cube streamlines installation and can help reduce installation time and costs. Its modular EQ5500 batteries offer storage capacities from 10.92 kWh to 49.14 kWh across two to nine modules, allowing homeowners to choose a system that suits their household energy needs. "Power Cube has been designed with the Australian market in mind," said Brooks Richard, Managing Director of APAC & Middle East at Fox ESS. "It delivers superior round-trip efficiency and a flexible range of capacities that align well with Australian household energy needs and available battery rebate tiers. Just as importantly, its integrated design simplifies installation, helping installers deliver a complete energy storage solution with greater ease." Power Cube combines this flexibility with features designed for everyday performance and convenience: - Power options for different homes: Single-phase models from 5–12 kW (CEC Approved) and three-phase models from 5–15 kW (coming soon), all supporting up to 200% PV oversizing. - A compact, integrated design and IP66 rating support indoor and outdoor installation. - An integrated gateway with 63A on-grid full-home backup support. - Built-in battery protection: Inter-cell insulation and an aerosol unit in each battery module provide two levels of protection, from cell to pack. - Integrated heating helps maintain battery performance in colder conditions. - Fox Cloud 2.0 with AI enables real-time monitoring and remote configuration, with Wi-Fi, LAN and Bluetooth connectivity. Backed by a 10-year product warranty, Power Cube brings installation simplicity, expandable storage and smart energy management together in one residential solution. For installers, it offers an integrated system designed to streamline delivery; for homeowners, it provides flexibility as their energy needs evolve. SOURCE Fox ESS

artigo.texto: SiC Ups Efficiency of Utility-Scale Battery Storage to Over 99% Battery energy storage systems (BESS) are building up behind the grid to help keep up with the rising demand for power driven by everything from electric vehicles (EVs) to AI data centers. By storing excess energy, including from non-constant sources such as solar and wind, they can deliver electricity to the grid during periods of peak demand. They can also supply backup power to facilities such as factories and data centers, helping the latter manage the highly variable power demands associated with AI workloads. But increasing the capacity and performance of these big lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) batteries is only part of the equation. Equally important is maximizing the amount of energy that power electronics can wring out of them. “At utility scale, even small improvements in power-conversion efficiency can have a meaningful impact on battery energy storage system performance and total cost of ownership,” said Sergio Fissore, vice president and general manager of the IPD power division at onsemi. To that end, the company is working with battery-storage supplier Sungrow to integrate its silicon-carbide (SiC) power-module technology into a new utility-scale BESS. Sungrow's PowerTitan 3.0 platform incorporates onsemi's power integrated modules (PIMs), optimized for the three-level inverter topologies widely used in grid-connected batteries. The "hybrid" module combines SiC MOSFETs, used in the high-frequency switching stages to maximize efficiency and power density, with silicon power devices, used in other portions of the design. This dual-material approach balances SiC's higher performance with silicon's cost to improve the “system economics” of energy storage. Compared with the previous-generation platform, the new architecture improves inverter-level efficiency by 0.4%, according to onsemi. It supports power-conversion units rated up to 450 kW, enabling higher-power storage deployments while maintaining high conversion efficiency. Peak efficiency exceeds 99.3%, helping minimize losses and the associated heat in utility-scale systems that convert DC from the battery to AC for grid delivery. In a large-scale BESS deployment, even small improvements in efficiency can make a big impact on both performance and cost, said Fissore. onsemi’s analysis revealed that a 0.4% efficiency boost delivered by the hybrid SiC module could add up to more than 475 megawatt-hours (MWh) of energy savings per year in a 100-MW battery energy storage installation compared to the previous module. These savings can increase the amount of energy available for grid delivery, reduce operating costs, and improve the overall economics of storage assets, according to onsemi. The same characteristics also enable higher overload capability and improved thermal performance, which helps energy storage systems handle the heavy demands of loads such as AI data centers while maintaining reliability. In these situations, the BESS acts as a shock absorber, supplying extra power to the data center during AI power spikes. Chen Peng, general manager of energy storage conversion products for Sungrow's Energy Storage business, said the new architecture would help with the "deployment of higher-performance storage solutions that deliver greater value throughout the lifecycle of energy assets. By integrating advanced technologies and collaborating with strategic partners such as onsemi, Sungrow is accelerating the deployment of higher-performance storage solutions that deliver greater value throughout the lifecycle of energy assets." About the Author James Morra Senior Editor James Morra is the senior editor for Electronic Design, covering the semiconductor industry and new technology trends, with a focus on power electronics and power management. He also reports on the business behind electrical engineering, including the electronics supply chain. He joined Electronic Design in 2015 and is based in Chicago, Illinois. The project is Times Digital’s first market-oriented overseas benchmark project, marking the formal export of its new-energy technical service capabilities. MAS is located in Ha’il province, about 590 km north of Riyadh, and is a key independent power producer project under Round 5 of Saudi Arabia’s National Renewable Energy Program, developed by a consortium of EDF, SPIC Yellow River Hydropower and Saudi SAPCO. The project is scheduled to begin pre-energization commissioning on November 15 and achieve partial grid connection by the end of November; once fully operational, it is expected to generate 4.4 billion kWh annually. Times Digital’s domestic new-energy O&M service portfolio has exceeded 34 GW.

artigo.texto: O Ceará abriga a construção de um data center que será o maior do Brasil em operação. Além disso, há outros 10 projetos hiperescala de processamento de dados na região do Pecém. Especialistas que participaram da terceira edição do Atlantic Convergence, em Lisboa, apontam o que está por trás desse boom: energia renovável em abundância e o hub de cabos submarinos de Fortaleza, que representa o segundo ponto de maior conectividade do mundo. Nesse contexto, o Estado caminha para se tornar uma potência global de processamento de dados, avalia o especialista em Transformação Digital e Inteligência Artificial do Banco Mundial, Luciano Charlita de Freitas. "O Ceará já tem histórico de investimentos em infraestrutura digital, um cinturão que cobre todos os municípios e recebe cabos submarinos. Entendemos que o Ceará pode se tornar um exportador global de dados, não só para o mercado brasileiro, mas também para fora do Brasil", lista. A agenda de expansão da geração e distribuição de energia foi desenhada antes do boom dos data centers, o que posiciona o Estado na dianteira, segundo o especialista. "A capacidade instalada de data centers no Estado deve aumentar muito nos próximos anos. O Ceará tem força de trabalho qualificada, conhecimento sobre o negócio e posição estratégica dentro do Brasil para continuar nessa agenda", observa. O Banco Mundial conversa com a gestão estadual para financiar projetos de tecnologia no Ceará. A instituição tem portfólio de US$ 1 bilhão no Brasil e já fez investimentos em Hdrogênio Verde. Data centers menores O Ceará também pode ficar na dianteira no mercado de data centers de menor porte, instalados o mais perto possível dos usuários finais, chamados de edge. Ao contrário dos grandes empreendimentos, esses data centers ficam em regiões periféricas, para permitir o processamento e a entrega de dados de forma mais rápida. De acordo com o CEO da holding de tecnologia e telecomunicações SAMM, Carlos Eduardo Sedeh, "os data centers menores vão permitir, por exemplo, que a população do Ceará tenha acesso a serviços como carros autônomos, inferências, internet das coisas, sensorização e cidades inteligentes". "Tudo isso a partir de data centers descentralizados", frisa. O executivo destaca que o Brasil deve registrar expansão dos pequenos empreendimentos nos próximos anos, em paralelo à atração de projetos em grande escala. "A economia digital está se tornando realidade. A demanda está aumentando muito, não só em telecomunicações, mas também em computação em nuvem e outros serviços", afirma. Segundo Sedeh, o ambiente de negócios criado na Zona de Processamento e Exportação (ZPE) do Pecém é um atrativo para as empresas. "Criar uma ZPE numa área que carece de desenvolvimento e direcionar energia e esforços para trazer as empresas é uma estratégia muito acertada. Não existe investimento dessa magnitude sem investimento do governo e estabilidade jurídica", diz. DE-CIX avalia levar interconexão a Fortaleza O Brasil desponta como um dos mercados com maior demanda por serviços de conectividade e processamento de dados, segundo o CEO do grupo DE-CIX, Ivo Ivanov. A empresa oferece interconexão premium e opera vários pontos de troca de tráfego ao redor do mundo. "No nosso negócio, o Brasil é o mercado com crescimento mais acelerado neste ano. Chegamos a mais de 100 clientes atendidos. Estamos oferecendo a primeira plataforma de interconexão de inteligência artificial do país", afirma. Com operação em São Paulo e no Rio de Janeiro, a empresa estuda levar seus serviços a Fortaleza, que caminha para se tornar o segundo maior mercado brasileiro, segundo Ivanov. "Temos muita vontade de construir do Brasil para o Brasil, e não entregar serviços de fora. Fortaleza está no nosso mapa. Vemos como a inovação impulsiona a infraestrutura e como a infraestrutura precisa ser implantada em todos os lugares", aponta. Ivanov ressalta que, com a crescente digitalização, as instalações devem ficar cada vez mais próximas dos usuários para diminuir o tempo de resposta. Para o executivo, com a chegada de pequenos e grandes data centers, o país deve atentar para a soberania e a proteção das informações processadas. "Dados de organizações e de pessoas que vivem no país devem ficar no país, e não ser enviados para treinamentos nos Estados Unidos ou na Europa. É uma questão de soberania. Também é preciso criar ambiente de inovação. Riscos sempre existem, mas temos de proteger e garantir que sejam mitigados", completa. *A repórter viajou a convite da DE-CIX para a Atlantic Convergence em Lisboa.

artigo.texto: POWERGRID Invites Bids for 187.5 MW/750 MWh Battery Storage Project 19 Oct 2026 2 Min Read CW Team Share Power Grid Corporation of India (POWERGRID) has invited online bids for developing a 187.5 MW/750 MWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) in Telangana. The project is intended to strengthen grid stability and support the integration of renewable energy into the electricity network. Designated as Package TS-BESS-01, the project carries Tender Reference Number CC/T/W-BESS/DOM/A02/26/14098. The proposed BESS will provide 187.5 MW of power capacity and 750 MWh of energy storage, equivalent to 4 hours of storage at full output. The tender is being conducted through the Tariff Based Competitive Bidding (TBCB) route and is classified as a power and energy project works contract. Eligible companies can access the tender documents through POWERGRID’s PRANIT Portal using RFX Number 5002005732, subject to the stated technical, financial and pre-qualification requirements. The participation fee has been fixed at Rs. 25,000, while the tender value and earnest money deposit (EMD) are listed as zero on the portal. Bidders are required to review the official documents for eligibility conditions, technical specifications, commercial requirements and other instructions before submitting their offers. The tender schedule set October 12, 2026, at 7:50 PM as the start of document sales and soft copy bid submissions. Document sales will close on October 17 at 11:55 PM, while bids must be submitted by October 19 at 11:00 AM and are scheduled to be opened at 11:30 AM the same day. The tender is being managed by Satyam Gupta, Engineer (CS), from POWERGRID’s corporate office in Gurugram, Haryana. The project will add flexible storage capacity that can absorb electricity when supply is available and discharge it during periods of higher demand or lower renewable generation, supporting grid balancing and the wider integration of solar and wind power. artigo.texto: IREN Co-CEO Daniel Roberts Says Firm’s Data Centers Carry No Debt As Funding Worries Hit Stock - After recent pressure on the IREN stock, co-CEO Daniel Roberts said that the company's data centers are supported fully by cash, and the company had no debt against assets. - Under recent three-year contracts, customer prepayments cover 45% to 55% of GPU expenses, Roberts said. - IREN's Microsoft agreement covered 96% of GPU expenses, with prepayments at 6%, and non-investment payment-grade customers paid 9%. Shares of IREN Limited (IREN) edged lower in pre-market trading on Tuesday after co-CEO Daniel Roberts said that the company's data centers did not carry any debt. Roberts responded to investors' concern over how the artificial intelligence (AI) cloud providers will fund their expansion. Roberts said on X that IREN has paid for their data center construction in cash so far. Adding to it, he said that the sites can support their own financing once they come online with contracted customers. Robert laid out the process step by step. Customers must first sign multi-year take-or-pay contracts, which require payment whether or not they use the capacity. On recent three-year deals, he said prepayments covered 45% to 55% of the cost of the graphics processing units (GPUs).https://x.com/danroberts0101/status/2112200081034129419?s=20 He added that lenders mostly fund the rest, with the GPUs serving as collateral. Robert added that Iren's Microsoft (MSFT) contract was supported by an A-rated facility at 6% or so. That, plus prepayments, accounts for 96% of the GPU spending. One customer without an investment-grade rating at Iren's McKenzie site in British Columbia was borrowing at a fixed 9%. The loan and prepayment more than pay for the whole cost of the GPU, the co-CEO added. He acknowledged that future debt will price at whatever the market charges. But he said a payback of about 2 years on recent contracts means "a wider spread barely moves the economics." Demand Outruns Build Capacity According to Roberts, customer demand exceeds what IREN can build. The company's 2026 capacity is largely sold out, he added, saying recent 3-year contracts are priced at more than double last year's level. Demand for capacity arriving in 2027 is several times oversubscribed, and discussions on 2028 have begun. The holdup in the industry is not signing deals, he said. Getting GPUs online is the issue, as announced capacity keeps sleeping across the sector. Pressure On Neocoloud Stocks Continue Neoclouds, the specialized AI cloud providers, have been under pressure through the past week. The stock has been down over 20% over the past week. Investors became increasingly worried after debt pressures at CoreWeave (CRWV) and a research firm warned that over 80% of neoclouds might no longer be able to operate independently by 2030. Retail Chatter For IREN Surges IREN stock was down over 4% in pre-market trade, trading at $26. On Stocktwits retail sentiment around IREN remained in the ‘extremely bullish’ zone, with ‘high’ chatter levels over the past day. According to platform data, chatter around IREN has been up over 952% over the past 30 days. One user on Stocktwits said that the IREN stock had erased all of the previous day's gain, and it would need to rise 70% to reach above $46 again.

artigo.texto: CATL Unveils Dual-Electric Range Extension Battery to Accelerate Electric Heavy-Duty Truck Adoption BEIJING, Oct. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- CATL today unveiled the innovative dual-electric range extension battery and the latest generation of heavy-duty battery-swapping solution to accelerate the electrification of road freight transportation. Competition in electric heavy-duty trucking is moving beyond technical specifications toward full-lifecycle value. While battery swapping has made energy replenishment faster and more predictable, concerns about battery utilization, operating costs and residual vehicle value continue to affect fleet economics. To address these challenges, CATL combines its dual-electric range extension battery with QIJI's strategy of standardization, new infrastructure and a full commercial ecosystem, bringing battery swapping and industry-wide collaboration together to accelerate heavy-duty truck electrification. A Dual-Electric Approach to Range Extension CATL's dual-electric range extension battery combines two independent yet complementary battery systems. The main battery uses QIJI's standardized chassis-mounted swappable battery to maximize efficiency. A behind-the-cab range-extension power system, currently equipped with a 77kWh battery capable of 3C charging, provides backup power. Together, the systems maintain uninterrupted power delivery and provide redundancy for demanding operating conditions. - Dual-System Power Redundancy In conventional battery-swapping trucks, drivers often return for a swap with unused capacity because they are reluctant to run the battery low. Backup power from the range-extension battery increases the main battery's depth of discharge (DOD) from approximately 70% to over 95%, allowing it to be returned at less than 5% state of charge (SOC). At this threshold, CATL's seamless switching technology transfers power delivery to the range-extension battery within milliseconds, maintaining a continuous and stable power supply. - "1+X" Architecture and Independent Upgrades The system uses a "1+X" architecture. One standardized main battery maintains compatibility with the QIJI battery-swapping network, while the range-extension battery can be customized for specific conditions with options including ultra-high energy density, low-temperature resistance for cold climates, or ultra-high power. The two battery systems can be developed and upgraded independently to meet their respective technical and operational requirements. - Flexible Leasing and Battery Asset Management The independently owned on-board range-extension battery stays with the vehicle as an asset throughout its service life, reducing reliance on immediate access to a swapping station. The main battery can be leased according to seasonal freight demand, helping fleets reduce rental costs during quieter periods and manage battery assets more flexibly. This architecture combines the benefits of standardization with flexible vehicle configurations, making electric heavy-duty trucks more practical and economically viable across a wider range of applications. QIJI Builds a Shared Battery Swapping Ecosystem QIJI complements these improvements with a three-pillar strategy of standardization, new infrastructure and a full commercial ecosystem. It seeks to speed heavy-duty truck electrification with a value-chain ecosystem co-created by all stakeholders, where benefits are shared collectively. - Standardization Supports Wider Adoption To accommodate a wider range of truck models and operating conditions, QIJI has introduced the 260# (432 kWh) and 300# (513 kWh) standardized battery-swapping blocks alongside the existing 75# block. The system enables battery swaps in just five minutes, with a 99.99% first-time success rate, helping fleets minimize downtime and maintain operational efficiency. QIJI has also pioneered a battery-as-a-service (BaaS) model in which customers pay for the net energy charged rather than the energy discharged. This allows customers to retain the value of energy recovered through regenerative braking, reducing per-kWh battery rental costs for users on basic plans by up to 20%. Flexible battery leasing options allow customers to tailor rental periods to their needs, from second-hand vehicle transitions to seasonal demand. This will minimize idle costs and offer more flexible options for off-season downtime, further helping fleets manage operating costs. - New Infrastructure Improves Resource Efficiency QIJI aims to make better use of four critical resources in long-haul freight: time, land, payload capacity and grid electricity. Rapid battery swapping reduces waiting times, while efficient station layouts serve more vehicles within the same footprint. Battery capacity is matched to transport needs, and centralized, coordinated charging makes better use of grid electricity. These measures aim to improve both resource efficiency and operational returns. CATL plans to deploy 900 battery-swapping stations by the end of 2026 and 2,000 by 2027, with a long-term target of 10,000 stations nationwide in collaboration with its partners. By connecting major freight corridors through a coordinated swapping network, QIJI aims to improve the efficiency and commercial viability of electric heavy-duty trucking. - A Commercial Ecosystem Supports the Full Vehicle Lifecycle QIJI connects truck manufacturers, financial institutions, insurers, channel partners and aftermarket service providers across the vehicle lifecycle, from purchase and operation to maintenance and resale, working together to build a comprehensive ecosystem of integrated products and services. QIJI has introduced two partnership models: Battery Asset Service Partners and Energy Replenishment Service Partners. These models allow partners to participate in battery asset services and energy replenishment, extending their role beyond one-off vehicle sales to ongoing operations. artigo.texto: Siga o Times Brasil - Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC no CEO do HSBC alerta que boom da IA não torna todos os data centers bons investimentos Publicado 20/10/2026 • 10:07 | Atualizado há 21 horas KEY POINTS Pexels A inteligência artificial (IA) é uma tecnologia transformadora que merece investimentos, mas os investidores precisam ser criteriosos ao escolher projetos de data centers, segundo o presidente-executivo de um dos maiores bancos do mundo. Em entrevista a Dan Murphy, da CNBC, nesta terça-feira (20), Georges Elhedery, CEO do HSBC, classificou a inteligência artificial como “um importante facilitador para reformular e reinventar todos os nossos negócios e atividades”. “Ela vai devolver muito poder aos nossos colegas por causa do nível de produtividade que proporciona. Portanto, será transformadora, e estamos certamente em uma jornada para adotá-la”, afirmou. Segundo ele, a IA também ajudará a “reformular o banco”. No entanto, ao abordar os investimentos em infraestrutura que sustenta essa tecnologia, Elhedery recomendou cautela, em vez de uma aposta indiscriminada no setor. Leia também: HSBC amplia receita e mantém lucro estável no 1º trimestre, com alta de depósitos e pressão de custos “É preciso ser seletivo”, afirmou. “É necessário avaliar a qualidade dos contratos de locação e os preços estabelecidos nesses contratos. Nem todos apresentam um nível de qualidade que permita sustentá-los com confiança. Alguns podem ser mais desafiadores.” O HSBC foi classificado pela S&P Global, no ano passado, como o sétimo maior banco do mundo e o maior credor da Europa, com ativos próximos de US$ 3 trilhões. Com sede em Londres, a instituição atua tanto no financiamento quanto na operação de data centers. Em seu relatório anual de 2025, o HSBC afirmou que pretende se tornar “o banco líder para ecossistemas de transição de rápido crescimento”, destacando que sua carteira de clientes abrange setores como data centers e inteligência artificial. Siga o Times | CNBC no Google e receba as principais notícias do Brasil e do Mundo. Siga o Times | CNBC Os complexos de data centers abrigam os servidores que sustentam a IA e a computação em nuvem. Nos últimos anos, o setor passou por uma expansão bilionária, impulsionada pela crescente demanda por capacidade computacional. Segundo a consultoria McKinsey, os gastos globais com data centers podem atingir US$ 7 trilhões até 2030. Para financiar a construção dessas instalações, grandes empresas de tecnologia têm recorrido cada vez mais ao crédito privado e à emissão de dívidas. O endividamento relacionado à IA, porém, está se tornando uma fonte de tensão nos mercados financeiros. O custo do capital está aumentando, enquanto empresas acumulam grandes volumes de dívida na corrida para financiar o desenvolvimento da inteligência artificial e a expansão da infraestrutura de data centers. Durante o GZERO Summit, organizado pela LSEG e pelo Eurasia Group em Londres no início deste mês, Mohamed El-Erian, principal consultor econômico da Allianz e ex-CEO da PIMCO, destacou a disputa por financiamento entre governos e empresas ligadas à IA como uma fonte de pressão sobre os mercados de títulos de dívida. Leia também: HSBC impulsiona Bolsas da Europa após elevar meta de rentabilidade “Os governos estão tomando emprestado o que precisam tomar, além de refinanciarem suas dívidas a taxas de juros mais altas”, afirmou. “E temos as grandes empresas de tecnologia que operam em larga escala na nuvem, que captaram US$ 200 bilhões em financiamento por meio de títulos de dívida no ano passado e provavelmente vão captar US$ 1 trilhão dessa forma neste ano. Elas não são sensíveis aos rendimentos. Não são sensíveis aos spreads de crédito, porque estão apostando em algo verdadeiramente transformador.” Os rendimentos dos títulos de dívida emitidos por diversas grandes economias atingiram, em 2026, os níveis mais elevados em várias décadas. O movimento ocorre em meio a preocupações com os elevados déficits públicos e o aumento do endividamento, além dos temores de que a inflação permaneça persistente e os bancos centrais adotem posturas mais rigorosas. No início deste ano, o JPMorgan Chase estimou que a emissão de dívidas relacionadas à inteligência artificial poderá alcançar US$ 4,1 trilhões até o fim da década, à medida que empresas de data centers e outros negócios ligados à IA ampliam os investimentos para expandir sua capacidade. 🔷 Canal 562 ClaroTV+ | Canal 562 Sky | Canal 592 Vivo | Canal 187 Oi | Operadoras regionais 🔷 TV SINAL ABERTO: parabólicas canal 562 🔷 ONLINE: www.timesbrasil.com.br | YouTube 🔷 FAST Channels: Samsung TV Plus, LG Channels, TCL Channels, Pluto TV, Roku, Zapping | Novos Streamings Este conteúdo foi fornecido pela CNBC Internacional e a responsabilidade exclusiva pela tradução para o português é do Times Brasil. artigo.texto: Pará tem potencial para liderar restauração florestal com créditos de carbono Conciliar a produção agrícola com a conservação das florestas, ampliar a restauração de áreas degradadas e transformar a preservação ambiental em oportunidades econômicas estão entre os desafios e as possibilidades para o Pará. Em entrevista ao Grupo Liberal, Leonardo Sobral, diretor de Florestas e Restauração do Imaflora (Instituto de Manejo e Certificação Florestal e Agrícola), destaca o potencial do estado para avançar nessa agenda por meio de incentivos econômicos, do mercado de carbono, da bioeconomia e das concessões florestais para restauração. O especialista também ressalta a importância de valorizar os produtos da floresta em pé e de fortalecer iniciativas que conciliem conservação ambiental, produção sustentável e geração de renda. * Repórter: Jéssica Nascimento Por Liberal Entrevista

artigo.texto: [SMM PV Flash] Times Digital Wins Commissioning and O&M Contract for 1.2 GW Solar Project in Saudi Arabia Times Digital Holdings’ subsidiary, through Concord New Energy’s O&M technology arm, has won the commissioning and operations and maintenance technical services contract for Saudi Arabia’s 1.2 GW Al Masa’a (MAS) solar PV project, per SMM understanding and public information. The project is Times Digital’s first market-oriented overseas benchmark project, marking the formal export of its new-energy technical service capabilities. MAS is located in Ha’il province, about 590 km north of Riyadh, and is a key independent power producer project under Round 5 of Saudi Arabia’s National Renewable Energy Program, developed by a consortium of EDF, SPIC Yellow River Hydropower and Saudi SAPCO. The project is scheduled to begin pre-energization commissioning on November 15 and achieve partial grid connection by the end of November; once fully operational, it is expected to generate 4.4 billion kWh annually. artigo.texto: BYD Pairs European Luxury Push With 3,000 Chargers as Shares Languish Near Yearly Low Published on 10/20/2026 at 03:31 | Editorial boerse-global.de BYD is betting that premium badges and its own charging infrastructure can lift its fortunes in Europe, even as its share price continues to sag. At the Paris Motor Show, the Chinese group rolled out its Denza marque with a technology-led pitch for what it calls intelligent luxury — a direct challenge to Europe's established premium names. The display came alongside the seven-seat ATTO 8 flagship SUV and the second generation of its Blade battery. Charging is central to the pitch. BYD plans to build 3,000 fast-charging stations across Europe by the end of 2027, a move aimed at winning drivers over to its rapid-charging technology. The company is also scaling up its local footprint: deputy chairwoman Stella Li told Bloomberg that European headcount will soon pass 10,000, with roughly 40,000 employees targeted in the region by 2030. A Two-Pronged Expansion The European push runs in parallel with a broader build-out beyond vehicle sales. BYD Energy Storage announced a global after-sales service network for battery storage systems, built around nine operations and maintenance centres and more than 200 field engineers. Additional sites in South Africa and Bulgaria are slated for 2027, and over 100 R&D specialists are tied into the network — a signal that BYD intends to stay close to commercial customers long after installation. At home, the group keeps widening its lineup. The Da Han EV, a new flagship sedan for the Dynasty range, launched on 13 October with a 1,000-volt architecture and a CLTC range of up to 1,008 kilometres; the entry version is priced at 235,900 yuan. BYD also introduced the second generation of its Seagull compact EV in China, according to media reports, shoring up its volume base. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying BYD? September Sales and a Hybrid Trade Deal Those model launches land in a testing market. BYD's September 2026 production and sales report showed 463,561 vehicles sold and 463,864 built during the month. Sales through September reached 3,131,576 units, down 3.9% on the same period a year earlier. Trade policy adds another variable. BYD has reportedly backed an agreement between China and the European Union on hybrid vehicle trade, though Reuters noted that such a deal — by capping exports of Chinese hybrid and plug-in hybrid models — could create headwinds for manufacturers. Details on how the arrangement would work in practice have not been disclosed. Investors Stay on the Sidelines The market has yet to be moved by the operational announcements. The stock closed Monday at EUR 8.30, down 0.5%, and slipped a further 0.1% to EUR 8.33 in today's session. That leaves the shares down 22% since the start of the year and well below the 52-week high of EUR 12.30 touched in mid-April. A nearer-term catalyst is on the calendar: the supervisory board meets on 29 October 2026 to review third-quarter results. For now, BYD is sticking to its strategy of putting technological innovation and higher-margin segments such as Denza at the forefront of its international drive. artigo.texto: Making Carbon Pay for Ireland’s Energy Transition: What a Modernised Emissions Trading System Could Mean for Ireland’s Energy Supply Could a modernised EU Emissions Trading System help Ireland ensure a more self-reliant and resilient energy supply? In response to rising energy prices and their impact on European industry, the European Commission published a proposal to modernise the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) on the 17 July 2026. Ireland has been severely impacted by the rising cost of energy caused by Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, and the ongoing conflicts in the Middle East. In addition to sparking public protests, the energy crisis has imposed significant costs on industry, the State, and consumers. With this in mind, this blog will explore how a modernised ETS could support Ireland in its energy transition. What is the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS)? The EU ETS is a European Union (EU)-wide carbon market on which carbon emission allowances, each worth the equivalent of one tonne of carbon dioxide, are exchanged via a cap-and-trade system. Under this system, companies must cover their carbon emissions with allowances that have either been freely allocated to them, that have been auctioned off by Member States, or that have been bought from other companies. This creates an economic incentive for companies to reduce their carbon emissions. Each year, the overall cap on allowances is lowered, in theory, driving a gradual reduction in carbon emissions. The EU ETS is the primary decarbonisation policy of the EU’s Green Deal and has proven to be fairly effective. Since is was launched in 2005, the ETA has helped emissions to be cut by around 50%, and since 2013, it has raised over 270 billion euros in auction revenues. Ireland has taken in 1.28 billion euros through EU ETS allowance auctions since 2013. From the 139 million euros raised in 2024 under the scheme, the vast majority (102.3 million euros) has gone to the Department of Transport and been invested in public transport projects. In addition the EU ETS revenue has also funded specific projects in Ireland through EU-level funds. For example, the ETS revenue funded an EU Innovation Fund grand of 39 million euros to the Saoirse Wave Energy Project located in Ireland. For these EU-level funds, the Irish National Contact Point is the Environment and Climate Research and Advisory Unit in the Department of the Environment, Climate and Communications (DCEE). Ireland’s energy supply vulnerability Recent geopolitical events have exposed one of Ireland’s strategic vulnerabilities as one of the most import-dependent economies in the EU when it comes to energy, with 80% of its energy supply being imported in 2024. This number can be explained by the fact that Ireland continues to rely heavily on fossil fuels. Of Ireland’s 168.0 TWh energy supply in 2024, fossil-fuel made up for 81.3%. Meanwhile, the country as yet does not produce or harvest much energy of its own. Therefore, to minimise the impact of future energy crises and to render Ireland’s energy supply more independent, policymakers should certainly consider how to foster the country's homegrown energy production capacity. For this, a modernised EU ETS, as proposed by the European Commission could be useful. How a modernised EU ETS could support Ireland’s energy transition In response to the ongoing energy crisis, the European Commission was invited by the European Council to draft a proposal for a review of the EU ETS. The aim of this review is to make the EU ETS a more effective instrument to strengthen independence, innovation and competitiveness in Europe. Its guiding idea is to redirect current expenditure on imported fossil fuel towards investments in the green transition. In the proposition published by the European Commission, two elements are particularly relevant to Ireland’s situation. First, the Commission’s proposal includes provisions to reform the Market Stability Reserve (MSR). The MSR was first established in 2018 as, at that time, carbon prices were considered too low to provide companies with a sufficient incentive to reduce their emissions. A mechanism that invalidates the carbon allowances surplus was thus introduced. Today, however, the opposite problem seems to be the case, as excessively high carbon prices are being passed on to electricity prices, thus increasing costs for businesses and consumers. Therefore, the proposal suggests stopping the invalidation of the surplus, and instead, sets it aside as a buffer that could be used if prices rise unexpectedly in the future. In principle, this reform of the MSR should ensure better market stability and reduce price volatility, which should be of interest to Irish policy makers. Second, the Commission’s proposal introduces a number of measures aimed at improving the use of EU ETS revenue. The underlying principle is that EU ETS revenue should go back to industry to support its decarbonisation efforts. If funds to that effect were already in existence, such as the aforementioned Innovation Fund, the proposal aims to establish an Industrial Decarbonisation Bank (IDB) that will enable investment at a bigger scale. The Commission also considers that there should be better control over the way Member States spend their EU ETS revenues. The revenue should be spent on genuine climate action, which, according to the WWF, is not always the case. How could this benefit Ireland? A modernised ETS with an amended MSR could protect the EU, and thus Ireland, from carbon-price volatility in the allowance market, limiting the extent to which fluctuations in allowance prices contribute to electricity costs. In the longer term, clean energy investments, such as those supported by a modernised EU ETS, can help reduce the impacts of energy crises. artigo.texto: Texas residents promised a state-ordered freeze on data center permits are instead watching approvals advance and public comment deadlines tick down. Nearly a month after Gov. Greg Abbott directed the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to pause issuing permits for data center projects on Sept. 12, the advocacy group said the agency had issued several water-related authorizations and continued reviewing air permit applications. Residents trying to understand what the pause actually stopped were advised by agency’s own staff to treat public comment as active, the group said. Communities struggling to link corporate names to construction sites face mounting confusion as state agencies continue issuing permits despite a promised freeze. That confusion plagues residents near Lufkin, where investigative reporting previously uncovered a web of separate corporate entities handling the proposed Amp Z development's air permits, land deals and political backing. The newspaper later found that a TCEQ reviewer asked whether the proposed power plant’s emissions could be lowered enough to avoid a more extensive federal pollution review, further minimizing’s the areas where residents can voice concerns. “The TCEQ’s own data indicates that it’s business as usual for data centers,” said Kathryn Guerra, director of Public Citizen’s TCEQ Watchdog Campaign. “Affected communities were promised a freeze. Instead, they’re getting another reason to distrust the TCEQ and ineffective attempts to govern by press release.” Public Citizen released its findings the same day the TCEQ was due to update Abbott’s office on its compliance with his directive. When the governor announced the pause through a late September directive, he formally called for state reviews of data centers before making permitting decisions. “Until they do, TCEQ will issue no permits sought by data center projects,” Abbott said in the announcement. Public Citizen identified 16 permit actions that came after Abbott’s directive, including seven new construction stormwater authorizations, one amended stormwater authorization and an industrial wastewater permit renewal. Stormwater authorizations were cited as examples of approvals that were issued after Abbott’s announcements by Guerra. Those authorizations allow stormwater discharges from construction sites. Public Citizen identified seven counties, with approvals dated from Sept. 22 through Oct. 13. Following the nonprofit’s investigation, Guerra said Public Citizen has not yet approached the governor’s office about its findings, which it began compiling late last week. Abbott’s directive followed months of pressure over the industry’s demands on electricity, water and rural communities. Some Republican leaders even crossed party lines, such as Agriculture Commissioner Sid Miller, who called for a temporary moratorium on new hyperscale data center developments, arguing that Texas needed to assess the effects on infrastructure and agriculture before the state could allow the rapid expansion to continue. Notably, Abbott’s September audit of data centers seeking to connect to the electric grid and subsequent pause on environmental permits has not accounted for facilities that plan to generate their own electricity, allowing them to proceed without relying on the grid-connection, The Texas Tribune reported. A separate Tribune analysis published Monday found Abbott had received about $9 million since July 2025 from donors with direct or indirect ties to data centers, representing about 13% of his fundraising during that period. Abbott’s campaign spokesman Eduardo Leal defended the governor’s position to the Tribune, saying his priorities remained on protecting the grid, requiring data centers to cover their costs and preventing disruption to communities. But for people living near the proposed facilities, the immediate concern is whether the promise of a pause could cause them to miss their opportunity to respond and voice their opinion. Public Citizen said the TCEQ mailed notices Sept. 22 for three major source air permit applications involving power facilities near Abilene and in Hill County. The notice for the Nexus project in Hubbard has a public comment deadline of Friday, Oct. 23, according to the group’s review. Guerra said a senior agency staff member told Public Citizen that residents should treat the deadline as active. Public Citizen asked commissioners Oct. 7 to clarify the situation or withdraw the notices, she said. Without state clarification on whether public comment periods remain active, residents are left scrambling to meet deadlines while navigating contradictory signals from Austin. The group also argued that people are being asked to comment on permit applications without truly knowing or being able to access the findings of the state’s review. When asked whether the Sept. 22 mailing dates could have simply been a reflection of notices that may have been prepared before the directive, Guerra acknowledged that possibility. But she said subsequent steps in the public participation portion have only continued. For Linda Polley of Save Hill County, residents also are still seeing work continue on the ground. Trucks traveling the roads with loads, cranes working, large piles of dirt and walls going up are what can be found at the Nexus construction site. Polley said nighttime lighting is visible even from her home 15 miles away. “What exactly did you pause?” Polley asked about Abbott, urging the governor to explain what communities should expect as the state’s review proceeds. In Caldwell County, resident Claudia Hollern said neighbors began examining and monitoring permits as they learned that proposed data centers would rely on large power-generating facilities to be built nearby. She described residents trying to follow applications filed under company names they did not initially recognize which had residents following one piece of infrastructure which led to another. artigo.texto: Both incumbent Rep. Eugene Vindman and Douglas Ollivant, his Republican challenger, say they want to put the brakes on data centers in sensitive areas but have different ideas about how to provide relief to people feeling the sting of higher prices. Vindman, 51, is a retired U.S. Army lieutenant colonel and former legal adviser for the National Security Council. Ollivant, 58, is also a retired U.S. Army lieutenant colonel and served as the director for Iraq on the National Security Council. He was recently diagnosed with an aggressive form of leukemia but chose to stay in the race. The 7th Congressional District includes parts of Prince William, Stafford, Spotsylvania, Culpeper, King George, Madison, Orange, Greene and Albemarle counties and the city of Fredericksburg. U.S. Rep. Eugene Vindman, D-7th, and his Republican challenger, Douglas Ollivant, submitted … The Prince William Times asked both candidates to weigh in on three issues ahead of the Nov. 3 election. The economy and rising prices Economic issues, including rising prices for everyday goods and fuel, are the top issue for voters going into this year's midterms, according to several recent surveys. Vindman said lowering costs has been “a top priority” for his office. He said he supports legislation to lower utility bills, provide relief from high diesel prices and lower healthcare prescription costs for military families. “Everywhere I go in Virginia's Seventh District, I hear the same thing: families are struggling to keep up with the rising cost of living. Whether it's filling up their gas tanks, putting groceries on the table, paying their utility bills, or affording health care, hardworking Virginians are being stretched to the breaking point,” Vindman said. Vindman also said he is committed to repealing Republicans’ “Big Beautiful Bill,” which slashed Medicaid funding and raised health-care premiums for people insured under the Affordable Care Act. Ollivant, however, said politicians need to be “more forthright” with the public about how government decisions impact kitchen table issues. “Politicians need to quit treating the public as infants and start leveling with us as adults. Prices are higher and are going to stay that way until the economy recovers and there is broader stability overseas — including Ukraine and Iran,” Ollivant said. Immigration enforcement The 7th District has one of the highest immigrant populations in the state, with 16% of residents having moved there from another country. The Prince William Times asked both candidates whether they support the Trump administration’s immigration policies andwhat should be done differently. Ollivant did not directly criticize President Trump’s approach. He said the country’s immigration laws need to be enforced and questioned adopting any policy that would “allow violent illegal immigrants to prey upon our communities.” He also said immigration officers should be treated better by opponents of the president’s agenda. “Few people put their lives on the line in the same way they do, enforcing our laws and keeping our families safe. They deserve a lot better than the broad brush applied by their detractors,” he said. Vindman, who immigrated to the U.S. from Ukraine as a child, said he opposes the Trump administration’s enforcement tactics. “Americans deserve an immigration system that keeps our communities safe, upholds the rule of law, and respects the dignity and rights of every person,” Vindman said. “As a former prosecutor and 25-year Army veteran, I know we can and must secure our borders without abandoning our values or treating our neighbors with cruelty.” Vindman said he would support reforms to immigration enforcement, such as requiring ICE officers to remove their masks, wear body cameras, issue judicial warrants, and ensure clear constitutional protections. He’d also like the agency to adopt enforceable use-of-force standards and conduct independent investigations when federal agents are accused of breaking the law. “As an immigrant whose family came to this country seeking freedom and opportunity, I believe deeply in the promise of America,” Vindman said. Data centers and electricity The rapid proliferation of data centers has provoked widespread backlash among Northern Virginia residents. It has also caused concerns about how those data centers will get their electrical power. New transmission line corridors and electrical substations have been proposed, some of which will be near homes, schools and businesses. Vindman said he is concerned about data centers being placed near sensitive areas, such as neighborhoods, schools and parks, but stopped short of calling for a moratorium. “Data centers should not be built near national parks, schools, or residential communities, and Virginians should not be stuck paying higher utility bills to support their growth. I firmly believe rural communities should not be forced to shoulder the costs and consequences of transmission infrastructure built to benefit everyone else,” he said. Vindman added that he is “deeply concerned” about the rapid expansion of transmission lines being built to serve data centers. “Hardworking Virginians should not be forced to pay higher utility bills, lose their land, or watch their communities transformed just so billion-dollar technology companies can turn a bigger profit,” he said. Ollivant said he is against data center development on farmland and on battlefields but did not respond to questions about whether he would support slowing data center development.The electrical grid in Virginia needs to be upgraded, Ollivant said, and he would consider “smart solutions” to boost the grid. “We can do a lot of good with advances in technology and economic growth in Virginia. We can't solve any of these problems, much less pay for basic services, without economic growth and technological innovation,” Ollivant said. artigo.texto: Agility Robotics, a humanoid robotics and physical AI company, has announced that Nyobolt, a pioneer of high-power, ultra-fast charging solutions, is the technology provider to Agility. The technology powers one of Digit 5’s most significant upgrades: a fast recharge battery system that enables Digit to work more than 20 hours in a 24-hour day. Agility recently unveiled Digit 5 as its first humanoid robot designed for cooperatively safe work at scale, allowing it to work in close proximity to people. As part of its upgrades, Digit 5 will feature a new battery system that delivers 90-minutes of runtime and charges in just 9 minutes, achieving a 10:1 run-to-charge ratio, up from Digit 4’s 2:1 ratio. This rapid charge capability is designed to keep Digit working, enabling more than two shifts in a single day and helping customers get more from each robot. Daniel Diez, chief business officer of Agility Robotics, says: “For our customers, Digit’s uptime is the business case. Digit 5 will deliver more than 20 hours of productive work in a 24-hour day, more than two full shifts. “That’s the kind of gain that materially improves the value customers get from Digit and the economics of deploying a humanoid robot fleet. Nyobolt’s ultra-fast charging technology gets us there, and it’s one of the pieces that makes Digit 5 ready for full-scale operation.” Nyobolt’s unique high-power battery technology is built for demanding industrial conditions, combining fast charging, exceptional cycle life, and reduced system weight. By removing the power bottleneck that has historically constrained autonomous robot fleet economics, the system addresses a key constraint on robot utilization: downtime. The result is a compelling potential advantage for Digit 5 customers, who can target longer operating windows, more productive shifts and more demanding task sequences. Combined with Agility’s experience deploying humanoid robots in real commercial environments, this battery performance is designed to strengthen Digit’s value proposition for warehouse, distribution and manufacturing operations. Sai Shivareddy, co-founder and CEO at Nyobolt, says: “Nyobolt’s technology was chosen because Digit 5 will need more power from a smaller, lighter pack, in environments where reliability isn’t optional. “Agility set an exceptionally high bar for what a battery has to withstand in live warehouse and manufacturing environments, and this partnership shows what’s possible when ultra-fast charging is engineered for the toughest conditions in physical AI.” Early access to Digit 5 equipped with Nyobolt’s battery technology is expected to begin in the first half of 2027, with increasing availability over the following six to nine months for manufacturing, warehouse and distribution operators. Agility is preparing to become a public company through its previously announced business combination with Churchill Capital Corp XI. The business combination is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026, after which the combined company will operate as Agility Robotics and is expected to trade on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol “AGLT”.
