artigo.texto: Huawei has stepped into the battery swapping track, joining hands with CATL to promote the energy replenishment for autonomous driving. From this very moment, the battery swapping track may truly take off at an unprecedented speed: The leading smart tech player Huawei and the top battery manufacturer CATL are joining forces to develop battery swapping services! The two sides have carried out cooperation before, and Huawei is not the only user of CATL's battery swapping service, but this collaboration is far from ordinary: It comes with an unprecedented technical chain, innovative and distinctive product solutions, and almost no restrictions on implementation scope... The combination of these elements is a signal that will subvert traditional business models. What exactly are Huawei and CATL going to do this time? First, let's sort out the division of responsibilities of all parties involved. The entities signing this agreement include Huawei's Zhiyuan Intelligent Technology Co., Ltd., CATL, and its battery swapping business-related entity EVOGO. Generally, Zhiyuan provides intelligent vehicle solutions, CATL provides battery technology and its chocolate battery swapping system, while EVOGO participates in the construction of battery swapping networks and related operation services. The goal put forward by the three parties is to promote Huawei Qiankun cooperative models to access CATL's chocolate battery swapping network, and realize the interconnection of the vehicle end, station end and cloud end. This means that the cooperation is not just adding several battery swapping station locations to the vehicle navigation system, nor is it just equipping a single car model with a swappable battery. The three parties aim to build a set of collaborative mechanism covering from vehicle demand to station service: when the vehicle needs energy replenishment, the system can plan a suitable battery swapping station; after arriving at the station, the vehicle can connect with the battery swapping equipment; after the battery swapping is completed, the vehicle can resume its normal trip. The 99-second battery swapping index announced by CATL corresponds to the battery replacement process alone. This cannot be directly equated with the total time from when the vehicle decides to replenish energy to when it drives away from the battery swapping station, let alone conclude that the entire set of unmanned battery swapping services has been realized solely based on this single index. What is really worth analyzing is how the intelligent driving system and the battery swapping station cooperate with each other. After all, there are still many technical details to be solved between the scenario that a vehicle can complete navigation and driving on open roads and the scenario that it can accurately drive into a specific workstation and park at the exact position required by the equipment. From self-searching for stations to automatic battery swapping, how to get through the technical chain? If we split the whole process apart, the first step actually happens on the vehicle side. First, the vehicle needs to judge whether energy replenishment is needed by combining its battery status, remaining driving range and travel plan. This capability can be provided by Huawei's on-board model, on the premise that the car manufacturer grants Huawei sufficiently high underlying permissions; of course, it can also be independently developed by the car manufacturer itself. If the user chooses battery swapping, the system will also comprehensively consider the location of stations, supported vehicle models and actual availability to determine which station to go to. Next, the vehicle needs to switch from road driving mode to station operation mode, which is the core value of Huawei in this cooperation. On open roads, the assisted driving system mainly deals with road structures, traffic participants, driving routes and dynamic obstacles and other issues. But after entering the battery swapping station, the environment and tasks will change: the entrance may be narrow, the internal passages and parking spaces in the station have clear restrictions, and the vehicle must finally park at the precise position where the battery swapping equipment can work normally. This puts forward higher requirements for the vehicle's positioning, environmental perception and low-speed control performance: Navigation that brings the vehicle near the station is only the first half of the whole process; the vehicle also needs to identify the entrance, understand the internal passage route of the station, and complete the parking alignment according to the requirements of the battery swapping workstation. Of course, the current ADS 5 version can easily handle scenarios such as passing through gates and toll stations, and it can also handle narrow and complex parking spaces with great ease. The only thing to do is to collect enough scenario data of CATL's battery swapping stations to ensure 100% reliability. After the vehicle is parked stably, the battery swapping equipment takes over the work, which is the home field of CATL. CATL's standard battery swapping station is compatible with vehicles with a wheelbase ranging from 2.55 meters to 3.1 meters. Each standard battery swapping station is equipped with 14 to 30 battery compartments, with a 99.99% battery swapping success rate and a 99-second swapping duration. In actual operation, the battery swapping process for users is as convenient as refueling, but the cost is greatly reduced. After the battery swapping is completed, the whole process is not over. The vehicle needs to confirm the battery status, safely drive away from the workstation, and reconnect to the navigation and driving tasks. Only when all the links before and after are connected, can users get a continuous experience from the road to the station, and then from the station back to the road. artigo.texto: In 2027, Chinese manufacturers only won half of the Dutch residential energy storage market. On September 23, Sungrow announced that its latest all-in-one residential energy storage system, PowerHarbor, has been officially launched for sale in Europe, with the Netherlands selected as its first stop. Product image of PowerHarbor. Image source: Sungrow Why the Netherlands, instead of familiar major residential storage markets like Germany? Because in just over two months, Dutch households will "have no choice but to buy home batteries". Around 3 million households in the Netherlands have installed solar panels on their rooftops. For more than two decades, they have been enjoying a favorable policy: Excess electricity generated during the day is fed into the grid; when there is a shortage of power at night, they draw electricity back from the grid. They can store as much as they take out, with almost no handling fees charged. The grid acts like a free power bank. On January 1, 2027, this free power bank will be taken away. Going forward, for each kilowatt-hour of electricity fed into the grid during the day, the law only guarantees a return of just over 40 euro cents; but buying one kilowatt-hour of electricity at night costs around 1.9 euros. After deducting various fees charged by power companies, the electricity fed to the grid by many households is almost given away for free. The most cost-effective solution is to install a residential storage battery at home: store the excess electricity during the day for self-use at night. Therefore, Dutch research institute Dutch New Energy Research forecasts that the new installed capacity of residential energy storage in the country will skyrocket from 0.86 GWh in 2025 to 4.5 GWh in 2027. A 5.2-fold increase in just two years. By that time, based on the average price of around 470 euros/kWh for residential batteries in the Netherlands in 2025, the 4.5 GWh of new capacity in 2027 corresponds to a hardware market of approximately 2.1 billion euros, or 160 billion RMB. This scale ranks third in Europe, only smaller than that of Germany and Italy. Chinese manufacturers have already taken the lead in this business. According to information from New Energy Industrialist, the two best-selling residential storage brands in the Netherlands at present, Votai and Sungrow Power Supply's residential storage brand Sinexcel, are both from China. Now, Sungrow is also entering the market. But when these Chinese-made batteries are actually installed in the basements of Dutch households, a deeper business reality emerges: the delivery of hardware is only the beginning. When to charge the battery, when to discharge it, and who to sell the excess electricity to at a high price — these issues that determine profit margins are not decided by Chinese manufacturers. The right to set these rules is held by local Dutch power companies. For example, an enterprise called Frank Energie does not manufacture a single battery itself, but it remotely manages more than 14,000 household batteries made by other manufacturers on the cloud every day. This is a bit like Didi: it does not manufacture a single car, but decides where the car goes and how much to charge for each order. Selling batteries is certainly profitable, but it is a highly competitive one-off transaction; those who hold the scheduling rights earn a steady stream of "toll fees" over time. In the feast of European energy transition, Chinese manufacturers, with their exceptional manufacturing capabilities, have won the first half of the "hardware selling" game. But the truly lucrative, compound-return second half of the energy storage business, as well as the other half of the large profits, are still firmly in the hands of those who send electricity bills to Dutch households every month. 01 In 2027, why do people have to buy batteries By the end of 2024, around 3 million households in the Netherlands had installed photovoltaic systems. For more than two decades, almost none of these households needed batteries. The reason is a policy implemented in 2004 called net metering. Excess electricity generated during the day is fed into the grid, which can be offset 1:1 when the household uses electricity. The grid is equivalent to a free power bank, where users can store as much as they take out without paying any handling fees. This "power bank" can no longer sustain the operation. There are too many photovoltaic systems installed, and at noon in summer, there is so much excess electricity that there is nowhere to send it. In June 2025, the Dutch wholesale electricity price dropped below zero for 127 hours, which means that power generators had to pay others to take their electricity, and still could not sell it. But power companies still have to record accounts for photovoltaic users at a retail price of more than 1 euro per kWh. Part of this loss-making business is ultimately passed on to neighbors who have not installed photovoltaic systems. Before the legislation was finalized, power companies took action first. Since the end of 2023, they have successively charged a "feed-in feedback fee" to photovoltaic users: the more electricity users send to the grid, the more fees they have to pay. According to a three-year fixed contract from a large power company in December 2025, if a household sends 2400 kWh of electricity to the grid every year, it has to pay more than 400 euros in feedback fees alone, equivalent to more than 3000 RMB. Users even have to pay extra to send electricity to the grid, and Dutch photovoltaic users have experienced the cost of doing good deeds in advance. The government also wants to reform the policy, but the process has been full of twists and turns. The gradual phase-out plan was rejected by the upper house of parliament in February 2024. artigo.texto: Pilot production system underway Commercialization targeted for late next year SK Nexilis, the copper foil unit backed by SKC's secondary battery investment arm, announced Tuesday it has successfully developed "high-adhesion carbon-coated copper foil" technology, a key material for next-generation batteries. The technology applies a specialized carbon coating to the surface of copper foil to suppress the volumetric expansion of silicon anode materials, improving electrode stability. It addresses a growing industry trend of increasing silicon content in anodes to boost energy density — a shift that makes maintaining strong adhesion between the anode material and the copper foil increasingly critical. The newly developed copper foil is also compatible with dry electrode processing, a next-generation battery manufacturing method drawing growing attention in the industry. SKC expects strong demand from that segment as well, given that adhesion between electrode materials and copper foil is equally critical in dry-process applications. To prepare for full-scale mass production, SK Nexilis is building a pilot production system for the high-adhesion carbon-coated copper foil. The company is currently verifying process stability and plans to secure the technology needed for mass production, targeting commercialization in the second half of 2027. "The development of this high-adhesion carbon-coated copper foil is a result of our efforts to respond to technological shifts in the next-generation battery market — including the expansion of high-silicon-content anode materials and the introduction of dry electrode processing," a company official said. "We will proceed with commercialization optimization without delay, while continuing to develop new technologies to strengthen our competitiveness in the next-generation battery materials market." klee@heraldcorp.com

artigo.texto: Region forging master key for next industrial revolution, proving that whoever can best store electricity holds future of power For a long time, electricity has been a unique energy commodity, with production and consumption happening almost simultaneously. You use it the moment it is generated. But today, as solar and wind power have become China's largest sources of installed capacity, energy storage is quietly building "warehouses" for the power grid. These massive facilities store surplus green electricity during the day and deliver it to factories, shopping malls and millions of households at night. This time-shifting magic has found its grandest stage in North China's Inner Mongolia autonomous region. Driven by the massive deployment of new-type battery facilities designed to support its vast wind and solar power bases, Inner Mongolia has overtaken California to become the world's largest energy storage region. READ MORE: China takes lead in global power storage As of the end of 2025, the region's cumulative installed capacity of new-type energy storage exceeded 25 million kilowatts, ranking first in the nation. Under the blueprint of the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30), this figure is projected to break the 50 million kW mark, cementing the region's role as the most critical power "reservoir" for the country's renewable mega-bases in the Gobi Desert and other arid areas. The sheer scale of this deployment has triggered a profound industrial metamorphosis. In the past, Inner Mongolia's vast Gobi Desert served merely as an application ground for energy storage, with complete sets of equipment largely purchased from manufacturing clusters in China's eastern provinces. Today, the narrative has shifted from isolated breakthroughs to a multi-city synergy. Hohhot, Baotou and Ordos are firing on all cylinders, forming a differentiated energy storage equipment manufacturing cluster. This has created a new paradigm of "desert application plus multicity collaborative smart manufacturing" — a concentrated reflection of the region's upgrading new energy industry chain. Each city brings a unique strength to the table, but the regional capital, Hohhot, stands out for its specialized focus on system integration and custom solutions engineered for extreme environments. Operating at the forefront of grid resilience, Hohhot's manufacturing sector produces energy storage equipment uniquely designed to withstand the severe cold and punishing sandstorms characteristic of the northern frontiers. While Baotou boasts the most comprehensive industrial chain and Ordos combines equipment manufacturing with ultra-large application scenarios at sites like Envision's zero-carbon industrial park, Hohhot's tailored approach to hostile climate operations ensures these massive systems remain reliable year-round. "Deploying gigawatt-scale battery facilities in the Gobi Desert is fundamentally different from installing systems in temperate coastal plains," said Lin Boqiang, head of the China Institute for Studies in Energy Policy at Xiamen University. "Extreme sub-zero winters can degrade battery performance and discharge efficiency by double digits, while seasonal sandstorms pose severe risks to thermal management and air filtration systems." Hohhot's focus on hostile-climate customization addresses the industry's biggest operational bottleneck — ensuring that massive desert storage parks don't just get built, but actually run safely and reliably 365 days a year, he said. Inner Mongolia's regional triumph mirrors a broader national strategy. Entering 2026, the strategic importance of new-type energy storage has reached unprecedented heights. For the first time, it has been listed among the nation's six emerging pillar industries for the 15th Five-Year Plan. The China New Energy Storage Development Report 2026, released recently by the National Energy Administration, said China's cumulative installed capacity of new-type storage had reached 136 million kW/351 million kilowatt-hours by the end of 2025, representing a year-on-year surge of 84.3 percent. Accounting for roughly 50 percent of the global total, new-type energy storage has surpassed pumped-hydro storage to become China's largest regulating resource, it said. Yet, after years of rapid expansion, the fundamental logic of the industry is evolving. Experts agree that the sector has bid farewell to the era of simple policy-driven scale expansion. "The industry has formally entered a new phase characterized by market-oriented selection, value priority and a focus on quality," said Dai Hongcai, director of the new energy institute at the State Grid Energy Research Institute. While the "forced pairing" of storage with renewable projects drove early growth, future expansion will rely on sustainable business models. The market is also demanding longer duration capabilities. While the average storage duration was around 2.5 hours at the end of 2025, four-hour storage has now become the mainstream, and eight-hour long-duration storage is moving from demonstration to commercial application. This shift ensures that "giant power banks" don't just respond quickly, but can actually sustain the grid through the entire evening peak. As the technology matures, the application boundaries of energy storage are expanding far beyond the traditional power grid. A new and highly lucrative frontier has emerged: the intersection of energy storage and artificial intelligence computing power. In the era of AI large models, a massive global "compute-power race" has sparked acute anxiety over electricity consumption. A single 10,000-GPU computing cluster can consume roughly 100 million kWh of electricity annually. While tech giants in the West are resorting to isolated gas turbines or small nuclear plants to power their AI ambitions, China is leveraging its robust wind, solar and storage ecosystems to pioneer a "compute-power and electricity synergy" model. artigo.texto: Hunterbrook Media’s investment affiliate, Hunterbrook Capital, does not have any positions related to this article at the time of publication. Positions may change at any time. Full disclosures below. This is the latest investigation in Hunterbrook Media’s series on the poisoning of American communities. For decades, polluters have released toxins across the U.S. We've built a nationwide database to expose harm to communities and ecosystems, then hold accountable those responsible. After reporting from Illinois, Nebraska, California, Texas, Louisiana, New Mexico, Indiana, and Virginia, this investigation takes us to Hawaii. Hunterbrook Media has also investigated environmental damage spanning from Namibia to Argentina to Peru. Please email ideas@hntrbrk.com if you suspect pollution or poisoning in your community. In 2025, Digital Realty spent $120 million to purchase a 97-acre parcel of land that was once part of Fort Gillem, a former United States Army post in Forest Park, Georgia. The company, one of the world’s largest real estate investment trusts, is constructing a massive data center complex on the site, returning valuable land to a “productive, tax-generating use,” as its executives put it. But the land came with a historical burden. From 1941 until around 1980 the Army dumped everything from gas masks and medical waste to solvents and sewage sludge on this parcel in the northwest corner of the former army base that now houses a maze of warehouses, including a Kroger distribution center and an Amazon delivery station. There’s quite a bit of environmental issues with the site,” a Digital Realty asset manager said at a meeting with county officials in 2025. “Tons and tons and tons of — physical tons — of trash and environmental hazards.” An investigation by Hunterbrook found that the hazards unearthed included military waste that was still combustible. Meanwhile, residents in neighboring communities are reporting cracks on their walls from explosive blasting on the site and say their questions about environmental and health threats stemming from Digital Realty’s Fort Gillem project are being ignored. The company plans to spend $3 billion on this project, and the first phase is expected to open in early 2028. But a document filed with the Georgia Environmental Protection Division suggests construction may surface some surprises. In December 2025, the company encountered white phosphorus on the property, which “reacted when exposed to air and exhibited a dense white smoke,” according to a letter an environmental consultant sent on behalf of Digital Realty to Georgia EPD. The company asked the Army for guidance and contacted the local police department, which sent a bomb squad to inspect and sample the material. The letter states that the white phosphorus was found in an area on the western side of the property that’s going to be under the planned data center. “Upon completion of the Property’s redevelopment, the area of concern will be encapsulated with a concrete building foundation,” the letter states. “At this time, the size of the area of concern is not known but is not anticipated to be larger than 100-feet by 100-feet by 8-feet deep based on grading already completed at the Property.” The material has since been removed, a Digital Realty spokesperson told Hunterbrook in an email. “Trained professionals carefully excavated the 100-foot by 100-foot by 8-foot area in accordance with an approved work plan, using appropriate equipment and personal protective equipment to identify any additional material containing white phosphorus,” the spokesperson wrote. “The excavation recovered five 30-gallon steel drums of material containing white phosphorus, far less than could have been encountered across the full area. The drums were then transported under a hazardous waste manifest to a permitted treatment, storage, and disposal facility.” The company also said that “work in the area where the material was initially discovered was stopped immediately upon the discovery of the material” and that “there were no reported injuries.” No other munitions and explosives of concern have been encountered since the white phosphorus discovery, according to Digital Realty. A Georgia EPD spokesperson confirmed the temporary work stoppage in the area where white phosphorus was found and that Digital Realty was in the process of removing the material in February, when EPD representatives visited the site. White phosphorus is used in artillery shells, rockets, and grenades to create dense smoke screens, provide battlefield illumination, mark targets, or act as an incendiary weapon. The use of white phosphorus weapons in civilian areas has been considered a war crime by human rights organizations like Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International. Its presence at the Digital Realty construction site “is assumed to be associated with historical Army disposal operations,” according to the letter to the Georgia EPD. “Measures are in place to protect construction workers, future occupants, and the public throughout remediation and development activities,” the Digital Realty spokesperson told Hunterbrook. Toxic Land Is Data Center Boom’s Next Frontier The frenzied AI build-out has turned Digital Realty into a digital infrastructure colossus. Amid the scramble to feed AI’s seemingly endless need for compute, other companies besides Digital Realty have resorted to building data centers on contaminated land. At its earnings briefing on Tuesday, CATL attributed the pressure on profitability to changes in its product mix, the resumption of battery consumption tax, and reductions in export tax rebates. The company management said it was discussing how to share the impact with customers while accelerating the introduction of new technologies and products to limit the impact on profitability, the Securities Times reported on Wednesday. And, more tax changes are expected in 2027. The consumption tax, reinstated at 2 percent in September, is set to rise to 4 percent in September 2027. And, battery export VAT rebates were reduced from 9 percent to 6 percent in April and are scheduled to be removed in January 2027. Regarding market demand, however, CATL pointed to more potential opportunities. Responding to investor concerns about 2027, the company cited rising electrification rates and battery capacity per vehicle in China, competitive new electric models in Europe and continued growth in global energy-storage demand. Industry figures showed continued year-on-year growth in both sales and exports. China's combined sales of power and energy storage batteries rose 57.6 percent to 1,681.7 GWh in the first nine months of 2026, while combined exports increased 51.6 percent to 302.9 GWh, according to data released by the China Automotive Battery Innovation Alliance on October 15. artigo.texto: US solid-state battery maker QuantumScape, backed by Volkswagen and Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates, is working with a South Korean equipment supplier. The development could expand the role of Korean companies beyond conventional lithium-ion batteries into the next-generation battery market. According to industry sources on Oct. 20, Mplus has developed assembly equipment for QuantumScape’s solid-state batteries and is conducting validation for mass production. QuantumScape completed its Eagle Line pilot production facility at its headquarters in San Jose, California, in February. The company is currently increasing sample production of its first commercial product, the QSE-5, at the facility. The uptime of key production equipment has exceeded 90%. Uptime refers to the proportion of available operating time during which equipment functions normally. “Among US solid-state and lithium-metal battery startups, QuantumScape has one of the most developed production infrastructures, including dry rooms,” an industry official said. “Because next-generation battery manufacturing processes differ among companies and mass-production viability has yet to be fully demonstrated, commercialization will depend on how quickly manufacturers can achieve sufficient production speeds and yields.” QuantumScape is supplying samples to Volkswagen’s battery subsidiary PowerCo and other companies to evaluate battery performance and practical applications. It has jointly developed next-generation batteries with Volkswagen since 2012 and has received more than $300 million in cumulative investment from the automaker. Volkswagen invested in QuantumScape to secure next-generation battery technology that could improve electric vehicle driving range and safety. Solid-state batteries replace the liquid electrolyte used in conventional lithium-ion batteries with a solid material. By eliminating flammable organic solvent-based liquid electrolytes, they reduce fire risks. They can also accommodate more energy within the same volume by reducing the components and space required to ensure internal battery safety. The core of QuantumScape’s technology is its proprietary ceramic separator. Conventional lithium-ion batteries use a porous separator between the cathode and anode, along with a liquid electrolyte that allows lithium ions to move between them. QuantumScape’s ceramic separator prevents direct contact between the electrodes while allowing lithium ions to pass through. The company has partnered with Corning and Murata to mass-produce the ceramic separators. Another distinguishing feature is its anode-free architecture. Instead of mixing and coating anode active materials such as graphite, the design uses only an anode current collector, reducing associated material and production costs. In QuantumScape’s manufacturing process, ceramic separators are laminated onto copper foil used as the anode current collector after the cathode electrode process. Cathodes are then attached to both sides to form individual units called monocells. The monocells are subsequently immersed in and removed from a solution containing catholyte, a liquid electrolyte that facilitates lithium-ion movement between cathode active materials. Multiple monocells are stacked to complete a battery cell. After packaging, QuantumScape simplifies the formation process, which stabilizes battery performance through initial charging and discharging, to reduce production time and costs. Beyond expanding its own manufacturing facilities, QuantumScape is pursuing a licensing business that would allow other companies to use its battery manufacturing technology. It has signed a technology licensing agreement with PowerCo covering battery production capacity of up to 85 GWh. QuantumScape is also considering outsourcing production line operations to external companies. It is reportedly holding related discussions with South Korean battery manufacturers. If its manufacturing technology expands to external production facilities, Mplus could secure additional equipment orders, having developed machinery tailored to QuantumScape’s processes. Mplus has secured equipment technologies required for QuantumScape’s battery manufacturing process. As with conventional lithium-ion batteries, the process involves notching, which cuts electrodes to specified dimensions; stacking, which layers multiple electrodes; and packaging, which encloses the cells in external materials. Mplus can supply a complete range of assembly equipment for these processes, as well as specialized high-temperature and high-pressure equipment required for solid-state battery production. Mplus has also diversified its customer base. SK On accounted for more than 80% of its revenue in 2022, but that share fell to approximately 22% in 2025, while other customers’ combined contribution rose to nearly half of revenue. The company has expanded its order base among US and European battery manufacturers. It recently supplied equipment for producing prismatic batteries for defense applications to a European battery company, believed to be France’s Saft. Mplus is pursuing additional orders and is reportedly close to signing a new contract. “We cannot confirm specific details concerning our customers,” an Mplus official said. “We intend to drive earnings growth by securing overseas customers and expanding new orders.” Mplus had an order backlog of 63.1 billion won at the end of the second quarter of 2026.

artigo.texto: 'Chinese Battery Maker' CATL Shares Plunge 11% on Profitability Concerns Third-quarter revenue rose, but net profit grew just 14.5%, its lowest rate in two years China's consumption tax reinstatement and reduced export tax rebates weigh on results CATL, China's leading electric vehicle battery maker, saw its shares plunge as much as 11% intraday after reporting third-quarter results that fell short of market expectations. The increase in quarterly net profit slowed to 14.5%, its lowest level in about two years. According to Bloomberg on October 21, CATL shares fell as much as 11% in early trading on the Shenzhen Stock Exchange and as much as 9.3% on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange. The declines followed the company's third-quarter results, announced on October 20, which fell short of market expectations. CATL's third-quarter revenue rose 58.6% year on year to 165.2 billion yuan (approximately 32.76 trillion won), while net profit increased 14.5% to 21.25 billion yuan (approximately 4.21 trillion won). The net profit growth rate was the lowest in about two years and well below the market forecast of 41.2%. Revenue surged, but profitability deteriorated because of rising costs and reduced tax benefits. China's tax reform plans are also weighing on the company. In July, the Chinese government ended a consumption tax exemption for lithium-ion batteries that had been in place for 10 years and began imposing a 2% consumption tax in September. It also reduced value-added tax rebates on battery exports and plans to eliminate them entirely starting in 2027. The measures are seen as an effort to curb overproduction and cutthroat competition in the battery industry. Markets expect the impact to extend beyond CATL, the industry leader, to small and midsize battery makers. Citigroup said, "If even CATL cannot fully pass the consumption tax burden on to its customers, it will be difficult for second-tier companies to absorb it." Inside the battery cell factory of Chinese battery maker CATL in Debrecen, Hungary, on October 1, 2026 (local time). AFP-Yonhap News View original image Automakers' efforts to reduce their dependence on CATL are also seen as a headwind. Some automakers are diversifying their suppliers by turning to small and midsize battery makers to reduce their reliance on CATL, intensifying price competition. CATL's shares on the Shenzhen Stock Exchange have fallen to about half their peak in May 2026. However, on its earnings conference call on October 20, CATL said it was "actively communicating" with customers to mitigate the impact together. The company added that it was "advancing new technologies and products to reduce the impact on profitability." CATL maintained a positive outlook for next year. The company said global demand for batteries used in electric vehicles and energy storage systems (ESS) "may not be as pessimistic as the market expects and has good growth potential." CATL (HKEX: 3750), the world's largest electric vehicle battery maker, reported higher third-quarter net profit from a year earlier, but earnings fell from the second quarter as profit growth failed to keep pace with its business expansion. Net profit attributable to shareholders rose 14.54% year-on-year to 21.25 billion yuan ($3.16 billion) in the third quarter, according to financial results CATL released on Tuesday. That was down 5.77% from 22.55 billion yuan in the second quarter, CnEVPost calculations show. Third-quarter revenue rose 58.58% year-on-year to 165.22 billion yuan. Net profit attributable to shareholders excluding non-recurring gains and losses increased 14.86% to 18.86 billion yuan. For the first 9 months of the year, CATL's net profit attributable to shareholders rose 31.60% year-on-year to 64.53 billion yuan, while revenue increased 56.19% to 442.14 billion yuan. The company attributed its revenue growth over the period to business expansion. However, cost of sales rose faster than revenue, increasing 61.61% to 341.7 billion yuan. Gross margin for the first 9 months was 22.72%, down about 2.59 percentage points from 25.31% a year earlier, according to calculations based on revenue and cost of sales in the financial report. Research and development expenses rose 22.89% year-on-year to 18.52 billion yuan over the same period. Investment income increased 73.11% to 9.07 billion yuan, which the company said mainly reflected its share of investee companies' net profits. Despite the earnings growth, net cash generated from operating activities fell 23.60% year-on-year to 61.63 billion yuan in the first 9 months. As of the end of September, CATL's accounts receivable had risen 47.78% from the end of last year to 112.91 billion yuan, while inventories increased 53.15% to 144.77 billion yuan. The company attributed both increases to business expansion. CATL maintained its lead in the global EV battery market. Its global battery installations rose 25.2% year-on-year to 333.0 GWh in the first 8 months, according to South Korean market research firm SNE Research. Its global market share increased to 39.4% from 37.7% a year earlier, ahead of second-place BYD (HKEX: 1211) at 15.1%. China's battery market also continued to expand. Domestic power battery installations rose 14.7% year-on-year to 87.2 GWh in September, setting a new high for the year for the second consecutive month, according to the China Automotive Battery Innovation Alliance (CABIA). Energy storage batteries grew faster. China's energy storage battery sales rose 104.4% year-on-year to 73.5 GWh in September, accounting for 33.0% of combined power and energy storage battery sales. CATL ranked first in China's power battery market in September, with installations of 35.49 GWh and a market share of 40.92%. ($1 = 6.7200 yuan)

According to the Korea Exchange on Oct. 16, the ETF posted a return of 22.76% over the past three months, the highest among Korea-listed equity ETFs, excluding leveraged and inverse ETFs. The SOL Solid State Battery&Silicon Anode Materials ETF, in particular, posted strong returns even among secondary battery ETFs, outperforming the KOSPI by more than 39 percentage points over the same period; the index recorded a return of -16.90%. The secondary battery sector has recently emerged from a prolonged correction triggered by slowing electric vehicle demand and is securing new growth drivers. Rising demand for energy storage systems (ESS) as AI data centers expand is improving battery companies' earnings, while expectations for the commercialization of next-generation technologies, including solid-state batteries and silicon anode materials, are also growing. ESS is emerging as a key growth driver reshaping the structure of the secondary battery industry. The importance of stable power supply and energy storage is increasing as AI data centers' power demand rises and renewable energy generation expands. Progress toward commercializing solid-state batteries is also encouraging. Samsung SDI is pursuing technology development and collaboration with customers with the goal of mass-producing solid-state batteries in 2027, while domestic materials companies are working to secure production capacity for key raw materials. The government also plans to provide about KRW 400 billion in research and development support for next-generation batteries over five years starting in 2027. The SOL Solid State Battery&Silicon Anode Materials ETF responds to these industry shifts by concentrating its investments in key companies involved in solid-state batteries and silicon anode materials. Its major holdings include Samsung SDI, which is working toward mass production of solid-state batteries; LG Energy Solution, a key ESS company; EcoPro BM, a solid-state battery cathode material company; Isu Specialty Chemical, a company involved in lithium sulfide; LOTTE Energy Materials, a battery materials company; and Daejoo Electronic Materials, a silicon anode material company. artigo.texto: SK Nexilis Develops Carbon-Coated Copper Foil for Next-Generation Batteries Improves Adhesion to Silicon Anode Materials to Prevent Electrode Delamination Also Suitable for Dry Electrode Processes Commercialization Targeted for the Second Half of 2027 SK Nexilis, the investment vehicle for SKC's copper foil business for secondary batteries, has developed copper foil for next-generation batteries that improves adhesion to silicon anode materials. The technology can extend battery life, improve safety, and be applied to dry electrode processes. Commercialization is targeted for the second half of 2027. SK Nexilis said on October 20 that it had successfully developed “high-adhesion carbon-coated copper foil,” a technology that coats the surface of copper foil with a special carbon material. The technology increases adhesion between copper foil and anode materials, helping suppress electrode delamination caused by the expansion of silicon anode materials. This is expected to improve the structural stability of electrodes and enhance battery life and safety. Recently, the battery industry has been increasing the silicon content of anode materials to boost energy density. However, silicon expands in volume during charging and discharging, making it important to ensure strong adhesion between copper foil and anode materials. The newly developed copper foil can also be used in dry electrode processes, which can reduce battery manufacturing costs and energy consumption. SK Nexilis said the material has strong potential for use in dry processes, where adhesion between electrode materials and copper foil is also important. SK Nexilis is currently validating process stability and plans to secure mass-production technology after establishing a pilot production system. artigo.texto: Samsung Asset Management's KODEX Solid State Battery ESS TOP2 Plus Surpasses 200 Billion Won in Net Assets Samsung Asset Management's exchange-traded fund (ETF) focused on energy storage systems (ESS) and solid-state batteries has surpassed 200 billion won in net assets just four months after its listing, buoyed by inflows from individual investors. On October 21, Samsung Asset Management announced that its KODEX Solid State Battery ESS TOP2 Plus ETF had surpassed 200 billion won in net assets. The milestone came four months after its listing on June 23, with net assets reaching 237.6 billion won as of the market close on October 20. The ETF's performance was driven by strong net buying from individual investors. Cumulative net purchases by individuals since its listing totaled 75.4 billion won, with approximately 23.3 billion won flowing in over the past month alone. Its return over the past month was 11.99%, and its return over the past three months was 34.98%, placing it among the top-performing ETFs listed in Korea. In particular, its return since listing was 6.88%, ranking first among battery and materials-related ETFs listed in Korea. This reflects the combination of expanding orders for Korean ESS companies and rising expectations for the commercialization of solid-state batteries. KODEX Solid State Battery ESS TOP2 Plus invests in both solid-state batteries and ESS, the two growth pillars of the battery industry. Solid-state batteries use solid electrolytes instead of liquid ones, reducing fire risks and increasing energy density, making them a next-generation battery technology. ESS are systems that store electricity generated and supply it when needed. Applications for solid-state batteries and ESS are steadily expanding beyond the industry's traditional focus on electric vehicles to include humanoid robots, urban air mobility (UAM), and aerospace. The ETF allocates approximately 50% of its investments to LG Energy Solution and Samsung SDI, leaders in the solid-state battery and ESS sectors. LG Energy Solution is targeting the North American market by successively bringing ESS production facilities in the United States online. artigo.texto: Protests against widespread state corruption have flooded the Philippines in recent weeks, putting pressure on the leadership of a country that for years has been one of the United States’ closest military and commercial allies in Southeast Asia. The domestic turmoil threatens to shake up the U.S.-Philippines partnership, particularly given that American-funded data center projects under President Donald Trump’s Pax Silica initiative are among the targets of the protesters’ rage. On September 21, 2026, President Ferdinand Marcos — whose national trust rating sits at just 28% — put the presidential palace under lockdown in anticipation of mass protests, as more than 17,000 police officers were deployed and tens of thousands of protestors marched through Manila to demand change in the face of the country's largest corruption scandal in years. The scandal revolves around more than $9 billion worth of proposed flood-control infrastructure projects, intended for construction since Marcos took office in 2022. The projects were designed to improve infrastructure like drainage and flood control systems to mitigate the effects of typhoons common in the Philippines. These projects are under legal investigation for being of poor quality or having never been built at all. The investigation into the matter has led to the arrest of former Philippines House Speaker Martin Romualdez, a cousin and formerly close ally of Marcos, on a $118 million plunder charge. Romualdez is only one of a number of officials currently detained under suspicion of pocketing money from the project, with Interior Secretary Ombudsman Remulla alleging that co-conspirators attempted to hide the money through the purchase of houses or Romualdez’s $1 million donation to Harvard University. Another layer of controversy involves the impeachment trial of sitting Vice President Sara Duterte. A major point of contention occurred on day 34 of the trial, when it was revealed that over 30 undeclared accounts showed Duterte’s net worth to be over $3 million — almost 15 times more than her declared net worth of $209,000. The public backlash and corruption-induced chaos currently surrounding the Philippines could affect relations with the U.S. at a time when the United States is trying to counterbalance China’s expansive aims in the South China Sea. The military alliance between the United States and the Philippines dates back to the 1951 Mutual Defense Treaty, which ensures mutual protection in the event of a foreign armed attack. This pact was preceded by the 1947 Military Bases Agreement, an executive order granting the U.S. 20 years of renewable access to bases in the Philippines, and later reinforced by the 2014 Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement, which currently provides the U.S. rotational access to nine military bases in the archipelago. This continued relationship has established the Philippines as a crucial node in Washington’s foreign policy strategy in regard to China. Although the number of stationed U.S. troops has remained at a few hundred since the 1990s, U.S. military activity has increased, as evidenced by the fact that U.S. troops made up more than 10,000 of the 17,000 personnel from seven countries that participated in the Balikatan military exercises this May. Congress has also authorized up to $2.5 billion in foreign military financing for the Philippines, and up to $1 billion in loans for military sales, for fiscal year 2026. This is the highest amount that the U.S. has given to the Philippines, an increase of $500 million from the prior year. Outside of military investment, the Philippines has also emerged as an increasingly important ally for economic collaboration. The United States has shown intense interest in the Luzon Economic Corridor (LEC), a trilateral infrastructure and technology initiative by the U.S., Japan, and the Philippines. The plan invests in the construction of infrastructure across Luzon island. The scale is large relative to current investment: the Philippines received $7.8 billion in net foreign direct investment in 2025, while Luzon alone attracted over $20 billion in projects at a September investor forum. Though the project is still mostly aspirational, Marcos is largely in favor of it, having told a crowd of investors at the forum to turn LEC “from a shared vision into concrete investments and projects.” “The United States is all-in on the Luzon Economic Corridor because it's good for the Philippines and good for America," stated Lee Lipton, Washington’s ambassador to the Philippines, in response. The U.S. private sector is also supportive of the initiative, with over fifty American companies reported to be engaged in investment opportunities in the LEC, according to the Subic Bay Metropolitan Authority. Despite the apparent enthusiasm from both governments, the court of public opinion seems skeptical of the initiative, particularly because of one aspect of the LEC: the proposed Pax Silica technology center in the industry hub of New Clark City, estimated to attract between $40 and $70 billion in investment and create nearly 200,000 new jobs. During city-wide protests throughout Manila on September 21, protestors held signs attacking U.S.-backed data center projects, which are a part of the Pax Silica initiative, as a major source of grievance with Marcos' government. Pax Silica, which aims to pursue similar initiatives across more than 20 other countries, has sparked worry from many Filipinos over the risks of heavy water usage, high electricity demands, and overdependence on foreign technology and capital. "[Pax Silica] threatens to permanently lock the Philippines into having the highest power rates not just in Southeast Asia but in all of Asia,” stated the Makabayan Bloc, a left-wing Filipino party that, although it lacks much representation in the country’s government, has a strong grassroots presence, and has often led anti-U.S. sentiment across the country. artigo.texto: TORONTO, Oct. 21, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- HiTHIUM, an integrated full-scenario energy storage solutions provider, has announced its entry into the Canadian market. Ranked in the top two globally for energy storage component, the manufacturer has surpassed 200 GWh in cumulative delivered capacity, focusing exclusively on stationary energy storage technologies. Canada's energy storage expansion requires reliable large-scale suppliers and local presence Mizhi Zhang, HiTHIUM President of Global Business, commented: "We are committed to delivering Canadian customers advanced, robust solutions, from 8-hour long duration energy storage to extreme-weather-ready sodium-ion BESS. But this also means being present for customers wherever they are, able to serve them quickly and locally. While Toronto serves as the main hub for our Canadian operations, we have subsidiary offices in British Columbia and Alberta, as well as operating sites in Quebec, Yellowknife, and Fort Smith." HiTHIUM has introduced 4-hour and 8-hour BESS solutions to serve the market's rapid buildout of utility-scale energy storage. With installed Canadian storage expected to double between 2025 and 2027, and the country's total wind, solar, and energy storage capacity on track to reach 50 GW by 2035, HiTHIUM is positioned to fill the growing demand for BESS on a large scale. The company has also revealed a new 4 MWh sodium-ion storage solution, which is designed for an extra-long service life, supports storage durations from 2 to 8 hours, and is perfect for extremely cold climates, like Northern Canada. "Canada's ambitious clean energy targets, as well as its high safety and regulatory standards, require partners who can deliver advanced technology that's also tested and compliance-ready. At the same time, project developers have to consider the tough climate. As a vertically integrated, global solutions provider, HiTHIUM is structured to meet exactly this nexus of challenges. Our strategy of advancing both lithium-ion and sodium-ion storage is designed to offer customers in markets like Canada the benefits of flexibility, since we see these technologies as highly complementary," continued Zhang. "Our partners, whether major energy developers, public utilities, or industrial enterprises, rely on our readiness for local certification and our long-term bankability to support them, from permitting through project commissioning," added Jordan Hebbert, HiTHIUM Senior Manager of Canada. "Likewise, they depend on the proven durability of HiTHIUM technology-including performance even in extreme weather conditions. In fact, long-term operational data from North American and European projects has recently demonstrated systems outperforming even our guarantees. And we offer customers a wider range of durations and choice of chemistries because we understand that they're coming to us with a very diverse range of energy storage needs." 4-hour or 8-hour BESS: Matching duration to project specifications The manufacturer's 4-hour BESS solution consists of its "∞Power" 6.25 MWh container, built on HiTHIUM's own 1175 Ah cell. Most Canadian projects are currently designed around the 4-hour unit. This enables them to shift wind, solar, and baseload output to later peak times, strengthen grid reliability, and drive the consumption of more renewables, particularly as electrification increases demand. The ∞Power system design fits more capacity into the typical 20-foot container but also reduces a project's overall footprint, because the containers can be placed back-to-back and side-to-side. In a groundbreaking step for long duration energy storage, HiTHIUM also developed the first ever native 8-hour solution based on lithium-ion technology. Its 6.9 MWh 8-hour BESS, built with HiTHIUM's own 1300 Ah cells, fewer components overall, and a 25-year lifespan, is designed to address issues like curtailments and to fill key gaps for zero-downtime industrial segments like AI data centers. For wind project developers and data center operators alike, 8-hour BESS offers risk reduction and greater revenue reliability. Extreme fire test validates safety architecture HiTHIUM additionally worked with UL Solutions at the start of 2026 on an independently conducted, extreme fire test of its 6.25 MWh block's intrinsic safety systems. A container was subjected to 24 hours of extreme combustion conditions, with its doors opened for maximum thermal spread, while neighboring containers were placed just 15 cm away. Only the containers' passive safety systems were enabled. The results validated HiTHIUM's multi-layer safety architecture, with the tested container structurally intact after the test, no thermal propagation across the containers, and the temperatures of cells in adjacent containers remaining below safety thresholds.

artigo.texto: The Xiaomi 18 Series is officially on its way, following its initial debut in China on September 23, 2026. Xiaomi 18 Series Launch in India: The Xiaomi 18 Series is officially on its way, following its initial debut in China on September 23, 2026. The upcoming flagship lineup introduces massive upgrades, including world-first 2nm mobile chipsets, dual 200MP camera systems, and revolutionary high-capacity silicon-anode batteries. Here is everything you need to know about what to expect from the India launch. While the series is already live in China, prominent industry insiders tip the Xiaomi 18 Series to launch in India by December 2026, matching the late-winter shopping rush. This represents an earlier launch cycle compared to previous generations, which typically arrived in India around March. The official launch events are expected to take place in the standard late-afternoon window (around 4:00 PM IST). India will likely receive the Xiaomi 18 Pro initially, while the standard Xiaomi 18 might follow in March or April 2027, and the top-tier Xiaomi 18 Pro Max might remain heavily limited or exclusive to global/China distributions. Xiaomi 18: Standard Xiaomi 18: Expected to start around ₹94,990. Xiaomi 18 Pro: Expected to retail between ₹1,29,990 and ₹1,39,990 depending on storage variants. The Silicon Battery Revolution: The standout upgrade of the 18 Series is battery density. Thanks to a new 32% silicon-anode composition, Xiaomi has packed a massive 7,000mAh battery into the Pro model without adding bulk to the body. The Pro Max pushes this boundary further with an 8,500mAh unit. Dual Display & Premium Design: The Xiaomi 18 Pro introduces a 2.7-inch secondary OLED screen on the back next to the camera module. This screen allows users to manage widgets, see incoming alerts, and use the high-quality 200MP rear camera to frame high-resolution selfies. The chassis features a premium glass-metal build protected by Xiaomi Dragon Crystal Glass 3.0. Extreme Leica Optics: Developed alongside Leica, the Pro variant boasts two massive 200MP sensors. The main lens uses a 1/1.28-inch Light Hunter 960 sensor for extreme low-light clarity, complemented by a 200MP periscope zoom lens capable of 3.2x optical telephoto macro shots. Hardware Privacy Display: Taking inspiration from secure display technologies, the 18 Pro series features a hardware-integrated privacy shield functionality, preventing side-angle snooping on your screen when you are in public areas. Next-Gen Connectivity: The devices are fully equipped for future network standards, integrating Ultra-Wideband (UWB) tracking, 5G-Advanced (5G-A), Wi-Fi 7, and Bluetooth 6.0. The series introduces the world’s first mobile platforms built on an ultra-dense 2nm architecture. Xiaomi 18 & 18 Pro: Equipped with the core Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 chipset, featuring Qualcomm's 4th-generation custom Oryon CPU architecture that hits clock speeds up to a massive 5.0GHz. Xiaomi 18 Pro Max: This top-tier model breaks away with the unthrottled Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 SoC, designed specifically to handle multi-stream 8K AI video processing and massive local generative AI large language models smoothly. All models support 100W HyperCharge wired charging (with the charging block included in the box), 50W wireless charging, and a powerful 27W reverse wireless charging capability to top up accessories or other phones on the go.

artigo.texto: OpenWorld Signs Term Sheet to Finance Solar-Powered, Distributed AI Computing Network Initially Integrated with Residential Battery Storage with Tokenized Financing Program of up to $1 Billion LAKE MARY, Fla., Oct 15, 2026 - (ACN Newswire) - OpenWorld, Inc. ("OpenWorld" or the "Company") (NASDAQ: OPNW), an innovation company advancing global real-world asset ("RWA") tokenization, today announced that it has entered into a non-binding term sheet with Meridian to establish a tokenized financing program of up to $1 billion to fund the purchase and deployment of a distributed AI computing network powered by on-site solar energy and residential battery storage. Under the term sheet, OpenWorld will serve as advisor, structuring agent and services provider for the program, and its OpenWorld Enterprise platform will finance and operate the orchestration of the network. The news follows recent OpenWorld tokenized financing announcements, including a proposed transaction to transform BeyondAI's industrial AI intellectual property rights into financeable collateral on OpenWorld's tokenization platform. Key Highlights - Meridian founded by Josh Raffaelli: Raffaelli was involved early in Tesla, Solar City, and SpaceX while at DFJ and Silver Lake. - Up to $1 billion in tokenized financing: OpenWorld structures and administers the tokenized financing program on OpenWorld Enterprise. Residential battery storage, solar panels and AI computing equipment form the asset base of the structure. - Meridian's role: Meridian holds purchase rights to Powerwall residential battery storage systems for the program and will own the storage assets within the structure. - AI inference without new data centers: AI providers pay to run trained models on the network with no new centralized data-center sites, no additional grid interconnections and no water-based cooling. The program is intended to supply capacity to one or more leading AI inference providers. - Initial deployment of 10,000 homes: Compute nodes at participating homes, with larger installations at local schools, hospitals and local commercial campuses. - Hosts get paid: Homeowners receive monthly hosting payments and lower-cost electricity, with household energy needs taking priority over computing workloads. Commercial hosts receive a share of site revenue and backup power. - Timeline: Initial installations scheduled to begin in the fourth quarter of 2026; first commercial site targeted for the first quarter of 2027. "Access to power is a major constraint on the growth of AI infrastructure," said Matt Shaw, CEO and Chairman of OpenWorld. "By bringing computing equipment to homes and commercial properties through solar generation and battery storage, we can build AI capacity closer to the power source instead of waiting years for a grid connection. Our term sheet with Meridian brings together the tokenization, financing and operating capabilities needed to develop this network at scale, and it shows what OpenWorld Enterprise is built to do: turn real-world assets into financeable, on-chain infrastructure." "Residential battery storage is the foundation of this program," said Josh Raffaelli, founder of Meridian and clean energy investor. "OpenWorld will help us finance the equipment, turning solar generation and battery storage at participating properties into infrastructure that can serve growing demand for AI computing." Solving the Power Problem in AI Infrastructure Access to power is a growing constraint on AI infrastructure. New data centers face lengthy grid interconnection timelines, local opposition and significant water demands. The planned network of home-hosted, distributed AI inference computing would place compute nodes at participating homes and larger installations at local schools, hospitals and commercial campuses, each powered by on-site solar generation and battery storage. AI providers would pay to use this computing capacity for inference, the process of running trained AI models, without requiring new centralized data-center sites, additional grid connections or water-based cooling. Participating homeowners would receive monthly hosting payments and lower-cost electricity, with household energy needs taking priority over computing workloads. Commercial hosts would receive a share of site revenue and backup power. How the Program Works Meridian, a privately held Delaware limited liability company, holds purchase rights to residential Tesla Powerwall battery storage systems for the program. The program's initial deployment is planned for 10,000 homes. Under the term sheet, OpenWorld will serve as advisor, structuring agent and services provider for the financing program. OpenWorld will establish and administer the tokenized financing structure on its OpenWorld Enterprise platform. The financing would support Meridian's purchase of residential battery storage systems, as well as the purchase by OpenWorld or a subsidiary of solar panels and associated AI computing equipment, all of which will be used within the structure. OpenWorld is also developing an integrated system to support each installation. The OpenWorld Enterprise platform will monitor equipment performance and provide investors with reporting on the underlying assets. The program is intended to supply computing capacity to one or more leading AI inference providers. Test installations are scheduled to begin in the fourth quarter of 2026, with the first commercial site targeted for the first quarter of 2027. Non-Binding Agreement The Term Sheet is non-binding, except for the provisions expressly stated to be binding, and the proposed transaction remains subject to the completion of confirmatory due diligence, negotiation and execution of definitive documentation, satisfaction of applicable conditions and completion of the contemplated transaction. artigo.texto: By JENNIFER McDERMOTT A battery system installed in a Buffalo, New York, apartment building will store excess energy when it’s plentiful and power the building when the grid is strained and electricity is costly. The manufacturer and state officials hope it will show that larger batteries can safely operate where people live and work. The 3.75 megawatt-hour lithium-ion battery system, which can power the Peace Bridge Place affordable housing complex for several days, is among the largest battery systems in a U.S. residential building, manufacturer Viridi and developer Good Carbon Co. said Tuesday. “We want our electric power to be resilient, affordable and available. Distributed battery storage accomplishes all three,” Viridi CEO Jon M. Williams said. “The only thing that has been holding up installations at scale is safety; a lot of the products on the market over the last 10 years have burned things down.” Deploying large batteries that can safely power apartment buildings is an important step toward replacing fossil fuels with renewables, experts say, but they’re uncommon because of the cost and concerns about fire risks. Already, larger batteries are paired with solar and wind projects, and homeowners are using smaller batteries to store excess energy from rooftop solar and for backup power. How batteries help keep electricity flow steady Batteries help maintain a steady flow of power when sources such as solar and wind are not producing. They charge when the sun is shining or when wind is blowing. That energy can then be used when demand is high. Batteries can also store excess electricity from hydropower, and New York is one of the top hydropower-producing states. Buffalo is close to Niagara Falls, where most of the state’s hydropower is produced. When electricity demand is high, Peace Bridge will use the battery. It will get paid by the utility for not drawing from the grid and for sending power back if needed. This helps lower the complex’s overall electricity costs, which benefits residents. The building can use the system during outages, too. The New York State Energy Research and Development Agency helped fund the Peace Bridge Place project, as part of its focus on including disadvantaged communities in the clean energy transition. “It goes a long way toward demonstrating the safety and viability of these types of projects,” said NYSERDA President and CEO Doreen Harris. Viridi has manufacturing facilities in Buffalo and Richmond, California, where a state grant assisted with renovations. California Energy Commission Chair David Hochschild said he’s impressed with the company. More than two-thirds of California’s electricity comes from clean energy and batteries get a lot of credit for that, Hochschild said. As electricity demand grows, batteries help ensure the grid is reliable, reduce pollution and contain costs, he added. “I believe the battery industry is the single most important energy industry for the next several decades,” said Hochschild, who co-founded the Electric Innovation Initiative to use electricity instead of fossil fuels more broadly throughout the U.S. economy. Viridi’s system passed a ‘near impossible’ test As large battery fires have garnered attention, some communities have opposed further development. However, the failure rate for batteries has decreased as more are installed, according to the Electric Power Research Institute. Viridi spent six years and $10 million figuring out how to make a fireproof container for batteries. Half the cost was for batteries Viridi destroyed during testing. Viridi uses plates, pouches and spacing to isolate each battery cell. If one fails, the energy dissipates instead of spreading to the next battery, so that no gas, smoke, heat or fire escapes the container, Williams said. Jigar Shah, an expert in clean energy financing and deployment, said the Peace Bridge Place system is a milestone in overcoming safety concerns. To ensure nothing would catch fire when used inside a residence, Viridi’s system had to pass a test where the battery was forced to fail while a cheesecloth covered the container. The cheesecloth did not char or ignite, according to the test report record. Viridi announced in April it met stringent Underwriters Laboratories safety standards so its system could be installed indoors without adding additional fire suppression to a building. Shah, who led the Department of Energy’s Loan Programs Office during the Biden administration, said Viridi is the only company to consistently pass this “near impossible” test. Shah thinks far more U.S. homes will use batteries for backup power by 2030. The U.S. can meet much more electricity demand and avoid costly upgrades to the grid if batteries are strategically deployed, he added. New York and California officials want forward-thinking energy solutions Viridi and Good Carbon Co. chose the Peace Bridge apartments because the all-electric building uses a geothermal system for heating and cooling rather than natural gas and needed additional, resilient power. The electricity demand locally can exceed the available supply, so the utility National Grid supported the endeavor, Williams added. Peace Bridge is considered affordable housing because renters earn no more than 80% of the area’s median income, Good Carbon said. It said energy storage will be an important part of future multifamily housing projects. Viridi has been manufacturing in Buffalo since 2018. A medical research building in the city is using its battery system, too. Viridi’s plant could build enough battery packs in a year to supply energy for about 14,000 average U.S. homes for 24 hours, Williams said. Harris, at NYSERDA, said the state needs more options like this for maintaining a reliable grid and managing costs. Gov. Kathy Hochul has made that a priority. “If we don’t need to build generation, we can utilize the grid that we have more effectively, that’s extremely valuable to us,” she said. In California

artigo.texto: Israel wants an AI data center boom. Its power grid may not be ready The Electricity Authority is preparing new rules for connecting energy-intensive facilities as data centers could account for 20% of national electricity consumption by 2030. Industry figures say transmission bottlenecks, gas dependence and national security concerns make local computing infrastructure both a challenge and a strategic necessity. During the August 2025 heat wave, Israel broke its electricity consumption record four days in a row. The new peak of 17,282 megawatts was 10% higher than the previous record, set just two years earlier. Israel’s current electricity generation capacity stands at approximately 18,800 megawatts. Despite the strain on the system, the Electricity Authority is expected to publish a regulatory framework today for connecting data centers to the grid. The move would allow more energy-intensive facilities to connect to an electricity system already operating close to its limits during periods of peak demand. According to the Authority’s load forecast, data centers could account for up to 20% of Israel’s electricity consumption by 2030. In July, the Electricity Authority halted approvals for applications to build data centers in Israel. The framework expected today is intended as a compromise, allowing construction to proceed while limiting the strain on the country’s infrastructure. Under the proposed rules, each data center would be capped at 200 megawatts of power consumption, roughly equivalent to the electricity demand of a mid-sized Israeli city such as Rehovot or Holon. According to estimates, as many as 15 facilities could be built at the maximum capacity of 200 megawatts. The proposed cap would apply to half of the 100 connection requests submitted to Noga, Israel’s electricity system operator. According to sources in the electricity sector, generation itself will be a challenge. “Electricity generation will be a problem. We see how hard it is to build a power plant in Israel, and how much politicians try to avoid decisions like that,” they said. The transmission grid, however, poses an even greater constraint, according to the sources. “There are problems in the transmission grid in the center of the country, and so it’s actually in the periphery that the risk is an opportunity. In the Negev there is renewable energy; instead of transmitting the electricity north, you can route it to data centers.” The challenge is not only how much electricity data centers consume, but also when they consume it. “Usually, there’s a kind of balance in electricity consumption: work zones and offices during the day, and residential areas in the evening. But data centers run 24/7 and raise the base load on the system, meaning several power plants need to run without stopping,” the sources said. Heavy electricity demand would also increase consumption of natural gas from Israel’s reservoirs. According to the Energy Ministry, those reserves could be depleted in less than 20 years, and greater reliance on gas-fired generation would also increase air pollution. Why, then, do data centers need to be built in Israel? Why not rely on facilities overseas, as Israeli companies and institutions do today? “The world is in the midst of a technological arms race, in which countries and giant corporations are investing hundreds of billions of dollars in building the computing infrastructure that will determine the balance of power in the global economy in the coming decades,” Shelly Lanzman, a partner and chair of the advisory board at NED, a company specializing in building and developing data centers and the former CEO of Microsoft Israel, told Calcalist. “Already today it’s clear that the scope of computing power, its strength and its availability will be decisive factors in the ability of countries to develop technologies and preserve a competitive advantage,” she said. In this context, Lanzman argues, data centers should be treated as national infrastructure on a par with power plants, airports and communications networks. “For Israel, whose economic and security standing relies to a large extent on technological superiority, this is a national interest of the first order.” National security is another argument for operating data centers locally. Government agencies and other organizations handling sensitive information, including the Shin Bet, the Mossad, the military and hospitals, increasingly rely on advanced AI and data systems. These organizations handle information with significant security or privacy implications, making local storage an important part of protecting it. Operational independence and continuity of service are also concerns. About a year ago, Microsoft restricted Unit 8200’s access to some of its cloud services after determining that the unit had violated the company’s terms of use. The decision followed reports that the service had been used to collect information on and track Palestinians, including by storing recordings of millions of their phone calls. Beyond security, a strong domestic data center industry could give Israeli entrepreneurs an advantage when launching startups and help attract international companies. Access to computing infrastructure is becoming an increasingly important consideration for businesses developing and deploying AI. “The global race is already creating growing competition for critical resources, from electricity supply and advanced chips to computing equipment, land and investment capital,” Lanzman added.

artigo.texto: Israel caps new data centers at 200 megawatts as demand overwhelms power grid The Electricity Authority will allocate an additional 1,000 megawatts to large data centers, bringing approved and planned capacity to about 3,000 megawatts. That would equal roughly 20% of projected national electricity consumption in 2030. After lengthy deliberations, the Electricity Authority published the main points of its new rules for connecting large data centers to Israel’s electricity grid on Sunday evening. As previously reported by Calcalist, the rules will cap the capacity of a new data center at 200 megawatts. The Authority will allocate an additional 1,000 megawatts to large data centers. Combined with approximately 2,000 megawatts in connections already approved, this would bring the total to around 3,000 megawatts, equivalent to about 20% of Israel’s projected electricity consumption in 2030. According to the Authority, the policy will make Israel “one of the world’s leaders in the rate of server farms relative to consumption.” The new rules became necessary after Noga, the company responsible for managing Israel’s electricity system, received requests to connect data centers with a combined capacity of 27,000 megawatts, roughly three times the country’s current average electricity consumption. In response to the surge in demand, the Electricity Authority issued a temporary order freezing responses to data center connection requests. To prevent developers from reserving grid capacity through projects with little chance of being built, or trading in connection approvals, the Authority will require developers to provide guarantees of NIS 2 million per megawatt of requested connection capacity, alongside additional conditions. The rules will also require backup mechanisms that allow data centers to be disconnected from the grid during periods of extreme demand. A 200-megawatt data center consumes electricity on a scale comparable to that of a mid-sized Israeli city, and construction costs are estimated at more than NIS 4 billion. The full decision is expected to be published in the coming days for a three-week public consultation. The Authority will consider the comments received and may make changes before the rules take effect. The decision would allow electricity consumption to grow as Israel attracts more data center investment, but it comes amid warnings that natural gas prices, and consequently electricity prices, could rise. A deal to supply natural gas involving NewMed and Ratio, partners in the Leviathan reservoir, collapsed. Last June, Israel Electric Corporation legal adviser Gershon Berkovitz warned that gas prices could increase. He also raised concerns about competition in the domestic market, warning that the problems could reach “the point of failure to meet the state’s energy needs.” While the new rules will restrict access to the grid for additional data centers and prevent the construction of some proposed megaprojects, including facilities with capacities of 500 megawatts and even 1,100 megawatts for which requests have already been submitted to Noga, limiting new connections will not eliminate the need for more electricity. Israel will still need to expand its generation capacity to meet growing demand from data centers and the wider economy.
