artigo.texto: [Stay on top of transportation news: Get TTNews in your inbox.] CATL bets big on electric truck market with new upgrades Offerings include battery upgrades and expanded swap stations Key Takeaways: - CATL is betting on the burgeoning electric-truck market to bolster growth, introducing battery upgrades and planning to open more so-called swap stations. - Electric trucks accounted for just over half of China’s vehicle sales last month, according to First Commercial Vehicle Network. - CATL plans to more than double its e-truck battery-swap stations to 2,000 by 2027 and ultimately operate 10,000 facilities. Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Ltd. is betting on the burgeoning electric-truck market to bolster growth, introducing battery upgrades and planning to open more so-called swap stations. The Chinese battery giant launched a slew of upgrades for the packs used in the cargo-hauling vehicles at an event in Beijing on Oct. 20, and said it has secured orders for swap products covering 13,000 units from major logistics companies including SF Holding Co. and China Postal Express & Logistics Co. The e-truck market is expanding rapidly in China, with vehicle sales accounting for just over half of the total last month, according to First Commercial Vehicle Network. CATL — which has seen its stock price slump this year amid concerns about rising competition — is due to release earnings later Oct. 20. The company plans to more than double its battery-swap stations for e-trucks to 2,000 by 2027, with a goal of running 10,000 facilities in the longer term, according to Yang Jun, CEO of CATL’s e-truck battery-swap business. The sites allow drivers to quickly exchange a depleted battery pack for a charged one, rather than waiting for a recharge of an existing unit. E-truck battery products introduced Oct. 20 included rear-mounted ultra-light and ultra-thin packs that can be suitable for weight- or space-sensitive applications. The company added that it will offer flexible battery leasing options for customers to tailor rental periods to their needs. “This will minimize idle costs and offer more flexible options for off-season downtime, further helping fleets manage operating costs,” according to a company statement.

artigo.texto: Near Arlington, Oregon, a 29,950-acre proposal combines 500 MW each of wind and solar with 4,000-MWh battery storage The Columbia River plateau desert of Eastern Washington lying above the Columbia River basin is an expansive area that is mostly windy, where rangeland stretches to the horizon beyond the small city of Arlington, Oregon, which has only 500 people living there. It would be hard for most Americans to locate it on a map. But it has drawn attention of energy experts and planners. An application is under consideration by the state regulators that proposes installing two kinds of renewable energy generation devices, along with a battery system large enough to overturn the assumptions about power grid reliability in the Pacific Northwest region. Remote Oregon plateau at heart of green energy gamble Arlington lies within the rain shadow of the Columbia River Basin – an area defined by high desert, created by the forces of wind, volcanic basalt, and hundreds of years of ranching and wheat farming. Arlington has some of the most consistent winds in the Pacific Northwest, as well as high-intensity summer solar radiation that few coastal areas can equal. The combination of natural features and existing power line routes in the area makes it increasingly attractive for renewable energy development. A developer filed a Notice of Intent with the Oregon Department of Energy on August 4, 2026, to pursue a site certificate for the Big River Renewable Energy Project. For perspective on the size of 29,950 acres, the urban land use in all of Portland occupies about 90,000 acres. This project alone would take up one-third of that space. This is no small project, but an extensive alteration of agricultural land visible from miles away. The Big River Renewable Energy Project proposal A developer filed a Notice of Intent with the Oregon Department of Energy on August 4, 2026, to pursue a site certificate for the Big River Renewable Energy Project. The Notice of Intent is the initial formal step in Oregon’s process of siting a facility and is not an approval in any way. There are four components to this proposal. A 500 MW wind turbine portion will place turbines on the plateau. Another 500 MW solar generation portion will overlay photovoltaic generation on the same footprint — co-location allowing wind and solar generation to share land and other infrastructure. Both will be supported by a 4,000 MWh battery energy storage system, able to store excess generation and dispatch it to the grid during peak times. Public comments can be submitted between August 7, 2026, and September 25, 2026, according to the Oregon Department of Energy – Big River. Why co-location of wind, solar, and storage is significant Wind energy and solar energy have often been referred to as intermittent forms of energy, but the generation patterns for these two in the Columbia Basin region are complementary. While wind blows the hardest at night and during the winter period, solar energy peaks at midday during the summer period. By combining both wind and solar energy together, the generation pattern becomes less intermittent. The addition of a 4,000 MWh battery system makes the entire process even better, as the battery takes care of the surplus generated during peak generation periods. The surplus energy is then used during the evening peak consumption times and when there are periods of cloudy weather without any wind blowing. The total 1,000 MW generating capacity will be enough to power hundreds of thousands of Pacific Northwest households. Grid operators have increasingly favored co-located hybrid projects because they reduce transmission congestion by delivering more usable power through a single interconnection point, improving overall capacity factors. Process review and role of the public in Oregon In Oregon, large energy projects need to get a Site Certificate from the Department of Energy before they can start construction. This process is purposely designed as such. The NOI phase, where Big River finds itself now, sets off environmental scoping, interagency coordination, and public participation. Submitting an NOI does not mean getting approval to build. An informational public hearing was held on August 20, 2026, and was available online and offline. The deadline for comments is set for September 25, 2026. Comments usually revolve around land use compatibility, effects on wildlife and habitats, landscape visual quality, water resources, and transmission corridor issues, given the size of the project. The future of Big River — and the energy situation in Oregon Once the comment period for the NOI is over, the developer will be required to file an application for site cacertificate. This application should respond to any issues identified during the public comment period and must meet all requirements of the Oregon Siting Standards. The project’s trajectory matters well beyond Arlington. Oregon has set ambitious clean energy targets, and the Pacific Northwest grid increasingly needs firm, dispatchable renewable power to replace retiring fossil fuel generation. A hybrid facility of this scale — if approved — would demonstrate that large co-located projects are viable in the American West, potentially accelerating similar proposals elsewhere. If it meets significant opposition or regulatory obstacles, that outcome would be equally instructive. For now, the project’s future remains genuinely open, shaped by the technical record, agency review, and the voices of people who live and work on that high desert plateau. Kelly is an experienced writer with 15 years of experience exploring the big stories that shape our world, from tech breakthroughs and space exploration to climate, energy, and the fascinating quirks of science. She has a talent for turning complex ideas into sharp, memorable insights that stay with readers long after they’ve finished reading.

artigo.texto: Tech CATL Unveils Five-Minute Battery Swapping for Electric Trucks, Targets 2,000 Stations by 2027 CATL introduces new electric-truck batteries and plans thousands of rapid-swapping stations. Chinese battery manufacturer CATL has unveiled a new generation of batteries for heavy-duty electric trucks and expanded its battery-swapping technology, offering a system designed to replace depleted truck batteries in approximately five minutes. The announcement marks another step in China’s efforts to electrify freight transportation, an industry traditionally dependent on diesel-powered vehicles. The new Tianxing II battery platform includes different configurations for commercial vehicles, while the company’s Qiji battery-swapping system is designed to reduce the time trucks spend waiting to replenish energy. According to Reuters, CATL is targeting 900 heavy-truck battery-swapping stations by the end of 2026, expanding to 2,000 stations in 2027 and eventually building a network of 10,000. The company’s plans reflect the growing importance of battery replacement technology as manufacturers seek to overcome some of the main obstacles to electric freight transportation, including charging times, battery weight, operating costs and infrastructure availability. How the Five-Minute Battery Swapping System Works Unlike conventional electric trucks that must remain connected to a charger while their batteries recharge, CATL’s system allows a vehicle to enter a specialized station where an automated mechanism removes its depleted battery and installs a charged replacement. The process is designed to take approximately five minutes, allowing drivers to resume operations without waiting for the original battery to recharge. CATL’s Qiji system uses standardized battery modules intended to work across compatible heavy-duty vehicle models. The battery-swapping approach can also separate battery ownership from vehicle ownership. Freight operators may be able to purchase or lease a truck without paying the full upfront cost of its battery, depending on the commercial arrangement. In an earlier company announcement, CATL said its standardized Qiji battery-swapping system could support a wide range of commercial trucks, with compatible designs developed alongside multiple vehicle manufacturers. The company says battery swapping can improve fleet efficiency, particularly for long-distance transportation, ports, mining operations and logistics services where vehicle downtime carries substantial costs. New Batteries Designed for Longer Truck Journeys The Tianxing II platform introduces batteries intended for different heavy-truck operating conditions. Its long-range configuration includes a battery pack with a capacity of 760 kilowatt-hours, which CATL says can support more than 600 kilometres of driving range under specified conditions. The company has also developed lighter battery configurations and chassis-mounted designs aimed at improving vehicle efficiency and preserving cargo capacity. CATL says its new standardized battery-swapping modules contain 52% fewer components and cost approximately 15% less than previous designs. These figures represent company-reported technical improvements. Actual vehicle range, battery performance and operating savings will depend on driving conditions, vehicle weight, climate, electricity prices and the availability of compatible swapping stations. CATL Plans Thousands of Battery-Swapping Stations CATL’s expansion strategy goes beyond developing new batteries. The company plans to establish a nationwide network of heavy-duty truck battery-swapping stations along China’s major freight transportation routes. The collaboration illustrates how the technology could be integrated into large commercial fleets that operate on predictable schedules and transportation routes. Heavy commercial vehicles consume substantial amounts of fuel and contribute to transportation-related emissions, making freight electrification an important part of China’s energy transition. artigo.texto: The Milwaukee Common Council unanimously passed a one-year moratorium last week on new data center projects while officials draft new zoning standards. Mayor Cavalier Johnson signed the ordinance the day after the council’s vote. Data center plans are facing public backlash across the state and the country. Milwaukee joins places like Superior, Madison and Wisconsin Rapids that passed their own data center construction moratoriums. Milwaukee’s moratorium comes in response to public controversy after a proposed project to redevelop a vacant Walmart on the city’s north side. Understanding Wisconsin, Together. WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter. Debate in the city mirrors what’s happening in other communities. Officials say they need time to write rules for projects that affect neighborhoods, utility costs and other issues. But business leaders say a pause may drive economic investment to other places. There are currently 53 data centers around the state, according to the Data Center Map. And at least 19 of varying sizes are in the Greater Milwaukee area. But while developers are moving quickly to build data centers, Milwaukee Common Council Ald. Marina Dimitrijevic told WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” that local government operates at a slower pace to weigh how major changes could affect residents. Before the moratorium, Dimitrijevic said the city had essentially no zoning rules or regulations regarding data center construction. “Government is not set up to move that fast, which is why we have to pause,” she said. “Zoning code has to account for land use; we have to look at how it would affect neighbors, the noise, the possible pollution; the list goes on and on. And I think there are very few Wisconsinites that want to live right next to one of these (data centers).” Dimitrijevic said she had concerns about how the boom in data centers would affect the region’s energy grid and utility costs for constituents. A Pew Research Center survey released in September found 54 percent of Americans believe that data centers would have a negative impact on the environment, up from 39% in January. The survey found half of Americans believe data centers would negatively affect home energy costs. “No one is asking for this, other than the corporations that are seeking to make money off of us,” Dimitrijevic said. But for the businesses hoping to build in Milwaukee and stimulate its economy, a moratorium like the one the city just passed could scare away potential investment, said Dale Kooyenga, president and CEO of the Metropolitan Milwaukee Association of Commerce. MMAC opposed Milwaukee’s moratorium. Kooyenga said he thought the data center pause could’ve been worse and that businesses still have opportunities to negotiate with the city, but that such a moratorium is essentially putting up a “we’re not open for business” sign on the city’s front door. “We understand that with any economic development, there’s a back-and-forth discussion, but you should have policies that invite a discussion, and then when you have those discussions, then share with the investor what you need to get to a yes,” Kooyenga said. “We just think (the moratorium) sends the wrong message for a city that really needs more economic development.” Building a new data center can take thousands of workers in construction jobs, from electricians to carpenters to engineers. But once built, the centers themselves host relatively few job openings, up to several hundred. Kooyenga said the years of construction jobs shouldn’t be discounted. And he said the jobs the centers host once operational are typically well above the median wage. Kooyenga said such projects raise significant property tax revenue for the area, which local governments could use to bolster schools, fire departments and other public services. Dimitrijevic said she was more skeptical over the long-term payoff of such projects after the construction is done and the builders have moved on to other projects. “I think we want the same (as businesses and developers) when we want investment in the city of Milwaukee, but we’ve got to do it in a way that serves the many, not just the few,” she said.

artigo.texto: Earlier this year, the German government laid out an ambitious plan: By 2030, it would double the scale of the country’s data center fleet, and quadruple the amount of compute available for running artificial intelligence models. The idea was to minimize Germany’s dependence on the United States for access to AI—a point of concern across Europe—and boost its faltering economy. However, Germany has found that its AI ambitions are butting up against its climate commitments. EU member states have committed to cutting greenhouse gas emissions by 55 percent by the end of the decade. But policies meant to help meet that target are interfering with attempts to trigger a data center building frenzy. As part of its broader climate commitments, the previous German administration voted through the Energy Efficiency Act in 2023. Among other things, it required all new data centers to recycle a portion of the waste heat generated by their computer equipment, ideally into nearby municipal heating systems. It seemed like a no-brainer, says Patrick Graichen, who served as a senior official at Germany’s Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy at the time, before resigning over cronyism allegations. “We need clean heat, and data centers are a source of clean heat,” Graichen tells WIRED. In June, a month before the rules were due to finally take effect, the German federal government walked them back. Data center firms had complained that the requirements made it almost impossible to build in the country; the German Data Center Association characterized an early version of the bill as a “data center prevention act.” Under an amended bill, which will be put to the German parliament for ratification imminently, data center operators would no longer be obligated to reuse waste heat, only to scope out the possibility. Graichen and others have accused the German government of sacrificing climate targets for a chance to ride the AI wave. But countries across Europe find themselves pulled between these same two poles, under simultaneous pressure to cash in on rapid growth in the energy-intensive AI sector—and limit dependence on the US—and to protect the climate. The German Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy did not respond to a request for comment. Among data center developers, the chief objection to the original Energy Efficiency Act was the chance it could land them in an impossible bind, obligated to reuse waste heat even when there was no available offtake—whether a municipal heating system or an industry, like greenhouse agriculture. “Some of the things they had to comply with were outside of their control,” says Barbara Smitten, associate director for critical systems at consulting firm Cundall. “It felt that [the burden] was all on the data center.” In the last 18 months, multiple data center proposals have fallen through in Germany: Stack Infrastructure canceled a $3 billion facility in Hesse, and state-owned Komm.ONE withdrew from a project in Baden-Württemberg. Though precisely what causes a data center development to fold is rarely clear, Komm.ONE pointed directly to the burdens of the Energy Efficiency Act. Graichen claims that the industry’s objections are groundless. He says the availability of a heat offtake should become a default criterion for any developer searching for a new site. “Stop complaining,” he says. When an offtake is available, recycling heat produced by a data center is straightforward. “There is no technical reason why a data center cannot use its waste heat. The technologies and concepts are well known,” says John Booth, managing director at IT consultancy Carbon3IT, who helped to devise EU-wide energy efficiency targets for data centers. “There is absolutely no reason except the will of the organization to do it.” Nevertheless, under the amended Energy Efficiency Act, data center developers are required only to assess whether recycling heat is economically and technically feasible. If not, they are exempt. “With practical rules for data centers, we are creating the conditions for digital sovereignty and economic growth,” wrote Katherina Reiche, federal minister for economic affairs and energy, when the cabinet approved the change. The amendment may unlock pent-up demand among data center developers to build in Germany, whose geographic centrality makes it easy to route data efficiently into Western and Eastern Europe. “It lessens the risk of people not seeing the German market as attractive,” says Smitten. But in a roundabout way, it could also undermine the aim to spark a building frenzy, inviting the type of climate-focused activism that has led to permitting freezes and data center moratoria in the US. Already, in February, the city council of a small German town voted to block the construction of a $2.5 billion data center development, partly over climate concerns. As policymakers contend with conflicting ambitions to improve domestic AI capabilities and meet climate objectives, some say the swelling public unease about that trade-off will complicate things yet further in Europe. In the last year, the attitude toward data centers “has switched completely,” claims Graichen. “First and foremost in the US, but the same will happen in Europe.”

artigo.texto: SK Nexilis, an investment company of SKC in the copper foil business for secondary batteries, said Tuesday that it has successfully developed 'high-bonding carbon-coated copper foil' technology, which is considered a core material for next-generation batteries. High-bonding carbon-coated copper foil is a product that applies special carbon to the surface of the copper foil to enhance adhesion with the anode material. It is characterized by suppressing the 'delamination phenomenon,' where silicon anode materials expand during charging and discharging processes, causing them to separate from the copper foil, thereby improving the structural stability of the electrode. The company explained that this can also contribute to enhancing battery lifespan and safety. SK Nexilis developed the related technology in line with the trend in the battery industry to increase the silicon content of anode materials to boost energy density. While silicon can store more lithium ions than conventional graphite, its significant volume change during charging and discharging processes is cited as a drawback. This is why adhesion between the anode material and copper foil becomes increasingly important as the silicon content rises. High-bonding carbon-coated copper foil can also be applied to dry electrode processes, which are gaining attention as a manufacturing method for next-generation batteries. Unlike conventional wet processes that use liquid solvents, dry electrode processes can reduce steps such as drying, thereby lowering manufacturing costs and energy consumption. However, since it is crucial to stably bond electrode materials with copper foil, the utilization of high-adhesion copper foil is expected to expand. SK Nexilis plans to build a pilot production system for high-bonding carbon-coated copper foil ahead of full-scale Yangsan. The company is currently verifying process stability and aims to commercialize in the second half of next year after securing Yangsan technology. An official from SK Nexilis said, "We will proceed with commercialization optimization work without any issues while strengthening our competitiveness in the next-generation battery materials market through continuous technological development."

artigo.texto: San Antonio is considering stricter regulations on data center development to address concerns about electricity use, water consumption, air quality, and neighborhood impact, with proposals requiring varying levels of City Council approval and community engagement. Public hearings are scheduled in October to decide on potential changes to the approval process for new data centers. - Data centers require significant electricity, cooling, and backup power, raising concerns amid rapid expansion in San Antonio. - Three regulatory proposals range from permitting data centers with specific requirements to requiring individual City Council approval and additional safeguards. - Mayor Gina Ortiz Jones proposes a 1,000-foot setback, advance community notice, neighborhood meetings, and green space replacement. - Council members are divided between ensuring resident input and maintaining economic development incentives. - Public hearings by the Zoning Commission and City Council are scheduled for October 20 and 29, respectively, allowing resident participation. San Antonio Moves Toward Tougher Data Center Restrictions as Residents Raise Concerns Over Water, Power and Neighborhoods San Antonio is moving closer to imposing stricter regulations on data centers as city leaders debate how to balance economic development with growing concerns about electricity consumption, water use, air quality and the impact of large industrial facilities on surrounding neighborhoods. The debate could change how data centers are approved throughout the city, potentially requiring developers to obtain City Council authorization before constructing new facilities. A public hearing before the Zoning Commission is scheduled for October 20, followed by an anticipated City Council vote October 29. Growing Industry Brings Growing Concerns Data centers house computer servers and other equipment supporting cloud computing, artificial intelligence and digital services. Their operations can require substantial electricity, cooling infrastructure and backup power systems. San Antonio has become an attractive market for developers because of available land, energy infrastructure and access to natural resources. However, the rapid expansion has raised questions about whether existing zoning regulations adequately protect residents. District 6 Councilman Ric Galvan has been among those pushing for stronger oversight, particularly as data center development expands across the city’s West Side. Galvan introduced a council consideration request last year calling for a comprehensive review of the industry’s impact on infrastructure and natural resources. “The residents of San Antonio deserve to have a say in where and how data centers are built in our city,” Galvan said in an October 15 statement. Three Proposals Could Reshape Development City officials are considering three approaches to regulating future facilities. One proposal would permit data centers in designated commercial and industrial districts if developers meet specific requirements, without requiring individual City Council approval. A second proposal would require developers to obtain specific use authorization, allowing council members to evaluate each project and providing opportunities for public comment. Mayor Gina Ortiz Jones has introduced a third approach combining individual council approval with additional safeguards. Her proposal includes a 1,000-foot setback, advance notice to affected communities, neighborhood engagement meetings and requirements to replace twice the green space eliminated during construction. The proposals also address concerns involving noise, lighting, emergency planning and environmental protections. Economic Growth Versus Neighborhood Protections Council members remain divided over how far the restrictions should go. Some argue that requiring individual approval for every facility would provide accountability and give residents a meaningful voice in decisions affecting their neighborhoods. Others warn that overly restrictive requirements could discourage investment and limit opportunities for economic development. Data centers could also generate additional revenue for municipally owned CPS Energy, potentially increasing funds transferred to the city. The central question is whether those economic benefits outweigh the demands placed on public infrastructure and surrounding communities. Residents Have Opportunity to Weigh In The Zoning Commission will consider the proposals October 20, with City Council expected to take up the issue October 29. Both meetings will provide opportunities for public participation. The outcome could determine whether data centers continue receiving approval under established zoning rules or face greater scrutiny from elected officials and residents. For communities already experiencing rapid development, the decision may establish how much influence neighborhoods have over the industry’s future expansion.

artigo.texto: Funding Strains, Power Shortages and Local Opposition Hit Projects, Squeezing Chip Demand At Least 47 Large Data Center Projects in the United States In the United States, the world’s largest artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure market, at least 47 large-scale data center projects have faced disruptions this year alone. Concerns are rising that cracks are forming in the U.S. AI infrastructure boom, estimated to be worth $10 trillion, due to a combination of practical issues such as worsening corporate financial conditions, power shortages, and opposition from local residents. On Oct. 18 (local time), the Financial Times (FT) cited data from regulatory intelligence firm RegLayer, reporting that at least 47 data center development projects in the U.S. have been delayed, withdrawn, or halted this year. RegLayer explained, “We surveyed primarily large-scale worksites, and the figures were compiled conservatively.” Recently, investment bank (IB) Bernstein also estimated that only 35% of the data center construction projects currently planned in the U.S. are feasible. Funding shortages are cited as the primary cause of the successive disruptions in AI infrastructure projects in the U.S. Concerns have grown over the structure in which new operators take out loans to bear massive costs for purchasing GPUs and securing sites. In particular, the controversy intensified recently as the corporate bond yield of AI infrastructure company CoreWeave surged to the 15% level. CoreWeave is a so-called ‘neocloud’ company that operates a business of buying Nvidia AI chips to build data centers and then leasing the infrastructure to tech companies. The FT stated, “The overheating of infrastructure competition among companies has turned the overall AI industry into a ‘Wild West’,” adding, “Interest rate hikes and the bond market slump are threatening the ambitions of AI infrastructure companies.” The increasingly severe power shortage and opposition from local residents, who have begun to perceive data centers as undesirable facilities, are also stumbling blocks. Big tech company Oracle notified the developer of the 2.45GW (gigawatt) ‘Project Jupiter’ underway in New Mexico of force majeure last month in preparation for disruptions in securing power. The intent is to delay rent payments if the set schedule is not met. PJM, the largest power grid operator in the US, recently decided to halt a previously planned special auction for 15 years’ worth of power for data centers to respond to the AI-driven power shortage. According to the FT’s own survey results, it was found that more than 1,000 communities in the US have attempted to introduce temporary halts or restrictive measures related to AI infrastructure development this year. Concerns over AI infrastructure companies are emerging in various parts of the market beyond the US. It is reported that Nscale, a British neocloud company, is also pursuing an initial public offering (IPO) with a corporate value of about $30 billion, but is facing difficulties as investors’ expectations are much lower than this. Bloomberg reported that due to the recently deteriorated industry conditions, some investors view Nscale’s corporate value at $16 billion to $19 billion. Previously, Australian AI infrastructure company Firmus also withdrew its IPO plan, which had been pursued at a scale of about $5 billion. It is pointed out that such crises for AI infrastructure companies could ultimately affect the earnings of semiconductor manufacturers. This is because if infrastructure companies increasingly struggle to secure investment funds and construction plans are consequently delayed, they may delay or reduce orders for semiconductor chips to be used in data centers. In fact, the stock prices of domestic memory companies such as Samsung Electronics and SK hynix have continued to show weakness recently. This is due to worsened investor sentiment caused by concerns over U.S. interest rate hikes and the pace adjustment of AI infrastructure. Bloomberg stated, “As borrowing costs rise and uncertainty about the long-term profitability of AI technology grows, investor sentiment regarding overall AI infrastructure, including server companies and semiconductor manufacturers, has deteriorated.”

artigo.texto: Energia limpa – O Google planeja construir um data center de 780 megawatts em Pine Island, Minnesota, nos Estados Unidos, acompanhado de investimentos em energia renovável e armazenamento. O acordo com a Xcel Energy prevê ampliar a capacidade da rede elétrica além da demanda da instalação, mas ainda depende de aprovação da Comissão de Utilidade Pública do estado. Segundo a CNBC, a empresa financiará a adição de 1.400 MW de energia eólica, 200 MW de energia solar e 300 MW de armazenamento em baterias. A capacidade adicional busca compensar a geração intermitente das fontes renováveis. LEIA: Consumo de água por IA varia conforme servidores e geração de energia Proteção contra a saída antecipada O contrato prevê que o Google pague pelo menos 75% da capacidade acordada, mesmo que utilize menos energia. Se encerrar o compromisso antes do prazo, poderá arcar com até oito anos de cobranças mínimas. “Ninguém quer ter uma grande expansão e depois não ter para onde mandar essa energia e ninguém para pagá-la”, diz Amanda Rome, vice-presidente executiva da Xcel Energy. “É aí que essas proteções entram.” A iniciativa ocorre em meio à crescente demanda por eletricidade dos centros de dados. A Corporação Norte-Americana de Confiabilidade Elétrica (NERC) aponta essas instalações como principal fator de expansão prevista do consumo na América do Norte na próxima década. Nos Estados Unidos, o envelhecimento da infraestrutura também pressiona o setor elétrico. Centros menores como alternativa Para Jigar Shah, sócio da consultoria Multiplier, empresas poderiam optar por instalações menores em regiões com capacidade disponível na rede, reduzindo custos para os consumidores. “Se você encaixar o crescimento de carga que os centros de dados querem na rede existente, as tarifas de todo mundo caem muito”, afirma. Segundo ele, construir unidades menores exige mais planejamento, mas pode evitar grandes expansões de infraestrutura. Incentivos das distribuidoras David Pomerantz, diretor-executivo do Energy and Policy Institute, observa que as distribuidoras têm incentivos financeiros para investir em novas estruturas. “Quando [as distribuidoras] constroem algo novo, financiam parte desse investimento com recursos de investidores de Wall Street e desfrutam de retornos incrivelmente altos, exorbitantes sobre esses investimentos, tipicamente em torno de 10%”, afirma. Uma alternativa seria os operadores de data centers financiarem melhorias na rede com capital mais barato. Pomerantz, porém, aponta que essa possibilidade gera conflitos com as distribuidoras. Apesar das ressalvas sobre o modelo, Shah avalia positivamente a proposta do Google, que aguarda autorização regulatória. artigo.texto: Two-Year LTA Covers 2027 Supply of High-Voltage Switchgear LS Electric has accelerated its push into the North American data center market after winning power infrastructure supply rights worth 170.0 billion won ($125.80 million) from a major U.S. tech company. LS Electric said on Oct. 19 that it signed a contract to supply power distribution solutions for data centers in North America. The agreement was structured as a long-term agreement, or LTA, running for two years from 2027 to 2028. The order value of 170.0 billion won ($125.80 million) corresponds to the volume scheduled for supply in 2027, while the scale of the 2028 business is to be finalized through additional consultations later. The main product to be supplied is 38kV-class high-voltage switchgear. The equipment serves as core infrastructure that stably distributes high-voltage electricity entering data centers and protects facilities when abnormalities occur in the power system. Given the nature of artificial intelligence, or AI, data centers, which must continuously receive large-scale electricity around the clock, product reliability and quality acted as key indicators in the contract. LS Electric is seeking to expand beyond this high-voltage switchgear supply. It is understood to be holding additional discussions on supplying other customized high-end power equipment for data centers, including low-voltage switchgear, distribution transformers, and ring main units, or RMUs. The latest result is seen as reflecting the effectiveness of the company’s strategy of strengthening its local response system in the United States. LS Electric has established bases at LS Electric Utah in Cedar City, Utah, and the Bastrop Campus in Texas. Through these operations, it has built a locally completed value chain that handles the full process on site, from sales and design to production, commissioning, and service, enabling it to respond quickly to customer demands. An LS Electric official explained that trust built through world-class technological capabilities and project execution experience led to the long-term contract. The company said it plans to further strengthen a stable revenue base and improve profitability by increasing supplies of high-value-added products for data centers in the future.

artigo.texto: Memphis leaders are set to consider a contentious plan Tuesday to pause new data center developments for up to a year — two weeks after a meeting on the issue led to protests, calls to police and a fist fight at City Hall. The moratorium vote comes more than two years after some communities in Memphis got a new life courtesy of trillionaire Elon Musk, as his artificial intelligence company moved in amid a local effort to make the city a hotspot for advanced technology. But the effort ended up angering residents as the company installed dozens of gas-powered turbines, known to produce a cocktail of toxic pollutants. A surge of new data center construction to fuel the booming AI industry is escalating public resentment and fear of both the energy-sucking infrastructure and AI itself in the US, roiling communities from coast to coast and transforming localized energy debates into a high-stakes, multi-million-dollar battleground for the 2026 midterm elections. At an early October council meeting in Memphis — a city used to fighting for clean air as the home to more than a dozen polluting facilities — fierce opposition was on full display. More than 100 people filed into the chamber to hear about the moratorium, bearing witness to clashes between anti-data center protesters and council members, and between the city officials themselves. Two women were also restrained in the lobby as they swung fists at each other. All eyes will be on City Hall as it considers the moratorium, which, if passed, would put a temporary pause on new data centers and on the expansion of existing ones, as well as develop a study committee to establish regulations. It would not shutter data centers already operating legally in Memphis, nor smaller data usages at facilities like hospitals and universities. Here’s what we know: How Memphis got here An abandoned factory in southwest Memphis got a makeover in June 2024, as the AI company owned by the world’s richest man, now called SpaceXAI, worked to turn the building into the “world’s largest supercomputer.” Dubbed “Colossus,” the data center was hailed by Musk at the time as the “most powerful AI training system in the world,” and the company’s website heralded plans for a second facility in the area to quickly follow. For some residents in the southwest Memphis suburb of Boxtown, a historic, majority Black and economically disadvantaged community that has long endured industrial pollution, the new gas-powered turbines represented yet another threat to their health. About 10 miles to the east in Southaven, Mississippi, more SpaceXAI turbines would chug to life at the new site of Colossus 2 — which fuels its Grok AI chatbot. CNN has reached out to SpaceXAI for comment. The NAACP filed a federal lawsuit against SpaceXAI in April of this year under the Clean Air Act, alleging it was operating dozens of unpermitted turbines in Southaven. The Department of Justice has since urged the court to throw out the lawsuit, saying the Grok AI chatbot was “critical” to national security. The case remains active, though tied up in appeals. The data centers have also caused a myriad of disruptions to daily life in Memphis, including relentless noise pollution and physical vibrations from the centers as described in a noise complaint filed by residents; concerns of dangerous emissions from the turbines brought by state officials; and an offer from SpaceXAI to buy Southaven residents’ homes in exchange for not signing onto a class action lawsuit against it. But it was at an August meeting — where the moratorium passed its first reading — that Memphis City Council Member JB Smiley Jr. said he proposed the measure to temporarily halt new data center builds after learning Musk’s company was planning a data center expansion in the city from a post on social media. “Not only did the council not know about the expansion of the data center, the community residents did not know,” Smiley said at the meeting. “I was intentional about bringing this ordinance because I think the people deserve an opportunity to voice their concerns; I think the council deserves to be treated with respect by the folks who are pushing these data centers in our community.” An earlier council meeting on data centers devolved into chaos Members of the Memphis City Council voted on whether to delay making a decision on the moratorium for two weeks at an October 6 meeting. When the effort to delay passed 7-5, the chamber erupted. “Officers, we need to clear it out,” council Chairwoman Jana Swearengen-Washington said from the podium as observers began shouting. As people rose from their seats in the chamber and a woman shouted chants into a megaphone speaker, the chairwoman repeatedly slammed her gavel, saying, “Get that f**king bullhorn!” A livestream of the meeting showed dozens of protesters gathering at the front of the room, fists in the air as they chanted above the council members’ shouts to stop, yelling, “Ain’t no power like the power of the people ‘cause the power of the people fight back!” before the livestream went dark. Councilwoman Yolanda Cooper-Sutton clashed with members of the crowd, according to CNN affiliate WMC, as she told one attendee, “You pipe down baby, I clap back.” She also lashed out at Smiley, who voted against postponing the vote on his moratorium, shouting that he “confuse(s) the people over and over,” as she was ushered out of the room by staffers. In the lobby of the building, a fist fight broke out between two women, WMC reported. Memphis police were called to the disturbance at City Hall, but according to WMC, a department spokesperson said no one was harmed or detained. artigo.texto: South Korea's Big 3 Battery Makers Race to Mass-Produce 'Salt Batteries,' Chasing CATL's Head Start South Korea's three major battery makers are accelerating commercialization of sodium-ion batteries, which replace lithium. Using sodium as a raw material, these batteries are seen as a technology that could reshape the next-generation energy storage system (ESS) market thanks to advantages in cost and low-temperature performance. However, China's CATL and BYD have already entered mass production, giving China the early lead. LG Energy Solution has built a sodium-ion battery pilot line at its Ochang Energy Plant in Cheongju, North Chungcheong Province, and is running sample tests for ESS applications at a scale of 30MWh with North American customers. The company aims for first mass production next year. In the early commercialization phase, it plans to target the vehicle auxiliary battery and ESS markets before expanding into affordable electric vehicles. Samsung SDI is developing sodium-ion batteries for uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems at AI data centers and for ESS. It has drawn up mass production plans and will disclose a detailed schedule by the end of this year or during next year. SK On aims to complete prototype development by next year, centered on ESS products, and pursue commercialization in 2028. It is also reviewing the possibility of using the technology in EV batteries. Sodium-ion batteries use sodium, the main component of salt, as a raw material. Unlike lithium, the mining and refining supply chain is not concentrated in a handful of countries, making supply stable and prices cheap. Another highlighted strength is that charge and discharge performance degrades less than lithium-ion batteries in subzero conditions. Energy density, long cited as a weakness, is also improving. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), recently developed products reach energy density of up to 175Wh/kg, approaching lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries at up to 205Wh/kg. Nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) batteries stand at around 255Wh/kg. ESS, where weight and volume constraints are relatively less binding, is the likely first application market. Global sodium-ion battery output last year was less than 1% of lithium-ion battery production, underscoring that the market is still in its early stages. Morgan Stanley expects sodium-ion batteries' share of total battery deployments to rise from 2% in 2027 to 20% in 2030 and 37% in 2035. Annual deployments are projected to reach 830GWh in 2030 and 2.4TWh in 2035, and the analysis estimates that about $800 billion in new investment will be needed by 2035 to achieve this. China is furthest ahead in seizing the market. In April, CATL signed a three-year supply contract for 60GWh with Chinese ESS company HyperStrong and entered a mass production regime. It plans to increase shipments through the end of the year and begin overseas supplies from June next year. BYD is also building a dedicated sodium-ion battery plant. The sense of urgency in South Korea's industry stems from memories of past failures in responding to LFP. The prevailing view is that while Korean companies focused on high-performance NMC batteries, they fell behind in LFP mass production and handed leadership of that market to China. There is a growing sense of crisis that if they are also outrun in sodium-ion batteries, they could lose leadership of the battery industry itself. If sodium-ion batteries are commercialized in earnest, the cost-competition landscape in the ESS market could change. The burden on existing supply chains exposed to lithium price swings would ease, and the economics of long-duration storage facilities could improve. However, a gap with LFP in energy density remains, suggesting it will take considerable time before sodium-ion becomes a mainstream EV battery. Whether South Korea's three companies can move up their mass production timelines is seen as a variable that will determine the supply landscape of the ESS market going forward.

artigo.texto: CATL Tries to Reassure Investors: Next Year's Battery Demand Not as Bleak as Feared, but Shares Still Plunge Nearly 10% CATL (03750.HK), China's battery leader, on the 21st took the rare step of proactively addressing market doubts. Responding to investor concerns about weakening demand in next year's new energy vehicle market and for batteries, the company said "next year's industry demand is still worth looking forward to," emphasizing that the global market size for power batteries and energy storage batteries may not be as bleak as outsiders imagine and still holds solid growth potential. The reassurance, however, failed to reverse the stock's slide. The shares touched an intraday low of HK$371.2 that day and last traded at HK$371.8, down 9.71%, on volume of 5.1631 million shares worth HK$1.964 billion (approximately $250.3 million), extending a run of new lows. CATL's weaker-than-expected third-quarter net profit was the direct trigger for the selloff. Breaking down the fundamentals, the company believes the market's assessment of demand is too conservative. In China, overall passenger vehicle sales have declined this year, but the electrification rate is climbing rapidly, and the battery capacity per vehicle is rising at the same time. Combined, these two forces are keeping shipment growth of power batteries for new energy passenger vehicles in positive territory. The electrification rate for new energy commercial vehicles is also in a rapid ascent. Overseas, the electrification trend in Europe has continuity, with new models continuing to launch and remaining competitive, while electrification potential in other markets may be underestimated. The energy storage business is another bright spot, maintaining solid growth in both China and overseas markets, with demand particularly strong in some overseas markets. Asked about capacity utilization, the company said utilization was at a very saturated level in the first half. In recent years it has accelerated capacity construction in line with market demand, and as new capacity added this year gradually comes on stream, the tightness has eased somewhat. But demand is also continuing to grow, so capacity utilization will remain at a relatively high level going forward and is overall healthy. The change in cash flow that has drawn outside attention is tied to an adjustment in supply chain strategy. The company noted that upstream lithium battery supply chain companies have faced relatively heavy cash flow pressure in recent years, and CATL has proactively adjusted payment arrangements with suppliers since the third quarter, giving priority to supporting partners with R&D capabilities, an innovative spirit and active cooperation in capacity expansion. Measures include shortening payment terms, making prepayments and providing R&D funding support, among others. This approach to supporting the supply chain may continue for some time, with the aim of fostering healthier and more sustainable development across the industry. It will have a phased impact on operating cash flow, but over the long term will not hurt the company's cash profitability, which is expected to return to a relatively healthy level. As for the quarter-on-quarter increase in third-quarter inventory, the company explained that the larger inventory figure is a natural result of business growth. Inventory turnover days have been relatively stable in recent quarters, with no sluggish sales or shipment disruptions, representing normal turnover. By composition, the increase was mainly goods shipped but not yet recognized as revenue, which will gradually be reflected in the company's revenue. In energy storage, the company is shifting from simply selling battery cells and DC-side products to offering AC-side and system-level products. The product mix and formats are richer than before, and the corresponding delivery and revenue recognition cycles have lengthened. In terms of market impact, CATL is a bellwether for the global power and energy storage battery industry, and its read on next year's demand is seen as an important gauge of conditions across the electric vehicle and energy storage sectors. The company's disclosures on capacity, cash flow and inventory in its earnings call and response help investors clarify the line items in its third-quarter report most likely to raise questions. Still, the stock's nearly 10% plunge after the results reflects short-term investors' heightened sensitivity to the profit miss and the phased pressure on cash flow. The strength of the demand recovery and the actual impact of the supply chain payment adjustments will be key focal points as the market re-evaluates the stock.

artigo.texto: AI Data Centers Snap Up Optical Fiber, Spot Prices Soar 5x Year-on-Year, Shortage Could Persist Through 2028 The AI data center (AIDC) construction boom is pushing optical fiber from a supporting role into the spotlight. TrendForce's latest communications industry research estimates that the global optical fiber supply-demand gap will reach 180 million fiber-kilometers in 2026. The supply crunch is directly reflected in pricing, with spot prices for finished optical fiber up 2.8 to more than 5 times compared with 2025, and the tight conditions are expected to last at least through 2028. The research notes that global optical fiber supply began tightening at the end of 2025, driven primarily by the massive new demand created by AI data center-related applications. There is no slack left on the supply side: global optical fiber capacity utilization is projected to rise to 92% in 2026, inventory levels have been compressed from four months in 2024 to just one month, and some major manufacturers' order books are already filled through the first quarter of 2027 — meaning existing capacity is running near full. Expanding capacity is not something that happens overnight. Optical fiber preform expansion involves the installation of deposition equipment and process setup, requiring roughly 18 to 24 months from planning to production. Even if manufacturers launch expansion plans now, new supply will take time to come online, making it difficult to effectively ease the shortage in the near term. Demand remains robust. The research estimates global optical fiber demand at 577 million fiber-kilometers in 2026, with growth driven mainly by data center construction, which accounts for roughly 18% to 20% of total demand and is expected to rise further to 30% to 35% in 2027. In addition to large Cloud Service Providers continuing to expand AI data centers, chipmakers and telecom operators are also investing in related infrastructure, driving optical fiber consumption for data center interconnect and high-capacity backbone networks. The supply-demand imbalance is already reflected in spot quotes across optical fiber product categories. Broken down by application, bend-insensitive fiber used for cabling inside data centers has seen the steepest increase, with average prices in 2026 more than 5x higher than in 2025. AI backbone fiber used for data center interconnect and high-capacity backbone networks has risen about 2.8x year-on-year. Mainstream fiber for telecom services has also climbed about 3.7x. Note: Year-on-year increases reflect the change in 2026 average prices versus 2025 average prices. Faced with persistently tightening supply, telecom operators' procurement strategies have clearly shifted. The previous model centered on short-term purchasing is gradually giving way to long-term contracts that lock in resources in advance. For example, Verizon and Corning signed a multi-year supply agreement in September 2026, planning to secure more than 129 million fiber-kilometers (about 80 million miles) of high-density optical fiber and connectivity solutions between 2027 and 2032. In addition to supporting broadband buildouts, the fiber will be used for high-capacity backbone networks connecting AI data centers. The nature of this tightness differs from past telecom buildout cycles. The research argues that the root of this shortage is the continuous expansion of new AI data center-related demand, rather than a cyclical rebound in traditional telecom capital spending. With supply unable to ramp up quickly in the short term and demand growing steadily, it will become increasingly common for telecom operators and large infrastructure players to lock in optical fiber resources through long-term contracts in advance. For the industry chain, optical fiber's shift from a buyer's market to a seller's market means upstream preform and fiber manufacturers have significantly strengthened their pricing power, along with extended order visibility. Conversely, telecom carriers and data center operators face rising construction costs, making procurement timing and cost control increasingly important. The market's focus has shifted from "is there demand" to "can we get the material" — and the pace at which optical fiber supply chain capacity comes online will be a key indicator for tracking AI infrastructure progress over the next two years.

artigo.texto: Shinhan Asset Management's SOL All-Solid-State Battery ETF Ranks No. 1 Among South Korean Equity ETFs With 22.76% Three-Month Return Shinhan Asset Management's "SOL All-Solid-State Battery & Silicon Anode" exchange-traded fund (ETF) has posted the highest return among South Korean-listed equity ETFs over the past three months. As of the 16th of this month, the product's three-month return stood at 22.76%, ranking first among South Korean-listed equity ETFs excluding leveraged and inverse products. That is 39.66 percentage points ahead of the KOSPI's -16.90% over the same period. The ETF concentrates investments in key companies tied to all-solid-state batteries and silicon anodes. All-solid-state batteries replace conventional liquid electrolytes with solid materials to boost safety and energy density, and expectations for their commercialization have recently been rising. Major holdings include Samsung SDI, which is pursuing mass production of all-solid-state batteries; LG Energy Solution, a key energy storage system (ESS) player; EcoPro BM, an all-solid-state cathode materials company; ISU Specialty Chemical, a lithium sulfide-related company; battery materials company Lotte Energy Materials; and silicon anode company Daejoo Electronic Materials. The portfolio is built around next-generation battery technology advancement and industrial structural change rather than short-term shifts in electric vehicle demand. The secondary battery sector has recently been shaking off a prolonged correction driven by slowing electric vehicle demand and securing new growth drivers. Rising ESS demand from the spread of artificial intelligence (AI) data centers is translating into improved earnings at battery companies, and investment sentiment is recovering as expectations build for commercialization of next-generation technologies such as all-solid-state batteries and silicon anodes. The fact that secondary battery-related ETFs have ranked among the top performers while the South Korean semiconductor sector's rally has stalled is seen in the same light. ESS is emerging as a key growth driver reshaping a secondary battery industry that had been centered on electric vehicles. As power demand from AI data centers grows and renewable energy generation expands, the importance of stable power supply and energy storage has increased. LG Energy Solution posted preliminary third-quarter operating profit of 756 billion won (approximately $566.2 million), topping market expectations. The company's earnings recovery is attributed to expansion of its North American ESS business and conversion of production facilities. The fact that commercialization timelines for next-generation batteries are taking concrete shape is also working in favor of investment sentiment. Samsung SDI is pursuing technology development and cooperation with customers with the goal of mass-producing all-solid-state batteries in 2027. South Korean materials companies are also moving to secure production capacity for key raw materials, and the South Korean government plans to support next-generation battery research and development worth about 400 billion won (approximately $299.6 million) over five years starting in 2027. All-solid-state batteries are expected to see their applications broaden beyond electric vehicles to humanoid robots and the aerospace sector. Kim Jung-hyun, head of Shinhan Asset Management's ETF business group, said, "The secondary battery industry is securing a new demand base through ESS, and growth drivers are diversifying as commercialization of next-generation technologies such as all-solid-state batteries and silicon anodes becomes visible." He added, "Going forward, earnings recovery through ESS and competitiveness in next-generation technologies such as all-solid-state batteries will be key factors determining corporate value."

artigo.texto: South Korea's LS Electric Signs approximately $125 Million AI Data Center Power Distribution Deal with U.S. Big Tech South Korea's LS Electric (010120) has signed a long-term supply agreement (LTA) worth approximately 169 billion won (approximately $126.8 million) with a U.S. Big Tech company for power distribution solutions for artificial intelligence (AI) data centers. As AI infrastructure expansion drives a clear shift in power equipment procurement from short-term orders to long-term volume commitments, analysts say the company has secured a bridgehead to broaden its supply range from high-voltage switchgear to high-end product lines. LS Electric said in a regulatory filing on the 19th that it had signed a $125.23 million (~169 billion won) contract to supply power distribution solutions for North American data centers. The contract runs for two years from 2027 to 2028, and the order value corresponds to volumes scheduled for delivery in 2027. The 2028 supply volume will be finalized through additional negotiations with the company. The main supply item is 38kV-class high-voltage switchgear. This equipment distributes extra-high-voltage power coming from outside at appropriate levels to each computing facility inside the data center and cuts off circuits when abnormal currents such as leakage or short circuits occur, protecting critical servers. In AI data centers where large-scale computation runs around the clock, continuity of power quality and equipment reliability determine operational success, and analysts say demand for high-reliability distribution equipment is bound to grow structurally. Global Big Tech companies have recently favored long-term supply agreements to secure stable power solutions for AI data center construction. As data center construction demand grows rapidly, the view that power equipment supply contracts themselves will be reorganized around long-term deals is gaining traction. Some skeptics argue that returns on AI infrastructure investment may be short-lived, but large-scale data center expansion continues on the judgment that AI will become fundamental infrastructure going forward. Building on this contract, LS Electric is also negotiating additional supply of data center-tailored power equipment such as low-voltage switchgear, distribution-class transformers, and RMUs (high-voltage gas-insulated load break switches). The goal is to expand its supply scope from a single high-voltage switchgear item to data center power infrastructure overall. The company is also strengthening its local North American response system. Centered on LS Electric Utah in Cedar City, Utah, and the Bastrop Campus in Texas, it has built a value chain that completes sales, design, production, and service locally, supplying products tailored to each customer's needs. The strategy is seen as aimed at reducing tariff and logistics risks while improving delivery responsiveness. An LS Electric official said, "Our world-class data center solution technology and the trust built through executing customized projects led to this long-term supply agreement," adding, "We will continue to expand supply of high-value-added products for data centers to secure a stable revenue base and maximize profitability." The deal is significant in that it is a case of North American AI data center-driven demand for power equipment translating into long-term results for a South Korean manufacturer, and could lead to expanded exports of adjacent product groups such as transformers and circuit breakers. However, since the contract value is limited to the 2027 portion and 2028 volumes remain undetermined, actual revenue recognition is expected to depend on the outcome of further negotiations and data center construction schedules.

artigo.texto: CATL's Q3 Institutional Ownership Falls 2.25 Percentage Points; Company Says 2027 Demand Still Has Upside CATL (300750.SZ) on October 21 disclosed its third-quarter 2026 financial report. As of October 20, a total of nine institutional investors had disclosed holdings of the company's A-shares, together holding 2.157 billion shares, or 46.61% of total share capital, down 2.25 percentage points from the previous quarter. At the earnings briefing the same day, management sent a relatively bullish signal on next year's market conditions, saying outright that global demand for power batteries and energy storage batteries "may not be as pessimistic as the market expects." Looking at the shareholder list, Xiamen Rueting Investment, Hong Kong Securities Clearing Company and Ningbo United Innovation New Energy Investment Management Partnership remain among the top holders. E Fund ChiNext Exchange-Traded Open-End Index Securities Investment Fund, Futaihua Industry (Shenzhen), China Life Insurance Traditional Ordinary Insurance Products and Beijing Huading New Power Equity Investment Fund were also within the disclosure scope. The more than 2 percentage point quarter-on-quarter decline in institutional ownership reflects some institutions trimming positions in the third quarter. Yet the company did not shy away from market concerns at its earnings briefing, instead proactively breaking down the structure of demand. CATL noted that some investors have recently worried about industry demand next year, but from the company's perspective, industry demand in 2027 is still worth anticipating. In China's passenger car market, although overall sales have weakened this year, the electrification rate has risen rapidly, and battery capacity per vehicle has increased markedly, keeping growth in power batteries for new energy passenger cars in positive territory. The electrification rate of new energy commercial vehicles is also accelerating. In Europe, the electrification trend is continuing, with competitive new models steadily being launched. Electrification potential in other markets may be underestimated. The energy storage business is likewise key to supporting the company's optimistic view. CATL said energy storage is maintaining solid growth both in China and outside it, with demand in some markets outside China particularly strong, providing an important buffer for overall demand. The company's conclusion is that the global power battery and energy storage battery markets still have solid growth potential, and actual market conditions may not be as weak as outsiders imagine. For investors, this disclosure presents two clues at once: on one hand, institutional ownership has declined, putting short-term pressure on the supply-demand picture for the stock; on the other, the company has offered a relatively positive framing of 2027 demand. The gap between the two will be a key focus going forward. If electrification rates and battery capacity per vehicle maintain their current pace, and demand for energy storage outside China remains strong, the shipment base of the power battery leader still has support. Conversely, if the market's conservative expectations for next year's demand prove correct, institutional trimming may continue.

artigo.texto: Li Xiang on "making cars doesn't mean making batteries": Li Auto aims to be the automaker that understands batteries best On October 19, Li Xiang, chairman and CEO of Li Auto (02015.HK), posted on social media to lay out the industry value of automakers developing core battery technology in-house. He argued that ultra-large-scale industries need "two legs advancing alternately"—one being specialized suppliers with a deep understanding of the product, the other being OEMs that delve deeply into core technologies. "The world needs both battery companies that best understand smart electric vehicles and smart EV companies that best understand batteries," Li wrote. He did not name names directly, but the remarks were widely interpreted as a response to earlier comments by Ni Jun, chief manufacturing officer of CATL (300750.SZ). In mid-to-late September, asked about automakers developing their own batteries at CATL's "Global Quality Open Month" event, Ni said: "Making cars doesn't mean making batteries. You still need professionals to do professional things." He also noted that how far a car can go and how long it lasts "is not determined by the best cell, but by the worst one." This time Li did not maintain a confrontational stance. He stressed that partner battery suppliers remain partners, and that which steps to do in-house and which to do with partners are choices made at different stages, with only one criterion—which approach is better for users. He also said Li Auto will hold an electric technology launch event on October 20 to announce its latest technological progress. This was not the first time Li has spoken publicly about the in-house development route. On September 28, he published a long post responding to discussion about "de-CATL-ization," saying zero-sum thinking is not how Li Auto defines its in-house strategy, and describing CATL as Li Auto's "comrade-in-arms." "Self-developed and self-manufactured PACK, self-developed cells with contract manufacturing" Li Auto sums up its battery approach as "self-developed and self-manufactured PACK, self-developed cells with contract manufacturing": Li Auto leads cell design and R&D, production is contracted to battery makers such as Sunwoda (300207.SZ) and CALB (03931.HK), while the battery pack, BMS and thermal management are developed and manufactured in-house by Li Auto. Capital-level ties are already in place. On September 4, Sunwoda announced that Li Auto had injected 2.65 billion yuan (approximately $396.6 million) into Sunwoda Power for an 8.79% stake; Li Auto and its affiliates hold a combined ~11.17%, making it the second-largest shareholder of Sunwoda Power. Business registration information shows that Shandong Li Auto Battery Technology Co., Ltd. was recently registered in Xuecheng District, Zaozhuang City, Shandong Province, with registered capital of 10 million yuan (approximately $1.5 million), wholly owned by Beijing Li Auto Co., Ltd., with a business scope focused on battery components and energy recovery systems. In October 2025, Li Auto had also set up a joint venture with Sunwoda Power, Shandong Li Auto Battery Co., Ltd., with registered capital of 300 million yuan (approximately $44.9 million), each holding 50%. The pace of battery deployment is accelerating in tandem. The L8, L6 and i8 already use self-developed batteries; new-generation MEGA models ordered through the Li Auto app from September 7 switch to self-developed 5C ternary lithium batteries, with deliveries expected to begin in November; the i9 launched in mid-September still uses CATL 5C batteries in its first batch; and the 2026 i6 to be launched in the fourth quarter will carry both self-developed 5C batteries and Li Auto's self-developed Mach chip, with plans to no longer offer a CATL version. Note: The above deployment plans are compiled from public reports; specific configurations are subject to Li Auto's official announcements. System integration innovation becomes the focus of competition and cooperation On cooperation models, Li Auto takes an open approach. Li Auto President Ma Donghui said in an earlier interview that as sales grow and capacity demand rises, the company very much wants to work with leading battery makers, but the prerequisite is that underlying data must be connected. He noted that OEMs do not think only from the perspective of battery components, but instead consider the battery together with all electrical components, thermal management and control systems of the vehicle, designing collaboratively from the vehicle architecture. This points to a shift in the innovation path for power batteries: as OEMs become more deeply involved in battery R&D, the industry's innovation focus may move from the performance of a single component to system integration innovation between the battery and the vehicle. For battery companies, this means the competitive dimension extends from cell metrics to data interfaces, thermal management and vehicle integration capability; for automakers, a model of parallel in-house development and contract manufacturing allows them to hold core definition rights while avoiding heavy-asset investment. In his latest post, Li reiterated that walking on two legs is not one company's choice but the entire industry's, and the progress it drives ultimately benefits users. He also warned that if the industry relies on only one leg for a long time, hopping on one foot is hard to sustain over long distances, and companies can easily fall into scale competition while the performance, quality, safety and lifespan that users truly care about stall in place. Notably, the pace of Li Auto's in-house battery push is rising in step with its supply chain bargaining power. From injecting capital into Sunwoda Power to setting up a battery technology company, and now to the gradual switch of mainstream models to self-developed cells, Li Auto is turning batteries from a purchased part into a defining component. artigo.texto: Yinwang Teams Up With CATL: Huawei Qiankun Smart-Driving Models to Plug Into 2,520 Chocolate Battery-Swap Stations On October 19, Yinwang, CATL (300750.SZ/03750.HK) and Shidai Dianfu formally signed a strategic cooperation framework agreement, announcing that partner models equipped with Huawei's Qiankun smart-driving system will gradually connect to CATL's Chocolate battery-swap network. It is the first major deal landed since Yang Jun, who heads CATL's battery-swap business, took on the additional role of co-president of CATL's marketing system, and it means Huawei has filled in the battery-swap piece of its energy-replenishment map beyond its million-plus charging piles. CATL Chairman and CEO Robin Zeng, Huawei Senior Vice President and Yinwang CEO Jin Yuzhi, and CATL marketing co-president Yang Jun all attended and witnessed the signing. The "Intelligent Energy-Replenishment Ecosystem Strategic Cooperation Agreement" signed by the three parties specifies cooperation around swap batteries and the swap network, as well as joint efforts with ecosystem partners to build an intelligent battery-swap ecosystem. Judging from the scope, this is not simply a matter of "adapting models to swap stations." Under the agreement, the three parties will link data and service ecosystems across the vehicle, the station and the cloud, using real-time battery status and users' travel patterns to enable intelligent forecasting and proactive scheduling. In terms of user experience, a vehicle can independently determine its energy-replenishment needs, find a station on its own, enter the bay autonomously, align automatically, complete a 99-second fully automated swap and then drive away — a fully intelligent closed loop. Yinwang sees the partnership as an extension of its energy-replenishment map. At the end of 2025 the company launched its "10-Minute Qiankun Smart Driving Life Circle," connecting assisted driving with high-frequency car-life scenarios such as parking payments, smart charging and smart car care. To date, convenient payments cover more than 300,000 parking lots, smart charging covers sites with 2 million charging piles, and smart car care covers more than 3,000 car-wash shops. With access to the swap network, the energy-replenishment link in this life circle will expand from "charging" to "charging and swapping combined." The scale figures on the swap side are also worth noting. As of September 29, CATL's Chocolate network had built 2,520 swap stations across 200 Chinese cities, with plans to expand to 30,000. For Qiankun, this is a ready-made energy-replenishment network that can be connected quickly; for CATL, it means the swap ecosystem has gained another heavyweight vehicle-side partner. On the pace of model rollouts, information from multiple channels shows that partner models equipped with Huawei's Qiankun smart-driving system will gradually connect to the Chocolate swap ecosystem. Yijing Auto, Huawei's earlier joint venture with Dongfeng, has already factored a swap version into the development of its new models. However, the three parties did not disclose a specific model list or launch timetable on the day of signing. It is worth noting that the battery-swap track has in recent years drawn a number of players, including Geely, NIO, Yinwang and CATL, with both competition and overlapping cooperation on station standards, battery specifications and operating models. By entering battery swapping as a smart-driving solution provider, Yinwang is in effect folding "energy replenishment" into the decision chain of intelligent driving — a car must not only know how to drive, but also judge for itself when and where to swap. Note: Swap-station figures are as of September 29; the rest reflect coverage of the "10-Minute Qiankun Smart Driving Life Circle" to date. For the industrial chain, the signal value of this cooperation outweighs any near-term orders. On one hand, the underlying interconnection between smart-driving solutions and the swap network requires deep integration of battery management systems, vehicle computing platforms and station operating systems, involving technical coordination among Huawei, CATL and automakers, so the implementation cycle will not be short. On the other hand, if the "smart driving plus battery swap" model proves out, it will offer a replicable energy-replenishment solution for other brands equipped with Qiankun and could push swap-station standards further toward concentration among leading companies. For investors, the variables that can be watched directly in the near term include the pace of Chocolate station expansion, the share of swap versions among Qiankun partner models, and whether station utilization can improve as the vehicle fleet grows. The shifting weight of CATL's swap business within the group is already visible in the arrangement under which Yang Jun, as head of the swap business, also serves as co-president of the marketing system.

artigo.texto: South Korea's Samsung Asset Management All-Solid-State Battery/ESS ETF Tops approximately $179 Million in Net Assets Four Months After Listing Samsung Asset Management's "KODEX All-Solid-State Battery ESS TOP2 Plus" exchange-traded fund (ETF) has surpassed 200 billion won (approximately $150.9 million) in net assets just four months after listing.
