artigo.texto: Is Finland’s data center boom getting out of hand? In early September, Google announced that it would invest €13 billion in Finland and build data centers in several locations. It would be the largest investment in Finnish economic history. This was big news and politicians were grateful. The Finnish economy has been depressed for years and investments are needed. By October, the atmosphere had changed and Google’s construction site stood still. It had turned out that a forest on the site had been cut down and work had started — despite the fact that Google hadn’t yet secured permission or submitted the environmental impact assessment required by law. The company had been in a huge hurry, which appears to have backfired. In Finland, the debate surrounding the construction of data centers is getting increasingly heated. It is almost impossible to keep up with how quickly data center plans are appearing all over the country. Since Google, there have been other announcements of the same magnitude involving billions upon billions of euros. In mid-October, the number of data center plans was somewhere between 150 and 200. Different sources use different figures, and there is no exact up-to-date information available. Most of them were still just plans, but construction is going on in many locations. The news headlines are listing American giants like Google, Meta and Microsoft, but there are also Finnish or international companies that have emerged, suddenly announcing their intention to invest billions in remote corners of small municipalities. Decision-making on data centers is highly decentralised in Finland. Companies approach small municipalities one by one. These are often places where decision-makers are used to people and jobs gradually disappearing into large cities. Then, suddenly, someone appears at their door promising a huge investment in the municipality and a lot of new jobs. At that point, it is very difficult to say no. Finland’s new reality As a result, the whole thing has gotten out of hand. Finland is gradually waking up to a new reality in which excavators are roaring along the country’s outlying regions, and in some cities building data centers — the owners and users of which are typically somewhere far away. What are the benefits that remain in Finland, and what are the risks? Among decision-makers and the general public, the reactions have ranged from enthusiasm to horror, not to mention confusion. The Finnish economy has been depressed for a long time, and new investments have been desperately needed. But the data center boom is so big that it’s already raising suspicions. Where does all the electricity come from? Where would all the builders come from? Will Finland be made into a sort of colony of data centers, which after completion employ only a few people and consume a large part of Finland’s electricity production and whose benefits drain abroad? Companies are drawn to Finland by the northern climate, which helps to cool the data centers. Companies are also attracted by the fact that electricity is readily available, and its production is often emission-free thanks to nuclear power, hydropower or wind power. Finns, on the other hand, are beginning to worry about whether there really is electricity available for all this, while people also want to have low electricity prices. Many of the new data center plans are in northern Finland. For example, Google’s new locations are Kajaani, Vaala and Muhos. Of these, Kajaani is a small town with an industrial tradition. Vaala is deep in the country, and Muhos is located quite close to Oulu — the largest city in the region. Key locations All of these places have one thing in common: they are close to good electricity transmission networks. In each case, there are municipalities nearby where other companies are planning data centers of the same size. Locations in Northern Finland (but mainly outside Lapland, the northernmost region of the country) have to do with the structure of the electricity transmission network. There are large trunk lines in that area that can be joined. Especially in Northern Finland, it has been noticed that “green transition” often refers to the appearance of windmills on the landscape or some other activity where one’s own area is seen only as a source of resources or raw materials. In Eastern Finland, on the other hand, there is concern that due to the structure of the electricity transmission network, new investments won’t be made in the area whose economy suffers the most from the break-up of connections with Russia anyway. Looking at the bigger picture, this debate is also related to the strategic independence of Europe. The companies and users behind the data centers are primarily in America. How does this fit into Europe’s desire to reduce its technological dependence on the U.S.? In October, Finland hurriedly began to prepare a new law which would significantly slow down the connection of data centers to the electricity network and thereby slow down their construction. As a result, the Finnish data center boom appears to have reached a temporary limit, though no one knows the outcome of all this yet. Any opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of Arctic Today. Markku Heikkilä is the Head of Science Communications at the Arctic Centre, University of Lapland, in Rovaniemi. As a former journalist at the Kaleva newspaper in Oulu, Heikkilä has followed Arctic cooperation from its early stages, and he received the State Award for Public Information for his work. He has written several books on these topics. The latest, Once We Had the Arctic – Journeys and Stories from the North, is available in English as an audiobook and e-book.

artigo.texto: “There are no more birds in the area,” Sterling, Virginia, resident Greg Pirio said at a public meeting of the Loudoun County Board of Supervisors in early July. “The sound has driven them away.” Pirio has lived in Sterling for more than a decade. Then, in 2025, Pirio and his neighbors began experiencing an “intolerable noise” stemming from the data centers that have swarmed their suburban community. Pirio said he and his neighbors, including children, suffer from headaches and sleep deprivation. Many have resorted to using mattresses and special plexiglass to keep the noise out, but this is only the beginning of the public health crisis they’re up against. “There’s a family up the street from me with four kids,” Pirio tells The Progressive. “All four children have come down with respiratory illnesses, and one had to be hospitalized.” Other residents of Pirio’s Northern Virginia suburb suffer from sinusitis and ringing in the ears as well as trouble breathing. Pirio himself says he has had to take sleeping pills to get rest amidst the noise and suffers from severely dry eyes due to the poor air quality. “I had to go to the emergency room twice in recent months,” he notes. “I have to keep my eyes lubricated all the time so I use eye drops every couple of hours along with a gel before bed.” As data centers transform the world through artificial intelligence (AI) connectivity, they are also transforming Black, brown, and working-class neighborhoods through strained infrastructure and depleted natural resources. These facilities are not hidden away in the middle of nowhere. More than half of all data centers in the United States are within a mile of a school, from Arizona and Texas to Georgia and Virginia. These data centers and the gas turbines that power them are not only looming over student playgrounds, they are also near parks, airports, office buildings, shopping malls, and even cemeteries. The epicenter of this global transformation, Northern Virginia, has been dubbed “Data Center Alley.” Three counties—Loudoun, Fairfax, and Prince William—are home to nearly 300 data centers and counting. Data centers in the region currently cover more than thirty million square feet, and more projects are proposed each year. A third of the world’s hyperscale data centers now sit in the backyard of our nation’s capital. Located near Dulles Airport, and with the greatest density of data centers on the planet, these Washington, D.C., suburbs have cashed in big time at 450,000 residents’ expense. “This issue felt distant initially,” says Bria Singleton, a Fairfax County resident who commutes into the capital five days a week for work. But the first time she heard that Northern Virginia had a data center problem, she was learning about towns like Ashburn and Sterling. “The metro line I take begins in Ashburn,” Singleton notes. Then, her Virginia town introduced a proposal to sell commercial property for a data center build-out. “As a health care consultant and Black woman, I knew what was coming and never supported data centers. There are no pros. Only cons,” she says. Now residents like her are demanding moratoriums and restitution, showing that the impacts of these centers are not tomorrow’s problem but today’s. When data centers first began popping up in the 1990s, residents were fairly out of the loop. Many of the initial data centers were no bigger than an average office building and seemed harmless enough while boasting of jobs and revenue that would benefit local residents. Data center developers often coordinate directly with local elected officials and invoke nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) in the name of “competitive interests.” By the time community members find out about a new data center, it’s because they’re seeing construction vehicles show up. After a series of tax incentives rolled out in the early 2000s, one approved data center proposal turned into two, which turned into ten, which quickly became more than 200 data centers statewide. The latest data centers are no longer mid-sized operations. They are what the industry calls “hyperscale”—meaning they are far bigger than earlier versions and create sprawling industrial parks. “In the NAACP’s People’s Report,” says Abre’ Conner, the NAACP’s director of environmental and climate justice, “we surveyed Virginians who expressed strong opposition to some existing infrastructure and new build-outs in the wake of a high concentration of data centers within the state.” Maryland’s Prince George’s County is the focus of the NAACP report, which found that residents of that county are “susceptible to air pollution from Data Center Alley located in Loudon [sic] County, Virginia” due to close proximity, cross-state wind patterns, and the sheer size of these facilities. With construction of the first beginning in 2018, the firm Vantage Data Centers built two data center campuses in the Ashburn-Sterling area. Within a few years, residents complained of incessant noise and fumes in the air. The first of the campuses was a massive fifty-two-acre compound with six data centers covering over 1.7 million square feet. The second sits on eighteen acres with three data centers, eight natural gas turbines, and fifty-one diesel generators. Gas turbines emit at least 188 different types of pollutants that increase the risk of asthma, pneumonia, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, cancer, and stroke—and they do so loudly. Pirio lives 150 yards away from the second campus. “I feel it in my throat and lungs when they run the backup generators,” he says. “This data center has been a curse on our life here,” another homeowner told a 7News reporter. Hugh Kenny/The Piedmont Environmental Council A recreational trail takes pedestrians and bicyclists past a data center in Loudoun County, Virginia. artigo.texto: Energy storage manufacturer HiTHIUM has announced that its cumulative energy storage product shipments have surpassed 200 GWh. Having begun shipments in late 2021, the company reached the 100 GWh milestone in August 2025 and added another 100 GWh in just over a year. HiTHIUM said it ranked among the world's top 2 suppliers by energy storage battery shipments in 2025 and the first half of 2026. Looking ahead, the company said it would remain focused on energy storage, with long-duration energy storage (LDES) as a strategic priority. Recall that HiTHIUM started mass production at its integrated LDES industrial park in Heze, Shandong Province, in August (see China Solar PV News Snippets). It aims to promote large-scale global deployment of its first integrated long-duration energy storage solution, featuring 1,000 Ah-class cells, and to develop integrated solutions that cover the value chain from battery cells to the grid. In its earnings forecast, Chinese inverter and energy storage equipment manufacturer Deye expects a net profit of RMB 4.22 billion to RMB 4.32 billion in the first nine months of 2026, up 79.81% to 84.07% year-over-year (YoY). Net profit excluding non-recurring items is projected to be RMB 3.95 billion to RMB 4.06 billion, up 73.33% to 78.16% YoY. The company attributed the expected earnings growth primarily to rising overseas demand for energy storage. Supported by energy security policies and tighter electricity supply-demand conditions in several countries, sales revenue from its residential and commercial and industrial (C&I) energy storage products increased significantly YoY. Deye also cited its global sales network and supply-chain cost management as contributing factors. Deye released its earnings results for H1 2026, reporting that its revenue rose over 92% during the period (see China Solar PV News Snippets). Power equipment manufacturers CEEG and SINEXCEL have jointly developed a 13,800 kVA transformer for energy storage applications. The oil-immersed, self-cooled, dual-split transformer is designed for a 40-foot high-cube containerized AC/DC integrated energy storage system (ESS), enabling a rated continuous output of 13.8 MW per container. According to CEEG, the transformer achieves 99.66% efficiency, exceeding the EU Tier 2 benchmark of 99.645%. Its design reduces overall weight by ~10% and is intended to be maintenance-free. The product series now covers single-unit power ratings from 6 MW to 13.8 MW, with grid-side voltage options of 13.8 kV, 22 kV, and 33 kV. The products target GW-scale energy storage and renewable energy projects with integrated storage. Guangdong's provincial development and reform commission and energy administration have issued pricing rules for local renewable energy consumption projects, including direct green power supply, integrated source-grid-load-storage projects, and zero-carbon industrial parks. Under the policy, annual self-consumed renewable generation must account for at least 60% of total available generation and at least 30% of total electricity consumption. The minimum share of electricity consumption supplied by self-consumed renewable generation will rise to 35% for new projects from 2030. Projects connected to the public grid must pay capacity- or demand-based transmission and distribution charges. Electricity imported from the grid will no longer incur separate system reserve charges or energy-based transmission and distribution fees. Other applicable charges, including system operation fees, government funds, and surcharges, will continue to apply under the relevant rules. China's renewable energy price settlement mechanism will not cover electricity exported by these projects. Renewable energy projects already covered by the mechanism price that switch to local consumption arrangements will be deemed to have voluntarily withdrawn from the mechanism. Guangdong recently launched a mechanism price auction for 2026 renewable energy projects, with a volume of 7.934 billion kWh for distributed PV (see China Solar PV News Snippets).

artigo.texto: Memphis fails to pass 1-year data center moratorium, instead opting for a shorter-term ban In a heated city council meeting on Tuesday, leaders in Memphis, Tennessee, voted against a moratorium that would have paused data center development for a year in the city, which has become a hotspot for the facilities driven by Elon Musk's SpaceXAI. Instead, city council members passed a substitute ordinance — which some said they received on short notice and did not have time to review — that would halt construction of data centers for 135 days. Residents and activists have pushed back against data center development in the region for years, starting with the construction of SpaceXAI's Colossus 1 data center in 2024. The company has also built two other data centers and has two under construction in Memphis and the surrounding region, including across the state border in Southaven, Mississippi. Also in Southaven, a plant powering the company's data centers is using methane gas turbines, which prompted a lawsuit from the NAACP and other organizations over alleged pollution. SpaceXAI did not reply to a request for comment. The Trump administration moved to dismiss the case, but earlier Tuesday, a Mississippi federal judge blocked that bid. Supporters of data centers argue they are needed to support the growth of artificial intelligence technology. Advocates also say they will create much-needed jobs, although experts counter many of those jobs are in the construction industry and therefore temporary. The moratorium would have paused the construction of new data centers for a year, allowing the city to adopt permanent zoning and development regulations as well as establish disclosure requirements for data center applicants. It also would have provided the opportunity to study impacts on air quality, electrical infrastructure, water protection and noise. The moratorium would not have halted existing data center operations. The language of the ordinance that was passed Tuesday states that it is intended to complement Memphis Mayor Paul Young's executive order to establish a 90-day period to study the impacts of data center development. Many attendees in the chambers appeared shocked and confused at the proposal for the new ordinance. A few members of the crowd remained in the chambers following the vote where they sang, chanted and vocalized their frustrations. The city council's move comes after a postponement of the vote earlier this month spurred protests in the chambers and resulted in an early end to an Oct. 6 meeting. Community members' opposition to data center development in Memphis is reflective of the broader attitude across America in recent months. According to a recent Pew Research Center survey, over half of Americans say they're not comfortable with a new data center operating in their area — a sentiment that's spilling over into city council meetings and town halls across the country. Ahead of the vote, KeShaun Pearson, the executive director of the Memphis Community Against Pollution, said that community members were concerned about what they feel has been a lack of transparency from local government officials and data centers' environmental impact. "It's as if the people who have been elected to protect us and to stand up to corporations and be that representative have just completely abdicated that responsibility, and left us to fend for ourselves," he said. Pearson and his brother, Tennessee Rep. Justin Pearson, were among a handful of people barred from city council meetings following the protests at city hall earlier this month. A federal judge lifted the ban and the two were present during the vote. Pearson and the group have sued the city council over the ban.

artigo.texto: Union workers line up for data center jobs Electricians travel from as far as Idaho and Virginia for a chance at Mid-South data center work MEMPHIS, Tenn. (WMC) - Hundreds of people lined up along the streets outside the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers union office in Midtown, hoping to get hired for jobs at Mid-South data centers. Workers travel from out of state The crowd included electricians from across the country, with some traveling from as far as Idaho and Virginia. They camped out for hours outside the union office. Workers said the big turnout was no surprise given the pay for the jobs. “When you got a big paying money job, you got people paying money job. It’s going to show up like this, like heavy,” said Sam, who traveled in hopes of data center work. “Well, to be honest, Elon Musk is paying the most money in the country right now with this SpaceX little job that they got down there in Southaven, you know what I’m saying. It’s a killing,” said Ray Massey, who also traveled in hopes of data center work. artigo.texto: In recent days, a Ukrainian drone strike hit Russia’s largest data center, owned by bank and technology company Sberbank. The strike came after Ukraine hit three data centers belonging to the tech giant Yandex, which is often referred to as “Russia’s Google.” After those attacks, Yandex’s traffic dropped 94%. Its users experienced heavy disruption to features such as email, search, navigation, music, ride-hailing, marketplace and financial services. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the strikes had made it “easier to breathe on many social media platforms”, by reducing Russian disinformation and bot activity. Later reports have cast doubt on Zelensky’s claim. Either way, the incident highlights the role of physical communication infrastructure in the online world. It also raises questions over what “digital sovereignty” really means, and hints at a way to fight disinformation. Data in the line of fire Data centers are an unconventional military target. However, that may be changing as their importance grows. Attacking data centers may disrupt an enemy’s military operations, as well as the ordinary civilian services that rely on these facilities. In Russia, these disruptions may slow down the economy in the long term, undermining its ability to continue the war. Ukraine’s strikes came after Russian attacks on Ukrainian data centers and internet service providers. They also follow a precedent set by Iran earlier this year when it hit data centers in the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain in response to American attacks. The Middle East data centers were run by Amazon Web Services, the world’s biggest cloud computing company with facilities around the globe. Typically, data centres use redundancy and backups to make sure losing a single facility does not have permanent negative consequences. Even so, the Iranian strikes resulted in long-term degradation of services and irrecoverable loss of some data. Russian data centres may have less in the way of international redundancy options. This is due to a particular vision of “digital sovereignty”, which Moscow has actively championed over the past decade. The idea that nations should have autonomy and control over their own digital data and infrastructure is a sound one. However, Russia’s pursuit of “sovereignty” has enabled it to censor online information and isolate Russian users from global internet services. Russia passed laws requiring certain data to be stored locally in 2015. These were followed by international sanctions after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. As a result, Russia’s options for maintaining backup infrastructure abroad have been significantly limited. Disinformation and influence Disinformation is often considered as the strategic spreading of deliberate falsehoods. Governments have often tried to fight it by removing or debunking these falsehoods on the platforms where they circulate. However, influence operations work in many different ways. Not all of them propagate falsehoods. Most of them aim to undermine public trust and delegitimise democratic processes and institutions. In Australia’s 2023 referendum on an Indigenous Voice to Parliament, for example, campaigners generated plausible competing narratives to exacerbate political polarisation. In New Zealand, influence operations have involved avalanches of misogynistic abuse to derail public support for policy initiatives. Russia is known for its orchestrated interventions in democratic politics around the world. The goal of these interventions has often been to sow dissent, distrust and dismay. Supporting candidates with pro-Russian stances can also be a goal. Civil society and activist communities have developed creative approaches to tackling this problem. These have included debunking, prebunking (preemptively countering false claims), reporting misleading content to platforms, or strategically using humor and memes. Digital sovereignty can create points of weakness The data center attacks in Russia are a reminder that Russian internet services – including influence operations – depend on physical infrastructure. Whether or not the strikes have led to a significant reduction in disinformation bot activity this time around, targeting the physical sources of disinformation may still be an effective way to contain it. There are over 100 data centers operating on Russian territory. Few of them have backups and resilience plans in place. Concentrating all digital operations in a relatively small number of physical sites creates a vulnerability. Once this infrastructure is hit, rebuilding can be slow and challenging, especially as Russia is reliant on China to supply advanced semiconductors. Lessons for democracies What does this mean for efforts to counter Russian disinformation and influence operations more broadly? One set of solutions might involve imposing physical or regulatory limits (such as sanctions) on Russian-based platforms and services such as Telegram. Other solutions would require international cooperation to undermine Russia’s capability to inflict harm in the digital environments. This may include supporting Ukraine’s efforts on the battlefront through bilateral security agreements. In any case, the recent events have shown that Russia’s digital influence extensively relies on physical infrastructures: data centers, scarce semiconductor materials and a domestic platform ecosystem that has been splintered from the world wide web. As the Kremlin continues to isolate itself in the name of sovereignty, it is also becoming more vulnerable to attacks and disruptions. Democracies can draw lessons from these events. Digital sovereignty is not achieved through isolation and vertical control over digital infrastructures. Instead, it is constantly negotiated through geographically distributed backups, frameworks for risk and governance, and strategic alliances that keep critical systems running and make them resilient to attacks. Olga Boich

artigo.texto: China continues to dominate global clean-tech manufacturing in 2026, while the United States, Europe and India are investing billions of dollars in solar panels, electric vehicle (EV) batteries, energy-storage systems and wind equipment. Major manufacturing projects by CATL, BYD, First Solar, Qcells, Toyota, Volkswagen, Reliance Industries and Tata Group demonstrate the growing competition for industrial leadership. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), the global market for key clean-energy technologies reached nearly $1.2 trillion in 2025. However, annual manufacturing investment declined from nearly $220 billion in 2023 to below $200 billion in 2024. The competition is increasingly determined by factory output, manufacturing costs, supply-chain integration, technology and exports rather than investment announcements alone. China Leads Global EV Battery and Solar Manufacturing China remains the world’s largest clean-tech manufacturing hub, supported by integrated supply chains, extensive production capacity and competitive manufacturing costs. According to the IEA Global EV Outlook 2026, China manufactured approximately 16 million electric cars in 2025, representing nearly 75 percent of global production. Chinese electric-car exports exceeded 2.5 million vehicles. China also accounted for more than 80 percent of global battery-cell production, approximately 85 percent of cathode active-material production and more than 90 percent of anode active-material production. Major Chinese clean-tech manufacturing projects CATL – Lithium-ion battery manufacturing CATL operates major battery manufacturing facilities in Ningde, Yibin and other Chinese industrial locations. Its manufacturing network supplies batteries for electric vehicles, commercial transportation and stationary energy storage. CATL’s extensive production capacity and investment in lithium iron phosphate (LFP) technology strengthen China’s position in global battery supply chains. BYD – Integrated EV and battery manufacturing BYD manufactures electric vehicles, Blade batteries, power electronics and other automotive components. Its vertically integrated operations reduce dependence on external suppliers and support manufacturing efficiency. LONGi Green Energy – Solar manufacturing LONGi produces solar wafers, cells and modules, including high-efficiency photovoltaic technologies. Its integrated manufacturing capabilities support China’s domestic solar market and international exports. JinkoSolar – Solar cells and modules JinkoSolar operates large-scale solar manufacturing facilities in China and international markets, producing photovoltaic wafers, cells and modules. China’s main challenge is overcapacity, particularly in solar manufacturing, where aggressive pricing has weakened margins despite strong global demand. United States Invests Billions in Solar and Battery Factories The United States is expanding domestic clean-tech manufacturing through investments in solar modules, battery cells and advanced energy-storage technologies. First Solar: $1.1 Billion Alabama Solar Factory First Solar invested approximately $1.1 billion in its Alabama manufacturing facility, adding 3.5 GW of annual thin-film solar module capacity. The factory, commissioned in September 2024, directly employed approximately 855 workers during 2025. First Solar’s cadmium telluride technology differentiates its products from conventional crystalline-silicon solar modules manufactured predominantly in Asia. Qcells: 8.4 GW Solar Module Manufacturing in Georgia Hanwha Qcells expanded its manufacturing operations in Georgia, with its Cartersville facility beginning solar-cell production in June 2026. The company’s integrated manufacturing programme targets 3.3 GW each of ingot, wafer and solar-cell capacity. Together, Qcells’ Cartersville and Dalton facilities have approximately 8.4 GW of annual solar-module manufacturing capacity, supporting a workforce approaching 4,000 employees. The investment is intended to strengthen domestic solar supply chains and reduce dependence on imported photovoltaic components. Toyota: $13.9 Billion North Carolina Battery Factory Toyota began production at its $13.9 billion battery manufacturing facility in Liberty, North Carolina, in 2025. The factory covers approximately 7 million square feet and is designed to accommodate 14 battery production lines. The facility will manufacture batteries for hybrid, plug-in hybrid and battery-electric vehicles, with planned employment reaching approximately 5,100. Toyota’s investment demonstrates the growing importance of localized battery production for the US automotive industry. Tesla: Battery and Energy Storage Manufacturing Tesla operates battery manufacturing facilities in Nevada and Texas, alongside Megapack energy-storage system production in Lathrop, California. These operations support electric vehicle production and utility-scale battery storage, two important segments of the US clean-tech market. Europe Expands EV Battery Manufacturing Despite Cost Challenges Europe is developing domestic battery production to reduce reliance on imported cells and strengthen its automotive manufacturing industry. However, European manufacturers face higher electricity, labor and financing costs than many Asian competitors. The IEA estimates that manufacturing efficiency accounts for more than 40 percent of the battery-cell production-cost difference between China and Europe. Volkswagen PowerCo: 40 GWh Battery Factory in Germany Volkswagen’s PowerCo commissioned battery-cell production at Salzgitter, Germany, in December 2025. The first expansion stage targets 20 GWh of annual production capacity, sufficient for approximately 250,000 electric vehicles, depending on battery size. The factory has the potential to expand to 40 GWh annually. Its manufacturing building covers approximately 69,000 square metres. PowerCo also plans to replicate its standardized battery factory design in Spai

artigo.texto: A battery system installed in a Buffalo, New York, apartment building will store excess energy when it’s plentiful and power the building when the grid is strained and electricity is costly. The manufacturer and state officials hope it will show that larger batteries can safely operate where people live and work. The 3.75 megawatt-hour lithium-ion battery system, which can power the Peace Bridge Place affordable housing complex for several days, is among the largest battery systems in a U.S. residential building, manufacturer Viridi and developer Good Carbon Co. said Tuesday. “We want our electric power to be resilient, affordable and available. Distributed battery storage accomplishes all three,” Viridi CEO Jon M. Williams said. “The only thing that has been holding up installations at scale is safety; a lot of the products on the market over the last 10 years have burned things down.” Deploying large batteries that can safely power apartment buildings is an important step toward replacing fossil fuels with renewables, experts say, but they're uncommon because of the cost and concerns about fire risks. Already, larger batteries are paired with solar and wind projects, and homeowners are using smaller batteries to store excess energy from rooftop solar and for backup power. How batteries help keep electricity flow steady Batteries help maintain a steady flow of power when sources such as solar and wind are not producing. They charge when the sun is shining or when wind is blowing. That energy can then be used when demand is high. Batteries can also store excess electricity from hydropower, and New York is one of the top hydropower-producing states. Buffalo is close to Niagara Falls, where most of the state's hydropower is produced. When electricity demand is high, Peace Bridge will use the battery. It will get paid by the utility for not drawing from the grid and for sending power back if needed. This helps lower the complex’s overall electricity costs, which benefits residents. The building can use the system during outages, too. The New York State Energy Research and Development Agency helped fund the Peace Bridge Place project, as part of its focus on including disadvantaged communities in the clean energy transition. “It goes a long way toward demonstrating the safety and viability of these types of projects,” said NYSERDA President and CEO Doreen Harris. Viridi has manufacturing facilities in Buffalo and Richmond, California, where a state grant assisted with renovations. California Energy Commission Chair David Hochschild said he's impressed with the company. More than two-thirds of California's electricity comes from clean energy and batteries get a lot of credit for that, Hochschild said. As electricity demand grows, batteries help ensure the grid is reliable, reduce pollution and contain costs, he added. “I believe the battery industry is the single most important energy industry for the next several decades,” said Hochschild, who co-founded the Electric Innovation Initiative to use electricity instead of fossil fuels more broadly throughout the U.S. economy. Viridi’s system passed a ‘near impossible' test As large battery fires have garnered attention, some communities have opposed further development. However, the failure rate for batteries has decreased as more are installed, according to the Electric Power Research Institute. Viridi spent six years and $10 million figuring out how to make a fireproof container for batteries. Half the cost was for batteries Viridi destroyed during testing. Viridi uses plates, pouches and spacing to isolate each battery cell. If one fails, the energy dissipates instead of spreading to the next battery, so that no gas, smoke, heat or fire escapes the container, Williams said. Jigar Shah, an expert in clean energy financing and deployment, said the Peace Bridge Place system is a milestone in overcoming safety concerns. To ensure nothing would catch fire when used inside a residence, Viridi's system had to pass a test where the battery was forced to fail while a cheesecloth covered the container. The cheesecloth did not char or ignite, according to the test report record. Viridi announced in April it met stringent Underwriters Laboratories safety standards so its system could be installed indoors without adding additional fire suppression to a building. Shah, who led the Department of Energy’s Loan Programs Office during the Biden administration, said Viridi is the only company to consistently pass this “near impossible” test. Shah thinks far more U.S. homes will use batteries for backup power by 2030. The U.S. can meet much more electricity demand and avoid costly upgrades to the grid if batteries are strategically deployed, he added. New York and California officials want forward-thinking energy solutions Viridi and Good Carbon Co. chose the Peace Bridge apartments because the all-electric building uses a geothermal system for heating and cooling rather than natural gas and needed additional, resilient power. The electricity demand locally can exceed the available supply, so the utility National Grid supported the endeavor, Williams added. Peace Bridge is considered affordable housing because renters earn no more than 80% of the area's median income, Good Carbon said. It said energy storage will be an important part of future multifamily housing projects. Viridi has been manufacturing in Buffalo since 2018. A medical research building in the city is using its battery system, too. Viridi's plant could build enough battery packs in a year to supply energy for about 14,000 average U.S. homes for 24 hours, Williams said. Harris, at NYSERDA, said the state needs more options like this for maintaining a reliable grid and managing costs. Gov. Kathy Hochul has made that a priority. “If we don’t need to build generation, we can utilize the grid that we have more effectively, that’s extremely valuable to us,” she said. artigo.texto: - The partnership will focus on vehicles using Huawei Qiankun solutions, aiming to deliver seamless energy replenishment for the autonomous driving era. - CATL has built 2,520 battery swap stations across 200 Chinese cities, with a long-term goal of expanding the network to 30,000 stations. Huawei's intelligent automotive business unit, Yinwang, or Newcool, has partnered with CATL (HKEX: 3750) on battery swapping, joining the battery maker's Choco ecosystem to further connect smart driving with energy replenishment services. Newcool, CATL and Contemporary Amperex Energy Service Technology (CAES) have signed a strategic cooperation framework agreement to jointly develop a smart battery swap ecosystem, according to a statement released by CATL on Monday. CAES operates CATL's battery swap business. The partnership will focus on vehicles using Huawei Qiankun intelligent automotive solutions, making them compatible with the Choco network and strengthening cooperation on swappable batteries and station networks. The 3 parties plan to integrate data and services across vehicles, swap stations and the cloud, using real-time battery status and users' travel patterns to anticipate energy needs and proactively schedule battery swaps. Under the proposed system, vehicles would independently determine when they need energy, locate and enter a station, align themselves for a fully automated 99-second battery swap, and drive away afterward. The partnership aims to extend assisted driving capabilities to battery swapping, creating a "seamless energy replenishment experience" for the autonomous driving era. However, the announcement did not identify specific vehicle models, a service launch date or initial coverage areas. This is similar to functionality Nio Inc (NYSE: NIO) already offers at some battery swap stations, where vehicles can automatically enter a station and complete a battery swap while using navigation-assisted driving. CATL chairman and CEO Robin Zeng, Huawei senior vice president and Newcool CEO Jin Yuzhi, and Yang Jun, co-president of CATL's marketing system, attended and witnessed the signing. For CATL, Newcool's participation provides a new avenue to expand vehicle partnerships for the Choco network as its station footprint extends from cities to highways. As of September 29, CATL had built 2,520 battery swap stations across 200 Chinese cities, according to the statement. Its long-term goal is to expand the network to 30,000 stations. Previously announced plans also call for building 1,000 highway battery swap stations in 2026 and 2027, creating a nationwide network spanning 11 north-south and 9 east-west highway corridors. Newcool grew out of Huawei's intelligent automotive solution business Unit, known as the car BU. It was formally established as a separate company in January 2024, initially wholly owned by Huawei. Huawei currently holds an 80% stake in Newcool, while Seres (HKEX: 9927) and Avatr, the EV unit of Changan Automobile (SZSE: 000625), each hold 10%. In April this year, Anhui Jianghuai Automobile Group Corp (JAC) announced plans to invest in Newcool without disclosing the proposed investment amount. Completion of the transaction has yet to be announced.

We asked the billionaire biotech businessman and former presidential candidate about his plans for public education, taxes, job creation, data centers and more, along with his views on his would-be status as the country’s third richest elected official, according to Forbes. This outlet extended a similar invitation to the Democratic gubernatorial nominee Amy Acton, the state’s former health director whom Ramaswamy has roundly criticized for what he sees as shirking opportunities to present her vision for Ohio or debate her ideas. Acton’s campaign agreed this week to schedule an interview with this news outlet; a story will follow. Public education Ramaswamy, who attended Ohio public schools before attending a private Cincinnati-area high school, has campaigned on the premise that Ohio should do more to reward its best teachers. By some measures, (it’s) $38,000 a year for entry-level first-year teacher salary. I don’t think that’s enough to attract the best of the next generation into the profession,” he said. When asked about how much he’d like to raise teachers’ starting salary, Ramaswamy said his administration would look into it. He said, “I think it’s got to be something that’s relatively meaningful to make this a more compelling profession for young people to want to go into.” Ramaswamy added that he believes too much of public school funding goes toward aspects of the education system outside of the classroom, and said he wants to prioritize in-classroom instruction. He went on to say that he believes teachers are “heroes, not magicians,” and said he believes that parents should be asked to take more accountability for their children’s education. “If the kid doesn’t show up at school and they’re chronically absent, there has to be some matter of accountability for the parent,” he said. “I think our public schools can also do a better job of setting standards and expectations for the family and for the parent, which I think will make it easier to set up our teachers for success in the classroom.” This outlet asked Ramaswamy about his stance on teacher unions, which he said he wanted to eliminate throughout his 2024 presidential campaign. He responded: “I’ve never, in this particular race, I’ve not proposed any of those changes, but what I do intend to look at is on a holistic basis, how are we going to improve education?” His wealth Forbes recently reported that, if elected, Ramaswamy would become the third richest public official in the country. His current net worth of $2.3 billion has more than doubled since March 2025, and it ranks only behind President Donald Trump and Illinois Gov. J.B. Pritzker among current elected officials. This fact has been used against Ramaswamy on the campaign trail, with Acton quick to say his status makes him inherently disconnected from the average Ohioan. When this outlet asked him if he was sympathetic about a voter being uncomfortable voting for a billionaire, here’s what Ramaswamy said: “I think what I am deeply sympathetic to is that families are struggling to get ahead and costs have risen faster than wages, and families are struggling to make ends meet when, in fact, they should be doing more than make ends meet, they should be getting ahead.” He said he had that experience growing up in what he described as a middle class family. “Having had that upbringing, I have seen the full arc of the American dream,” Ramaswamy said. “That’s the place I come from to say, the more we celebrate success and upward economic mobility, the more of it we will get. artigo.texto: BEIJING, Oct. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- CATL today unveiled the innovative dual-electric range extension battery and the latest generation of heavy-duty battery-swapping solution to accelerate the electrification of road freight transportation. Competition in electric heavy-duty trucking is moving beyond technical specifications toward full-lifecycle value. While battery swapping has made energy replenishment faster and more predictable, concerns about battery utilization, operating costs and residual vehicle value continue to affect fleet economics. To address these challenges, CATL combines its dual-electric range extension battery with QIJI's strategy of standardization, new infrastructure and a full commercial ecosystem, bringing battery swapping and industry-wide collaboration together to accelerate heavy-duty truck electrification. A Dual-Electric Approach to Range Extension CATL's dual-electric range extension battery combines two independent yet complementary battery systems. The main battery uses QIJI's standardized chassis-mounted swappable battery to maximize efficiency. A behind-the-cab range-extension power system, currently equipped with a 77kWh battery capable of 3C charging, provides backup power. Together, the systems maintain uninterrupted power delivery and provide redundancy for demanding operating conditions. - Dual-System Power Redundancy In conventional battery-swapping trucks, drivers often return for a swap with unused capacity because they are reluctant to run the battery low. Backup power from the range-extension battery increases the main battery's depth of discharge (DOD) from approximately 70% to over 95%, allowing it to be returned at less than 5% state of charge (SOC). At this threshold, CATL's seamless switching technology transfers power delivery to the range-extension battery within milliseconds, maintaining a continuous and stable power supply. - "1+X" Architecture and Independent Upgrades The system uses a "1+X" architecture. One standardized main battery maintains compatibility with the QIJI battery-swapping network, while the range-extension battery can be customized for specific conditions with options including ultra-high energy density, low-temperature resistance for cold climates, or ultra-high power. The two battery systems can be developed and upgraded independently to meet their respective technical and operational requirements. - Flexible Leasing and Battery Asset Management The independently owned on-board range-extension battery stays with the vehicle as an asset throughout its service life, reducing reliance on immediate access to a swapping station. The main battery can be leased according to seasonal freight demand, helping fleets reduce rental costs during quieter periods and manage battery assets more flexibly. This architecture combines the benefits of standardization with flexible vehicle configurations, making electric heavy-duty trucks more practical and economically viable across a wider range of applications. QIJI Builds a Shared Battery Swapping Ecosystem QIJI complements these improvements with a three-pillar strategy of standardization, new infrastructure and a full commercial ecosystem. It seeks to speed heavy-duty truck electrification with a value-chain ecosystem co-created by all stakeholders, where benefits are shared collectively. - Standardization Supports Wider Adoption To accommodate a wider range of truck models and operating conditions, QIJI has introduced the 260# (432 kWh) and 300# (513 kWh) standardized battery-swapping blocks alongside the existing 75# block. The system enables battery swaps in just five minutes, with a 99.99% first-time success rate, helping fleets minimize downtime and maintain operational efficiency. QIJI has also pioneered a battery-as-a-service (BaaS) model in which customers pay for the net energy charged rather than the energy discharged. This allows customers to retain the value of energy recovered through regenerative braking, reducing per-kWh battery rental costs for users on basic plans by up to 20%. Flexible battery leasing options allow customers to tailor rental periods to their needs, from second-hand vehicle transitions to seasonal demand. This will minimize idle costs and offer more flexible options for off-season downtime, further helping fleets manage operating costs. - New Infrastructure Improves Resource Efficiency QIJI aims to make better use of four critical resources in long-haul freight: time, land, payload capacity and grid electricity. Rapid battery swapping reduces waiting times, while efficient station layouts serve more vehicles within the same footprint. Battery capacity is matched to transport needs, and centralized, coordinated charging makes better use of grid electricity. These measures aim to improve both resource efficiency and operational returns. CATL plans to deploy 900 battery-swapping stations by the end of 2026 and 2,000 by 2027, with a long-term target of 10,000 stations nationwide in collaboration with its partners. By connecting major freight corridors through a coordinated swapping network, QIJI aims to improve the efficiency and commercial viability of electric heavy-duty trucking. - A Commercial Ecosystem Supports the Full Vehicle Lifecycle QIJI connects truck manufacturers, financial institutions, insurers, channel partners and aftermarket service providers across the vehicle lifecycle, from purchase and operation to maintenance and resale, working together to build a comprehensive ecosystem of integrated products and services. QIJI has introduced two partnership models: Battery Asset Service Partners and Energy Replenishment Service Partners. These models allow partners to participate in battery asset services and energy replenishment, extending their role beyond one-off vehicle sales to ongoing operations. artigo.texto: The debate over data centers in Mason County has taken on a new wrinkle thanks to a report last week estimating the county’s schools could bring in $90 million a year — but only if residents renew a levy on the ballot in two weeks. That estimate — part of a report put out last week by Treasurer Larry Pack’s office — is based on projected property tax revenue from two new controversial data centers, the Monarch Compute Campus, currently under construction, and the proposed Project Tamarack data center. Last year, Mason County Schools brought in $10 million from the excess levy, according to data from the state Tax Division, meaning that the schools would get a 9-fold jump in levy revenue if the estimates are correct. However, Mason County Schools will only get the money if voters approve a renewal of the school excess levy on Nov. 3. Pack and some county officials are worried that may not happen. “We were hearing people say that Mason County is going to get all this tax money from the data center, so they don't need to pass this excess levy,” said Pack. “That’s not how the bill works, and that's not the impact.” Pack said he believes opposition stems from a misunderstanding about how the data centers are taxed. Under House Bill 2014, the controversial 2025 law that established state-wide regulations for high impact data centers, county boards of education do not immediately get access to data center property tax revenue. The money is contingent on voters passing the levy renewal. “If a county school board has no excess levy, they get zero money from the construction and operation of data centers in their county,” Pack said. Mason County officials have been trying to get the message out: The vote isn’t for or against the two data centers, which will stay either way. But if the levy fails, the data centers will, in effect, get a $90 million tax break and Mason County Schools will lose out on the extra tax revenue. “We’re talking not only academics, but band trips, athletic trips on busses. We're talking about helping out the extracurricular activities in the county as well as the academics,” said Rick Handley, president of the Mason County Commission. He said he supports the levy and is encouraging others to vote for it as well. Elaine Matheny is an advocate with Mason United, a group that has been fighting against the two data center developments. While she plans to vote for the levy, she said it hasn’t changed her opposition to the projects, and she’s skeptical about promises of how much money they will bring in. “Look at all the other extract industries that we've had in this state,” she said. “Look at the promises for the lottery and all the funds that were going to take care of the school system. Has that happened? No. We still have lots of problems funding our schools.” The levy question comes as Mason County — and West Virginia more broadly — debates how to handle the data center development. Proponents, including Gov. Patrick Morrisey and many Republicans in the Legislature, have argued that data centers will be an important economic boon for the state that will bring in money and growth. Opponents, however, have raised concerns about issues like water usage and pollution from the power plants needed to generate the enormous amounts of electricity the data centers require. Residents also worry about rising electricity prices and noise pollution created by the thousands of servers these centers house. In the background of it all is HB 2014. The law prevents local county zoning officials from blocking data center development and allows the developers to keep information about their projects from the public. It also spells out how the tax revenue from data centers will be split, with the state getting 50% while the local county keeps 30%. Regardless of how the vote shakes out, Pack expects lawmakers to reevaluate the law next year, especially when it comes to how revenue is split. “I do think that generally local folks know better how to spend the money than Charleston does,” he said. “So I think we'll have a spirited discussion about these allocations next session.” Election Day is Nov. 3. O portfólio abrange quatro vertentes de tecnologia de baterias — chumbo-ácido, íons-lítio, íons-sódio e estado sólido — para aplicações que incluem veículos elétricos de duas e três rodas, veículos de baixa velocidade, força motriz industrial e armazenamento de energia para residências, data centers voltados a IA, usuários comerciais e industriais, além de projetos em escala de concessionária. Parceiros da Argélia, Indonésia, Nigéria, Camboja e Brasil participaram de uma mesa redonda sobre produção local, eletrificação de veículos de duas rodas, armazenamento de energia e transformação da distribuição, concordando que as raízes locais e a sinergia do ecossistema são essenciais. artigo.texto: Schneider Electric’s third quarter organic revenue jumped 17% to €11.5 billion euros ($12.9 billion US) — a record high for any quarter — the French multinational energy technology company said in an Oct. 16 earnings release. The company’s business associated with data centers “continues to be exceptionally strong with another quarter of triple digit demand growth in Q3, further improving our visibility into 2027 and 2028,” said Schneider’s CFO, Nathan Fast, during an earnings call. Schneider Electric has seen triple digit demand growth in orders associated with data centers for “three out of the last four quarters,” Fast said during the call. Morgan Stanley analyst Max Yates asked how much exposure the company has to neocloud businesses like CoreWeave. Fast said, “We do not break down exactly the impact or the split of hyperscaler, colo, neocloud, et cetera.” Schneider CEO Olivier Blum added, “We are extremely careful to select those companies that will be there in the long term.” Schneider Electric’s Energy Management segment made its most revenue in North America in the third quarter, but saw a higher organic growth rate of 32.4% in China and East Asia, compared to 20.3% That continues a trend in 2026, where North America led overall revenue volume but Asia saw a higher organic revenue growth rate. The sales growth in China was “led by everything to do with investment in AI infrastructure, driving growth in the data center and [semiconductor] segments, in particular,” said Fast during the call. “In our geographic trends, we add China alongside the U.S. and India in the countries we expect to drive growth. This is based on the strength of what we have seen over the recent quarters and which we believe is set to continue.” North American demand continues to grow, driven by momentum in data centers, “where we saw sustained high demand for prefabricated solutions and cooling,” Fast said. Blum said the company has also been bolstered in the European market by the “massive acceleration” of electric car adoption, as well as heat pumps. “We see very fast growth,” Blum said. “This fast growth is not only the growth of the EV charger, but every time you install an EV charger, you have to extend your electrical panel, so that creates a great opportunity, great synergy in a place where, for instance, in Europe, we have a very strong market share.”

artigo.texto: Vietnam Eyes Battery Storage to Unlock Rooftop Solar Potential Industry groups and policymakers identify energy storage infrastructure as critical bottleneck for distributed generation expansion across residential and commercial buildings. - ·Vietnam's rooftop solar expansion depends on battery storage deployment to address grid integration limits and intermittency challenges affecting distributed generation. - ·The Ministry of Industry and Trade is developing regulatory frameworks including time-of-use tariffs and capacity payments to incentivise storage systems alongside photovoltaic installations. - ·Lithium-ion battery costs fell 14 per cent globally in 2025 to USD 139 per kilowatt-hour, improving project economics for solar-plus-storage systems in Vietnam's industrial zones. Storage Gap Slows Distributed Generation Vietnam's rooftop solar sector faces a structural constraint that battery storage systems could resolve, according to industry stakeholders and government officials assessing the country's renewable energy transition. The Southeast Asian nation installed significant rooftop photovoltaic capacity during earlier subsidy programmes, but grid integration limits and the absence of storage infrastructure now restrict further expansion. Electricity demand in Vietnam grew 9.8 per cent year-on-year in the first eight months of 2025, driven by manufacturing export growth and rising household consumption. Rooftop solar offers a distributed generation pathway that reduces transmission losses and defers grid upgrade costs, yet the technology's intermittent output creates operational challenges for state utility Electricity of Vietnam without accompanying storage. Battery systems allow building owners to capture midday generation peaks and discharge during evening demand surges, smoothing supply curves and reducing strain on distribution networks. The technology also enables self-consumption models that improve project economics for commercial and industrial users facing higher tariff structures. Policy Framework Under Development Vietnam's Ministry of Industry and Trade is evaluating regulatory mechanisms to incentivise storage deployment alongside rooftop solar installations. Current feed-in tariff structures do not differentiate between solar-plus-storage projects and standalone photovoltaic systems, removing financial incentives for developers to add batteries despite grid benefits. Policymakers are examining time-of-use tariffs and capacity payment schemes that would reward storage operators for providing grid services. Such frameworks exist in Thailand and the Philippines, where battery systems participate in frequency regulation and peak shaving programmes. The ministry has not announced a timeline for new regulations, though industry participants expect pilot programmes to launch in major industrial zones during 2027. Manufacturing hubs in the southern provinces of Binh Duong and Dong Nai present logical test cases, given high daytime electricity consumption and existing rooftop solar penetration. Cost Trajectory Improves Economics Lithium-ion battery prices declined 14 per cent globally in 2025, reaching USD 139 per kilowatt-hour at the pack level. Analysts project further reductions as Chinese manufacturers expand production capacity and new chemistries enter commercial deployment. Vietnam imports most battery storage components, primarily from China and South Korea, with domestic assembly limited to a handful of renewable energy firms. Lower equipment costs improve payback periods for solar-plus-storage projects, though financing remains constrained for small and medium enterprises without access to green credit facilities. State-owned commercial banks have increased lending for renewable energy projects under central bank directives, yet loan terms typically require collateral exceeding project asset values. Development banks and multilateral lenders are exploring guarantee mechanisms to reduce perceived risks for rooftop solar storage investments. Grid Modernisation Parallel Track Energy storage deployment must proceed alongside broader grid infrastructure upgrades if Vietnam is to meet its 2030 renewable energy targets. The national power development plan calls for 47,000 megawatts of solar capacity by the end of the decade, with rooftop systems expected to contribute approximately one-third of that total. Transmission congestion in southern provinces already curtails utility-scale solar output during low-demand periods, a problem that distributed generation with storage could partially alleviate. However, distribution network operators lack real-time monitoring systems and advanced inverter controls necessary to manage high penetrations of behind-the-meter generation. International donors have committed funding for smart meter rollouts and grid management software, though implementation timelines extend beyond 2028 in most provinces. The sequencing challenge requires storage incentives to align with grid readiness, avoiding stranded assets or curtailment that undermines project viability. Vietnam's rooftop solar trajectory will depend on how quickly storage costs fall and whether policy frameworks create sufficient returns for combined systems. The country's manufacturing sector offers substantial demand for daytime generation paired with evening storage discharge, positioning industrial rooftops as the most viable near-term market segment.

artigo.texto: Invinity Energy Systems (LSE:IES) has announced plans to raise at least £20 million through a combination of institutional investment and a retail share offer, with proceeds intended to support product development, manufacturing expansion and working capital requirements. The vanadium flow battery manufacturer is proposing a fundraising at 10 pence per share, comprising a cornerstone subscription from the National Wealth Fund, an institutional placing and a separate offer to retail investors. The National Wealth Fund, an existing major shareholder, has committed to invest at least £10 million, with the potential to increase its participation to £12.5 million. The fund may also match retail investor subscriptions on a pound-for-pound basis, subject to the proposed arrangements. The total fundraising is capped at £25 million. Invinity intends to allocate approximately £10 million of the proceeds to accelerate product development and reduce manufacturing costs. A further £8 million is earmarked for working capital, while £2 million is expected to support additional manufacturing capacity in the UK and US. The planned investment forms part of the company's efforts to increase production efficiency and support the delivery of its existing commercial commitments. Management said the fundraising would strengthen Invinity's ability to execute its revenue plans for 2026 and 2027, which it considers well supported by existing commercial activity. The company also reported a commercial pipeline exceeding 12.5 gigawatt-hours (GWh), although this figure represents potential business opportunities rather than confirmed revenue. Invinity is working towards introducing an investment-grade insurance arrangement intended to improve the financial acceptability of its battery systems for prospective project customers and financing partners. The company is also progressing projects including FlexBase's Technology Centre Laufenburg, while implementing measures to reduce corporate overheads. Invinity develops and manufactures vanadium flow batteries designed for long-duration energy storage applications, including electricity grid infrastructure and renewable energy integration. For investors, the proposed fundraising represents a significant financing development, providing additional capital for operations and expansion if completed. However, the issuance of new shares at 10 pence would increase the company's share count and dilute the percentage ownership of existing shareholders who do not participate.

artigo.texto: Overview: - Van Buren Township Planning Commission approved final site plans for Google's 1-gigawatt data center and accompanying utility substation on 282 acres north of I-94. - The facility will use 2-3.6 million gallons of water daily and employ 50-200 people. - Read details on the projected noise, water usage, and power demands from the hyperscale data center. The site plans for a 1-gigawatt Google data center and an accompanying electrical substation received final approval last week from the Van Buren Township Planning Commission. 🗳️ Civic Action Toolbox — see how you can get involved Why it matters The Van Buren Township data center could affect nearby residents' quality of life through noise, dust, and climate impacts. Who's making public decisions The Van Buren Township Planning Commission granted the site plan approval. The Michigan Public Service Commission oversees DTE's contracts and proposed gas plants, and EGLE regulates wetland and stream impacts. Upcoming Meetings Contact Your Representatives Civic Actions: What You Can Do What to watch for next Watch whether Van Buren Township adopts stricter data center zoning rules, and how regulators rule on DTE's proposed natural gas plants in Milan and Handy townships ahead of the planned December 2027 startup. Are you taking action? Let us know. Powered by Civic Action Toolbox Residents have said the “Project Cannoli” data center proposed by developer Panattoni could bring noise to the nearby Haggerty subdivision, harm water resources, and impact energy reliability and affordability. Project backers say it represents a boon for jobs and investment that will bring significant tax dollars to the area. The commission is compelled to approve the project because it’s a principal permitted use under the township’s zoning rules, Van Buren Township Planning Commissioner Jeffrey Jahr said Wednesday, Oct. 14. “I feel that the applicant has met all of the objective specific requirements for us to grant the request,” he said. Saline Township, in neighboring Washtenaw County, was sued by a data center developer that alleged exclusionary zoning in September 2025 after the township board denied the rezoning needed for Oracle and OpenAI’s 1.4 GW data center. Whether Van Buren Township places more restrictions on data centers will need to be evaluated, Jahr said, adding that he is leaning toward doing so. Residents say they’re already dealing with noise, dust Township residents said Wednesday they are already dealing with noise and dust from the project. Several people played recorded dump truck noise on their phones. Over 2,700 people have signed an online petition opposing the data center. Van Buren Township resident Tracy Osborne, who lives next to the data center site, said he’s concerned about the impact constant data center noise could have on his daughter with special needs. “My concern is not simply whether this facility meets a number on a noise report,” he said. “It is whether neighboring families will be able to enjoy their homes without continuous disruptive equipment noise.” A Panattoni spokesperson told Planet Detroit in a statement that the company takes resident concerns seriously, including noise and dust, and is committed to minimizing impacts. Multiple parties are working in the area, including utility providers, and not all work is associated with the project, the spokesperson said. Representatives for Panattoni said Wednesday that the I-94 Service Drive will be used for site access during construction — not Haggerty Road — to minimize resident impacts. Here’s how the data center could impact residents. How big will the project be? The project is set to occupy 282 acres north of I-94, east of Haggerty Road, west of Hannan Road, and south of Wayne County Community College. The project will permanently impact 13.55 acres of wetlands, require six culverts in regulated streams, and fill and abandon 573 linear feet of a stream, John Jones, an environmental quality analyst with Michigan’s Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy (EGLE), said in June. Developers will offset wetland and stream impacts by purchasing wetland mitigation bank credits in the Huron River watershed and creating 1,174 feet of new stream channel on the property itself, Jones said. Forty-five percent of the acreage at the site will remain undeveloped under a conservation easement, Josh Capps, Panattoni’s director of data center delivery, said Wednesday. The data center will use roughly 1 GW of electricity, according to the township’s frequently asked questions document. One gigawatt is roughly equivalent to the power used by 800,000 homes. What are the economic impacts? The project represents a “generational investment from one of the best companies in the world,” Adam Kramer, president of data centers for Panattoni, said Wednesday. The data center will require 9.8 million labor hours for its construction and employ 50-200 employees on site, he said. Developers have already awarded $2 billion in contracts to Wayne County businesses, he said. The data center is projected to be the largest taxpayer in Van Buren Township and one of the top five taxpayers in Wayne County, Kramer said in February. How much noise will the project produce? Modeling shows the data center will comply with Van Buren Township’s noise limit of 67 dBA, Paul Kammer, an engineer with the consulting firm Fishbeck, said Wednesday. dBA is a weighted decibel scale for judging loudness, with 67 falling between the volume of a normal conversation and a vacuum cleaner, according to a Yale University decibel chart. Panattoni’s Capps said sound from the facility would largely fall below the area’s ambient nighttime noise. The loudest noise will be to the south and east of the facility, with anticipated dBA readings of 62.1 and 59.7, respectively, he said. artigo.texto: Leilão de baterias Aneel: transmissoras podem ficar de fora A área técnica da Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) defende que a participação de transmissoras nos leilões de baterias depende da reversão de parte da receita da atividade para reduzir as tarifas. O entendimento consta de Ofício Conjunto enviado à diretoria da agência. A medida, se confirmada, pode impactar diretamente a competitividade das empresas do setor elétrico. Reversão de receitas para modicidade tarifária O ofício conjunto vincula a participação das empresas à destinação de parte ou total da receita dos projetos à redução das tarifas de transmissão. O documento cita: “Além disso, mantém-se a necessidade do benefício à modicidade tarifária, mediante reversão total ou parcial das receitas auferidas com a atividade da SPE para a concessão, em favor dos usuários do SIN [Sistema Interligado Nacional]”. Ainda segundo o ofício, os contratos firmados exigem autorização prévia para atividades estranhas ao objeto da concessão e estabelecem que parte ou toda a receita desses negócios contribua para a modicidade das tarifas de transmissão. No entanto, o ofício não define percentual, base de cálculo ou metodologia para a reversão. O texto usa a expressão “receitas auferidas com a atividade da SPE”, sem individualizar a receita fixa do CRCap (Contrato de Reserva de Capacidade para Potência). Essa lacuna gera insegurança jurídica para as transmissoras interessadas no leilão. Manifestação técnica, não deliberação da diretoria Vale destacar que a manifestação é das áreas técnicas; o documento não registra uma deliberação da diretoria colegiada da agência sobre os editais ou sobre a legitimidade dessa captura. Ou seja, o posicionamento ainda pode ser revisto ou ajustado pela instância superior da Aneel. A diretoria colegiada é responsável pelas decisões finais sobre regras de leilões e regulação do setor elétrico. Fontes ouvidas pela reportagem dizem que se o entendimento for mantido, as empresas transmissoras podem ficar de fora do leilão por perda de concorrência e desequilíbrio dos investimentos. A incerteza regulatória pode afastar players importantes e reduzir a competitividade do certame, com reflexos no preço final da energia para consumidores e empresas. Taesa contesta reversão da receita fixa “A Receita Fixa do CRCap não se sujeita a reversão à modicidade tarifária da transmissão”, sustenta a Taesa em um dos tópicos da contribuição enviada à Aneel. A transmissora argumenta que a receita fixa do contrato de reserva de capacidade tem natureza distinta e não deveria ser capturada para reduzir tarifas de transmissão. A empresa defende que a reversão comprometeria a viabilidade econômica dos projetos de armazenamento. Como os certames selecionam propostas de menor receita fixa, uma subsidiária de transmissora sujeita à reversão precisaria incorporar esse custo ao lance ou aceitar remuneração líquida inferior à de concorrentes com as mesmas obrigações contratuais. Isso criaria uma desvantagem competitiva clara para as transmissoras, que poderiam optar por não participar do leilão. Impacto no setor elétrico e na economia O leilão de baterias é visto como estratégico para ampliar a flexibilidade do sistema elétrico e integrar fontes renováveis intermitentes. A eventual exclusão das transmissoras pode reduzir o número de proponentes e elevar os custos dos projetos vencedores. Para o comércio e a indústria do interior paulista, como Araçatuba e região, tarifas de energia mais altas pressionam os custos operacionais e a competitividade das empresas locais. A definição sobre a reversão de receitas deve ocorrer antes da publicação do edital definitivo do leilão. Empresários e associações setoriais acompanham o tema de perto, pois a energia elétrica é um insumo essencial para a produção e os serviços. A fonte não detalhou se haverá nova rodada de contribuições ou audiência pública sobre o assunto. Perguntas Frequentes O que a área técnica da Aneel defende sobre a participação de transmissoras no leilão de baterias? A área técnica da Aneel defende que a participação de transmissoras nos leilões de baterias depende da reversão de parte da receita da atividade para reduzir as tarifas, conforme consta em Ofício Conjunto. Como a reversão de receitas das transmissoras no leilão de baterias afetaria a competitividade? Como os certames selecionam propostas de menor receita fixa, uma subsidiária de transmissora sujeita à reversão precisaria incorporar esse custo ao lance ou aceitar remuneração líquida inferior à de concorrentes, podendo ficar de fora do leilão por perda de concorrência e desequilíbrio dos investimentos. A Receita Fixa do CRCap está sujeita à reversão para modicidade tarifária da transmissão, segundo a Taesa? Não, a Taesa sustenta que ‘A Receita Fixa do CRCap não se sujeita a reversão à modicidade tarifária da transmissão’, conforme um dos tópicos de sua contribuição.
