artigo.texto: It was as if Connie Lane were standing on the precipice of the Grand Canyon, she said, staring in disbelief at its enormity. The hyperscale data center near Milwaukee, where Lane had been visiting with friends from law school for a June reunion, left her incredulous. “I can’t begin to describe the scope. They brought in these huge lines to feed them electricity. I was stunned. It’s one thing when you read about it; it’s another thing to see it,” she said. Lane, a Democratic state representative, is running for reelection in Merrimack District 13, or Concord’s Ward 2. In her response to the Monitor’s general election survey, she cited energy policy and the feared effect of data centers on the power grid and ratepayers as one of the most salient issues facing the state of New Hampshire. There are currently ten data centers in New Hampshire, four of which are clustered in Manchester, according to the tracking platform Data Center Map. Proposals in Bow and Nottingham have spurred public outcry that, in the latter case, prompted the developer to withdraw his plan just hours before the town’s planning board was scheduled to review it. That opposition is hardly exclusive to the Granite State. Data centers have unified Democrats and Republicans, progressives and conservatives, in forceful resistance as local disputes over land use, municipal transparency, tax incentives and environmental impacts repeat themselves nationwide. “They’re going to come in, electricity is going to soar, and are we really ready for this vast use of our land? Is this the way we really want to develop acres and acres and acres?” Lane said. Earlier this year in New Hampshire, a group of Republican lawmakers inverted an effort to affirm municipalities’ ability to regulate data centers, amending the language of the bill, Senate Bill 439, to do the opposite: allow data centers by right in areas zoned for commercial or industrial development. The bill was ultimately tabled and didn’t advance further. Gov. Kelly Ayotte, a Republican, told WMUR at the time that she opposed those alterations to the bill. In the months since, she’s stated she will impose a moratorium on new data center developments with the upcoming state budget, citing concern that, at an average energy consumption of 100 megawatts, even one hyperscale development could overburden the regional grid. “I’ve been clear that I oppose siting data centers in New Hampshire, including the proposed projects in Nottingham and Bow. Data centers would drive up our already too-high energy costs, and I share the concerns raised about their impact on our water and environment,” she said in a statement to the Monitor. Her gubernatorial challenger, Democrat Cinde Warmington, said she doubts the governor’s intentions based on her perceived lack of leadership on data center-related bills, like SB 439, and that she would like to see the state act more expediently. If elected, Warmington said she would impose a temporary moratorium on the permitting of new data centers on “day-one.” Her campaign’s “data center bill of rights” outlines some of the safeguards she’d push for in a regulatory framework: limits on noise pollution, requirements that construction draw on local labor through protected agreements and protections for clean air and water. “I think it is really hypocritical that Gov. Ayotte now suddenly is calling for a moratorium,” Warmington told the Monitor. “Now she says she’s for a moratorium in her budget next year — by next year we could have a massive data center in our state. We know there’s one proposed in Bow. So too little, too late, and pretty disingenuous.” Imagining how the legislature might devise more permanent regulations on data centers, Lane told the Monitor the state “would certainly want to do a lot of study” to inform the drafting process, but that “personally, I don’t want them at all.” The hyperscale data centers recently proposed in New Hampshire provide a window into the rabid acceleration of development to keep pace with artificial intelligence’s demand for computing power, and the imposing dimension of data centers being built in other parts of the country. One colossal data center development, imagined by technology company Fermi America for the Texas Panhandle and dubbed “Project Matador”, is expected to have a capacity of 17 gigawatts. The development’s first power-generating equipment, three 480,000-pound gas turbines, arrived on site near Amarillo last month, according to local reporting. By comparison, the proposal that public filings indicate is in the very early, exploratory stages of being permitted for development in Bow could draw between 200 and 350 megawatts of power — two percent of that capacity. William Lynch, the Democratic candidate for Merrimack District 10, which includes Hooksett and Dunbarton, said he worries not only about the unmistakable environmental consequences of such large developments but the possibility that, if the AI bubble bursts, today’s enormous investments will produce warehouses full of data storage no one uses tomorrow. “I’ve seen commitments to build out data centers that progress as far as building. But some data centers are not keeping pace with their commitments, and I’m concerned that it might come to a point, in two or three years, where the overall investment and use of the computing power won’t keep up,” he said. Lynch had an eight-year career with tech giant Oracle, a major cloud and AI data center operator. He described his work — first as a cloud applications engineer, then pivoting to health applications — as building the software infrastructure on top of which other software engineers iterate. His software could be adapted for use on websites like Facebook or the New York Times, or it could be deployed into traditional data centers. artigo.texto: Microsoft desiste de acordo para data center no Reino Unido em momento crucial para planos de IPO da Nscale Segundo o jornal The Telegraph, não foram apresentados os motivos para que a gigante americana abandonasse o acorfo referente ao empreendimento em Loughton, no condado de Essex A Microsoft desistiu de um acordo para um data center no Reino Unido com a britânica Nscale, especializada em infraestrutura de computação em nuvem para inteligência artificial, em um momento crucial para as perspectivas de abertura de capital da startup, informou o jornal The Telegraph. O jornal não apresentou uma razão específica para a decisão da gigante americana de tecnologia de abandonar o acordo referente ao empreendimento em Loughton, no condado de Essex, mas afirmou que o projeto vem enfrentando uma série de atrasos. Segundo a publicação, as autoridades informaram à Nscale que não esperam fornecer energia à instalação antes da década de 2030. O principal empreendimento da Nscale na Noruega também está seis meses atrasado, com apenas 6,4 megawatts dos 30 megawatts de capacidade previstos para o data center em operação. De acordo com um documento apresentado no âmbito dos preparativos para o IPO, a Nscale depende da Microsoft e da Anthropic para cerca de 85% de seus contratos. A Microsoft estava prestes a se tornar a principal cliente do primeiro data center britânico da Nscale, em Essex. A saída da Microsoft representaria um revés para a empresa, que pretende captar até US$ 3 bilhões em uma oferta pública inicial de ações (IPO, na sigla em inglês), possivelmente ainda neste mês, e que já vinha enfrentando a apreensão dos investidores em relação aos riscos da expansão mais ampla da infraestrutura de inteligência artificial. A Nscale é uma das empresas mais proeminentes do segmento conhecido como neocloud, formado por companhias que buscam construir enormes complexos computacionais voltados à inteligência artificial. Essas empresas querem aproveitar os centenas de bilhões de dólares que as gigantes de tecnologia se comprometeram a investir nessa área e representam um elo fundamental na cadeia de suprimentos que sustenta o boom da IA. Um porta-voz da Nscale disse ao The Telegraph: “Continuamos comprometidos com o projeto de Loughton e com o Reino Unido, e estamos estudando fontes alternativas de energia para o local, além de outros locais para expansão no país. “Nossa relação com a Microsoft continua sólida e é de longo prazo, e esse lamentável problema na rede elétrica de Londres não afeta nossos outros contratos.” A Microsoft não comentou o assunto ao The Telegraph e não respondeu imediatamente a um pedido de comentário da Bloomberg feito fora do horário comercial habitual. O cenário para os planos de abertura de capital da Nscale ficou mais desfavorável nos últimos dias. Na semana passada, a também neocloud CoreWeave ganhou destaque depois que seu cofundador afirmou que a empresa estava estudando formas de captar recursos nos mercados de dívida com grau de investimento, que oferecem amplos volumes de capital provenientes de investidores como seguradoras. Os investidores já vinham demonstrando cautela em relação aos fornecedores de capacidade computacional para IA, diante das dezenas de bilhões de dólares em empréstimos contraídos por essas empresas e por seus clientes para financiar a enorme expansão da capacidade dos data centers. As ações da CoreWeave despencaram nas três primeiras sessões da semana e depois se recuperaram parcialmente. Na sexta-feira, porém, as preocupações voltaram a pesar sobre os papéis, provocando a pior semana da empresa desde novembro, com uma queda de 25%. O episódio também ocorreu após a australiana Firmus, do setor de data centers, abandonar seus planos de abertura de capital porque a oferta não conseguiu atrair apoio suficiente ao preço das ações proposto ao mercado.

Coordinating Economic Affairs Minister Airlangga Hartarto said the government was prioritizing the digital economy to help reach a 6% growth target in 2027. Indonesia currently has 600-700 megawatts of operational data-center capacity, with a further 1.3 gigawatts in the pipeline, representing an estimated $15-20 billion in potential investment. Such projects, he said, require ample land, reliable electricity and adequate water. Those requirements have drawn scrutiny. Timothy Wong, head of research at DBS Group, said Indonesia needed to rethink its approach given how much electricity and water the facilities consume. “Data centers are very intensive users of electricity and water, and the Indonesian government actually needs these resources for its population,” he said. A DBS colleague, Amit Sinha, said AI projects must plan for power, cooling, water and community impact, pointing to options such as renewable energy, closed-loop liquid cooling and recycled water.

artigo.texto: - The launch comes as Li Auto shifts its batteries from CATL to in-house developed ones produced by its joint venture with Sunwoda. - The Lianshan system covers batteries, electric drive units and the charging network. Li Auto (NASDAQ: LI) has launched its in-house developed electric powertrain technology system named Lianshan, covering batteries, electric drive units and charging network. The company pledged two lifetime guarantees — against battery self-ignition and against fire after collisions — as it seeks to ease consumer safety concerns while expanding the use of its in-house batteries. The Chinese automaker announced the system at its Power Day electric technology event on Tuesday. It said the Lianshan battery, Lianshan electric drive and charging network are all developed in-house, and that it will take care of "everything about electricity." Under the Lianshan battery guarantee program, if a vehicle self-ignites due to quality problems with the original battery and meets scrapping criteria, Li Auto will compensate the owner with a new vehicle of the same configuration. If a battery catches fire following a collision or chassis scraping and the vehicle is scrapped, the company will cover the gap between the vehicle damage insurance coverage amount and the actual insurance payout. The program is subject to eligibility conditions. The launch comes as Li Auto accelerates the switch of its models' batteries from CATL (HKEX: 3750) to in-house developed batteries, which are produced by a 50-50 joint venture it established with Sunwoda (SZSE: 300207) in 2025. Li Auto also disclosed on September 4 that it plans to invest 2.65 billion yuan ($394 million) in Sunwoda's power battery subsidiary, Sunwoda Electric Vehicle Battery Co Ltd (Sunwoda EVB), and will directly hold an 8.79% stake after the deal closes, becoming its second-largest shareholder. CATL is the world's largest power battery maker, and its batteries are generally seen by Chinese consumers as safer and more premium. Persuading potential customers to accept batteries made by Sunwoda will not be easy for Li Auto, and the raft of safety commitments unveiled on Tuesday appears to be aimed at that concern. When CATL signed a 5-year strategic cooperation agreement with Li Auto in September 2025, the battery maker said more than 1 million Li Auto vehicles equipped with its batteries had been delivered, with no thermal runaway incidents caused by the batteries themselves. In January, Li Auto delayed some Li i6 deliveries due to insufficient battery supply and encouraged order holders to switch to versions equipped with Sunwoda batteries, offering an additional 2-year or 40,000-kilometer battery warranty extension. Sunwoda EVB was sued in December 2025 by Vremt, a Geely-affiliated company, which sought 2.31 billion yuan in damages, alleging quality problems with the battery cells it had delivered. At Tuesday's event, Li Auto said the Lianshan battery uses a high-stability cathode, a low-lithium-consumption anode and a dual-formula electrolyte for long life, supporting continuous dynamic repair. Batteries across all models will retain at least 75% health within 8 years or 160,000 kilometers, it said. The company said cell-level material improvements, highly integrated battery packs and vehicle-level energy management have increased range across all models. Under the CLTC standard, the new Li L8 offers 430 kilometers of pure electric range and the 2026 Li i6 offers 780 kilometers, an overall improvement of more than 8% over the 2025 versions. On safety, Li Auto said the underside of the Lianshan battery can withstand a 500-joule impact without catching fire or exploding, remain watertight after 48 hours submerged in 1 meter of water, and that the full pack will not catch fire for 24 hours after a single cell goes into thermal runaway at 50 degrees Celsius. The company said its new-generation 5C ternary lithium cells run 12 degrees Celsius cooler during supercharging than ordinary 2C ternary lithium cells. For lithium iron phosphate batteries, its adaptive algorithms keep state-of-charge estimation error within 3% and increase peak power output at low charge in winter by more than 40%. The Lianshan electric drive uses a proprietary patented CAR119 cast aluminum rotor material, adding more than 15 kilometers of pure electric range in urban driving and more than 8 kilometers on highways. Li Auto also restructured the power module so that current flows directly to the chip, adding another 30 kilometers of range and freeing up 24 millimeters of headroom. The company said 4 million of its in-house developed silicon carbide power chips have gone into production vehicles over the past year with zero failures. The next-generation electric drive system will deliver more power and range without increasing in size, it said. On the charging network, Li Auto's supercharging stations now exceed 4,200, covering cities, highways and scenic areas, and span the "12 vertical and 13 horizontal" expressway corridors, with an average of one station every 100 kilometers to be achieved within the year. The company said equipment availability stands at 99.9 percent, and all highway supercharging stations are equipped with 5C superchargers. Li Auto founder, chairman and CEO Li Xiang said on Monday that the company decided in 2020 to develop its own batteries, and that its existing battery suppliers remain partners to this day. artigo.texto: Pittsylvania County’s Berry Hill megasite will eventually have 21 data center buildings, built in phases over 15 years, according to permits filed by Stack Infrastructure. The project, an AI data center campus, “represents the largest private single-investment commitment” on record with the Virginia Economic Development Partnership, according to permit information. When formally approved, the project will also be the largest economic development deal in Southside Virginia’s history. It’s expected to create up to $100 billion in investment and more than 2,500 jobs with salaries of more than $80,000 over a 20-year period. At full build-out, the campus — called Project Crossroads — will require about 3,000 megawatts of capacity power, mostly generated on-site, said the permit application. The application requests construction and environmental permitting from multiple agencies at once. It lays out project details, like power infrastructure, wetlands impact mitigation and community engagement for Project Crossroads. The project was first made public in March through a land sale between data center developer Stack Infrastructure and the Danville-Pittsylvania County Regional Industrial Facility Authority. Many of the details in the joint permit application were not available until now. Through the land sale and a local performance agreement, Stack claimed nearly 3,000 acres at the 3,528-acre megasite in Pittsylvania. According to the joint permit application, 1,715 acres of that land are developable. The 21-building data center campus, along with its on-site power and other infrastructure, would encompass those 1,715 acres, with a total of 1,733 acres disturbed during construction. The application also included expected property tax revenue for Pittsylvania County: up to $48 million per year at full buildout. That’s about $16.5 million in taxes per year on the first 1,000 acres and an additional $16,250 per acre for every developed acre after that. The county will also receive tax revenue on data center equipment at a rate of $1.62 per $100 of assessed value. This would almost certainly make the project the county’s largest taxpayer. The biggest chunk — about 42% — of the county’s revenue for fiscal year 2027 comes from real estate taxes. The project is not receiving any local discretionary monetary incentives. Though no formal announcement about the project has been made, Project Crossroads is expected to be the second tenant at the megasite, after lithium-ion battery separator manufacturer Microporous announced that it would build a facility on about 200 acres in 2024. The Berry Hill megasite was purchased jointly by Danville and Pittsylvania in 2008. Since then, over $217 million in public and private funds have been invested in grading, infrastructure and other preparations to ready the site for development. The megasite is now “shovel-ready,” meaning it has all the resources necessary for development. In January, the planning commission and board of supervisors in Pittsylvania County unanimously approved a fast-tracked zoning change to allow “special heavy industrial” developments, including data centers and power generation, at the megasite. On-site power generation Project Crossroads is expected to use on-site power generation for its massive energy needs, according to the application. A large part of the energy will likely be supplied by natural gas, via existing transmission pipelines to the megasite. Stack also plans to build a 150-megawatt substation at the megasite, which is expected to be operational by 2028, the application says. “The utilization of onsite power generation will reduce constraints on existing grid infrastructure, while providing reliability for operations,” the joint permit application says. “The project will also require backup and emergency power capabilities to maintain operational continuity during utility interruptions.” Specifics on the type, capacity and configuration of these systems will be determined later, based on requirements of future tenants, but they may include diesel generators, natural gas-fired generators, battery energy storage systems or a combination of these. The March performance agreement includes a condition on power use. It says that there will be a minimum load capacity of 299 megawatts for the project, provided by Appalachian Power by the end of 2028. There will be no restrictions on a load capacity higher than 299 megawatts, it says. The total projected capacity for on-site power at Project Crossroads is 3,000 megawatts. By comparison, a conventional nuclear power plant can deliver more than 700 megawatts, according to the International Atomic Energy Agency. For instance, Dominion Energy’s North Anna nuclear station’s two reactors supply, together, 1,890 megawatts. The joint permit application identifies two “energy generation campuses” as part of the facility — the 80-acre Southwest Energy Generation Campus and the 125-acre Northeast Energy Generation Campus. The combined 205 acres are the minimum acreage necessary to meet the project’s planned energy needs, the application says. The company is making efforts to minimize the on-site power’s environmental impact to streams and wetlands, according to the application. Where feasible, the energy generation facilities and infrastructure were consolidated to reduce environmental impacts, according to the document. Also released with the joint permit application were thousands of other pages of permitting information, submitted to the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and other agencies. In an April community outreach meeting, Pittsylvania County Economic Development Director Matt Rowe said it’s a misconception that the project will raise electric bills for ratepayers. artigo.texto: Yankton County is going to take its time to study the economic and environmental effects of electrical energy storage facilities. During its regular meeting on Tuesday, the Yankton County Commission approved temporary Zoning Ordinance No. 23, which imposes a 12-month moratorium on these types of facilities in the county and directs the “Planning Commission, zoning staff, emergency management officials, fire departments, highway officials, and other appropriate advisors to study such facilities, conduct public proceedings and recommend permanent zoning regulations.” According to this ordinance, “Upon the effective date of this temporary zoning ordinance, no application for a building permit, use permit, zoning or rezoning permit shall be accepted by Yankton County, or its offices, specifically for electrical energy storage facilities exceeding a capacity of 1 (megawatt hour), nor shall any permit be issued for the same.” Energy storage systems for electricity generation use electricity — or some other energy source, such as solar-thermal energy — to charge an energy storage system or device, which is discharged to supply, or generate, electricity when needed at desired levels and quality, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. According to Yankton County’s temporary ordinance regarding these systems, commercial- and utility-scale electrical energy storage facilities are an emerging land use not presently addressed with sufficiently specific siting, fire protection, emergency response, environmental protection, road use, financial assurance and decommissioning standards in the county’s zoning regulations. Batteries (electro-chemical) are one of the five types of energy storage systems for electricity generation in commercial use within the United States. “The reason I brought this to the commission is that we do have a company that is interested in putting in an electrical energy storage facility — a battery storage facility,” Yankton County Commissioner Ryan Heine said. “It’s not really well covered in our zoning. There’s been some toss-around of exactly where and how this should be permitted under our zoning. None of the places really work out good. Rather than trying to let this muddle through, we’re just going to put a clear hold on it.” He said this “hold” imposed by the temporary ordinance on electrical energy storage facilities will allow the Yankton County Planning Commission to work on a permanent ordinance on this topic. “We just want to put this in so that we have our zoning code done right and clear,” Heine said. “That’s to the benefit to our community. That’s also to the benefit to any businesses that are going to be putting in a facility like this. They know exactly what the ordinances are, and we can hopefully make a good, clean ordinance that addresses real problems and that also tries to open our county up for real opportunity.” About the temporary ordinance, Yankton County Commissioner Wanda Howey-Fox added that, “just for clarification, we need to do it as an emergency,” addressing meeting attendees and online viewers. Heine said the “emergency part is simply because we do have a business that’s looking at” potentially installing an electrical energy storage facility in Yankton County. “We do have lots of questions around it,” he said. “I like these emergency ordinances only if they’re kind of specific, so that’s why I’m trying to be very specific. I don’t want to be inadvertently affecting other things. … We don’t want to inadvertently make problems for other things … that we shouldn’t be concerned about. “The emergency part of this is simply because we do have questions and we do have a business interested in this, and we want to get it cleared up so that we have a clear field for them to start on,” he said. “An ordinance like this also definitely puts some fire for our zoning committee to get it done.” While he acknowledged that the temporary ordinance says 12 months, Heine said he hopes a permanent and “proper zoning ordinance” can be prepared by the Yankton County Planning Commission much sooner than that, adding that the permanent ordinance will eventually replace the temporary one. “I really hope it’s something fast,” Heine said. “Two to three months would be great. They could do it in two to three months.” He said electrical energy storage facilities present “a few new safety things” that Yankton County has not considered before in its zoning. “We also want to make sure that we are also in a good alignment with the (South Dakota Public Utilities Commission),” Heine said. “There’s a size of things where we don’t want to intrude on things. We don’t want to create an issue for, say, someone who has battery storage for their solar farm or their solar panels on their farm or something like that of personal use. There are sizes to make sure that we are in a good place for that. “There’s also making sure that we’re … making a good law that does not inadvertently have negative effects,” he said. “I like to make sure that we make good laws like that. As I’ve always (said) a lot to the Planning Commission and in general is to not rely entirely on setbacks because setbacks are a poor way of regulating a real problem. If there’s a real problem, let’s make a real regulation to address it, but only address real problems.” Tom Glanzer, NorthWestern Energy’s community relations manager for South Dakota and Nebraska, spoke to the Yankton County Commission about the county’s temporary ordinance on electrical energy storage facilities. “I appreciate your comments, Commissioner (Heine), on doing this sensibly,” Glanzer said. “What we’re here to do is just to explain a little bit where we’re at with it and why we’re interested in battery storage.” He said NorthWestern Energy respects Yankton County’s responsibility to protect public safety, landowners and the community through responsible zoning and permitting standards. “However, even a temporary 12-month blanket m

artigo.texto: Carbon market plan offers income opportunities — BBM Revenue from carbon credits could also help finance climate adaptation projects, including resilient infrastructure, water facilities and other essential services. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has issued Executive Order (eo) 127, which seeks to create income opportunities for Filipinos through environmental protection activities, including tree planting, forest conservation and pollution reduction. The order mandates the formulation of the Philippine Carbon Market Policy Framework to support the country’s climate commitments under the Paris Agreement, attract investments in green projects and establish rules for the trading of carbon credits. Executive Secretary Ralph Recto said communities, farmers, businesses and other groups that help reduce pollution or absorb greenhouse gases could earn additional income through qualified environmental projects. Under the framework, eligible projects could generate carbon credits that may be sold to companies or other buyers seeking to meet their climate commitments. Recto cited communities that plant and protect trees as potential beneficiaries, since trees absorb carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. “In other words, people can earn from planting and caring for trees, using clean energy, and engaging in other activities that help protect the environment. You will be given carbon credits for every activity proven to have reduced greenhouse gases, which can be sold,” Recto said. He stressed, however, that projects must meet government standards and undergo proper verification before qualifying for carbon credits. Registry Recto said the initiative could encourage investments in reforestation, sustainable agriculture, renewable energy and waste management while creating livelihood opportunities, particularly in rural communities. “We’re hitting two birds with one stone. The President wants to protect the environment while helping people earn more,” he said. Revenue from carbon credits could also help finance climate adaptation projects, including resilient infrastructure, water facilities and other essential services, Recto added. Under EO 127, the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) will develop rules on project eligibility, carbon credit measurement and verification, and the sharing of revenues and other benefits. The DENR will also establish a Philippine National Carbon Registry to monitor carbon credits and prevent double counting and other irregularities. An interagency committee chaired by the Climate Change Commission, with the Department of Finance as vice chair, will oversee the development and implementation of the policy.

artigo.texto: O Google quer construir um data center de 780 megawatts em Pine Island, cidade de cerca de 4 mil habitantes a uma hora a sudeste de Minneapolis, e aposta que o projeto pode ajudar a financiar uma rede elétrica mais limpa e confiável. O modelo, apresentado pela empresa como a forma correta de atender à demanda da inteligência artificial, é tema de reportagem da CNBC, que ouviu especialistas e moradores céticos. O acordo proposto com a Xcel Energy prevê que o Google financie a adição de 1.400 megawatts de energia eólica, 200 megawatts de solar e 300 megawatts de armazenamento em baterias à rede da concessionária. O volume supera a capacidade do próprio data center porque eólica e solar não geram eletricidade o tempo todo. Segundo a Xcel, a nova energia atenderá todos os clientes da região, não apenas o Google, e ajudará a avançar no fornecimento local de energia livre de carbono. O contrato depende de aprovação da comissão de serviços públicos do Minnesota. O desenho inclui proteções para a concessionária: o Google pagará por pelo menos 75% da capacidade contratada mesmo se consumir menos e, em caso de rescisão antecipada, deverá arcar com até oito anos de cobranças mínimas de demanda. “Ninguém quer fazer uma grande expansão e depois não ter para onde mandar essa energia”, disse Amanda Rome, vice-presidente executiva da Xcel, à CNBC. O projeto também mira a meta do Google de operar com energia livre de carbono 24 horas por dia até 2030. A empresa diz que a área de nuvem, que sustenta seu modelo Gemini, teve receita de quase US$ 25 bilhões no segundo trimestre, alta de 82% em um ano. A corrida da tecnologia por capacidade computacional é o que vem impulsionando a demanda por eletricidade. Resistência dos moradores Pesquisa do Gallup feita em março mostrou que 71% dos americanos se opõem à instalação de um data center em sua vizinhança, com o consumo de energia no topo das preocupações. Levantamento do Pew Research Center de julho e agosto indicou que metade dos entrevistados avalia que os data centers serão majoritariamente ruins para o meio ambiente e para as contas de luz das famílias. Rede envelhecida e críticas A North American Electric Reliability Corporation, entidade sem fins lucrativos que atua como reguladora do setor, afirma que os novos data centers responderão pela maior parte do aumento projetado da demanda por eletricidade na próxima década. O Departamento de Energia, sob o governo de Joe Biden, informou que mais de 70% das linhas de transmissão e transformadores dos EUA têm pelo menos 25 anos. Para Amanda Peterson Corio, chefe global de energia do Google, o momento é ideal para usar capital privado na correção da infraestrutura envelhecida, segundo a CNBC. Jigar Shah, sócio da consultoria Multiplier, disse à CNBC que os operadores poderiam erguer instalações menores em locais onde a rede já tem capacidade ociosa, o que reduziria a necessidade de construir nova geração e transmissão. David Pomerantz, diretor-executivo do Energy and Policy Institute, afirmou que as concessionárias têm retornos em torno de 10% sobre novos investimentos — e por isso têm pouco incentivo para acomodar data centers na rede existente.

artigo.texto: TORONTO, ON / ACCESS Newswire / October 20, 2026 / Polaris Renewable Energy Inc. (TSX:PIF) ("Polaris" or the "Company") is pleased to announce that it has awarded and executed a contract with Trina Energy Storage Solutions (Singapore) Pte. Ltd. ("Trina Storage") for the supply of battery energy storage systems ("BESS") for the Company's Punta Lima project in Puerto Rico. Trina Storage is a global utility-scale energy storage provider with 30 GWh of BESS projects commissioned and under execution worldwide, including more than 6 GWh across Latin America and the Caribbean. The Punta Lima BESS project is being advanced under Puerto Rico's Accelerated Storage Addition Program ("ASAP"), a strategic initiative designed to strengthen grid reliability through the deployment of utility-scale battery energy storage systems co-located with existing generation facilities. As background, on June 5, 2026, Polaris Power US, Inc. ("PPUS") fully executed the BESS Standard Offer Agreement (the "SO1 Agreement") with the Puerto Rico Electric Power Authority, establishing the framework for its participation in ASAP. The award and execution of the supply contract with Trina Storage represents the next key milestone in advancing the Punta Lima BESS project. The Punta Lima BESS will consist of a single 35.7 MW system with an 8-hour duration. Under the SO1 Agreement, the Storage Capability of 71.4 MW will be served by the BESS through two four-hour energy delivery blocks. Total estimated gross capital expenditures for the ASAP project, including the BESS, medium-voltage transformer, tariffs and balance of plant, are expected to range from US$55 million to US$60 million and will be funded with cash on hand. Once constructed and fully operational, the project is expected to contribute approximately US$12.5 million of EBITDA in the first year of operation. PPUS, as Resource Provider, will be entitled to receive monthly fixed and performance-based payments from the Puerto Rico Electric Power Authority in exchange for providing energy storage services, including capacity and grid support. The agreement with Trina calls for deliveries of the BESS containers to take place March/April 2027. Accordingly, commercial operation of the project is currently expected in the third quarter of 2027, and the agreement will run for a 20-year term from the commercial operation date. Marc Murnaghan, CEO of Polaris, commented: "The execution of the supply contract with Trina Storage is a significant milestone in advancing our investment in Punta Lima, moving the project from its contractual framework into equipment procurement and implementation. This investment reflects our confidence in Puerto Rico's long-term energy transition and our commitment to delivering critical storage capacity that will enhance grid reliability and resilience. We look forward to working with Trina Storage and our partners to advance the project toward construction and commercial operation." Polaris remains committed to delivering long-term, sustainable energy solutions across Latin America and the Caribbean and looks forward to working with Trina Storage and other stakeholders through the implementation of the Punta Lima BESS project. About Polaris Renewable Energy Inc. Polaris Renewable Energy Inc. is a Canadian publicly traded company engaged in the acquisition, development, and operation of renewable energy projects in Latin America and the Caribbean. We are a high-performing and financially sound contributor to the energy transition. The Company's portfolio includes a geothermal plant (~82 MW), four run-of river hydroelectric plants (~39 MW), three solar (photovoltaic) projects (~35 MW) and an onshore wind park (~26 MW).The Company's development portfolio also includes three projects in Mexico comprising approximately 250 MWdc of solar generation capacity and 61.6 MW / 192.0 MWh of battery energy storage, currently in the planning stage and progressing toward financial close. artigo.texto: Shares of Australia's NextDC plunged 39.5% on Wednesday after the data center operator slashed its annual earnings forecast, citing power supply delays at its Melbourne facility amid local community and stakeholder opposition. The company lowered its fiscal 2027 revenue guidance to between $475 million Australian dollars and A$500 million, from A$615 million to A$640 million forecast earlier, while cutting its underlying earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, or EBITDA, forecast to A$245 million to A$265 million from A$385 million to A$410 million. The delays to power stem from the suspension of infrastructure upgrades at the company's M3 Melbourne data center amid community opposition, with electricity distributor Jemena not expecting to resume work before February 2027, according to NextDC. Jemena cited safety concerns and restricted access to work sites due to community opposition, as well as a lack of consent from the local council pending further community consultation. Citi said in a note that NextDC's power delays could affect earnings beyond fiscal 2027, citing delays to approvals for the M3 expansion and a longer-than-expected timeline for transformer upgrades. As Australia grapples with growing concerns over the impact of data center developments on local communities, Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the government was working to establish national standards for investment. Chalmers told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia" on Wednesday that the government welcomes investment in data centers and AI infrastructure, provided it aligns with the country's national interest, adding that the government was finalizing national investment standards to address concerns surrounding AI deployment. Australia is not alone in facing opposition to data center projects, there has been growing push back against data center developments worldwide, amid concerns over their impact on local communities and the environment. NextDC shares have declined for seven straight weeks, and are on course to end lower for the eighth week.

(NASDAQ: XOS) (“Xos” or the “Company”), a leading energy storage and fleet electrification solutions provider, today announced its participation in RE+ 2026, North America's largest clean energy event. Xos will share Booth W15500 with Pioneer eMobility at the Las Vegas Convention Center from November 16 to 19, 2026. At the show, Xos will present the Power Hub line and display the AC Power Hub on the booth floor. Visitors will see how Power Hub storage arrives fully integrated, connects to any source, and powers a site in days instead of the years a new grid connection can take. Xos Highlights at RE+ 2026: - Power on your terms. The Power Hub bridges data centers and industrial sites through multi-year grid delays and powers site growth ahead of utility upgrades. It also runs standalone microgrids where EV fleets can power the site, delivers grid-independent power to remote mining and agriculture operations, supports construction, events, disaster relief, and mission-critical sites, and combines into multi-megawatt utility-scale plants. - Built to scale. The Xos Power Hub™ comes in four configurations, 210 kWh, 420 kWh, 630 kWh, and 3.1 MWh of storage per unit, with up to 1.5 MW of power output per unit. Up to 32 units connect in parallel for multi-megawatt sites, and more than 250 MWh is already deployed across North America. - Any source, any site. Power Hub units arrive fully integrated on a trailer, skid, or 20-foot container: connect and power on. They pair with the grid, generators, or solar arrays, and the 210, 420, and 630 kWh units can also recharge from a DC fast charger. Grid-forming controls let a site run with the grid or on its own, switching between the two without interruption, with real-time remote monitoring, diagnostics, and control from anywhere. - On display: the AC Power Hub. Attendees at Booth W15500 will see the AC Power Hub, a towable, battery-buffered mobile generator with 210, 420, or 630 kWh of LFP storage. Dual bi-directional AC channels each deliver up to 150 kW with independent voltage and frequency control. It needs no permits, excavation, or permanent installation, and carries UL1973, UL9540A, and UL1741 certifications. - Built in America. Power Hub systems are designed in California, manufactured in Tennessee, Buy American compliant, and backed by domestic service. Public agencies can purchase the AC Power Hub through Sourcewell, OMNIA Partners, NPPGov, GSA, and California CORE. “Energy infrastructure has traditionally been a permanent, multi-year bet. Demand for new power is outpacing the grid’s ability to connect it. According to Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory’s 2026 “Queued Up” report, 2,061 GW of generation and storage capacity is waiting to connect to the U.S. grid, and projects can take more than five years to reach commercial operation. artigo.texto: Australia-based battery energy storage system (BESS) company Akaysha Energy has established an AUD 1.75 billion portfolio financing platform. It will refinance the company’s four BESS projects in Australia: Brendale, Orana, Ulinda Park and Elaine. The financing is backed by 11 banks, including ANZ, BNP Paribas, Bank of China, CIBC, Commonwealth Bank of Australia, Deutsche Bank, DNB, ING, Mizuho, MUFG, and Rabobank. The financing will support the company’s development pipeline of approximately 6 GW/25 GWh of large-scale battery storage projects across Australia’s National Electricity Market (NEM). Akaysha Energy owns and operates the 850 MW/1.68 GWh Waratah Super Battery in New South Wales that’s touted to be one of the world’s most powerful BESS projects (see Australia Powers Up 850 MW Waratah Super Battery Project). Blackstone has closed its fifth energy transition fund, Blackstone Energy Transition Partners V, with $8.7 billion in capital commitments. This is more than 50% higher than its predecessor fund. Blackstone says this fund has already invested in power generation, electric transmission, energy efficiency, and infrastructure businesses, including three platform companies focused on power generation and transmission development. Blackstone said it has committed more than $11 billion in new equity investments across the energy transition sector since January 2025. UK-based renewable energy company Low Carbon has launched the Dengie Peninsula Energy Park Project in Essex, UK. It is planned to have a potential capacity of 1 GW, combining solar power and battery energy storage to export clean electricity to the grid. Low Carbon says the project is intended to support the UK’s clean energy transition, with public consultation planned for early 2027. It qualifies as a Nationally Significant Infrastructure Project (NSIP) since it will have a generation capacity exceeding 100 MW. Low Carbon plans to submit a Development Consent Order (DCO) application to the Planning Inspectorate. Earlier this year, in July 2026, the UK government announced planning reforms aimed at reducing up to 12 months from the approval process for major infrastructure projects in Britain, including solar farms (see Britain Cuts NSIP Planning Process By Up To 12 Months). Shandong Electric Power Construction Corporation, a subsidiary of POWERCHINA, has secured a contract for a 500 MW/2,000 MWh standalone BESS project in Saudi Arabia. The Saudi Group 1-KSB independent energy storage power station project is part of the country's initial battery storage program, with Saudi Power Procurement Company (SPPC) as the offtaker. Once operational, it is expected to support grid flexibility, improve power supply resilience, and facilitate the integration of renewable energy. India’s ACME Solar has signed a power purchase agreement (PPA) with Solar Energy Corporation of India (SECI) for a 300 MW/1,200 MWh assured peak supply project under the FDRE-IX tranche at a tariff of INR 6/kWh. The project will combine solar power and battery energy storage to supply electricity for four hours daily during non-solar hours, with a minimum monthly availability of 90%. Following the agreement, ACME Solar says its signed PPAs for projects under construction reached 4.31 GW, out of a total contracted capacity of 5.38 GW under construction. Fortis Green Renewables Investment Management and Zeitinger Invest have invested in GRIPS Energy Group to support the expansion of commercial and industrial (C&I) solar and battery energy storage projects across Sub-Saharan Africa. The investment will finance the acquisition of operational renewable energy assets in Senegal, Botswana, Zambia, and Uganda, while providing growth capital for new projects. GRIPS aims to build a portfolio of more than 100 MW of solar and storage assets by 2030.

artigo.texto: Memphians react to failed data center moratorium MEMPHIS, Tenn. (WMC) - The Memphis City Council passed a new data center ordinance Tuesday night, but it is not the legislation activists and environmentalists fought for and supported. New security rules instituted after the chaotic Oct. 6 council meeting kept disruptions at a minimum, but not the disappointment. The council passed an ordinance that calls for a 135-day pause on the permitting process for data centers, far less than the 12 to 18 months the activists endorsed. The meeting lasted more than five hours, filled with emotion. Citizens expressed doubt in the council’s decision-making. “History will find us on the right side of this issue,” one man told the council. “Data centers don’t belong in neighborhoods and communities,” said another woman. “And we can’t accept an ordinance, Councilman Warren, drafted by ChatGPT and rubber stamped by SpaceXAI,” another speaker said. Councilman Jeff Warren and Councilwoman Rhonda Logan sponsored the legislation OK’d by council, which was updated at the last minute. And while Councilwoman Jerri Green said council needed more time to understand the changes, Logan disputed that. “My ordinance has not changed. Everything you talked about tonight is not under our purview. The only thing we can address is land use,” said Logan. City Council Chairwoman Jana Swearengen-Washington told Action News 5, “This item is still going to have a pause in it and it’s going to have some guardrails. It’s more of what they need and what they requested.” KeShaun Pearson, founder of Community Against Pollution, said what is needed is more community input and further study of the impact of data centers on Memphis’ air, water and electricity. What council passed, he said, doesn’t come close to addressing that. “It’s not good enough because it’s not what the people wanted,” he told Action News 5, “It’s not good enough because it was presented to the people 45 minutes before it was voted on.” His brother, State Rep. Justin J. Pearson, who successfully challenged the council’s ban on his and five others’ attendance at the meeting in federal court, said the next step in the fight against data centers will be taken at the polls. “It is apparent that the Chamber of Commerce and Elon Musk have significant sway over some of these city council members,” Pearson said, “and it’s the responsibility of the people of this city to see them for who they are and to vote them out next year.” The council has requested a data centers study. Mayor Young issued an executive order earlier this month asking for a review of policy to determine the appropriate guardrails for the facilities. Data center critics said it’s too little, too late and the ordinance passed lacks the teeth to protect the people. “It was a big missed opportunity for the City of Memphis to be a leader in the region,” said Sarah Houston, Executive Director of Protect Our Aquifer, “We could be talking with our neighbors in DeSoto County and in Millington, where they just passed a moratorium and have a collaborative approach to data center regulation so it’s more uniform. It’s a missed opportunity.” The five council members who voted no against the ordinance were: Easter-Thomas, Green, Smiley, Walker and Swearengen-Washington. Councilwoman Cooper-Sutton was not in attendance. Action News 5 was told she’s handling a family emergency in Mississippi. Click here to sign up for our newsletter! artigo.texto: Data center air pollution permit under public review MASON COUNTY, W.Va. (WSAZ) - An air permit application for the Monarch Cloud Campus outlines plans for the site and its’ proposed power system that would operate independently of the traditional electric grid. The plans call for more than 800 primary engines, along with six natural gas heaters, 12 emergency generators and six diesel-powered firewater pump engines. During a public meeting, the West Virginia Department of Environmental Protection explained how the state evaluates whether a project like this meets air quality standards. “They want to install a power generation facility that would power their data center campus. And so they’ve applied for an air quality permit for that power-generating equipment. We’ve conducted a technical review of that application,” Terry Fletcher with WVDEP said. The application also calls for testing, emissions monitoring and record-keeping to demonstrate compliance. The permit falls under the state’s major-source permitting program, known as Prevention of Significant Deterioration. The process is intended to allow industrial development while limiting how much air quality can deteriorate. That includes modeling how emissions could affect surrounding areas, including nearby residents, farmland and the river. The review does not require a full environmental impact statement or consider broader issues such as traffic, property values or the project’s economic costs and benefits. Instead, the focus is on whether the facility meets applicable air quality requirements. “The purpose of air permitting is to ensure that a facility is in compliance with the federal and state air quality standards,” Fletcher said. “And so, this puts limits on their operating hours and how much emissions they can emit during their operation. Make sure that there are proper controls in place to make sure that they have all the emission control requirements and things like that in place to ensure that we don’t impact the air quality negatively in the air.” The state received Monarch’s application in April and revised it in May. The public comment period is now underway, with comments due Oct. 30. A virtual public meeting is scheduled for Oct. 29. Copyright 2026 WSAZ. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: - The system pairs a swappable main battery with a 77-kWh range-extension battery to improve battery utilization and lower fleet operating costs. - CATL plans to have 900 heavy-duty truck battery swap stations operating by the end of 2026 and expand to 2,000 by 2027. CATL (HKEX: 3750) has unveiled a dual-electric range extension battery for heavy-duty trucks, pairing a swappable main battery with an independent on-board battery as it expands its push in freight electrification. The world's largest EV battery maker introduced the system in Beijing on Tuesday, alongside upgrades to its Qiji battery-swapping system aimed at reducing fleets' energy replenishment and battery costs. The system consists of 2 independent battery systems: a standardized, chassis-mounted swappable main battery and a 77-kWh range-extension battery behind the cab. The latter supports 3C charging and provides backup power. Drivers of conventional battery-swapping trucks typically return to swap stations with about 30% charge remaining to avoid running out of power en route, leaving part of their leased battery capacity unused, CATL said. With the backup battery, the system can increase the main battery's depth of discharge (DOD) from about 70% to more than 95%, allowing trucks to return to a swap station with less than 5% charge remaining in the main battery. The system can switch power delivery to the range-extension battery within milliseconds, maintaining uninterrupted power and providing redundancy under demanding operating conditions, the company said. It uses what CATL calls a "1+X" architecture. The main battery remains standardized for compatibility with the Qiji swapping network, while the range-extension battery can be tailored to requirements such as low-temperature performance, high energy density or high power. The 2 battery systems can be upgraded independently. The range-extension battery stays with the vehicle as an on-board asset, while the main battery can be leased flexibly according to seasonal freight demand, helping fleets reduce rental expenses during idle periods. Alongside the new system, Qiji introduced the 260# and 300# standardized swappable batteries, with capacities of 432 kWh and 513 kWh, respectively, complementing its existing 75# battery. The new-generation Qiji station can complete a battery swap in 5 minutes and reduces construction costs by 10%, CATL said. It requires no excavation pit and can be deployed in as little as 5 days. The company also changed the billing method for its battery-as-a-service (BaaS) offering, charging customers for net energy charged rather than energy discharged, allowing them to retain the benefits of regenerative braking. The change can reduce per-kWh battery rental costs for users on basic plans by up to 20%, further improving the economics of operating electric heavy-duty trucks, according to CATL. The company plans to have 900 heavy-duty truck battery-swap stations operating by the end of 2026 and expand to 2,000 by 2027. Its long-term goal is to deploy 10,000 stations across China with partners. Agreements covering 13,000 vehicles were signed at the event, with orders for battery-swapping products from major logistics companies including SF Holding and China Postal Express & Logistics. The launch comes amid a rapid increase in new energy vehicle (NEV) penetration in China's heavy-duty truck market. New energy heavy-duty trucks accounted for 50% of the segment in September, up from 29% a year earlier, according to China Passenger Car Association (CPCA) analysis of compulsory traffic insurance data. CATL launched its Qiji Energy heavy-duty truck battery-swapping solution in June 2023 and introduced the 75# standardized swappable truck battery in May 2025, expanding its presence in logistics. On June 30 this year, the company signed a strategic cooperation agreement with J&T Express to provide swappable batteries, swap-station equipment, and operation and maintenance services for more than 5,000 heavy-duty trucks. Beyond the dual-electric range extension system, CATL also unveiled truck batteries for different transport applications, including ultra-light and ultra-thin packs mounted behind the cab, as well as chassis-mounted batteries for short-haul and long-haul operations.

artigo.texto: San Diego County may soon establish new regulations for energy storage facilities. Documenter Melina Jimenez sat in on a presentation at the latest meeting for the Sweetwater Community Planning Group. The battery energy storage systems, or BESS, use rechargeable batteries to store excess electricity, mostly from the electric grid, solar panels or wind turbines. They are a tool used to help with reliable energy, though communities nationwide have raised concerns about fire risks, water and air contamination and impacts on property values. A county proposal aims to set zoning, safety, development and decommissioning standards for storage facilities in unincorporated San Diego. The item will come before the Board of Supervisors for consideration next year. — Written by Brisa Karow, Documenter and freelance reporter

artigo.texto: 3.75 MWh fail-safe system provides energy resilience and grid support at Buffalo's 105-unit affordable housing apartment building while helping lower energy costs for residents BUFFALO, N.Y., Oct. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Viridi, the industry leader in fail-safe distributed energy storage systems, and Good Carbon Co., today announced the deployment of a 3.75MWh lithium-ion battery energy storage system (BESS) at Peace Bridge Place, a 105-unit affordable housing apartment building in Buffalo, New York. The project is one of the largest indoor lithium-ion battery systems in an occupied residential building in the United States. At Peace Bridge Place, Viridi's RPSLinkIN indoor BESS is part of a broader clean energy strategy that includes geothermal heating & cooling, domestic hot water, and high efficient building envelope upgrades. The 3.75 MWh system is designed to provide extended backup power for the fully electrified building during outages, while also helping reduce demand on the local grid during peak periods. Good Carbon Co., which focuses on revitalizing multifamily properties in communities throughout Western New York, selected the system to strengthen energy resilience for residents and enable the property to enable flexible, grid-responsive energy management. "Energy is one of the biggest operating costs in multifamily housing, and how you manage it directly affects the long-term performance of a property," said Adam Serbert, CEO of Good Carbon Co. "At Peace Bridge Place, Viridi's battery and energy management technology will help us reduce peak demand, avoid higher-cost periods and participate in demand response programs. That means lower operating costs, new revenue opportunities and a stronger economic foundation for keeping the property affordable and well maintained. For us, this is not just about one building — it is about creating a model we can apply across future multifamily projects." Viridi's intelligent Energy Management System automatically stores and discharges electricity based on the needs of the fully electrified property and the local grid. It allows Peace Bridge Place to reduce electricity demand during peak periods and respond to utility signals when additional grid flexibility is needed, while providing greater energy resilience for residents. By reducing peak demand and participating in demand response programs, the system can help lower the property's energy costs while creating new revenue opportunities. The New York State Energy Research and Development Agency (NYSERDA) is providing support to Good Carbon Co. for the Peace Bridge Place project through its Future Grid Challenge. The Peace Bridge Place project is a National Grid pilot focused on integrating flexible, grid-responsive technologies into its distribution network. Viridi's energy storage and energy management technology will work in coordination with EnergyHub's Edge Distributed Energy Resource Management System (DERMS), enabling the property to respond to National Grid signals during periods of peak electricity demand. "Peace Bridge Place demonstrates how forward-thinking energy storage solutions can ensure New York's multifamily buildings are meeting the energy needs of its residents while creating a more reliable and resilient electric grid," said Doreen M. Harris, President and CEO, NYSERDA. "Projects like this embody NYSERDA's mission to spur innovation that drives New York toward a clean energy future." Distributed across seven battery rooms, the 3.75MWh system is integrated with Viridi's proprietary Energy Management System (EMS), which optimizes the property's electricity use while enabling it to respond to changing conditions on the local grid in two key ways: - Peak Shaving: As the building's grid energy draw approaches a monthly peak, the battery automatically discharges to keep demand below a target threshold, reducing peak demand and associated $/kW demand charges. - Seasonal Demand Response: During peak events, National Grid dispatch signals are delivered through EnergyHub's platform to Viridi's energy management system, which then coordinates the response across the building's battery and other energy systems. For participating residents, smart thermostat setpoints can be adjusted to "pre-cool" or "pre-heat" apartments before the event, enabling reduced HVAC consumption during the event while the battery discharges. Residents can opt out of individual events at any time. Together, these actions allow the property to reduce its net electricity demand while the local grid is under the greatest strain. Deploying lithium-ion battery storage indoors at this scale requires rigorous safety standards. The risk of thermal runaway — and its potential to propagate from cell to cell — has historically constrained where lithium-ion systems can be installed. The RPSLinkIN system is designed to address that challenge through Viridi's proprietary Fail-Safe Anti-Propagation architecture, a passive safety layer designed to prevent thermal runaway from spreading between cells. That safety architecture has undergone industry-standard testing designed to evaluate how battery systems behave during a thermal runaway event. During UL 9540A testing, a cell was intentionally driven into thermal failure to determine whether the event would spread to surrounding cells. Viridi's technology prevented cell-to-cell propagation, with no detectable release of heat, sparks, smoke, gas or flames. RPSLinkIN has also earned UL 9540 Listing from TÜV Rheinland, providing third-party certification of the complete energy storage system. "This project demonstrates what becomes possible when energy storage is designed to serve the building and the grid at the same time," said Jon M. Williams, CEO of Viridi. "Peace Bridge Place will now be able to reduce peak demand, respond when the grid needs support and strengthen resilience for the people who live there. artigo.texto: Maily Kocinski grew up in Beaver Dam, Wisconsin, a rural town 70 miles northwest of Milwaukee. She still lives there on a small farm — complete with a creek — with her husband, Robert, along with “two horses, barn cats, a dog, and four peacocks.” Kocinski is worried about her new neighbors. Meta Platforms Inc., the technology giant that owns Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, is building a hyperscale data center in Beaver Dam. The facility, currently under construction with a $1 billion price tag on a 520-acre site of former Wisconsin farmland, is part of an estimated 3,000 new technology developments proposed or underway across the U.S. to serve as the backbone of the artificial intelligence and machine learning wave. Kocinski is concerned about the Meta project’s impact on water flows and quality on her farm, house and neighboring properties. She contends the water problems began after construction started last year. “It was bone dry. It smelled like fertilizer,” Kocinski said of the creek the first time she noticed the issues. “We have had a couple of neighbors whose wells have gone dry.” Soon after, the water returned with a gush — bringing new concerns, including erosion that might require rebuilding a small bridge over the creek. Kocinski said these fits and starts in water flow have occurred approximately 30 times since she first noticed the issue in May 2025. She also said that the water supply to her farm and home has turned murky. “It was cloudy, too,” Kocinski said. She has reached out to government agencies, Meta and other companies involved in building the new data center. “Every time I called, I was told to talk to a different department,” she said. “This is a big old mess.” Kocinski eventually commissioned her own water study, which showed higher-than-acceptable levels of strontium — an alkaline earth metal that can cause cardiovascular or kidney issues in high doses. A new water filtration system for her farm to lower those levels could cost as much as $40,000, she said. She worries the spike in strontium stems from the construction site less than two miles away, questioning whether blasting caused the shift and whether ample environmental due diligence was conducted before work began. In a response provided to Adams MultiMedia, Meta stated that a review of geographic information systems (GIS) data and a third-party analysis indicate the creek originates at a quarry near Kocinski’s property and does not extend into the data center parcel. Meta added that construction is occurring on the portions of the property farthest from her farm. Roberta “Bobbi” Marck, mayor of the city of Beaver Dam, said she has met with the Kocinskis twice, including once alongside Meta and its water engineering consultant. Meta — which currently operates 28 data centers in the U.S. — emphasizes that it uses more efficient, closed-loop cooling systems that recycle and reflow water used to cool servers and equipment. Facebook’s parent company also stated it will invest in operational water efficiencies at its facilities and fund local water restoration projects. ‘A LOCAL STORY’ The Kocinski family’s concerns represent a single snapshot of a much wider national debate over how the surge of AI infrastructure will affect local water systems. Data centers are undeniably thirsty. Water-fueled cooling systems are essential to keep rows of servers and computing equipment from overheating. Larger facilities can consume up to 5 million gallons of water per day, according to the Environmental and Energy Study Institute (EESI). Globally, water use by data centers could double to 2.46 trillion gallons by 2030, according to a United Nations report. By 2030, AI data centers are projected to use “enough water to meet the needs of all 1.3 billion people in sub-Saharan Africa for an entire year,” according to UN Secretary General António Guterres. AI and data centers are national and global waves with machines learning programs poised to change the nature of work, creativity and innovation. AI could also potentially displace workers from their livelihoods. “But water is really a local story,” said Rich “Raz” Razgaitis, a clean water and sustainability expert and CEO of FloWater, a Denver-based purification company. Razgaitis said that a data center’s impact varies widely depending on local water supplies and infrastructure. “That’s why small towns really need to be at the table,” he said, stressing the need for transparency. “We’re in uncharted territory.” He added that water systems across the nation have historically been underfunded compared to other utility infrastructure. FARMERS’ FEARS Tim Negris, executive vice president with MOCA Systems Inc., a Boston tech firm working with contractors, architects, and engineers, said that community resistance is often driven by local farmers and agriculture advocates worried about lost land and a potential strain on water supplies. “The fear around water is being driven by agriculture,” Negris said, pointing to similar tensions playing out in Minnesota, Wisconsin, Maryland and Iowa. In Dubuque County, Iowa, County Supervisor Harley Pothoff said local concerns about water, energy and farmland helped drive a local data center moratorium approved in May. He said a one-year pause gives the community time to evaluate the impacts of a proposed data center on a 400-acre parcel — including on a nearby local airport. “I have some concerns,” Pothoff said. “It just seems awfully big.” Opponents of the Iowa project claim it could consume up to 3 million gallons of water daily. Conversely, developers argue it could generate as much as $6.2 billion in long-term economic impact, including construction jobs, permanent operations, and tax revenue. ‘SO MUCH MONEY’ Shelley Copsey, CEO and co-founder of FYLD, a fieldwork and infrastructure AI technology company, believes this wave of projects presents opportunities alongside its challenges. “I think we will see a whole new way of thinking whe

artigo.texto: SHENZHEN, China, Oct. 19, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- BYD Energy Storage has built a comprehensive after-sales service network in a multi‑tier framework: station O&M, project centers, regional centers and global headquarters. BYD Energy Storage operates nine O&M centers globally, each spanning 2,500 square meters. Its after-sales service network covers China, Chile, South Africa, the UK, the US, Australia, Japan, Poland, and the Middle East. New service centers will open in South Africa and Bulgaria in 2027 to further expand its global service footprint. The centers deliver core functions including spare parts storage and management, batteries repair and maintenance, regional spare parts allocation, batteries recycling, and training for locally hired engineers. BYD Energy Storage's regional centers fully comply with local regulatory requirements, deliver structured workforce training and enable rapid on-site response. The professional service team comprises over 200 field engineers and more than 100 R&D specialists. The company enforces standardized service SLAs: response within 24 hours, on-site arrival within 48 hours, and fault troubleshooting within 7 days. The company's global service network has achieved widespread coverage. It forms a multi-point supply network that ensures rapid spare parts delivery worldwide. Furthermore, leveraging localized production lines, its O&M teams integrate regional resources to deliver local battery repair services, providing global customers with fast, convenient, and localized after-sales support. "Our global service footprint is tailored to our fast‑growing BESS deployments. Trustworthy after‑sales support underpins the long‑term stable operation of energy storage assets," commented Mr. He Dehong, Head of Global After-sales Service at BYD Energy Storage. Guided by its vision, empower global energy storage industry with digital and intelligent service, BYD Energy Storage's mature global O&M system strongly supports its expanding battery energy storage footprint. The company topped global BESS shipments at over 60 GWh in 2025, and has delivered more than 650 energy storage projects in total, supported by standardized, localized after-sales services for reliable asset operation. artigo.texto: Group holds Lexington walkout against AI and data centers LEXINGTON, Ky. (WKYT) - A small but vocal group of Lexington residents is working to shape the rules before more data centers move in. The group, No AI in KY, welcomed speakers and singers Tuesday to show unity against artificial intelligence. Members describe reasons for walkout Reva Russell English, a member of No AI in KY, said singing was included because of a long history of using song as resistance in the United States and around the world. No AI in KY is not just an organization, but words members live by as artificial intelligence use grows daily. The group gathered outside the Lexington government center Tuesday, joining a nationally organized walkout against AI. English said the National Walkout to Freeze AI was organized by Irreplaceable. “We don’t have like a set location to walk out from so a lot of people did leave their jobs early or called out sick today,” English said. Moratorium approved, zoning changes ahead English said Lexington city leaders are listening. In early October, the council approved a one-year moratorium on new data centers. English said the fight is only beginning. During that time, leaders will strengthen the zoning ordinance text amendment, or ZOTA, to decide where and how centers can be built. “We’re going to be around the whole time when they build that new ZOTA and they build that new zone we’re going to make sure that they keep data centers in a way isn’t going to harm this place and its people,” English said. Students raise concerns about AI and creativity “I can only imagine what that will do to the next generation of artists and creatives and how their creative ability will be impacted and the thing is that we don’t know because it’s not been around long enough for us to know,” Mehta said. Mehta said AI does not just impair creativity — it plagiarizes it, using human work to mimic human creativity. He said that is why he is fighting against AI and data centers. English said the group wants more people to join its effort. “It’s a fight for the future, it’s a fight for our lives and we would like more people to be a part of it with us,” English said. The Urban County Council will hear public comments on data centers at its 6 p.m. council meeting Thursday. Copyright 2026 WKYT. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: STL (Sterlite Technologies) has expanded its Neuralis Data Center portfolio with pre-terminated fiber trunk assemblies supporting fiber counts from 48 to 6,912. The new high-density cabling solutions are designed to help hyperscale and enterprise data centers accommodate growing bandwidth demands from AI, cloud computing and high-performance computing (HPC) workloads. The launch addresses a key challenge for data center operators: increasing network capacity while reducing installation time and making better use of limited cable routing space. For European data center operators and infrastructure designers, the assemblies offer an approach to scaling optical connectivity without significantly expanding existing pathways, trays and conduits. High-density fiber for space-constrained data centers The portfolio includes two product families covering indoor data hall connectivity and larger-scale indoor/outdoor installations. STL’s indoor pre-terminated fiber trunk assemblies support 48 to 576 fibers, with cable diameters ranging from 5.8 mm to 12.2 mm. Designed for high-density MMC, MPO and LC terminations, the assemblies meet ANSI/ICEA S-83-596 requirements and are available with UL OFNP plenum or OFNR riser-rated cables. For campus, inter-building and inter-row connections, STL offers indoor/outdoor assemblies supporting 144 to 6,912 fibers. The highest-density version accommodates 6,912 fibers in a single cable with an outer diameter of 32 mm. These assemblies feature OFNR/LSZH jacketing and UL 1651-rated sunlight resistance, making them suitable for installations requiring outdoor exposure. Factory termination targets faster deployment Both product families are factory-terminated and 100% tested before delivery, reducing the need for on-site connector installation and helping operators accelerate network deployment. Connector options include MMC, MTP/MPO and LC, with Base-8, Base-12, Base-16 and Base-24 configurations to support different switch and patch-panel architectures. The assemblies are available with bend-insensitive ITU-T G.657.A2 single-mode fiber in 200 µm or 250 µm formats. Indoor versions also support OM4 multimode fiber for shorter-distance connections. STL has integrated its patented IBR rollable ribbon technology into both product families. The color-coded bonded ribbon design is intended to simplify fiber identification and improve splicing efficiency in high-fiber-count installations. Ultra Low Loss connector performance options are also available for applications with demanding optical loss budgets. Supporting AI infrastructure expansion The new assemblies reflect the growing importance of cable density and installation efficiency as data center operators expand optical infrastructure to support AI workloads. “Every data center customer we work with is trying to solve the same equation – more capacity, less time. That’s exactly what this extension of Neuralis portfolio is built around. Our Pre-Terminated Trunk Assemblies are designed for dense networks, they are pre-tested, ready to connect on arrival, and flexible. This is connectivity built for how data centers are actually being constructed today; high density, tight timelines, zero room for error”, said Dr Badri Gomatam, CTO, STL. The expanded portfolio gives operators additional options for increasing fiber capacity within existing physical infrastructure while limiting field termination work.
