artigo.texto: Gelion PLC (AIM:GELN, OTC:GELNF, FRA:X0S) told investors it expects to generate its first commercial revenues from its sulfur battery technology in the current financial year, backed by a strengthened cash position and development agreements with major industrial and automotive partners. The company reported pro forma cash of £9.6 million at 30 June 2026, up from £4.1 million a year earlier, following an oversubscribed £9.9 million net fundraising. Its adjusted EBITDA loss widened to £4.4 million from £4.1 million, although this was 10.4% better than analyst expectations. Total income slipped to £2.5 million from £2.7 million but exceeded consensus forecasts by 17.1%, with government grants and R&D incentives covering 63.2% of research expenditure. Customer revenue fell to £49,000 from £912,000 following the completion of a legacy energy storage project. Gelion has since secured a £2 million funded development agreement with Japan's Mitsui Kinzoku and a co-funded proof-of-concept programme with a top-five global automotive manufacturer. Both are expected to contribute modest commercial revenue in FY27 as the company advances its Nano-Encapsulated Sulfur technology towards customer qualification and manufacturing scale-up. Chief executive Matt Wood said the company was moving "from technology validation towards customer programmes, qualification and scale-up", with a focus on converting technical progress into commercial adoption. "2026 has been an important transition year for Gelion, marked by continued advancements in our sulfur battery technology and growing commercial validation of our NES™ cathode platform through partnerships with leading global industrial and battery sector participants," Wood said. He added: "Supported by a strengthened balance sheet, strong partner engagement and a clear focus on commercial execution, we are confident in our strategy and the opportunity ahead. "As we move from technology validation towards customer programmes, qualification and scale-up, our focus remains on converting our technological leadership into commercial adoption and long-term shareholder value." Gelion also noted on Wednesday that it is winding down its Integration Solutions business and pursuing the sale of its Battery Minerals subsidiary to focus investment on sulfur cathode materials designed for use in existing battery manufacturing infrastructure.

artigo.texto: Long County weighs temporary moratorium on data center development Long County leaders are considering a temporary moratorium on future data center development. The discussion comes as data centers draw increasing scrutiny nationwide and neighboring Liberty County recently paused new data center applications in unincorporated areas for 120 days. Although no project is currently proposed in the county, Long County’s Planning and Zoning Commission discussed Monday night whether to recommend a temporary moratorium to county commissioners, who have the final say. “My concern is that Long County has not touched on this subject at all, and it’s becoming a hot button item,” said Lisa Ruise, with Long County Planning and Zoning. Ruise also expressed concern about the potential community response to a proposed data center. “I don’t think our community can withstand the drama and the anger and outrage that a possible data center would bring,” she said. However, some planning and zoning commissioners were not on board. One commission member said they were not ready to support a moratorium without first exploring whether data center development could provide additional revenue for the county. “I’m not saying yes or no, but I’m not willing to just go and put that stop light on this right now without looking into it,” the commissioner said. Questions about the county’s ability to support a large-scale facility also have emerged. “I personally do not believe we have the infrastructure, power, water or ground to be able to hold such possibilities,” said Long County resident Ramsey Sleevar, who attended the meeting Monday. “I don’t think it needs to be dead in the water, but it definitely needs to be in place where people can be more educated." The Planning and Zoning Commission is scheduled to hold a public hearing and vote on a proposed data center moratorium at its next meeting, Nov. 16. If the measure advances, it will go to county commissioners for final approval.

artigo.texto: Gelion PLC (AIM:GELN, OTC:GELNF, FRA:X0S) shares rose over 12% to 18p on Wednesday morning after the sulfur battery technology company reported that its £9.6 million pro forma cash balance and new partnerships with global automotive manufacturers strengthened its position to commercialise its battery technology. Gelion reported total income of £2.5 million for the year to 30 June 2026, down from £2.7 million a year earlier but 17.1% above analyst consensus, mainly reflecting government grants and research and development tax incentives. The adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation loss widened to £4.4 million from £4.1 million in the previous financial year, although it was 10.4% better than analyst consensus as the company continued investing in technology development, partnerships and commercialisation. Pro forma cash and cash equivalents stood at £9.6 million, with no debt, and were 21.1% above analyst consensus, providing funding for the next phase of development. Operational progress included expanded collaborations with TDK Corporation, QinetiQ UK, Nissan Technical Centre Europe and the University of Oxford, alongside development work on its nano-encapsulated sulfur technology, designed as a lower-cost alternative to critical minerals used in lithium-ion battery cathodes. After the financial year ended, Gelion signed a £2 million funded development and scale-up agreement with Mitsui Kinzoku and agreements with two major global automotive manufacturers to test its sulfur cathode technology for electric vehicle batteries. The company also reported that independent testing by the National Laboratory of the Rockies showed cells retained 92% of reference capacity at a 20-fold higher cycling rate, supporting further evaluation for defence, aerospace and drone applications. Chief executive Matt Wood said the company was moving from technology validation towards customer programmes, qualification and scale-up, with a focus on converting its technology into commercial adoption. Gelion said it had strengthened its intellectual property portfolio with six new patent grants across the US, Europe and Asia, and will hold an investor presentation on Thursday, 22 October.

artigo.texto: A U.K. homeowner shopping for battery storage got sticker shock after receiving a quote where the installation cost was about as much as the hardware. The homeowner wanted to add a Fogstar 32-kWh battery paired with a 6-kW inverter package, and they got a quote for £6,999. After finding what appeared to be the same hardware online for £3,995, the shopper turned to Reddit to ask whether the roughly £3,000 installation charge was standard. Here's what to know On Reddit, the homeowner said the plan was for a battery-only setup at a three-bedroom semi. They were aiming for a larger battery because a heat pump was expected to be installed. "I can see on the fogstar website that this combo is available for £3995 so a 3 grand installation cost feels steep?" the original poster wrote. One commenter joked, "Must be nice to make £3k for one days work." Battery storage can be one of the most effective ways to improve energy independence and keep a home better protected during outages. A system sized with a future heat pump in mind can also help cut energy costs by storing power for use when it is needed most. EnergySage has teamed up with electrification brand Qmerit to help homeowners get the best price on home battery storage solutions. A reply agreed the price looked elevated and focused on the system layout, saying, "It does seem a little bit high." More background Another Redditor offered a price comparison, writing, "I'm getting 2x16kwh fogstar with 6kw inverter for £4900." While that example does not represent an exact match, it gave the original poster a much lower installed price for roughly the same total storage capacity and inverter size. That led the OP to note that Equivolt also worked in their area, suggesting they should get another quote. Adding battery storage to a house is a major investment, and comparing options can have a meaningful impact on the experience. In this case, the homeowner went to Reddit and got a good lay of the land, but that is likely not enough in itself. What can be done? Getting multiple quotes from competing companies and understanding all the charges is important. Also, separating hardware costs from installation costs can make a quote easier to understand and compare. In this case, the homeowner was able to compare a £3,995 online bundle with a £6,999 installed quote, making the labor and other installation-related charges easier to examine. One clear takeaway is to gather more than one estimate. The original poster had initially been looking for a "sense check," and the shared quotes that commenters provided gave them a concrete baseline to pursue. artigo.texto: Pitt County to hold public hearing on data center moratorium GREENVILLE, N.C. (WITN) - Pitt County commissioners voted unanimously Monday night to schedule a public hearing on a proposed temporary moratorium on data centers. The hearing is set for Nov. 16. The vote followed a presentation by Pitt County Planning and Development Director Jonas Hill. Hill said a moratorium would give the county time to study the impact of data centers. He highlighted regulatory gaps including a lack of standards for electrical load infrastructure, low-frequency noise compliance and air quality from generators. “They use and consume a tremendous amount of water. There’s no standards for water usage in our current ordinance at all,” Hill said. Hill said current ordinances regarding data centers do not distinguish between small or hyperscale facilities. Hill said 24 counties in North Carolina currently have moratoriums on data centers, including Greene County and Wake County. Several residents spoke in favor of a data center moratorium at the meeting, saying it is important for county leaders to have enough time to make an informed decision. “Often it’s in community of color or working class communities because the billionaires impact these monstrous things. I think they can do that and get away with it because people might not know their rights,” Pitt County resident Don Cavellini said. Another resident, Zoey Dixon, said data centers pose environmental, social and employment threats. “I had nearly 10 years of tech experience. I am somebody who will not use AI, for example, and this has already cost me multiple job opportunities,” Dixon said. Copyright 2026 WITN. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Oct 21 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday that companies building data centers should pay a "dividend" to the communities where they are sited if they want to make the developments popular. "I have watched the process closely, and data centers that were highly unpopular in a certain area, have become extremely popular when a financial deal is struck," Trump said in a Truth Social post. Data centers fueling the rise of AI have become a political flashpoint in communities across the country given the high quantities of water and power they require, with opposition uniting voters across ideological lines. The Trump administration, which has prioritized rapid AI development to compete with China, has also noted the shifting voter sentiment. "New and large, in some cases gigantic, Data (centers) are mandated by me to make their own electricity, and give or sell any excess back to the local community, or grid," Trump said in his post. Trump said in February that major technology companies must build their own power plants for their data centers in order to protect consumers from rising bills. AI giant Anthropic and Elon Musk have laid out blueprints in recent days for sharing some of the spoils of the AI boom. The creator of Claude models said over the weekend it is committing 5% of its shares to a new fund for the "public good", while Musk pledged on Monday to give one SpaceX share to "every kid in America", arguing for such direct distributions as the burgeoning sector faces public scrutiny. (Reporting by Akanksha Khushi in Bengaluru; Editing by Tom Hogue and Jan Harvey)

artigo.texto: At an Oct. 13 meeting on a proposed data center, more than 200 residents crowded into Elizabeth Forward Middle School's auditorium in Elizabeth Township, Pa. Opposition emerged, petitions circulated, and Elizabeth Township officers escorted one attendee out after a disturbance. Here's what to know Commissioners were first approached in June about locating a possible data center at a power plant site, and the gathering at Elizabeth Forward Middle School was the township's first public move since then, according to the Mon Valley Independent. About 330 questions were submitted beforehand, and township resident Eric Piper condensed them into roughly four dozen for the discussion. According to the Mon Valley Independent, Bucks County developer Tim Hendricks, who said he has 35 years in real estate, is looking at a 550-acre Henderson Road site in the Buena Vista area next to the Youghiogheny River. Preliminary concepts presented at the meeting included 20 two-story buildings and stormwater basins. Hendricks said the development might generate $125 million in tax revenue for the township and school district and create 200 to 300 permanent jobs with salaries ranging from $60,000 to $100,000, according to the Mon Valley Independent. He also said residents' energy service would stay the same and that the facility would not emit pollutants. Key details were still unavailable. Asked by Commissioner Jim Benedek about expected electricity and water use, Hendricks said he did not want to offer figures until he had dependable information, according to the Mon Valley Independent. Residents also disputed the claim that nearby homes would be about 2,000 feet away, saying some properties across the river sit closer than that. More background To illustrate the site's scale, Piper said the property is about 2.5 times the size of Kennywood Park, while Hendricks said, according to the Mon Valley Independent, "There's hundreds of acres proposed that would not be built on out of the total. This is an evolving process. Things change as we get more information. As I start to get answers, we can update the plan to make it more usable and hopefully better for the community." Hendricks said he learned about the property from a colleague's brother, who had been exploring it for a possible solar project. He added that existing utility lines and earlier environmental cleanup made the site more appealing for redevelopment, according to the Mon Valley Independent. The debate arrives amid broader concerns about data centers, artificial intelligence, and pressure on the electric grid. Hendricks told the audience that people often view data centers only through the lens of AI, but said they also support ordinary online activity such as texting and streaming movies. Data centers can add computing capacity that helps optimize cleaner energy systems. Residents and local officials often focus on the tradeoffs, including heavy electricity demand, significant water use, security concerns, and the possibility that large new loads could strain local infrastructure and utility bills. Residents pressed environmental and quality-of-life concerns. Resident Candy Woy raised questions about wildlife at the site and possible environmental effects, while Mary Jane Carnahan, who identified herself as a Terrytown Drive neighbor, said underground mines and prolonged construction could disrupt daily life and reduce property values, according to the Mon Valley Independent. What's being done? For now, Hendricks said, the proposal is still at a very early stage. As of Oct. 13, nothing formal had been filed, and he said the concept would need many permits and approvals before it could move ahead, according to the Mon Valley Independent. He added that if construction ever happens, the eventual company behind the site would step into his role. According to the Mon Valley Independent, Hendricks said he is trying to place any data center as far from homes as possible and is still talking with gas providers while deciding whether the project fits the community. He told residents the plans would be revised further if the process continues. Residents are organizing their own response. Attendees signed anti-project petitions on the way in, and Megan McDonough, state director at Food and Water Watch, questioned whether public opposition would matter if commissioners were later asked to change zoning, according to the Mon Valley Independent. Protect Elizabeth Township has another town hall set for 6:30 p.m. Oct. 29 at Butler's Golf Course on Rock Run Road, featuring a speaker panel and opponents of data centers from other communities. Piper said, "This community is my home. My family has been in this township for nearly 100 years. I care about this community just as I know everyone in this room does. And whether you support this proposed development, oppose it or simply want to learn more, I believe we all have something in common. We want what's best for Elizabeth Township, and the people that call it home." Where can I learn more? What's happening in Elizabeth Township echoes fights in other communities over proposed data centers. artigo.texto: O RN não pode perder a corrida dos data centers No próximo dia 23, a FIERN sediará a Data Center Conference 2026, reunindo investidores, empresas de tecnologia, especialistas e autoridades em torno de um dos setores mais disputados da economia global. O momento não poderia ser mais oportuno para o Rio Grande do Norte. Enquanto a inteligência artificial amplia a demanda por processamento e armazenamento de dados em escala sem precedentes, estados brasileiros começam a definir suas estratégias para atrair um mercado que movimentará bilhões de reais nos próximos anos. Levantamento da consultoria Innova Assuntos Públicos identificou 20 projetos de lei relacionados a data centers em 11 assembleias legislativas entre 2025 e outubro de 2026. Dos projetos mapeados, nove possuem caráter restritivo, sete são favoráveis aos empreendimentos, dois combinam incentivos e exigências e dois são neutros. O que antes era visto quase exclusivamente como um tema restrito a uma parcela pequena da sociedade ganha impulso e chega aos legislativos com visões de mundo diferentes e mostra o quanto a temática ganha centralidade nas decisões dos governos daqui para a frente. Ceará e Goiás, os únicos a transformar propostas em legislação, optaram por oferecer previsibilidade regulatória. O Ceará criou um modelo de licenciamento escalonado de acordo com o porte e o potencial poluidor dos empreendimentos. Goiás combinou incentivos, zonas prioritárias e procedimentos simplificados. Em ambos os casos, a mensagem que deixam é que investimentos dessa magnitude procuram regras estáveis e segurança jurídica. O Rio Grande do Norte ainda não possui uma política ampla para atração de data centers, mas deu um passo importante ao aprovar, por meio do Conema, uma regulamentação específica para o licenciamento ambiental do setor. Ao estabelecer critérios conforme a potência instalada e diferenciar exigências de acordo com o sistema de refrigeração utilizado, o Estado sinaliza que compreende o momento, mas ainda precisa que o tema se consolide com uma legislação específica que dê a segurança jurídica para quem pretende investir. Essa discussão ganha importância adicional diante da reforma tributária. Durante décadas, a disputa por investimentos esteve associada aos incentivos de ICMS. Esse instrumento perderá relevância nos próximos anos. A vantagem competitiva passará a depender de fatores mais duradouros, como rapidez no licenciamento, segurança energética, disponibilidade hídrica e qualidade da infraestrutura. Em outras palavras, os estados deixarão de competir por benefícios fiscais e a previsibilidade do licenciamento e regras relacionadas à água e à energia terão mais relevância. Às empresas também cabe entrarem cedo nesses debates, com dados e diálogo com as comunidades locais para a construção de regras mais favoráveis, mostrando a importância desses investimentos para o desenvolvimento do Estado. A liderança na geração eólica, o crescimento da energia solar, os projetos de hidrogênio verde e a posição estratégica na agenda da transição energética colocam o RN em uma situação privilegiada. A Data Center Conference será uma excelente oportunidade para fazer esse debate de forma madura. O RN precisa definir a estratégia. Porque, na economia digital, os investimentos tendem a chegar primeiro aos lugares que sabem exatamente o que querem. Os que se planejam costumam colher os resultados antes dos demais. Quem hesitar correrá o risco de assistir ao futuro passar pela janela.

artigo.texto: Snyder outlines plans for 7th term, addresses data center ad Incumbent discusses school funding and data center regulations ahead of Nov. 3 election WAUSAU, Wis. (WSAW) -Representative Pat Snyder says he has a plan in mind if he is reelected to a seventh term representing the 85th District, which covers Wausau and Weston. School funding Snyder has previously worked in the Assembly to get more funding for special education departments at public schools. That effort did not pass. Snyder said he is confident it will pass if he can bring it back to the state Assembly if reelected. Snyder and his opponent, John Kroll, agree there should be more funding for public schools. Snyder said there needs to be a plan in place and that the policy should not be generalized. “When they say fully funded, they don’t ever have a number of what fully, because I asked the three when we had our executive session, what is fully funded? Well, just enough to make sure everything’s covered. We got to have a number because the taxpayers would like to know,” Snyder said. Data centers Snyder’s view on data centers differs from Kroll’s. While Kroll does not want data centers, Snyder said they are an inevitability given how much media is consumed. Snyder said that does not mean he is against regulations and protecting Wisconsin’s nature. He said local governments have been doing the right thing by making data centers follow their set rules. “If you do come in, get the local control taken care of, it has to be enclosed water and it has to be your own generation. You bring your power and you can’t put the excess or taxpayers to be anywhere troubled by that,” Snyder said. Response to political ad One political ad running against Snyder says he gave $2 million to a data center near Milwaukee. Snyder said that is not true. He said when utility rates go up, the Public Service Commission sets and approves the rate increases, not legislators. “When they say that I gave $2 million for Microsoft down in Southeast Wisconsin, that was the 2023 budget that Governor Evers signed and passed. He could have vetoed that,” Snyder said. Snyder helped propose a bill that would put restrictions on data centers in 2025. He originally voted no. Amendments included an AI review council, which earned his yes vote. Snyder said technology growth should be possible in Wisconsin, but done in a responsible and controlled way. artigo.texto: Wisconsin regulators will conduct a full statewide review of the environmental impacts of data center development under a legal deal reached among environmental groups, a data center developer and the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources. The settlement reached Friday stems from a lawsuit filed in July by Midwest Environmental Advocates, or MEA, on behalf of Sierra Club against the DNR in Ozaukee County Circuit Court. The DNR, Sierra Club and Denver-based Vantage Data Centers signed off on the deal. The groups sued over the agency’s decision to issue permits for the $15 billion Lighthouse data center campus in Port Washington without conducting an environmental impact statement. The project is being developed by Vantage Data Centers and tech companies Oracle and OpenAI to expand capacity for artificial intelligence, or AI. Under the deal, the DNR will conduct a strategic analysis of the anticipated build-out of AI data centers and associated infrastructure to power them under current plans and projections. The review will analyze the direct, indirect and cumulative effects of the buildout on the state’s agriculture, air and water quality, climate, energy, economy, cultural resources and more. MEA attorney Michael Greif said the DNR approached environmental groups about settling the lawsuit by either agreeing to an environmental impact statement for the Port Washington project or a broader statewide review of data centers. “That second option was really exciting to Sierra Club because it would provide a holistic, comprehensive look at the environmental impacts and the financial impacts of these AI data centers on the state and on communities, and that’s something that very few states have done across the country,” Greif said. In July, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul enacted the nation’s first statewide moratorium on data centers while the state reviews their effects on the environment and energy use. The deal reached Friday among the DNR, groups and Vantage does not pause permitting of data center projects while the state completes its review. “That’s something that the next governor certainly could put in place, and I think that’s something that would be the right approach for the state,” Greif added. Crowley supports ‘pause’ in development during yearlong review Democratic candidate for governor David Crowley said in a statement that he would support halting new data center projects while the environmental analysis is taking place. Understanding Wisconsin, Together. WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter. “David Crowley has been clear that he doesn’t believe we should move forward with any new projects until firm guardrails are in place. As governor, he will work with the legislature to pause development until the review is complete and the new guardrails are in place,” a Crowley campaign spokesperson said. Both Crowley and Republican Tom Tiffany have called for new standards or guardrails before any new data centers move forward. A spokesperson for Tiffany’s campaign said Tiffany has consistently said there should be no new data centers without five standards that include ending subsidies for data centers and barring non-disclosure agreements. “Under my administration, the DNR will hold every proposed project to Wisconsin’s environmental standards before a permit is issued, ensuring our water, land, and natural resources are protected. If a project doesn’t meet these standards or the local community doesn’t support it, it will not move forward,” Tiffany said on his website. Tiffany’s spokesperson did not address the new statewide environmental analysis announced in the legal settlement. Vantage will pay all costs tied to the strategic statewide analysis A Vantage spokesperson said it supports a thoughtful, fact-based discussion about responsible data center development and has agreed to fund all costs tied to the strategic statewide analysis led by the DNR. “The analysis will examine the environmental and economic considerations associated with data center development, providing policymakers and communities with additional information as the state considers the industry’s continued growth,” said Mark Freeman, Vantage’s vice president of global marketing. The DNR will retain sole control over the review, and the agency will have full authority to determine whether any future application or project complies with state laws. The DNR must complete its strategic analysis by Jan. 31, 2028, according to the deal. A DNR spokesperson said late Monday that the statewide analysis will be an important tool to understand impacts and inform future policy decisions. “We are also pleased that, under a negotiated settlement agreement with Sierra Club and Vantage, the DNR will be able to conduct the independent strategic analysis at no additional cost to Wisconsin taxpayers,” the agency said. The DNR must seek public comment and hold one or more public hearings on the analysis, and it will include summaries of the effects of data center development on energy bills. Under the settlement, permits for the Lighthouse data center campus will remain valid, and further environmental review of those approvals is not required. Ward said the deal is an opportunity to ensure the state understands the impacts of projects, including future phases of the Port Washington campus. Sierra Club will withdraw its petition for a contested case hearing on the agency’s decision, but the DNR will provide records requested by environmental groups. artigo.texto: October 21, 2026 Introduction Critics often argue that data centers bring large buildings and heavy power demand but few jobs, and on its face the argument is easy to accept.[i] A finished hyperscale campus can run with a relatively small permanent staff.[ii] Yet a count of the people working inside a finished facility captures only a fraction of the sector’s economic footprint. Before a campus opens, electricians, ironworkers, and engineers spend years building it, and specialized manufacturers supply the power and cooling equipment that runs it.[iii] Once it opens, operators buy electricity, maintenance, and security from Iowa businesses and replace servers and other hardware every few years.[iv] That activity matters more in Iowa than in most states. Iowa ranks among the Midwest’s leaders in data center capacity, both in facilities already operating and in projects still in development.[v] National research finds that counties with data centers see “positive effects on total employment, construction employment, establishments, payroll, tax returns, adjusted gross income, and wages.”[vi] This report estimates how much Iowa employment, income, and output these data center lifecycles support. It first documents the size, location, and development of Iowa’s data center sector. It then estimates the direct investment owners and operators have made to date and have announced for the coming years. Common Sense Institute then uses the Regional Economic Models, Inc. (REMI) Tax-PI+ model to simulate the direct, indirect, and induced effects of two phases of spending—construction and initial equipment, and ongoing operations and equipment replacement. Finally, the report opens the door to future CSI research on the sector’s tax impacts, community investments, and resource demands. Key Findings - Data center owners and operators have invested or announced at least $53 billion in Iowa buildings and equipment through 2031 (table 1). - Investments in Iowa data centers to date total an estimated $15.1 billion, or about $4,700 for every Iowan. - Announced investments from 2027 through 2031 would add an additional $38.0 billion. At an average of $7.6 billion per year, these direct investments represent roughly 2.8% of Iowa’s current annual GDP. - Ongoing operating and replacement spending totaled an estimated $4.4 billion in 2026, and announced projects would add about $10.6 billion a year by 2031. - Announced construction and initial equipment purchases would support about 12,775 jobs by 2031, counting direct, indirect, and induced effects. - From 2027 through 2031, they would add about $10.4 billion to GDP and $6.3 billion to personal income (table 3). - The ongoing operations of Iowa’s data centers produce more sustained jobs and more economic activity than their initial construction. - Operations at existing data centers support an estimated 12,647 Iowa jobs in 2026, or nearly three jobs for every direct job (tables 4 and 6). - Once operating, announced projects would support about 29,597 jobs in 2031. From 2027 through 2031, they would add about $18.5 billion to GDP and $9.0 billion to personal income (table 4). - Job gains reach well beyond technology, to electricians, construction workers, retail workers, teachers, and motor vehicle operators (table 5). - Data centers pay more than other employers for the same job titles, from 12% more for security officers to almost 100% more for electrical engineers (figure 4). - Average annual pay in the industry that includes data centers reached $125,759 in 2025, nearly double the $63,469 average for all Iowa workers. - Relative to its population, Iowa is the Midwest’s data center leader, with more operating capacity per resident than any other state in the region (figure 1). - Iowa’s data centers have 71.8 megawatts (MW) of operating capacity per 100,000 residents. Megawatts measure how much electricity a facility can draw at once, which is the most reliable gauge of a data center’s size. - Iowa ranks second in the Midwest in total operating capacity (2,324 MW), behind only Ohio. Including planned projects, it ranks fourth in total capacity and second per capita, behind only Indiana. - Iowa’s data center sector is on track to more than triple in size by 2031 (table 1). - Announced projects would add 5,257 MW to today’s 2,324 MW of operating capacity in about five years. Building what exists today took more than two decades (figure 3). Iowa’s Data Center Landscape This section describes Iowa’s data center sector and what its jobs pay. It begins with the size, location, and development of the state’s data center facilities and compares Iowa with the rest of the Midwest. It then compares pay at data centers with pay at other employers. Iowa’s Data Center Facilities Figure 1 displays the combined operating and planned data center capacity, measured in megawatts, for each of the 12 Midwest states, ranked from smallest to largest total capacity. Operating capacity—facilities already in service—is shown in blue at the base of each bar. Planned capacity, representing projects in development or under construction, is shown in red above it. Cleanview provides the data.[vii] Planned capacity figures for all states are a snapshot. Additional projects will likely be announced or finalized in the coming years, which would raise total planned megawatts across the region. At the same time, these figures assume no currently planned projects are canceled or indefinitely delayed. Figure 1. Only Ohio, Indiana, and Illinois rank higher, at 25,759 MW, 16,837 MW, and 9,962 MW, respectively, and all three have much larger economies. Iowa stands out more on operating capacity alone. artigo.texto: A First Nation community in Canada is using a data center to preserve its heritage The Wiikwemkoong First Nation in Canada is using a data center to help preserve its heritage The Wiikwemkoong First Nation in Canada is using a data center to help preserve its heritage. The data center on the Wiikwemkoong Unceded Territory in rural Ontario stores digital files, including Anishinaabe language videos. Chief Tim Ominika emphasizes the importance of protecting the community's language and data. The idea of digital sovereignty has gained momentum in places like Europe, where leaders are wary of the widespread influence of American Big Tech. For the Wiikwemkoong First Nation and other Indigenous communities, it is also about asserting authority over their own information after historically being excluded from its collection and use by colonizers. WIIKWEMKOONG UNCEDED TERRITORY, Ontario (AP) — For thousands of years, Indigenous peoples have passed down their traditions and culture through oral storytelling. Now, a Canadian Indigenous community is using a data center to help preserve its heritage. The Wiikwemkoong Unceded Territory in rural Ontario installed a small data center as it modernized its recordkeeping systems. Among the digital files it holds are video recordings of Anishinaabe speaking their native language. “Our language is one of the biggest things that most First Nations across the country are losing,” said Wiikwemkoong Chief Tim Ominika. “We will have our knowledge keepers, our language speakers who may be moving on to the spirit world, but their legacy is still going to be protected for many years to come by having our own data systems in place and protecting that.” The idea of digital sovereignty has gained momentum in places like Europe, where leaders are wary of the widespread influence of American Big Tech. For the Wiikwemkoong First Nation and other Indigenous communities, it is also about asserting authority over their own information after historically being excluded from its collection and use by colonizers. About the size of a single-car garage, the data center installed last year also stores the community's corporate documents, health data for residents, and security camera footage. “The purpose of all of this is having the ownership, access, control and possession of our information,” Ominika said. It’s about preventing anyone else from “having authority or setting their guidelines on what they could do with our data.” The First Nation has been transferring all its information from a Microsoft data center in Toronto, about 190 miles (305 kilometers) south, said Michael McCormick, the community’s chief technical officer. Other Indigenous communities have been taking an interest Wiikwemkoong is on the eastern end of Manitoulin Island in Lake Huron, an area that attracts visitors with its rugged wilderness, extensive waterways and Anishinaabe cultural offerings. The reserve prides itself on being Canada’s only “unceded territory,” because it never signed a treaty surrendering its land. The data center, which underpins a modernization of Wiikwemkoong’s administrative services, also has paved the way for new public safety infrastructure, including a drone fleet and a network of surveillance cameras. A backup data center on the mainland and public Wi-Fi transmitters are also planned for the community of about 4,000 people. The chief declined to disclose how much is being spent on the projects. Improvements to data storage gained urgency after a flood in 2022 resulted in the loss of some of its digital records, which had been scattered in various offices. “That information is very important to us. And in order to protect it, keep it safe, we said ’Why can’t we not look at developing and creating and implementing our own data sovereignty program?'” Ominika said. Wiikwemkoong’s upgrade program is among the first for Indigenous communities in Canada that include First Nations, Inuit and Métis. Delegations from other Indigenous communities in Ontario and neighboring Manitoba have come to check out the project, McCormick said. The chief said he has to explain to visitors that their data center is not like the giant ones relied on by artificial intelligence companies that require vast amounts of land and water. Wiikwemkoong's data center sits in a secure bunker next to the administrative office, accessed by a facial recognition scanner. Its four racks of computer servers are cooled by a pair of fans — not water — and it has “a relatively small carbon footprint,” McCormick said. In the U.S., a few Native American tribes like the Navajo Nation have for years been operating their own data centers for local infrastructure services. Wiikwemkoong's data center is believed to be the only one on Indigenous territory in Canada, but McCormick said other Indigenous leaders are increasingly savvy about control of their data. The Chiefs of Ontario, which represents 133 First Nations in the province, held a data sovereignty conference earlier this year that included a panel on AI and data centers. For generations, Indigenous communities worldwide have had no say in how information on them has been collected, interpreted and held by governments, researchers and institutions, said Carmen Jones, director of research and data management for the Chiefs of Ontario. “As more information is collected and stored, it is critical that First Nations determine how that data is accessed, managed, and used,” she said. The technology has addressed some issues — and raised new ones Amid the island's natural splendor, the community faces its share of problems that community leaders hope the technology can help address. Since installing the data center, McCormick’s team has added 700 surveillance cameras around the community, and a dozen drone docking stations on the administrative office’s rooftop housing a fleet of DJI drones. artigo.texto: CATL bets on battery swapping for heavy trucks with Tianxing II CATL unveils its Tianxing II heavy-truck range and argues for battery swapping on long-haul routes, while the Qiji station network remains to be built. CATL (Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Limited), listed in Shenzhen and Hong Kong and described as the world's largest maker of batteries for electric vehicles, unveiled its Tianxing II (å¤©è¡II) heavy-truck range on October 20, 2026. The group used the occasion to defend battery swapping as the preferred route to electrifying long-distance freight. The principle is simple: rather than recharging the battery while the truck sits idle, the haulier replaces it at a station with a full one in a few minutes. The battery sector is also driving projects in Europe, such as the construction of battery parks in Bydgoszcz by Tavion. A range tailored to different markets The range also carries an international name, Tectrans II, and varies by market. The version for the global market emphasizes very high-power charging, while the Chinese presentation, led by Gao Huan, chief technology officer of CATL's passenger car and commercial vehicle division for China, puts swapping first. CATL's heavy-truck swapping offer is called Qiji (éªéª¥) and covers swap blocks, stations and a cloud platform. The Chinese range includes batteries mounted behind the cab, suited to converting diesel trucks, and batteries placed under the chassis, including a very large-capacity version aimed at long-distance haulage. It also features a new two-battery configuration. In this setup, a large swappable battery, leased rather than purchased, provides most of the traction, while a small fixed battery, permanently installed on the truck, takes over when the large battery is nearly empty. According to information relayed after the event, leasing of the large battery would be billed on energy charged, with no unit price published to date. CATL says this configuration is already in production and that commitments covering a significant number of vehicles have been signed. Arguments put forward by the company CATL justifies its choice on physical grounds: faster charging requires higher currents, which generate more heat, so swapping would be the only route to maximum refueling efficiency. This is the company's position; it also sells a global version based on very high-power charging, and it does not reflect an industry consensus. In support of swapping, CATL cites a total cost of ownership, meaning the combined purchase and operating costs of a vehicle, lower than diesel's, as well as operating savings. These estimates rest on mileage assumptions specific to CATL, and the savings announced have changed from one presentation to another, on different bases. Deployment requires building a network of stations. Yang Jun, head of CATL's swapping business and CEO of Qiji Energy (æ¶ä»£éªéª¥), the group's heavy-truck swapping subsidiary, oversees this activity. Qiji's technology relies on "under-chassis" swapping, while Qiyuan Green Power (å¯æºè¯å¨å), an operator of swapping networks, favors "rear-mounted" swapping, with the battery behind the cab. CATL is becoming the top shareholder of Qiyuan Green Power, whose seller is China Power International Development, a subsidiary of the state-owned group State Power Investment Corporation.

artigo.texto: O Google e sua parceira Xcel Energy afirmam que seu projeto de data center de 780 megawatts em Minnesota ajudará a modernizar a rede elétrica com fontes de energia mais limpas, sem transferir o ônus dos custos de infraestrutura para os clientes existentes. No entanto, especialistas dizem que grande parte dessa expansão poderia ser evitada e alertam que as empresas de energia têm um incentivo financeiro para construir continuamente mais infraestrutura. A corrida para fornecer energia a centros de dados com inteligência artificial está remodelando a rede elétrica dos EUA. Se há algo em que a maioria dos americanos concorda, é que eles não querem um centro de dados perto de onde moram. Uma pesquisa da Gallup realizada em março de 2026 revelou que 71% dos americanos se opõem à construção de data centers em suas localidades. A principal preocupação era o consumo de energia. Enquanto isso, de acordo com uma pesquisa do Pew Research Center realizada entre julho e agosto, metade dos entrevistados acreditava que os data centers teriam um impacto negativo no meio ambiente e nos custos de energia das famílias. Atualmente, o Google aposta que um centro de dados de IA em grande escala pode ajudar a financiar uma rede elétrica mais limpa e confiável. O acordo que está propondo com a Xcel Energy inclui a adição de capacidade proveniente de sistemas de energia eólica, solar e de armazenamento em baterias — totalizando mais energia do que o centro de dados deverá consumir. Nos termos deste acordo, o Google subsidiará o custo dessa energia adicional e continuará pagando mesmo que não utilize toda a eletricidade fornecida. Pine Island, uma pequena cidade com cerca de 4.000 habitantes, localizada a uma hora a sudeste de Minneapolis, é onde o Google espera que seu projeto de data center de 780 megawatts receba apoio da comunidade local. Ao mesmo tempo, este projeto também aproxima o Google de sua meta de operar inteiramente com zero emissões de carbono, 24 horas por dia, 7 dias por semana, até 2030. O Google, cujo negócio de serviços em nuvem dá suporte direto ao seu próprio modelo de IA Gemini, viu sua receita no segundo trimestre atingir quase US$ 25 bilhões (um aumento de 82% em relação ao ano anterior), afirmando ter encontrado o modelo certo para isso. O Google planeja financiar a adição de 1.400 megawatts de energia eólica, 200 megawatts de energia solar e 300 megawatts de armazenamento em baterias à rede da Xcel. A capacidade total dessas fontes adicionais supera em muito as necessidades do próprio data center; segundo o Google, isso ocorre porque a energia eólica e solar não conseguem gerar eletricidade continuamente. A Xcel Energy afirmou que essa nova fonte de energia atenderá a todos os clientes da região, não apenas ao Google. A Xcel também afirmou que essas melhorias contribuirão para aumentar o fornecimento de energia livre de carbono para a rede elétrica local. O acordo proposto entre o Google e a Xcel inclui cláusulas relativas a taxas mínimas de demanda e multas por rescisão. O Google afirma que esses termos garantem que a empresa continue responsável pelo pagamento da infraestrutura construída especificamente para ela, mesmo com a diminuição do interesse em inteligência artificial. O Google se compromete a pagar por pelo menos 75% da capacidade contratada, independentemente do consumo real; além disso, caso rescinda o contrato unilateralmente antes do prazo, deverá pagar uma multa equivalente à taxa mínima de demanda por até oito anos. Segundo Amanda Rome, vice-presidente executiva e chefe de relações com o cliente da Xcel Energy, ninguém quer investir em grandes obras de construção para depois se deparar com a falta de mercado para a eletricidade gerada e de quem a pagar. É exatamente por isso que essas medidas de segurança são necessárias. O acordo entre o Google e a Xcel Energy aguarda atualmente a aprovação da Comissão de Serviços Públicos do Estado de Minnesota. Os centros de dados estão impulsionando uma expansão sem precedentes da infraestrutura energética. De acordo com as previsões da North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC), os novos centros de dados serão responsáveis pela maior parte do aumento projetado na demanda de eletricidade na próxima década. Sob a gestão do ex-presidente Joe Biden, o Departamento de Energia declarou que mais de 70% das linhas de transmissão e transformadores nos EUA estão em operação há pelo menos 25 anos. O departamento também observou que, para atender à demanda futura com o custo mais otimizado, o sistema nacional de transmissão de energia precisa dobrar de tamanho até 2050. No entanto, os operadores de centros de dados de grande escala argumentam que podem fornecer o financiamento necessário para modernizar a rede elétrica, tornando-a também mais limpa e confiável. Amanda Peterson Corio, diretora global de energia e eletricidade do Google, acredita que o momento desta revolução industrial é particularmente oportuno, já que a empresa precisa de capital para modernizar sua infraestrutura obsoleta nos Estados Unidos. Será que os centros de dados podem utilizar a rede elétrica existente sem modificações? Jigar Shah, sócio da Multiplier, uma consultoria que auxilia startups de energia limpa em suas ofertas públicas iniciais (IPOs), sugere que os operadores de centros de dados poderiam construir instalações menores em locais onde a rede elétrica existente possui capacidade excedente. Essa abordagem minimizaria a necessidade de novas construções e os custos de investimento em novos equipamentos de geração ou transmissão de energia. Shah argumentou que a integração da crescente demanda por eletricidade dos centros de dados na rede elétrica existente reduziria significativamente os custos de eletricidade para todos os outros usuários. Ele citou a colaboração entre o Google e a Xcel em Minnesota como um excelente exemplo de como os centros de dados podem servir de catalisadores para novas tecnologias mais ecológicas. Segundo o jornal VNA/News and

artigo.texto: Is battery storage the quick fix for apparel’s energy crisis? Battery energy storage systems could offer Bangladesh’s apparel industry a rapid path to energy security. However, the government must ensure affordable financing for factory installations If you ask anyone in Bangladesh's apparel industry what the sector needs most to survive and thrive in the years ahead, you will hear the same answer, almost without exception: energy security. The urgency is not hypothetical. A recent survey of 134 knitwear factories found that 55% had seen buyers cancel or cut orders because of gas and power shortages since late August. Across the sector, energy shortfalls are cutting output by as much as 25–30%, and the diesel needed to keep backup generators running now comes at a heavy premium. Let me be fair to those in charge. The government has been doing its best through careful rationing and prioritisation of available energy to keep the apparel industry, and industry at large, running without interruption. Entrepreneurs, for their part, are managing somehow. But managing somehow is not the same as operating smoothly. Flawless operations, the kind global buyers expect when they place their orders, require a steady supply of energy that is simply not available at the moment. So, what is the solution? The permanent answer is, of course, a long-term one. According to media reports, there has been little meaningful effort to explore domestic gas reserves over the past 17 years. Even if exploration began today, it would take a minimum of 10 to 20 years for that gas to reach our factories. We cannot ask the country's largest formal employer to wait two decades. Nor are we alone. The energy crisis is a global one, driven by turmoil in the Middle East, and the world's more forward-thinking economies are not waiting either. One quick solution they are turning to is the battery energy storage system, or BESS. What remains missing is access to finance. Few manufacturers, battered by falling orders and rising costs, can commit nearly a million dollars upfront. If the government were to extend financing directly to manufacturers — interest-free or at a low rate — installation could be completed within two to three months. No other measure on the table offers relief this quickly. The case for BESS has never been stronger. An all-inclusive turnkey system now costs around $135–165 per kWh globally, down from more than $380 per kWh as recently as 2022. A typical 5 MWh industrial system, suitable for a large apparel factory in Bangladesh, costs roughly $900,000, all-inclusive. The technology has matured, too. Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) chemistry now dominates industrial storage, valued for its safety and long cycle life. A system typically lasts 10–15 years, or 6,000 to more than 9,000 cycles. With periodic augmentation, it can continue delivering power for 15–20 years. I do not speak merely as an observer. At 4A Yarn Dyeing, we have never relied on a single energy source, and our rooftop solar and backup systems have helped us absorb rising costs. Even so, more expensive diesel has increased 4A's production costs by 2–3%. If a factory with multiple backup systems feels the squeeze, one can only imagine the strain on those without them. Here, the government deserves credit for a far-sighted move. The FY2026-27 budget has removed import duties, VAT and other taxes on BESS and solar equipment until 2031 and set the corporate tax rate at 0% for solar power generation until 2035. With diesel costly and outages frequent, these incentives have made the payback period shorter and the post-tax returns on BESS more attractive than they were even a year ago. What remains missing is access to finance. Few manufacturers, battered by falling orders and rising costs, can commit nearly a million dollars upfront. If the government were to offer financing directly to manufacturers, interest-free or at a low rate, installation could be completed within two to three months. No other measure on the table offers relief this quickly. We are well aware that the economy is currently facing a cash crunch. Nevertheless, since assuming office, the government has shown a clear willingness to support industry, and rightly so, because the only way to strengthen the economy is to help its industries grow. For example, Bangladesh Bank has rolled out a Tk60,000 crore stimulus package specifically aimed at reviving closed, sick and underutilised industrial and service-sector enterprises. It is a well-intentioned initiative. If even a portion of that fund were made available for BESS installation at existing, operational factories, the impact would be immediate. Reviving closed factories carries considerable risk, and the benefits will take time to materialise. By contrast, existing factories struggling to survive today could not only stay afloat by overcoming the energy crisis but also double or even triple their capacity in the years ahead. This is not an argument against long-term energy planning. Domestic exploration must begin in earnest, and renewable energy capacity must continue to grow. But the long term will mean little if our factories cannot survive the short term. Bangladesh's apparel industry has weathered far greater storms over four decades, and each time, it has come back stronger. With the right financial support at the right moment, it can do so again and, in doing so, give the wider economy the strength it needs to grow. Abdullah Hil Nakib is the Deputy Managing Director of Team Group. artigo.texto: Cincinnati residents voice data center concerns as city leaders provide zoning update City leaders are studying new zoning rules for data centers as residents raise concerns about their potential effects on local communities, utility costs and the environment. Dozens of people attended a public forum Monday in Walnut Hills to discuss how Cincinnati should regulate future development. While no large-scale facility has been proposed, officials said they want rules in place before an application is submitted. “Is that what Ohio wants to be known for? Is that what Cincinnati wants to be known for?” Over-the-Rhine resident Cayley Baker asked. Residents questioned where data centers could be built and how their heavy water and electricity use might affect ratepayers. Robert McCracken of Cincinnati’s Office of Environment and Sustainability anticipated increases costs but called for protections to keep costs down. “How can the state and Public Utilities Commission look at rules that pass on the costs to the end user, the data center, and not to us?” said Ohio ranks among the top states for data center facilities. About 28 are operating in the Greater Cincinnati area, including smaller-scale sites such as CyrusOne. Cincinnati has imposed a moratorium preventing data center construction within city limits until February 2027 while officials consider zoning regulations. Baker called the process an important first step but said residents must hold city leaders accountable. “Time will tell if the city will help developers feet to the fire," she said. "I think city members do a lot of talk but when it comes down to holding people accountable and making real changes, words are cheap."

artigo.texto: Sepco wins Saudi 500MW/2,000MWh BESS project contract The project is being developed by a consortium of French energy major Engie and Saudi group Haji Abdullah Alireza & Co The Saudi Arabia Group 1-KSB Independent Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) project has been secured by Shandong Electric Power Construction Corporation (Sepco). The project is said to form part of the Kingdom’s first wave of large-scale battery energy storage projects. The Al Khushaybi Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) project has a planned capacity of 500MW/2,000MWh. It supports Saudi Arabia’s energy transition ambitions under Vision 2030, particularly the development of energy storage infrastructure to complement its expanding renewable energy capacity. The project is being developed by a consortium of French energy major Engie and Saudi group Haji Abdullah Alireza & Co. The Saudi Power Procurement Company (SPPC) is the offtaker for the project, which is mainly aimed at strengthening grid flexibility and supporting the integration of renewable energy into Saudi Arabia’s power system, said a report. Upon completion and commissioning, the BESS facility will help balance electricity supply and demand by storing energy during periods of lower demand and discharging it when demand increases, it added. The project is expected to improve grid stability, enhance the resilience of electricity supply, and support the integration of solar and wind power into the national grid.

artigo.texto: Almost everyone agrees that data centers should pay their fair share — even data center developers. The newest proposal out of Congress poses the question: What’s fair? Congress has put forward its most aggressive proposal yet to protect electricity prices from massive new data center developments. The bipartisan permitting reform bill would allow utilities to charge data centers more than other customers for using the grid and would let states charge data centers more on top of that. “I think policymakers are seeing an opportunity for a good deal to take place here between extremely wealthy technology companies and regular everyday consumers, where the technology companies put many tens of billions of dollars into the power system to pay for the upgrade and keep the costs off of everybody else,” said Rob Gramlich, president of Grid Strategies, a firm that focuses on integrating clean energy into the power grid. The bill errs on the side of “over-collection,” Gramlich said, meaning data centers could pay more than their impact on the system and effectively subsidize other customers. Trending So far, major data center developers seem to be on board — though as negotiations continue things could change. “There are many devils in the details,” Gramlich said. “Regulators at the state and federal levels will have a lot of work to do.” The data center provisions in the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would change a longstanding federal policy that allows utilities to charge customers only one of two costs: the general “embedded” costs of operating on the energy grid or the “incremental” cost of any grid upgrades necessary to serve a new project. Utilities usually only charge customers the embedded cost of operating on the grid, Gramlich said. Incremental costs are difficult to calculate and can vary widely based on the kinds of grid upgrades that are needed at the time a new customer is coming onboard. Data centers, cryptocurrency miners and other “high-density computing facilities” would be subject to both of those costs together under the bill. Awhite paper created for utility company Exelon Corporation earlier this year found that data centers could still shift costs onto other customers if they were only charged the “incremental” costs without the continued embedded cost charges. The bill would also require data centers and similar facilities to provide financial guarantees before the grid is upgraded and to continue paying grid costs even if they abandon projects early. The bill also notes that states could charge data center customers extra, beyond the incremental and embedded grid costs, using the proceeds as rebates for others on the grid. It also tells states they could choose which projects can connect to the grid first based on how much extra money they’re willing to spend to subsidize other customers. The idea of data center developers paying for the cost of upgrading the grid for their projects has been widely embraced; several of the data center provisions in the permitting bill seem directly related to President Donald Trump’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge. But past attempts to avoid shifting data center costs onto the general public have included only voluntary commitments. The permitting bill would turn that directive into law. Despite the new potential costs, the data center and AI industries have been quiet and moderately supportive of the permitting reform bill, highlighting the support for energy and infrastructure projects from the bill as a whole. Staci Pies, senior vice president of government affairs and policy at Incompas, an AI infrastructure association, said data center companies have “been very clear” that they will bear appropriate costs. “They’ll contribute their fair share of whatever kind of incremental infrastructure costs are necessary in order to increase and upgrade the grid,” she said. But, she added, the costs and analysis “needs to be transparent” — particularly if states decide to charge data centers above the embedded and incremental costs. “In some instances data centers are going to say ‘we’re willing to live by this additional charge so long as it’s transparent and we understand the implications.’ And in other instances, they may not,” she said. OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta didn’t respond to requests for comment on whether they supported the bill’s data center provisions. Lobbying disclosures show the Data Center Coalition spent $480,000 on lobbying between July and September, including on the permitting reform bill. Michele Nellenbach, vice president of federal affairs at the Data Center Coalition, said the organization was still reviewing details of the bill and noted members were “investing hundreds of billions of dollars in the U.S. annually to build America’s digital infrastructure.” Some progressives have aired concerns that the bill as a whole would amount to a giveaway for data centers because of the easing of environmental laws and the provisions to limit legal challenges to projects. At the same time, there’s been concern that the proposed changes amount to overcharging data centers for grid connection. Travis Fisher, director of energy and environmental policy studies at the libertarian Cato Institute, wrote the bill’s data center provisions risk “shifting costs in the opposite direction,” which, he says, might be necessary to counter the opposition to AI infrastructure developments. Over the course of the last year, data center development has faced an incredible rise in political pushback. Communities across the country have rallied against the centers being built in their backyards out of fear of higher utility costs, pollution and other concerns. Data center developers have responded by leveling up efforts to sweeten the deal for communities. artigo.texto: (The Center Square) – Companies operating data centers should be the ones that pay for upgrades to the electric grid, most voters say according to a new poll. The Center Square Voters’ Voice Poll found that 66% of voters believe that data center companies should be paying for the increased power demand and infrastructure required to get that electricity to the data centers. Fourteen percent of those registered to vote say the costs of the upgrades should be shared by both data center companies and the public while 8% believe the upgrades are the responsibility of federal, state or local taxpayers and 6% believe that all electricity customers should pay for the upgrades. Another 6% said they were unsure who should pay. The results come from a survey conducted by Noble Predictive Insights from Oct. 5-7 that polled registered voters nationally via opt-in online panel and text-to-web cell phone messages. The sample included 2,527 respondents comprised of 1,011 Republicans, 1,011 Democrats, and 505 Independents. Among independent voters, 220 respondents were classified as true independents, which are individuals who do not lean toward either major party when given the choice. The margin of error is +/- 1.95%. The cost of electricity infrastructure to power data centers has been debated across the country as more energy sources are required as well as new transmission lines and power storage equipment. The U.S. House of Representatives nearly unanimously passed the Ratepayer Protection Act in September before it failed in the Senate on a 57-43 vote. The bill would have required state public utility commissioners “commence consideration” of implementing rules that would protect ordinary ratepayers within one year of the bill becoming law. President Donald Trump announced a Ratepayer Protection Pledge along with several hyper-scale data operators in 2025 with a goal of preventing Americans from paying for rising electricity costs associated with increased demand from data centers. The pledge states that companies including Amazon, xAI, Oracle, Microsoft, Meta, Google and OpenAI will pay for the new electricity generation and grid infrastructure needed to accommodate new data centers.

artigo.texto: ABDC pede corte de 90% no ICMS e cobra regulamentação do Redata Entidade relata projetos represados à espera das regras federais e defende ampliar os pontos de chegada de cabos submarinos. A Associação Brasileira de Data Center (ABDC) defende uma redução de 90% do ICMS sobre equipamentos de TI sem fabricação nacional e cobra a regulamentação do Redata para destravar investimentos. Segundo o presidente da entidade, Renan Alves, há operações com infraestrutura pronta que aguardam as regras do regime para importar hardware e ocupar a capacidade disponível. Em entrevista à TV Síntese, gravada durante o Futurecom, em 8 de outubro, Alves afirmou que a associação mantém conversas com governos estaduais sobre o benefício tributário. A proposta envolve uma deliberação no Conselho Nacional de Política Fazendária (Confaz) e a identificação dos equipamentos contemplados por meio da Nomenclatura Comum do Mercosul (NCM). “A ideia é você ter 90 por cento de redução do ICMS, nesses ativos de TI”, declarou. O dirigente ressaltou que o pleito se concentra no hardware que o país não produz. Segundo ele, a proposta não abrange todos os investimentos e despesas de um data center: construção, consumo de energia e outras atividades da cadeia continuariam sujeitos à tributação correspondente. Alves relatou receptividade de parte dos estados, mas também resistências. Lista de equipamentos condiciona decisão dos estados Na avaliação do presidente da ABDC, a definição dos produtos contemplados pelo Redata é necessária também para que os estados dimensionem o alcance de uma eventual redução do ICMS. O dirigente afirmou compreender a posição dos governos que aguardam a regulamentação federal antes de decidir sobre o benefício estadual. Sem a lista de NCMs, argumentou, faltam elementos para quantificar e qualificar os efeitos da medida. “Ninguém vai tomar uma decisão de olhos fechados”, afirmou. Além dos equipamentos elegíveis, Alves cobrou a definição dos critérios de habilitação das empresas, dos procedimentos de apresentação dos projetos e das eventuais exigências de auditoria. Estruturas prontas aguardam hardware A demanda imediata, segundo o executivo, inclui empresas que já operam no Brasil e precisam instalar equipamentos para ampliar seus negócios. Ele distinguiu esses investimentos dos projetos de novos entrantes, cuja implantação exige mais tempo. “O benefício é de quem já está com a estrutura pronta e você está fazendo só um crescimento orgânico”, explicou. Alves afirmou que existem projetos represados à espera do regime. Sobre a data limite para que as empresas conseguissem importar equipamentos ainda em 2026, diz que isso depende da complexidade das regras e da velocidade de aprovação dos pedidos. “O tempo que a gente perdeu, até agora ele não volta mais”, resumiu. Na avaliação do dirigente, o mercado brasileiro continuará crescendo para atender à demanda doméstica. A função do Redata seria ampliar a competitividade do país na disputa por investimentos que poderiam ser destinados a outras localidades, especialmente operações voltadas ao atendimento de clientes no exterior. Cabos submarinos para ampliar destinos dos investimentos Além da questão tributária, a ABDC defende ampliar os pontos de chegada de cabos submarinos para permitir que mais regiões disputem esses projetos. Alves argumentou que a conectividade internacional precisa integrar as políticas de infraestrutura, ao lado de estradas e linhas de transmissão. “Se você quiser que o data center venha, você precisa também fazer investimento em fibra”, afirmou. O executivo reconheceu que os empreendimentos dependem de operadores e de viabilidade econômica, mas defendeu participação do poder público na criação das condições para sua implantação.

artigo.texto: Fox ESS has introduced Power Cube, an all-in-one residential energy storage system combining an inverter and batteries in a compact, stackable design. Announced in Melbourne on 20 October 2026, the system is designed to simplify installation and allow households to expand their storage capacity as their energy needs change. The launch follows a SunWiz announcement which, according to Fox ESS, ranked the company first in Australia for installed energy storage capacity in the first half of 2026. Power Cube integrates key components into one system, with the aim of reducing installation time and associated costs. Its modular EQ5500 batteries offer storage capacities from 10.92 kWh to 49.14 kWh across two to nine modules. “Power Cube has been designed with the Australian market in mind,” said Brooks Richard, Managing Director of APAC & Middle East at Fox ESS. Richard said the system’s capacity options were designed to suit a range of Australian household energy needs, while its integrated design aimed to simplify installation. System features According to Fox ESS, Power Cube includes: - Power options: CEC-approved single-phase models from 5–12 kW, with three-phase models from 5–15 kW planned for release. Both ranges support up to 200% PV oversizing. - Installation options: A compact, integrated design with an IP66 rating for indoor and outdoor installation. - Backup capability: An integrated gateway with 63A on-grid full-home backup support. - Battery protection: Inter-cell insulation and an aerosol unit in each battery module, providing protection at cell and pack level. - Integrated heating: Designed to help maintain battery performance in colder conditions. - Monitoring and connectivity: Fox Cloud 2.0 with AI functionality, real-time monitoring and remote configuration, alongside Wi-Fi, LAN and Bluetooth connectivity. Power Cube comes with a 10-year product warranty. Its modular design allows households to select an initial storage capacity and expand it as their requirements change. Ends. artigo.texto: CATL Unveils Dual-Electric Range Extension Battery to Accelerate Electric Heavy-Duty Truck Adoption BEIJING , Oct. 20, 2026 /CNW/ -- CATL today unveiled the innovative dual-electric range extension battery and the latest generation of heavy-duty battery-swapping solution to accelerate the electrification of road freight transportation. Competition in electric heavy-duty trucking is moving beyond technical specifications toward full-lifecycle value. While battery swapping has made energy replenishment faster and more predictable, concerns about battery utilization, operating costs and residual vehicle value continue to affect fleet economics. To address these challenges, CATL combines its dual-electric range extension battery with QIJI's strategy of standardization, new infrastructure and a full commercial ecosystem, bringing battery swapping and industry-wide collaboration together to accelerate heavy-duty truck electrification. A Dual-Electric Approach to Range Extension CATL's dual-electric range extension battery combines two independent yet complementary battery systems. The main battery uses QIJI's standardized chassis-mounted swappable battery to maximize efficiency. A behind-the-cab range-extension power system, currently equipped with a 77kWh battery capable of 3C charging, provides backup power. Together, the systems maintain uninterrupted power delivery and provide redundancy for demanding operating conditions. - Dual-System Power Redundancy In conventional battery-swapping trucks, drivers often return for a swap with unused capacity because they are reluctant to run the battery low. Backup power from the range-extension battery increases the main battery's depth of discharge (DOD) from approximately 70% to over 95%, allowing it to be returned at less than 5% state of charge (SOC). At this threshold,CATL 's seamless switching technology transfers power delivery to the range-extension battery within milliseconds, maintaining a continuous and stable power supply. - "1+X" Architecture and Independent Upgrades The system uses a "1+X" architecture. One standardized main battery maintains compatibility with the QIJI battery-swapping network, while the range-extension battery can be customized for specific conditions with options including ultra-high energy density, low-temperature resistance for cold climates, or ultra-high power. The two battery systems can be developed and upgraded independently to meet their respective technical and operational requirements. - Flexible Leasing and Battery Asset Management The independently owned on-board range-extension battery stays with the vehicle as an asset throughout its service life, reducing reliance on immediate access to a swapping station. The main battery can be leased according to seasonal freight demand, helping fleets reduce rental costs during quieter periods and manage battery assets more flexibly. This architecture combines the benefits of standardization with flexible vehicle configurations, making electric heavy-duty trucks more practical and economically viable across a wider range of applications. QIJI Builds a Shared Battery Swapping Ecosystem QIJI complements these improvements with a three-pillar strategy of standardization, new infrastructure and a full commercial ecosystem. It seeks to speed heavy-duty truck electrification with a value-chain ecosystem co-created by all stakeholders, where benefits are shared collectively. - Standardization Supports Wider Adoption To accommodate a wider range of truck models and operating conditions, QIJI has introduced the 260# (432 kWh) and 300# (513 kWh) standardized battery-swapping blocks alongside the existing 75# block. The system enables battery swaps in just five minutes, with a 99.99% first-time success rate, helping fleets minimize downtime and maintain operational efficiency. QIJI has also pioneered a battery-as-a-service (BaaS) model in which customers pay for the net energy charged rather than the energy discharged. This allows customers to retain the value of energy recovered through regenerative braking, reducing per-kWh battery rental costs for users on basic plans by up to 20%. Flexible battery leasing options allow customers to tailor rental periods to their needs, from second-hand vehicle transitions to seasonal demand. This will minimize idle costs and offer more flexible options for off-season downtime, further helping fleets manage operating costs. - New Infrastructure Improves Resource Efficiency QIJI aims to make better use of four critical resources in long-haul freight: time, land, payload capacity and grid electricity. Rapid battery swapping reduces waiting times, while efficient station layouts serve more vehicles within the same footprint. Battery capacity is matched to transport needs, and centralized, coordinated charging makes better use of grid electricity. These measures aim to improve both resource efficiency and operational returns.CATL plans to deploy 900 battery-swapping stations by the end of 2026 and 2,000 by 2027, with a long-term target of 10,000 stations nationwide in collaboration with its partners. By connecting major freight corridors through a coordinated swapping network, QIJI aims to improve the efficiency and commercial viability of electric heavy-duty trucking. - A Commercial Ecosystem Supports the Full Vehicle Lifecycle QIJI connects truck manufacturers, financial institutions, insurers, channel partners and aftermarket service providers across the vehicle lifecycle, from purchase and operation to maintenance and resale, working together to build a comprehensive ecosystem of integrated products and services. QIJI has introduced two partnership models:Battery Asset Service Partners andEnergy Replenishment Service Partners . These models allow partners to participate in battery asset services and energy replenishment, extending their role beyond one-off vehicle sales to ongoing operations.
