artigo.texto: Marcos directs DENR to develop Philippine carbon market rules - October 19, 2026 - 0 President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has directed the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) to develop a national carbon market policy framework and submit it for inter-agency approval within 30 days of Executive Order (EO) No. 127 taking effect. Signed on October 13, the order seeks to establish rules for Philippine participation in domestic and international carbon markets, facilitate access to climate financing, technology and investments, and support projects that generate carbon credits. “There is a need to formulate a national carbon market framework aligned with international standards, through a whole-of-government approach, to support the achievement of the country’s NDCs (nationally determined contributions),” the EO stated. NDCs outline countries’ climate commitments under the Paris Agreement, including efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and address climate change. Carbon markets allow companies and countries to buy and sell credits generated by projects that reduce or remove greenhouse gas emissions. The Philippine Carbon Market Policy Framework will establish requirements for participating companies, project approvals, carbon-credit trading, transaction monitoring and benefit-sharing arrangements. It will also provide safeguards to ensure compliance with national policies and international standards. The order designates DENR as the country’s national authority for carbon markets, responsible for overseeing and authorizing emission-reduction projects and ensuring compliance with environmental policies. DENR will also establish and maintain the Philippine National Carbon Registry, a digital system for tracking carbon credits and related transactions. To oversee the framework’s implementation, Marcos created the Inter-Agency Committee on Carbon Markets (IACCM), chaired by the Climate Change Commission, with the Department of Finance as vice chair. Its members include DENR, the Department of Energy, Department of Agriculture, Department of Transportation, Department of Trade and Industry, and Securities and Exchange Commission. The committee will coordinate government policies, review implementation of the framework, and approve reasonable processing fees for carbon market applications and certifications. DENR must submit the proposed framework to the IACCM for review and approval within 30 days of the order’s effectivity. — How can the Philippines’ carbon market framework attract investment while ensuring credible emission reductions and fair benefit-sharing? artigo.texto: North Huntingdon officials are considering passing an ordinance to govern the development of data centers that would be permitted in 20 sites in the 27-square mile township. The township commissioners Thursday decided the proposed 16-page ordinance needs revisions regarding the size of data centers. They plan to revisit the issue in November. The proposed ordinance would permit the data centers on a 10-acre parcel with setbacks of 500 feet from the property line, as a conditional use on land zoned for industrial purposes, as well as parcels designated as planned economic development districts 1 and 2. The ordinance was developed by the township solicitor in conjunction with the municipality’s engineers. Township Commissioner Ron Zona said he would want language in the ordinance that would address smaller data centers, possibly those less than 20,000 square feet, as well as larger ones. Board Chair Commissioner Zachary Haigis said he is comfortable with the draft ordinance as proposed. Township Solicitor Ashley Puchalski said the language in the ordinance must not exclude the development of data centers. Any data center also would have to be 1,500 feet from any school, daycare center, hospital, nursing facility and place of worship. The developer would need the township’s approval of a land development plan, as well as all applicable building permits, Department of Environmental Protection permits, as well as any other state and local permits. The ordinance addresses the issue of how much power a data center would use by requiring a qualified professional to document electricity demand. An expert also must document water demand on an average daily basis and identify the source for water to address an issue regarding water usage that data center opponents have raised. Like data center ordinances passed by other municipalities, North Huntingdon’s regulations would set requirements for decommissioning a data center, including removing buildings when it becomes inactive. A bond must be obtained to cover the estimated decommissioning costs and the cost to restore the site. By passing the ordinance in November, a public hearing could be held in 2027, Puchalski said. If approved by the township commissioners, North Huntingdon would join East Huntingdon, Hempfield, Ligonier, Rostraver, Sewickley and South Huntingdon townships in setting rules to govern data center development. Upper Burrell already has a data center at the former Alcoa Technology Center that’s operated by TECfusions. The Upper Burrell supervisors are scheduled to vote on a data center ordinance Thursday, Oct. 22, but that ordinance would pertain to future development, not the data center currently in operation. A Department of Environmental Protection website on data centers shows the TECfusions data center, where a 3-gigawatt power plant is planned, is the only data center in the county that is under review by environmental regulators. In South Huntingdon, a Sewickley developer, TriEnergy Inc., has applied for a land use permit for a $25 million project that would contain a data center within a 1 million square-foot warehouse to be built on a former farm along Route 31, east of the intersection with Interstate 70. DEP has yet to approval a sewage permit for the project, so the township has not reviewed a land development plan submitted in May.

artigo.texto: Data center anxiety plays out in Senate campaign debates Democrats seek to capitalize on public sentiment over local impacts In debates and advertisements ahead of the midterm elections, Democratic candidates for Senate are consistently pressing their opponents on artificial intelligence data center policy, often as a proxy for voter fears about the economy and local impacts. In Ohio, former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown is fond of calling Republican incumbent Sen. Jon Husted “the face of data centers.” Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., tied the vote by opponent Rep. Mike Collins, R-Ga., for the Republican “One Big Beautiful Bill” health and tax cuts measure last year to data centers. And James Talarico is accusing his opponent in the race for the Senate, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, of “selling off Texas” to data center firms. In addition to attacking each other’s policy positions on tech, candidates of both parties are attacking each other’s campaign donations from Big Tech groups and investments in data center companies. Both pro-AI and regulation-focused groups are spending millions on Republican and Democratic candidates. As Democrats have sought to put Republicans on the back foot by tying data centers to rising energy costs and the larger issue of affordability, polling data appears to support the choice. A Pew Research Center survey conducted in July and August found that 50 percent of U.S. adults think data centers are “mostly bad” for home energy costs, compared with 38 percent in January. Those polled have also gotten more pessimistic about data centers’ effects on the environment, jobs, tax revenue and quality of life for those living nearby. Dan Cassino, a professor of government and politics at Fairleigh Dickinson University, said because voters believe data centers are the cause of their higher electricity bills, the construction projects are part of affordability concerns. “President [Donald] Trump campaigned for office in 2024 saying he was going to make things more affordable, was going to break down inflation, and he hasn’t delivered on that,” Cassino said. “And that means it’s a real point of vulnerability for Republicans.” As a result, Cassino said, Democrats are “hitting Republicans really hard” on the need to regulate data centers. Pocketbook issues In a Georgia Senate debate earlier this month, Ossoff used last year’s budget reconciliation bill, which included tax breaks that Ossoff said are being used by data center companies, to criticize Collins. “Just think about this, when you are paying more for your health insurance, when a hospital in your community is closing down,” Ossoff said. “Mike Collins voted to take that money out of your pocket and out of your community and give it instead to data center developers.” Collins, in turn, said he favored “local control” over data center decisions. Data center attacks may work differently, however, against sitting members of Congress. Cassino posited that candidates like Collins who have already been on Capitol Hill may have an easier time on this issue than their counterparts coming from state and local government. “They might have been doing something indirectly, but they weren’t on zoning boards,” he said. Talarico’s race with Paxton highlights the local nature of the data center backlash, with ads tying data centers both to the cost of living and to accusations of corruption against Paxton. “The data centers bankrolled Paxton, they get tax breaks and you get stuck with the bill,” Talarico said in one ad. In another, he promised that if elected he would “take on the data centers raising our costs.” Husted, as well, is being challenged for actions during his time in state government. He served as lieutenant governor before his appointment to the Senate early last year when fellow Republican JD Vance became vice president. In an ad, Brown pointed to tax breaks his state agreed to for tech companies building data centers. Husted “gave away two and a half billion dollars to these out-of-state corporations and billionaires,” Brown said in the advertisement. “He gave up Ohio’s money, our tax money, to Meta, a company worth $2 trillion, to make sure they come to Ohio.” Other Brown ads connect data centers to rising residential electricity costs. He also pledged to “require the data centers pay the full cost of their electricity, not you.” While Husted’s own ads don’t seem to mention data centers, his work in the Senate has. He sponsored the Senate version of a bill, dubbed the “Ratepayer Protection Act,” that would encourage states to adopt standards to make data centers take on the cost of electrical grid upgrades needed to meet their new energy demand. The House-passed version stalled on a procedural vote last month on the Senate floor after Democrats said it wasn’t strong enough. In a debate last week between Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson, Collins responded to Jackson’s data center attacks by pointing to her support for the Husted bill. She also said that “guardrails” on energy use are particularly important because of Maine’s high energy prices, which she blamed on Jackson, who previously served as state Senate president. Jackson agreed on the need for “real guardrails” to ensure that data centers don’t cause higher electricity costs for other consumers or hurt local water quality. Democrats’ data center arguments, while not the central issue of most campaigns, seem to be part of a successful strategy. Inside Elections rates Georgia as Lean Democrat, while Maine, Ohio and Texas, all seats currently held by Republicans, are rated as Toss-up. Effectiveness As sitting senators talk about the Ratepayer Protection Act bill, Cassino cautioned that voters may not care about Capitol Hill procedural votes. “Anything incumbents say about, ‘oh, this is what I’m doing to protect you,’ is going to ring hollow because everyone sees their electricity prices going up,” Cassino said. artigo.texto: À medida que empresas de inteligência artificial (IA) com infraestrutura de hiperescala e incorporadoras aceleram a construção de data centers, elas estão deixando de depender da rede elétrica e passando a construir, cada vez mais, sistemas privados de energia atrás do medidor (behind-the-meter, ou BTM, na sigla em inglês), que operam de forma independente das conexões com a rede pública. Isso ocorre porque as filas de espera para conexão à rede se transformaram em um gargalo estrutural. Desde 2017, o prazo entre a entrada na fila e o início da operação comercial aumentou aproximadamente 60%. Atualmente, esse período supera, em média, 2.100 dias para projetos que tinham como meta começar a receber energia em 2025. Esse é um dos fatores que fazem da geração de energia no próprio local uma solução que deixou de ser apenas temporária e vem se consolidando como uma alternativa amplamente adotada. A Bloom Energy estima que, até 2030, 38% das instalações de data centers utilizarão algum tipo de geração própria como fonte primária de energia. O percentual representa um aumento de 13% em relação ao ano anterior. A mesma fonte prevê que, dentro de quatro anos, aproximadamente 27% dessas instalações serão abastecidas integralmente por energia gerada no próprio local. No entanto, ao contornar as filas de espera de vários anos para garantir acesso à rede elétrica e resolver um problema, essas empresas se depararam com outras dificuldades que não haviam previsto. Um exemplo é o fato de que as cadeias de suprimentos de equipamentos não acompanharam o ritmo de expansão dos data centers. Os prazos de entrega de transformadores e turbinas a gás estão muito acima das estimativas iniciais, que variavam de 24 a 48 meses. Na prática, a Wood Mackenzie, empresa de pesquisa, análise e consultoria sediada em Edimburgo, na Escócia, informou que os prazos de entrega de turbinas a gás atualmente chegam a seis anos. Isso levou a consultoria a observar que o atraso “mudou fundamentalmente o mercado, que deixou de tomar decisões orientadas pela economia dos combustíveis e passou a priorizar estratégias de aquisição e a viabilidade dos produtos”. Cronogramas diferentes Há também outros problemas. A complexidade dessas instalações não tem precedentes, já que muitos projetos combinam diferentes tipos de tecnologia em uma única microrrede integrada. Ao mesmo tempo, as empresas responsáveis pela operação e manutenção precisam estruturar e operar as instalações conforme os equipamentos chegam, seguindo cronogramas escalonados. A disponibilidade inédita de equipamentos e a complexidade operacional resultante impuseram uma pressão inesperada sobre os responsáveis pela operação das usinas de energia. “Os incorporadores não estão mais esperando pela rede elétrica; eles não podem se dar a esse luxo”, afirma Doug Machon, vice-presidente de desenvolvimento de negócios da Kyuden Energy Partners, empresa de operação e manutenção de usinas de energia sediada em Aliso Viejo, na Califórnia. “A fila de espera para conexão à rede é um gargalo significativo, mas não é o único. O problema se ampliou e passou a abranger a cadeia de suprimentos da infraestrutura energética, desde turbinas e transformadores até sistemas de controle e equipamentos auxiliares das usinas. Como resultado, somos cada vez mais solicitados a estruturar uma capacidade operacional antes mesmo de todos os ativos físicos previstos para a instalação definitiva terem sido entregues e a colocar em operação sistemas integrados compostos por diferentes tecnologias, cujos equipamentos chegam em cronogramas distintos. Trata-se de um trabalho fundamentalmente diferente da operação de uma usina convencional.” A Kyuden Energy Partners, assim como empresas como Consolidated Asset Management Services (CAMS) e Ethos Energy, está entre os diversos fornecedores de serviços de operação e manutenção que ajudam os participantes do setor a superar esse desafio. Desafios de execução Embora cada projeto atendido por esses fornecedores tenha características próprias, determinadas complexidades se repetem. Entre elas estão a integração de diferentes tecnologias de geração em uma microrrede; o uso de fontes temporárias ou provisórias de energia até que a infraestrutura permanente esteja disponível; a contratação, integração e capacitação de grandes equipes técnicas e de manutenção para garantir operações presenciais ininterruptas; e a coordenação do comissionamento e da entrada em operação de diferentes fases do projeto, que ocorrem de forma escalonada. Em comparação com projetos tradicionais de geração de energia em grande escala, a Kyuden constatou que cada um desses obstáculos representa um desafio de execução. A CAMS, fornecedora de serviços de operação e manutenção (O&M) e gestão de ativos sediada em Houston, nos Estados Unidos, tem experiência em projetos que somam 70 gigawatts (GW) de capacidade de geração. A empresa oferece um programa que combina processos simplificados de licenciamento e gestão comercial com serviços diários de operação e manutenção. Sua resposta à demanda energética decorrente das cargas de trabalho de IA e da computação em nuvem está inicialmente concentrada na geração a gás natural e em fontes renováveis. Com experiência na gestão de mais de 100 instalações e de mais de 40 GW de capacidade de geração de energia em todo o mundo, a Ethos Energy desenvolveu seu Centro de Desempenho 24 horas por dia, sete dias por semana (24-7 Performance Center), para oferecer um modelo de operação remota voltado aos desafios dos sistemas BTM. artigo.texto: Microsoft abandona projeto de centro de dados no Reino Unido A Microsoft desistiu de um centro de dados no Reino Unido que estava a ser construído pela Nscale, depois de atrasos no acesso à eletricidade terem impedido a entrada em funcionamento das instalações. Neste artigo encontras: A decisão representa um revés para a Nscale e surge numa altura delicada para a empresa, que prepara uma oferta pública de ações este mês. A saída da Microsoft poderá aumentar as preocupações dos investidores sobre a capacidade da empresa para executar os seus projetos. Microsoft deixa projeto da Nscale devido a atrasos Segundo um porta-voz da Nscale, a Microsoft abandonou o plano para utilizar o centro de dados. O principal obstáculo terá sido a dificuldade em garantir a ligação à rede elétrica necessária para colocar o local a funcionar. O acesso à energia tornou-se um dos maiores desafios para os operadores de centros de dados. A expansão dos serviços de computação na nuvem e da inteligência artificial está a aumentar rapidamente a procura de eletricidade e de novas infraestruturas. Porque este projeto era importante Os centros de dados são fundamentais para alojar serviços cloud, aplicações empresariais e ferramentas de inteligência artificial. Sem energia suficiente, mesmo uma instalação concluída pode ficar impossibilitada de operar à capacidade prevista. Para a Nscale, perder um cliente de grande dimensão como a Microsoft pode afetar a perceção sobre o projeto e levantar dúvidas quanto aos prazos de outros empreendimentos. Não foram divulgados detalhes sobre o valor do contrato nem sobre os próximos passos para o local. Possível impacto na oferta pública da Nscale A notícia surge pouco antes da oferta pública planeada pela Nscale. Embora o impacto final dependa das condições do mercado e dos restantes ativos da empresa, os atrasos e a saída da Microsoft poderão pesar na avaliação atribuída pelos investidores. O caso também mostra como a falta de capacidade energética pode travar a expansão da indústria tecnológica. A procura por centros de dados continua a crescer, mas os projetos enfrentam cada vez mais limitações relacionadas com licenças, redes elétricas e disponibilidade de energia. O que acontece agora Ainda não foram reveladas novas datas para a entrada em funcionamento do centro de dados nem foi indicado se a Nscale procura outro cliente para as instalações. A Microsoft, através da Azure, que também enfrenta pressão para cortar custos, não apresentou até ao momento detalhes públicos adicionais sobre a decisão. - A Microsoft deixou o projeto de centro de dados da Nscale no Reino Unido. - Os atrasos no acesso à eletricidade terão estado na origem da decisão. - A saída poderá afetar a oferta pública planeada pela Nscale. - O episódio reforça os desafios energéticos associados à expansão da inteligência artificial. Huawei's automotive technology company Yinwang, or Newcool, and CATL (HKEX: 3750) have tentatively set an initial lineup of 5 battery swap models for launch in 2027, according to a media report. Newcool, CATL and the battery maker's battery swap operator are developing the vehicles, LatePost reported on Tuesday, offering further details on the initial scope of their partnership. Newcool reiterated the core provisions of the 3 parties' strategic cooperation agreement to the outlet but declined to comment on the model count or launch plans. Those details have yet to be officially confirmed. Cailian reported earlier today that the first model would come from Epicland, a brand jointly developed by Dongfeng and Huawei, with a launch planned for 2027. The specific model has not been disclosed. The 2 reports add details on the product lineup and timeline to the newly announced battery swap partnership. The strategic cooperation framework agreement announced on October 19 did not identify specific models or launch dates. Under the agreement, Newcool is joining CATL's Choco swap ecosystem to help adapt partner models using Huawei's Qiankun intelligent automotive solutions for compatibility with the battery swap network. The partnership also includes Contemporary Amperex Energy Service Technology (CAES), CATL's battery swap operator. The 3 parties plan to integrate data and services across vehicles, battery swap stations and cloud systems, using real-time battery conditions and users' travel patterns to anticipate energy needs and proactively arrange battery swaps. Under the plan outlined in the earlier statement, vehicles would autonomously locate and enter stations, position themselves for a fully automated 99-second battery swap, and then drive away. Additional partner models would help CATL expand the user base for its battery swap network. The business can generate recurring revenue from battery rentals and energy replenishment services, but requires sufficient vehicle volume to support investment in stations, battery inventories and operations. CATL had built 2,520 battery swap stations across 200 Chinese cities as of September 29, according to information it previously released. Its long-term goal is to expand the network to 30,000 stations. The company also plans to build 1,000 highway battery swap stations between 2026 and 2027, extending the network beyond cities to support long-distance travel. Newcool took over Huawei's former intelligent automotive solution business and supplies automakers with systems for smart driving, smart cockpits and vehicle control.

artigo.texto: The University of Illinois Springfield is hosting a presentation on Wednesday, Oct. 21, focused on the environmental impacts of artificial intelligence and data center development. The talk is free and open to the public. Mary Willis, assistant professor of epidemiology at the Boston University School of Public Health, “will investigate the local effects of data centers built in the United States and propose policy solutions to help mitigate environmental impacts and protect local communities,” according to a promotional annoucement. The event, at 6 p.m. in Brookens Auditorium, is a part the UIS Engaged Citizen Common Experience speaker series. Earlier this year, Willis, who previously studied fracking, told Illinois Times research on animals could reveal more information about the effects of hyperscale data centers on surrounding residents, animals and land. “The first study that really linked tracking to adverse health outcomes was on horse or cattle,” she said. “That’s how we kind of figured out that there was even something going on here, and so I would be 0% surprised if local animal studies are what help us actually figure out the effects of data centers faster than we will in humans.” The most immediate concern regarding the CyrusOne data center project planned for rural Sangamon County, according to Willis, is likely going to be the 420 backup emergency generators. While they will only need to run for 15 hours per year for maintenance, they would run for longer if the data center needed emergency power. “This fine, particulate matter can very quickly become a regional problem,” Willis said, though she noted it’s more of a concern for those near the site. “If you live near a coal-fired power plant, that’s probably a far more important source to consider than the data center if that’s not right near you – but this is likely contributing overall to regional air pollution.” Almost half of all Americans are living in areas with heavily polluted air, according to the American Lung Association. Sangamon County and the surrounding counties, according to the American Lung Association, rank middle of the road in particle pollution when compared to more than 200 more metropolitan areas. Polluted air is “associated with increased risks of mortality, asthma and preterm birth,” Willis said. She said she was surprised that CyrusOne plans to install that number of diesel-powered backup generators, a sentiment echoed by another researcher. In March, Max Zhang, a professor at Cornell University who researches air pollutants produced by diesel-powered generators, told Illinois Times that was the largest number of backup generators he’d ever heard of for a data center. Rising land temperatures Researchers at The University of Cambridge published a study in March that used remote sensors to observe temperature increases around active data centers. Data centers located in non-urban environments resulted in “heat islands,” where surface temperatures can rise as far as six miles away. Illinois Times asked CyrusOne about the study’s conclusions in July and whether the company had previously sampled land surface temperature around its data centers. “At CyrusOne, our facilities are designed, developed, and operated in accordance with applicable health, safety, environmental, and land-use requirements, while following established industry practices for site design, cooling, energy efficiency, and environmental performance,” wrote Blair Felter, vice president of communications. “We do not have surface-temperature data to share.” It’s unclear how nearby farmland might be impacted by the CyrusOne data center and the heat it gives off from running continuously; farmland is assessed by soil quality, which then affects the sale price and, ultimately, the tax assessment. Byron Deaner, the county’s chief assessment officer, told IT in July even if that study bears out in Illinois, farmland values wouldn’t change much until parcels of land are actually sold and the market potentially adjusts. “You really wouldn’t see any impact to those values until you started to see some farmland with those different productivity indexes sell at different rates,” he said. “Maybe that would force the Illinois Department of Revenue to revisit the values associated with those soils, if they could contribute the environmental impact of the heat to those particular soil types within the particular distance.”

artigo.texto: Brasil e China buscam ampliar a cooperação na construção de mercados de carbono, com foco no intercâmbio de experiências, na medição das emissões de gases de efeito estufa e no desenvolvimento de mecanismos capazes de contribuir para a transição econômica de baixo carbono. A possibilidade de aprofundar essa parceria foi destacada por Cristina Reis, secretária extraordinária do Mercado de Carbono do Ministério da Fazenda, após sua participação na Conferência de Mercado de Carbono da China 2026, realizada em setembro, na cidade de Wuhan. O evento reuniu representantes de 27 países, regiões e organizações internacionais para compartilhar experiências sobre a criação e o funcionamento de mercados de carbono e discutir caminhos para a cooperação climática. Segundo Reis, a experiência chinesa oferece referências relevantes para o Brasil, especialmente na implementação gradual de mecanismos de precificação de emissões e na estruturação de sistemas de monitoramento, relato e verificação de gases de efeito estufa. A aproximação ocorre enquanto os dois países desenvolvem seus próprios instrumentos de política climática e participam de uma iniciativa internacional voltada à convergência entre mercados regulados de carbono. A cooperação pode contribuir para aprimorar metodologias, aumentar a transparência na contabilização das emissões e criar condições para uma maior compatibilidade entre os sistemas nacionais. Experiência chinesa pode orientar a estruturação do mercado brasileiro A China lançou seu mercado nacional regulado de comércio de emissões em julho de 2021. Desde então, o sistema passou por uma expansão gradual, com o objetivo de utilizar mecanismos econômicos para estimular a redução de gases de efeito estufa. Até o fim de agosto de 2026, o mercado regulado chinês havia acumulado negociações equivalentes a 961 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono equivalente, com movimentação financeira de 65,7 bilhões de yuans, aproximadamente US$ 9,71 bilhões, segundo os dados divulgados pela Xinhua. O país também desenvolve um mercado voluntário de redução de emissões. Até o mesmo período, 41 projetos haviam sido registrados nesse sistema, com volume acumulado de negociações de 21,71 milhões de toneladas e valor total de 1,74 bilhão de yuans. Os mercados regulados e voluntários têm características diferentes. No primeiro caso, o governo estabelece regras e obrigações para os participantes abrangidos pelo sistema. No segundo, projetos podem gerar créditos de carbono segundo metodologias específicas, que são adquiridos voluntariamente por organizações interessadas em compensar emissões ou apoiar iniciativas de redução e remoção de gases de efeito estufa. A secretária brasileira destacou a experiência da China na implantação progressiva desses mecanismos, começando por projetos-piloto, avançando para o mercado regulado e, posteriormente, fortalecendo o mercado voluntário. A troca de experiências, entretanto, não significa que o Brasil precise reproduzir o modelo chinês. As características econômicas, a estrutura produtiva e as prioridades ambientais de cada país exigem soluções próprias. O objetivo da cooperação é identificar práticas e metodologias que possam contribuir para o desenvolvimento dos respectivos sistemas, respeitando suas particularidades. Brasil implementa seu sistema regulado de carbono No Brasil, a estruturação do mercado regulado ganhou base legal com a Lei nº 15.042, sancionada em dezembro de 2024, que instituiu o Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa (SBCE). O sistema prevê a criação de regras para monitorar emissões, estabelecer obrigações para os agentes regulados e organizar a negociação de ativos relacionados às emissões e às reduções verificadas de gases de efeito estufa. Sua implementação está prevista em etapas. O processo envolve a regulamentação da lei, a preparação dos instrumentos de monitoramento e a definição de mecanismos para alocação e negociação de ativos de carbono. Em julho de 2026, o Ministério da Fazenda abriu uma consulta pública sobre uma proposta de cronograma para a implementação das obrigações de monitoramento, relato e verificação. A medida integra a preparação da infraestrutura necessária ao funcionamento do sistema. Esse processo torna a cooperação internacional particularmente relevante. A elaboração de metodologias confiáveis para contabilizar emissões é um dos requisitos para que os mercados funcionem com transparência e para que os resultados ambientais possam ser comparados de maneira consistente. Segundo Cristina Reis, Brasil e China podem aprofundar a colaboração justamente nessa área, compartilhando experiências sobre os sistemas de monitoramento, relato e verificação, conhecidos pela sigla MRV. Esses procedimentos permitem determinar a quantidade de gases emitidos por atividades econômicas, registrar as informações e verificar se os dados apresentados seguem critérios técnicos definidos. A confiabilidade dessas informações é fundamental para evitar a contabilização incorreta de emissões e preservar a credibilidade dos créditos de carbono. Coalizão internacional reúne Brasil, China e União Europeia A aproximação bilateral também está ligada à Coalizão Aberta para Mercados Regulados de Carbono, iniciativa lançada durante a COP30, realizada em Belém, em novembro de 2025, sob liderança brasileira. O mecanismo busca promover o diálogo entre países que adotam sistemas de precificação de carbono, com o objetivo de aproximar metodologias de contabilização, regras para créditos e procedimentos de verificação das emissões. Brasil, China e União Europeia ocupam posições de liderança na iniciativa. O Brasil exerce a presidência até 2027, enquanto China e União Europeia atuam como copresidentes. Em setembro de 2026, durante uma reunião de alto nível realizada em Wuhan, os participantes aprovaram um plano de trabalho até 2030 e definiram uma estrutura provisória para o secretariado da coalizão. artigo.texto: Can larger batteries safely power residential buildings? A project in New York aims to show how A battery system that stores excess energy when it’s plentiful will power an apartment building in Buffalo, New York, when the grid is strained and electricity is costly A battery system that stores excess energy when it’s plentiful will power an apartment building in Buffalo, New York, when the grid is strained and electricity is costly. The manufacturer and state officials hope it will show that larger batteries can safely operate where people live and work. Buffalo-based battery storage manufacturer Viridi and developer Good Carbon Co. say the lithium-ion battery system is connected to the electric grid for Peace Bridge Place. Viridi says the 3.75 megawatt-hour system can power the building for several days. It's among the largest of these systems in a U.S. residential building. A battery system installed in a Buffalo, New York, apartment building will store excess energy when it’s plentiful and power the building when the grid is strained and electricity is costly. The manufacturer and state officials hope it will show that larger batteries can safely operate where people live and work. The 3.75 megawatt-hour lithium-ion battery system, which can power the Peace Bridge Place affordable housing complex for several days, is among the largest battery systems in a U.S. residential building, manufacturer Viridi and developer Good Carbon Co. said Tuesday. “We want our electric power to be resilient, affordable and available. Distributed battery storage accomplishes all three,” Viridi CEO Jon M. Williams said. “The only thing that has been holding up installations at scale is safety; a lot of the products on the market over the last 10 years have burned things down.” Deploying large batteries that can safely power apartment buildings is an important step toward replacing fossil fuels with renewables, experts say, but they’re uncommon because of the cost and concerns about fire risks. Already, larger batteries are paired with solar and wind projects, and homeowners are using smaller batteries to store excess energy from rooftop solar and for backup power. How batteries help keep electricity flow steady Batteries help maintain a steady flow of power when sources such as solar and wind are not producing. They charge when the sun is shining or when wind is blowing. That energy can then be used when demand is high. Batteries can also store excess electricity from hydropower, and New York is one of the top hydropower-producing states. Buffalo is close to Niagara Falls, where most of the state’s hydropower is produced. When electricity demand is high, Peace Bridge will use the battery. It will get paid by the utility for not drawing from the grid and for sending power back if needed. This helps lower the complex’s overall electricity costs, which benefits residents. The building can use the system during outages, too. The New York State Energy Research and Development Agency helped fund the Peace Bridge Place project, as part of its focus on including disadvantaged communities in the clean energy transition. “It goes a long way toward demonstrating the safety and viability of these types of projects,” said NYSERDA President and CEO Doreen Harris. Viridi has manufacturing facilities in Buffalo and Richmond, California, where a state grant assisted with renovations. California Energy Commission Chair David Hochschild said he’s impressed with the company. More than two-thirds of California’s electricity comes from clean energy and batteries get a lot of credit for that, Hochschild said. As electricity demand grows, batteries help ensure the grid is reliable, reduce pollution and contain costs, he added. “I believe the battery industry is the single most important energy industry for the next several decades,” said Hochschild, who co-founded the Electric Innovation Initiative to use electricity instead of fossil fuels more broadly throughout the U.S. economy. Viridi’s system passed a ‘near impossible’ test As large battery fires have garnered attention, some communities have opposed further development. However, the failure rate for batteries has decreased as more are installed, according to the Electric Power Research Institute. Viridi spent six years and $10 million figuring out how to make a fireproof container for batteries. Half the cost was for batteries Viridi destroyed during testing. Viridi uses plates, pouches and spacing to isolate each battery cell. If one fails, the energy dissipates instead of spreading to the next battery, so that no gas, smoke, heat or fire escapes the container, Williams said. Jigar Shah, an expert in clean energy financing and deployment, said the Peace Bridge Place system is a milestone in overcoming safety concerns. To ensure nothing would catch fire when used inside a residence, Viridi’s system had to pass a test where the battery was forced to fail while a cheesecloth covered the container. The cheesecloth did not char or ignite, according to the test report record. Viridi announced in April it met stringent Underwriters Laboratories safety standards so its system could be installed indoors without adding additional fire suppression to a building. Shah, who led the Department of Energy’s Loan Programs Office during the Biden administration, said Viridi is the only company to consistently pass this “near impossible” test. Shah thinks far more U.S. homes will use batteries for backup power by 2030. The U.S. can meet much more electricity demand and avoid costly upgrades to the grid if batteries are strategically deployed, he added. artigo.texto: China's CATL third-quarter profit growth slowest in nearly two years as competition intensifies Synopsis CATL reports slower third-quarter profit growth as intense competition in China’s EV battery market weighs on earnings. Net profit rises 14.5% to 21.2 billion yuan, below estimates, while revenue grows 58.6%. CATL also unveils new heavy-duty truck batteries and plans to expand its battery-swapping network. The third-quarter net profit growth, which follows a 36.5% rise in the second quarter, is the slowest in nearly two years Revenue climbed 58.6% year-on-year to 165.2 billion yuan, undershooting forecasts for a 60.2% increase, after growing 56.9% in the previous quarter. The EV battery specialist on Tuesday unveiled a new generation of batteries for heavy-duty trucks and announced plans to expand its battery-swapping network CATL, which broadened supplies to overseas automakers, accounted for 39.4% of global EV battery usage in the first eight months of the year, up from 37.7% a year earlier, while second-ranked BYD's share slipped to 15.1% from 17.1%, industry data showed CATL's share of China's power battery installation market fell to 40.9% in September from 49.8% in January, while BYD increased its share to 21.1% from 17.4%, according to industry data. While China's domestic auto market extended a 12-month downturn in September, exports continued to support industry growth as manufacturers expanded abroad. CATL expects energy storage to contribute half of its global revenue by 2030, up from about a quarter currently, Reuters reported in June. (You can now subscribe to our ETMarkets WhatsApp channel)

artigo.texto: Siga o Times Brasil - Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC no Entrelinhas de Mercado: Energia vira gargalo para data centers e limita avanço da IA, diz Márcio Aguiar, diretor da Nvidia para a América Latina Publicado 20/10/2026 • 21:43 | Atualizado há 9 horas KEY POINTS A disponibilidade de energia se tornou um dos principais obstáculos para ampliar data centers e a capacidade de processamento de inteligência artificial, afirmou Márcio Aguiar, diretor-executivo da divisão Enterprise da Nvidia para a América Latina, em entrevista ao programa Entrelinhas de Mercado, do Times Brasil – Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC. “O grande gargalo da expansão de um data center, da expansão de um poder computacional é: tem energia suficiente para isso?”, disse Aguiar ao apresentador Júnior Gornelli. Segundo ele, as limitações do setor mudam conforme a tecnologia avança e já envolveram a oferta de GPUs e de memória. Para enfrentar a demanda crescente, a companhia busca otimizar o software e aumentar a eficiência dos servidores, reduzindo consumo de energia e espaço físico. O executivo explicou que a Nvidia também desenvolve CPUs, DPUs e tecnologias de conexão entre equipamentos, além das placas gráficas pelas quais é mais conhecida. “O foco tem sido sempre ao máximo otimizar o uso do software, no sentido da atualização do software para que ele consuma menos energia e traga mais poder de processamento ao cliente final”, afirmou. Aguiar citou a evolução da infraestrutura: a Nvidia já oferece um rack com 72 GPUs e anunciou outro que, segundo ele, deverá reunir 544 GPUs no mesmo espaço físico em cerca de dois anos. A concentração de capacidade exige soluções de refrigeração e aproxima a empresa de fornecedores especializados. Leia também: Nvidia vira termômetro da IA e sustenta aposta do mercado; entenda “A gente começa a atrair também mais próximos de nós empresas que têm especialização na parte de refrigeração”, explicou o executivo, ao descrever o crescimento do ecossistema ligado aos data centers. Na adoção de inteligência artificial, a recomendação de Aguiar é não investir automaticamente na GPU mais avançada. Ele defende que as companhias avaliem seus softwares, suas necessidades de processamento e a infraestrutura já disponível antes de definir novos investimentos. “Comecem pequeno, pensem grande, comecem pequeno”, aconselhou. Segundo ele, o primeiro passo é reunir uma equipe para conduzir a transformação e testar aplicações que possam demonstrar o retorno do investimento. O executivo afirmou que cerca de 80% do trabalho da Nvidia com seu ecossistema envolve educação e orientação. A companhia procura mostrar que a inteligência artificial não se restringe às grandes empresas e que projetos podem começar com equipamentos de gerações anteriores. Leia também: EXCLUSIVO: IA entra na era dos milhares de agentes autônomos, diz diretor da Nvidia para América Latina “Faz o teu benchmark, porque quem define a arquitetura de hardware são os softwares”, destacou Aguiar. Ele acrescentou que GPUs adquiridas há cinco ou seis anos continuam sendo oferecidas por empresas que comercializam capacidade de processamento na nuvem. Siga o Times | CNBC no Google e receba as principais notícias do Brasil e do Mundo. Siga o Times | CNBC Sobre robôs humanoides e veículos autônomos, Aguiar afirmou que a Nvidia pretende fornecer a capacidade computacional dessas máquinas, em vez de se tornar uma fabricante de robôs próprios. Para ele, a expansão da inteligência artificial ainda está em estágio inicial. “A gente vai ser sempre o cérebro de tudo isso”, disse o diretor, ao explicar o papel da empresa no desenvolvimento da chamada IA física. Leia também: Nvidia quer ensinar robôs a entender o mundo real; veja como Aguiar mencionou aplicações que vão além da robótica, como previsões meteorológicas, planejamento urbano, produção e distribuição de alimentos. Na avaliação dele, o processamento de grandes volumes de dados amplia as possibilidades de pesquisa e de tomada de decisões. “O intuito não é você simplesmente sair comprando só o que há de melhor”, ressaltou. Para o executivo, o objetivo é combinar ferramentas diferentes que efetivamente agreguem valor às operações das empresas. Aguiar relembrou que a Nvidia identificou novas possibilidades para suas GPUs em 2012, quando pesquisadores utilizaram plataformas originalmente voltadas a games em uma competição de classificação de imagens. A partir dali, a companhia intensificou o desenvolvimento de hardware e software para aplicações de inteligência artificial. Leia também: EXCLUSIVO CNBC: CEO da Gecko Robotics destaca parceria com Nvidia para ampliar segurança de robôs com IA “O hardware por si só […] não adianta”, explicou o executivo, ao destacar que os programas precisam estar preparados para aproveitar o processamento das placas. Após 16 anos na Nvidia, Aguiar afirmou que não imaginava a dimensão atual da transformação tecnológica. Segundo ele, a orientação da empresa é desenvolver soluções a partir das necessidades dos clientes e continuar abrindo mercados. Leia também: Nvidia supera projeções e segue à frente da concorrência na corrida pela inteligência artificial “O foco sempre foi abrir novos mercados e nunca focado em disputar mercado”, afirmou. artigo.texto: CATL Unveils Dual-Electric Range Extension Battery to Accelerate Electric Heavy-Duty Truck Adoption BEIJING , Oct. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- CATL today unveiled the innovative dual-electric range extension battery and the latest generation of heavy-duty battery-swapping solution to accelerate the electrification of road freight transportation. Competition in electric heavy-duty trucking is moving beyond technical specifications toward full-lifecycle value. While battery swapping has made energy replenishment faster and more predictable, concerns about battery utilization, operating costs and residual vehicle value continue to affect fleet economics. To address these challenges, CATL combines its dual-electric range extension battery with QIJI's strategy of standardization, new infrastructure and a full commercial ecosystem, bringing battery swapping and industry-wide collaboration together to accelerate heavy-duty truck electrification. A Dual-Electric Approach to Range Extension CATL's dual-electric range extension battery combines two independent yet complementary battery systems. The main battery uses QIJI's standardized chassis-mounted swappable battery to maximize efficiency. A behind-the-cab range-extension power system, currently equipped with a 77kWh battery capable of 3C charging, provides backup power. Together, the systems maintain uninterrupted power delivery and provide redundancy for demanding operating conditions. - Dual-System Power Redundancy In conventional battery-swapping trucks, drivers often return for a swap with unused capacity because they are reluctant to run the battery low. Backup power from the range-extension battery increases the main battery's depth of discharge (DOD) from approximately 70% to over 95%, allowing it to be returned at less than 5% state of charge (SOC). At this threshold,CATL 's seamless switching technology transfers power delivery to the range-extension battery within milliseconds, maintaining a continuous and stable power supply. - "1+X" Architecture and Independent Upgrades The system uses a "1+X" architecture. One standardized main battery maintains compatibility with the QIJI battery-swapping network, while the range-extension battery can be customized for specific conditions with options including ultra-high energy density, low-temperature resistance for cold climates, or ultra-high power. The two battery systems can be developed and upgraded independently to meet their respective technical and operational requirements. - Flexible Leasing and Battery Asset Management The independently owned on-board range-extension battery stays with the vehicle as an asset throughout its service life, reducing reliance on immediate access to a swapping station. The main battery can be leased according to seasonal freight demand, helping fleets reduce rental costs during quieter periods and manage battery assets more flexibly. This architecture combines the benefits of standardization with flexible vehicle configurations, making electric heavy-duty trucks more practical and economically viable across a wider range of applications. QIJI Builds a Shared Battery Swapping Ecosystem QIJI complements these improvements with a three-pillar strategy of standardization, new infrastructure and a full commercial ecosystem. It seeks to speed heavy-duty truck electrification with a value-chain ecosystem co-created by all stakeholders, where benefits are shared collectively. - Standardization Supports Wider Adoption To accommodate a wider range of truck models and operating conditions, QIJI has introduced the 260# (432 kWh) and 300# (513 kWh) standardized battery-swapping blocks alongside the existing 75# block. The system enables battery swaps in just five minutes, with a 99.99% first-time success rate, helping fleets minimize downtime and maintain operational efficiency. QIJI has also pioneered a battery-as-a-service (BaaS) model in which customers pay for the net energy charged rather than the energy discharged. This allows customers to retain the value of energy recovered through regenerative braking, reducing per-kWh battery rental costs for users on basic plans by up to 20%. Flexible battery leasing options allow customers to tailor rental periods to their needs, from second-hand vehicle transitions to seasonal demand. This will minimize idle costs and offer more flexible options for off-season downtime, further helping fleets manage operating costs. - New Infrastructure Improves Resource Efficiency QIJI aims to make better use of four critical resources in long-haul freight: time, land, payload capacity and grid electricity. Rapid battery swapping reduces waiting times, while efficient station layouts serve more vehicles within the same footprint. Battery capacity is matched to transport needs, and centralized, coordinated charging makes better use of grid electricity. These measures aim to improve both resource efficiency and operational returns.CATL plans to deploy 900 battery-swapping stations by the end of 2026 and 2,000 by 2027, with a long-term target of 10,000 stations nationwide in collaboration with its partners. artigo.texto: Premier Energies is advancing its planned 12 GWh BESS manufacturing agreement with RCT with a shareholders’ agreement The initial 6 GWh phase is expected to become operational in FY2027–28 RCT Nexor Energy can acquire a 15% stake in the JV in four tranches linked to project milestones, with an option to acquire an additional 5% India’s Premier Energies Limited has finalized a shareholders’ agreement for a joint venture (JV) to establish a 12 GWh battery energy storage system (BESS) manufacturing facility in Telangana. The agreement was signed between Premier Battery Technologies Private Limited (PBTPL), a wholly owned subsidiary of Premier Energies; Premier Energies Storage Solutions Private Limited (PESSPL), the JV company; and RCT Nexor Energy Private Limited, part of Germany’s RCT Group. The facility is planned to come up in Seetharampur, Telangana, with an initial capacity of 6 GWh expected to be established in FY2027-28. The duo signed a binding term sheet for the facility in September 2026 (see India Solar PV News Snippets). The proposed facility will manufacture and assemble BESS for residential, small business, commercial, industrial, and utility-scale applications. Under the agreement, RCT Nexor Energy will have the right to acquire a 15% stake in the JV through four tranches linked to project milestones. It will also have the option to acquire an additional 5% equity stake for cash consideration at the end of the first phase, subject to the agreement’s terms. The JV’s board will comprise two nominees from PBTPL and one from RCT Nexor Energy. With this joint venture, solar cell and module manufacturer Premier Energies will enter BESS manufacturing, targeting both domestic and international markets. The company recently announced that it secured new orders worth INR 4,001 crore in Q2 FY2027 (July-September 2026). The orders cover 2,308 MW of solar cell and module supplies, along with EPC projects. It said the orders came from power producers, module manufacturers, EPC companies, and other customers, excluding the retail segment. Premier Energies’ module manufacturing capacity has nearly doubled to 11.1 GW, while its solar cell capacity has increased to 10.6 GW following the commissioning of a 7 GW TOPCon cell manufacturing facility in Andhra Pradesh (see Premier Energies Commissions India’s ‘Largest’ Solar Cell Fab).

artigo.texto: Na manhã de 18 de outubro, a Ucrânia lançou um ataque com drones em grande escala, visando uma instalação petrolífera, um centro de dados e uma ponte na cidade de São Petersburgo, localizada no noroeste da Rússia. A mídia russa noticiou que drones atacaram o porto petrolífero de São Petersburgo e o centro de dados do VKontakte, empresa que opera a maior rede social do país. O governador Aleksandr Beglov confirmou que um incêndio deflagrou na zona portuária do petróleo e em várias instalações civis em quatro distritos da cidade. As equipas de resgate atuaram imediatamente no combate às chamas e, até ao momento, não foram registadas vítimas. O incidente também afetou diversos voos no Aeroporto Internacional de Pulkovo. Na província de Leningrado, que circunda São Petersburgo, o governador Aleksandr Drozdenko anunciou que as defesas aéreas abateram 127 drones. Os destroços danificaram quatro carros em um estacionamento e causaram vários focos de incêndio. Fontes que monitoram o conflito disseram que o ataque começou por volta das 2h50 da manhã. Imagens registradas por moradores mostraram múltiplas explosões iluminando o céu noturno sobre São Petersburgo – uma cidade de 5,6 milhões de habitantes localizada a cerca de 856 km da fronteira com a Ucrânia. Alguns vídeos mostraram drones atingindo uma ponte de oito faixas e causando um grande incêndio na área portuária. O porto petrolífero de São Petersburgo tem capacidade para receber e transportar aproximadamente 12,5 milhões de toneladas por ano por via marítima, ferroviária e rodoviária, sendo um dos maiores centros de armazenamento e exportação de combustíveis da Rússia. A fabricante ucraniana Fire Point afirma ter utilizado seu avião de ataque FP-1 nessa operação. Diversos canais de notícias locais relataram que uma subestação de energia também foi danificada, causando cortes de energia localizados e redução da pressão da água em algumas áreas. Esses ataques fazem parte da operação de longo prazo da Ucrânia para pressionar intensamente o fornecimento de combustível e a infraestrutura digital da Rússia, em meio a uma complexa e contínua troca de ataques contra a infraestrutura energética entre os dois países. artigo.texto: The abandoned San Francisco Centre mall could find new life as a massive data center and artificial intelligence lab under a newly revealed proposal, though the idea faces immediate hurdles from city leadership and community members. The multistory shopping mall has been closed and boarded up since late January. According to a proposal confirmed by Jared Kreiger, CEO of the Maryland-based property development firm KG Growth Partners, a confidential client is exploring purchasing the entire property to convert the upper floors into a data center and AI lab. Watch NBC Bay Area News free wherever you are The plan would include public space on the ground level and water for a rooftop community garden that could be donated to nonprofits focusing on food insecurity. However, Kreiger declined to reveal the identity of the prospective buyer. The proposal comes at a complicated time for downtown San Francisco. Last week, Mayor Daniel Lurie approved a 45-day moratorium on City Hall approving any permits to build new data centers in the city. Addressing the proposal, Mayor Lurie said he was unaware of the plan and emphasized that the building remains on the market. "I am not aware of that proposal," Lurie said. "The building is still up for sale. There is not a buyer yet. I'm hopeful that we get someone in there that will bring a lot of people downtown." Communities across the country have increasingly raised concerns over data center developments, pointing to issues such as heavy water usage, environmental impacts, round-the-clock noise, and vibrations. Local reactions to the downtown San Francisco concept were mixed. Local "I've heard bad things about data centers," said San Francisco resident Paul Bodner. "By default I would not support it," added Guillaume Le Ster, also of San Francisco. Nicholas McNely, who lives a couple of blocks from the shuttered mall, questioned the motives behind such a project. "They're more trying to extract from whatever community they're trying to extract the resources from to enrich themselves so, I don't really see the reason for a data center here," McNely said. Conversely, some visitors saw potential upside. Janet Li of Burlingame noted, "If it's an AI center here, more people would work here so, I think it's good for the street." The proposal was first reported by the San Francisco Chronicle and confirmed to NBC Bay Area by development consultants.

artigo.texto: Ahead of iPhone Duo’s launch on Friday, accessory maker BMX is releasing what appears to be one of the first MagSafe batteries designed specifically for Apple’s foldable. The BMX Duo is available to order now and can wirelessly charge your iPhone Duo (or any other iPhone) at up to 15W. You can pick it up on Amazon for $79.99. The iPhone Duo supports MagSafe, but because it’s shorter than a standard iPhone, many existing MagSafe accessories likely won’t fit—or will hang awkwardly off the bottom. The BMX Duo 5000mAh Power Bank is designed to fit exactly on the iPhone Duo: A custom-size 5,000mAh cell is shaped to the iPhone Duo’s folded footprint, so it sits flush on the cover panel instead of hanging past the edges. It was built around the Duo, and it snaps onto the iPhone 12 through 18 series just as securely. In addition to attaching via MagSafe for 15W wireless charging, it also has a built-in USB-C cable that can charge at up to 20W speeds. The BMX Duo also features a built-in ring that rotates a full 360 degrees. The full-color display on the back shows the exact battery percentage and live charging wattage. It uses semi-solid-state cells, which BMX says “use significantly less liquid electrolyte than conventional lithium-ion cells, which helps reduce the risk of battery fires.” The BMX Duo 5000mAh Power Bank is available to order today for $79.99. We expect to see a bunch of iPhone Duo accessories roll out to the market soon. More iPhone Duo accessories: Follow Chance: Threads, X, and Instagram

artigo.texto: By Vũ Hoa HƯNG YÊN — Combining rooftop solar power with battery energy storage systems (BESS) could help Việt Nam strengthen energy security, improve electricity efficiency and ease pressure on the national grid, but policy gaps, high costs and technical requirements remain barriers to wider adoption, experts said. Speaking at a conference on self-produced and self-consumed rooftop solar power in northern province of Hưng Yên on October 16, Mai Duy Thiện, chairman of the Việt Nam Clean Energy Association (VCEA), said the country’s target of average annual GDP growth of more than 10 per cent in 2026-30 would require sufficient, stable and safe electricity supplies. Resolution No 70-NQ/TW on national energy security and Government Directive No 10/CT-TTg, issued on March 30, 2026, identify renewable energy development, electricity savings and rooftop solar power as priorities. The Government has also called for research into preferential credit mechanisms to support investment in rooftop solar and BESS. However, market development remains constrained by high initial investment costs, limited access to finance, gaps in technical standards, fire safety requirements and complicated implementation procedures. Thiện called for closer coordination among regulators, local authorities, power companies and businesses to improve the legal framework, facilitate grid connections, enhance product quality and expand financing options. He also stressed the need to strengthen domestic research, manufacturing and technical capabilities to reduce reliance on imported equipment. Storage capacity set to expand Võ Quang Lâm, former deputy general director of Vietnam Electricity (EVN), said the country’s installed power capacity reached 87,616MW at the end of 2025, ranking second in Southeast Asia. As of August 2026, Việt Nam had 134,410 rooftop solar systems with a combined capacity of more than 11,450MWp, while the number of self-produced and self-consumed installations equipped with BESS remained very limited. On larger storage projects, Hà Nội Power Corporation (EVNHANOI) had completed 50MW of BESS capacity, while Northern Power Corporation (EVNNPC) had completed 155MW and aimed to reach 305MW in October 2026, Lâm said. Electricity Project Management Board No 2 and Power Generation Corporation 3 (EVNGENCO3) were pursuing investment procedures for centralised storage projects in northern Việt Nam, with planned capacities of 550MW and 300MW, respectively. Lâm said factories, commercial buildings and industrial parks could combine rooftop solar, battery storage and smart energy management systems to optimise electricity consumption and reduce dependence on grid power. He called for technical standards, grid-connection requirements, fire safety regulations, testing procedures and pricing mechanisms for BESS services. He also proposed publishing the PVout coefficient used to estimate rooftop solar generation at ward and commune level to improve calculation accuracy and support investment decisions. Bùi Xuân Bình, chairman and general director of GG Power, said Việt Nam should build its capacity to research, manufacture and export energy technologies rather than remain primarily a consumer market for products developed elsewhere. GG Power is developing energy storage manufacturing capacity, targeting an annual scale of 5GWh to serve residential, commercial, industrial and large-scale projects. Bình said a competitive domestic industry would require a complete value chain covering research, design, manufacturing, installation, maintenance and battery recycling. Cooperation among businesses, research institutions, distributors and financial institutions would also be needed to improve technology and access to finance. He stressed that product safety, quality, customer protection and effective battery collection and recycling systems were essential to sustainable market development. Representatives from Goldwind Group, Cornex Group, SRNE Group, Đan Khuê Solar, Ngọc Long Energy and Solar Kinh Bắc, among others, expressed interest in cooperation with GG Power. At the conference, the company introduced its “Made in Vietnam” energy storage products and signed cooperation agreements with several businesses to strengthen industry links and expand distribution networks. Participants said the market had significant growth potential but needed more consistent policies, affordable products and reliable warranty and maintenance services to improve the competitiveness of domestic technologies. — VNS

artigo.texto: Microsoft (MSFT:NASDAQ) has pulled out of a planned AI data center in Loughton, Essex, that British cloud provider Nscale was building for it, Reuters reported on October 18, citing the Telegraph. Microsoft is one of Nscale's two largest customers. Reuters said the Telegraph did not specify why Microsoft withdrew, and Microsoft declined Reuters' request for comment. The site did have an obvious problem: power. The Telegraph reported that grid officials told Nscale they didn't expect to supply electricity until the 2030s. That matches a September report that UK Power Networks couldn't connect the site before the early to mid-2030s. Nscale says it remains committed to Loughton and is looking at other power sources. Loughton Was a Small Slice of Microsoft's Buildout Loughton was planned to house about 23,000 Nvidia (NVDA:NASDAQ) chips for Azure, starting at 50 MW. Nscale agreed to supply Microsoft with about 200,000 Nvidia chips across the UK, Norway, Portugal and Texas, so Loughton was about 11.5% of the program. Microsoft added roughly a gigawatt of capacity in the June quarter alone, which makes Loughton's starting load about 5% of one quarter. The spending shows no sign of a pullback. Cash capital expenditure reached $35.80 billion in the June quarter, more than double the $17.08 billion a year earlier. Fiscal 2026 cash capex totaled $115.95 billion, up about 80%. On management's broader measure including finance leases, June-quarter capex was approximately $41 billion, with more than $50 billion expected in the September quarter. Demand is keeping pace. Intelligent Cloud revenue hit $39.31 billion in the June quarter, up about 32% from $29.88 billion, and CFO Amy Hood said customer demand still exceeds available supply. Microsoft has the customers and the cash. What it can't buy quickly is electricity. Power First, Then Chips Microsoft has been picky with Nscale before. It signed a letter of intent for up to 1.35 GW at Nscale's West Virginia campus in March, then walked away over the summer, and Anthropic took the capacity. Meanwhile, it is paying up for sites with a power date. On October 16, two days before the Loughton report, NiSource (NI) announced a 20-year agreement with Microsoft, with service expected to begin in 2028 and approximately 1,100 MW of generation resources to be added in Indiana. The other workaround is making power on-site, which is where Bloom Energy (BE:NYSE) comes in. Nscale reportedly held talks with Bloom about fuel cells for Loughton. Bloom's revenue reached a record $1.065 billion in the June quarter, up 166% from a year earlier. Its last four quarters brought in about $3.12 billion, nearly double the $1.63 billion of the four before. Grid delays are already showing up in someone's income statement.

artigo.texto: Next Upcoming Virtual event Hold onto Your Tax Credits: How to Get Ahead of the 2027 Deadline By Canary Media Illinois has built out large amounts of renewables in the past decade to reach its mandate of 100% clean energy by 2050. So far, though, it has lagged on building battery storage, which advocates say is especially necessary now as data center development drives up energy demand. Last fall, Illinois passed an ambitious law requiring 3 gigawatts of batteries on the state’s grid by the end of 2030. In August, the Illinois Power Agency, which procures electricity on behalf of the state’s large utilities, ran an auction-type proceeding to hand out incentives for companies promising to develop these batteries. The results were mixed. Statewide, deals were made for 600 megawatts of storage — less than two-thirds of the target that the law set for the initial procurement. The state sought to get 588 MW of storage in the utility ComEd’s territory in northern Illinois, but the procurement ended with just one company planning to build an 80-MW battery project there. In utility Ameren Illinois’ territory, which stretches over much of the state, three developers’ bids were chosen to supply 520 MW. Advocates said that while they were disappointed in the outcome in northern Illinois, the results overall were encouraging. James Gignac, Midwest policy director for the climate and energy program at the nonprofit Union of Concerned Scientists, called it “a strong start” that indicates “there is interest in developing energy storage in Illinois.” He noted that the new deals will increase Illinois’ total energy storage manifold: The state currently has only 102 MW, according to energy data firm Cleanview. The Illinois Power Agency is collecting feedback from developers through Oct. 28, with the goal of improving the next procurement process. Already some important takeaways have emerged that Illinois can use to entice more developers to build battery storage over the next few years. “I believe storage developers see Illinois as a strong market for new utility-scale storage, especially with our policies in place and state agencies focused on expanding batteries’ role on the power grid,” Gignac said. Across the country, states are turning to battery storage to bank renewable energy that is abundant when the wind is blowing and the sun is shining. This helps meet clean energy goals and spiking demand. A few states — notably Texas with over 18 GW and California with over 16 — have already installed large amounts of energy storage on their grids. Indiana tops the list of Midwestern states with 587 MW, over five times Illinois’ capacity. Overall energy storage has increased dramatically on U.S. grids, from 4.7 GW total in 2022 to over 50 today, according to federal data, but that surge took time to ramp up. Massachusetts, for example, launched an energy storage initiative in 2015 and an official target in 2018, but progress was slow until an uptick the past couple years. The state passed legislation in 2024 and the governor issued an executive order this year to boost battery deployment. New York, like Illinois, has a goal of 3 GW of utility-scale storage on the grid by 2030, as part of its goal of getting off fossil fuel-fired electricity by 2040. New York has 288 MW of storage installed, according to Cleanview, and in September the state secured promises for 950 MW using the same incentive mechanism that Illinois has employed. Two of the four companies chosen in Illinois’ procurement are New York-based. In the regional grid known as the PJM Interconnection, which handles the flow of power in parts of 13 states, including New York and the ComEd territory in Illinois, long delays to connect batteries to the system have been a significant barrier to deployment. Brett Sproul leads regulatory work in Illinois for Advanced Energy United, a national industry organization whose members include renewable and battery storage companies. He said there are multiple developers that could build batteries in Illinois by 2030, “however because of the interconnection queue at PJM there’s a lot of uncertainty” as to whether those projects could actually start storing power by the deadline. “That uncertainty led to some cold feet,” he added. States like Illinois can have a hard time convincing developers to build batteries, because of the structure of their energy market. In states with vertically integrated energy markets, utilities can include batteries in their plans to meet energy demand, and with the approval of state regulators, charge customers for the cost. But in states such as Illinois, New York, and Ohio that have “restructured” markets where generators compete to get contracts to supply the grid, a different model is often needed to incentivize developers to invest in batteries and sell their storage services on the open market. In Illinois, that’s taken the form of an incentive program under the Clean and Reliable Grid Affordability Act signed into law in January that uses “indexed storage credits” to guarantee a certain amount of revenue to storage developers. During the bidding process that culminated Aug. 26, storage developers stated how much payment they would need in order to build batteries connected to the grid. If regional wholesale energy prices available to battery owners end up being below those amounts, the utilities will make up the difference — using customers’ funds to pay the storage companies. If wholesale prices are higher, the storage company will pay excess funds back to the utility. While the model means battery developers could feasibly earn less than they would without participating in the program, the guarantee of a certain revenue level is crucial to jumpstarting the state’s still-new industry, experts said. Existing investors AENU and Daphni participated alongside WEPA Ventures, OVNI Capital, and Aurum Impact. Epyr develops thermal energy storage systems that use electricity during periods of low prices to generate and store heat for industrial applications. Its technology uses electric resistors to heat air, which transfers thermal energy to firebricks. The bricks store energy at high temperatures, allowing industrial facilities to use the heat when required. Sébastien Léger, co-founder and GP at SlateVC, said, “We were convinced by the quality of the entire Epyr team, their speed and their customer-centric approach. They deliver climate impact, energy cost savings and resilience to industrial sites. Epyr has the potential to become a European leader in electrifying the €100 billion (~$118 billion) industrial heat market. We are delighted to enable their growth in France and beyond.” The funding comes 18 months after Epyr’s pre-seed round, in which the company raised €3 million (~$3.1 million), co-led by AENU and Daphni. OVNI Capital, WEPA Ventures, and several other European angel investors also participated. Epyr has been selected to deploy a 35 MWh thermal energy storage unit at Papeco’s Orval-sur-Sienne facility in France. The company described the installation as France’s largest thermal energy storage project, replacing all natural gas consumption at the Papeco facility. The company said it is prioritizing industrial steam, mainly in paper, food and beverage, and chemicals. Epyr deployed an industrial thermal energy storage unit at WEPA Group, a hygiene paper manufacturer, in Troyes, which went into operation in early 2026. artigo.texto: Itália desponta como importante polo de data centers no sul da Europa A Itália vem se consolidando como um mercado de data centers de destaque na Europa, à medida que cresce a demanda por superinteligência, computação em nuvem e infraestrutura digital, segundo informações de inteligência de mercado da Administração de Comércio Internacional dos Estados Unidos. O país se apoia em sua localização, que liga a Europa, o Norte da África e a Ásia, além de conexões submarinas de cabos em expansão, imóveis industriais acessíveis e necessidades crescentes de computação em SI, observou o órgão. O mercado italiano tinha um valor de aproximadamente €7,5 bilhões em 2025 e deve crescer de forma substancial. O Observatório de Data Centers do Politecnico di Milano estima o investimento em cerca de €25 bilhões no período de 2026–2029, enquanto a Associação Italiana de Data Centers prevê que a capacidade nacional possa superar 1 GW até 2028 e chegar a 2 GW até 2031, ante cerca de 287 MW em 2024. Milão lidera a capacidade, enquanto Roma desempenha um papel complementar Milão continua sendo o principal polo, representando cerca de 68% da capacidade instalada de data centers na Itália. A Lombardia oferece infraestrutura de fibra existente, proximidade de grandes clientes corporativos, terrenos industriais, um ecossistema tecnológico maduro e conexões com redes europeias. Essa concentração, porém, também pressiona a infraestrutura elétrica, o uso do solo e os processos de licenciamento. Roma atua como um mercado complementar, dada sua proximidade com instituições governamentais e com a infraestrutura digital do setor público, com o Polo Estratégico Nacional e programas mais amplos de transformação digital gerando demanda por infraestrutura de computação segura e hospedada no país. Governo passa da estratégia à implementação Os data centers têm sido tratados pelo governo italiano como infraestrutura estratégica. A estratégia nacional de data centers do MIMIT busca atrair investimento estrangeiro, simplificar os procedimentos de autorização e posicionar a Itália como um polo digital europeu e mediterrâneo. Ao longo de 2026, o governo passou da estratégia à implementação, por meio de reformas no licenciamento, medidas para o sistema elétrico e a designação de grandes projetos como de relevância estratégica nacional. A disponibilidade de energia continua sendo a maior restrição estrutural do mercado. Em 2026, o governo adotou legislação para tratar dos custos de eletricidade, da competitividade industrial e da integração dos data centers ao sistema elétrico, reconhecendo que o desenvolvimento de data centers é indissociável do planejamento nacional de energia e da rede elétrica. Oportunidades para investidores dos EUA Para os investidores dos EUA, a Itália oferece a oportunidade de participar da próxima fase da infraestrutura europeia de SI e nuvem, ao mesmo tempo que ganham exposição ao corredor digital do Mediterrâneo. As oportunidades mais fortes devem surgir em campi de hiperescala preparados para SI, empreendimentos com energia garantida, reurbanização industrial de áreas já ocupadas, infraestrutura de conectividade e nos sistemas de energia que dão suporte aos data centers, segundo o órgão de comércio.

artigo.texto: AI data centers boost Arizona construction jobs: Here’s why BuildStrong Academy offers free training as demand for skilled labor grows PHOENIX (AZFamily) — Artificial intelligence is affecting industries from healthcare to education to commerce, and now attention is turning to construction and skilled labor in Arizona. Signing up for a skilled labor class is getting harder as demand for workers continues to climb. Jordan Gil, 39, is one of many aspiring carpenters and electricians looking for a new career path. “I’ve been waiting to find something to work with my hands and develop a career and learn some skills and I found info online and seen a couple videos,” Gil said. “There’s a lot of work out here — everything from new construction and remodels,” Gil said. Demand for workers remains strong The need for construction workers is out there, according to Becca Haro, operations manager at the BuildStrong Academy in Phoenix. Haro said the construction industry in Arizona remains strong, with job openings for skilled laborers. She said that is encouraging amid fears about AI eliminating jobs across the labor market. “Everybody is scared that robots and computers are going to take over — but from my perspective and from what I see in the industry, I think this is actually creating a great opportunity — especially for us in Arizona,” Haro said. Data centers drive need for labor Haro said as AI continues to grow, more data centers will be needed across the state, and building them requires a strong skilled labor workforce. “I think people forget — there’s only so much you can automate or use AI for but when it comes to swinging hammers and using drills and wiring buildings, it still takes a human body to do,” Haro said. The BuildStrong Academy offers nine-week classes for free. The classes are paid for by companies and businesses that need skilled workers. For more details, visit https://homebuilding.academy.
