artigo.texto: The 15-Minute Space TPU: Why Orbital Data Centers Are a Radiator Problem Google's prototype can only run for 15 minutes before it has to cool down. The radiator, not the chip, explains the entire economics of space compute. Google's first Project Suncatcher prototype satellite has reached orbit on SpaceX's Transporter-18 rideshare mission. The spacecraft, built with Planet Labs and roughly the size of a refrigerator, carries four Google TPUs. Google says the ground team has made contact and that the satellite is operating as expected. The detail that traveled fastest was this: the TPUs can run for about 15 minutes, then must shut down while the radiator rejects the heat. That sounds like a thermal failure in orbit. It is not. The 15-minute window was written into the mission profile before launch. Google designed an intermittent operating cycle because, in vacuum, the radiator rather than the chip sets the long-run compute ceiling. That distinction matters. It moves the question from "can a TPU survive space?" to "what kind of system can run continuously in space?" A data center is judged by sustained average power, not by a 15-minute burst. On that measure, the radiator is the main character. Three problems, one still open Google's public test results divide the engineering risk into three buckets. Launch vibration: the TPU assembly passed three-axis vibration testing, with local loads of 50 to 100 g. Google's team described the result as better than expected. Radiation: at UC Davis, Google ran the Trillium TPU under a proton beam while it was executing workloads. The chip absorbed a total ionizing dose exceeding the cumulative dose of a five-year mission. That is a positive early signal for inference workloads. Training would face a higher risk profile. Heat rejection: Google tested the thermal path in a thermal vacuum chamber. The result was an intermittent operating mode. Vibration and radiation have fairly clear answers. Heat is being bypassed by duty cycle. Why the radiator sets average compute In space, there is no air convection and no atmospheric sink. Heat moves from the chip through heat pipes to a radiator, then leaves as infrared radiation. The radiator's continuous rejection rate is fixed by its area, its temperature, and its emissivity. The Stefan-Boltzmann relationship makes temperature the dominant term: rejection scales with the fourth power of absolute temperature. A rough estimate shows the scale. At a radiator surface temperature of 20°C (293 K) and emissivity 0.9, one square meter rejects about 376 W on one side. Two sides give roughly 750 W before accounting for Earth infrared and albedo inputs. The net figure is lower, around 600 W per square meter in a realistic low-Earth-orbit environment. A ground-based high-density AI rack now draws well over 100 kW. At 600 W per square meter net, one such rack maps to nearly 170 square meters of radiator area. That is one rack. This is why a space data center is a radiator-area project. The compute boards are a small part of the mass and volume. Most of the structure goes to radiators, heat pipes, and deployment mechanisms. Google's project lead has said the radiator is one of the heaviest components on the prototype. In an industry that charges by launch mass, the heaviest component also sets the compute ceiling. The economics follow the radiator. The design logic also flips. On the ground, cooling engineers push chip temperatures down: colder water, lower PUE, lower junction temperature, less leakage, longer life. In space, a hotter radiator is better. Raising the radiator surface from 20°C to 60°C (333 K) lifts single-side rejection from about 376 W per square meter to about 627 W per square meter, an increase of nearly 70%. A space-optimized compute chip should tolerate higher junction temperatures and accept a modest efficiency penalty in exchange for radiator mass reduction. Today's TPUs and GPUs are optimized for ground data-center temperature windows. Sending them up is a test under the wrong conditions. For a prototype, that is acceptable. For a scalable architecture, it is not. The long-run metric changes accordingly: from performance per watt to sustained performance per square meter of radiator area, or sustained performance per kilogram of launched mass. The duty cycle does not create extra compute The heat sink, heat pipes, and structure have thermal capacitance. During the 15-minute run, the chip's heat output exceeds the radiator's continuous rejection rate. The difference goes into thermal capacitance, and the temperature rises. When the chip shuts down, the radiator drains that stored heat. Averaged over a full run-and-cool cycle, the continuous heat rejection equals the radiator's capacity. The burst does not add a watt of long-run compute. It moves the radiator's capacity into a 15-minute window. For a single inference demo, one question and one answer, 15 minutes is enough. For a data center, the number that matters is the average. That number is set by radiator area and temperature. What the orbital test should measure Google says the satellite will run the Gemma open-weight model to observe how the chip behaves in space. The thermal chain matters more than the model output. Three measurements matter more than benchmark scores. First, whether thermal interface materials degrade under vacuum and repeated thermal cycling. Second, how far heat-pipe performance in microgravity diverges from ground measurements. Third, whether the 15-minute window shrinks over a year. A shrinking window would indicate thermal-path degradation. That is a more serious problem than radiation-induced bit flips, because it directly erodes average compute. Google plans to launch two more satellites in 2027 to test high-bandwidth laser inter-satellite links and formation flying. That work is as important as heat rejection. artigo.texto: da Agência iNFRA A EPE (Empresa de Pesquisa Energética) publicou a metodologia que será utilizada para calcular o custo marginal de referência, que servirá de base para a definição do preço-teto do leilão de baterias, marcado para dezembro. A nota técnica disponibilizada na segunda-feira (19) não apresenta os preços, uma vez que o dado é considerado estratégico para o certame, mas detalha como será feito o cálculo para os projetos. A metodologia utiliza um modelo de fluxo de caixa descontado, que avalia os investimentos, os custos e as receitas esperadas ao longo do empreendimento. A EPE calculará uma TEQ (Tarifa de Equilíbrio), isto é, a receita necessária para que o projeto cubra seus custos e remunere o capital, considerando os riscos e as condições financeiras adotadas. A EPE destaca que o preço-teto não será baseado apenas no custo inicial das baterias, mas também considerará os valores necessários para manter os sistemas de armazenamento aptos a operar conforme o contrato. Assim, o cálculo do custo marginal de referência considerará, além do investimento, as despesas com operação e manutenção, degradação das baterias, augmentation (reposição de componentes), tarifas de uso da rede, financiamento, seguros e tributos. Nacional x importado Quanto à divisão do leilão em dois, um para produto nacional e o outro que permite equipamentos importados, a nota técnica da EPE destaca que não se deve presumir que equipamentos nacionais serão mais caros ou mais baratos que os importados, uma vez que vários componentes entrarão na conta. “O efeito final decorrerá da avaliação conjunta dos custos, das condições de financiamento, dos prazos e dos riscos associados à cadeia de fornecimento”, diz o documento, que cita por exemplo que projetos nacionais podem ter condições diferenciadas de financiamento. Com a publicação da metodologia, a EPE agora deve avançar nos cálculos do custo marginal de referência, com as recomendações de preços-tetos. Isso será feito a partir informações dos projetos cadastrados, diligências técnicas, estudos nacionais e internacionais, referências de mercado e informações de fabricantes e bancos. A decisão final sobre o preço-teto caberá ao MME (Ministério de Minas e Energia).

artigo.texto: Georgia candidates up and down the ballot are campaigning on an issue that has struck a nerve across the political spectrum: data centers. A wave of data center projects across Georgia has been met with outrage in many communities in the last year or so, causing state lawmakers from both parties to push a flurry of legislative solutions during the 2026 legislative session. But in the end, none of the bills passed. Since then, Georgia has become the leading state for data centers. Gov. Brian Kemp, a Republican who is term-limited and leaving office after this year, has welcomed the facilities, saying at a data center-related event in Washington this summer that "we cannot let China win this race, and that's what some people want," referencing the race between the U.S. and China to develop increasingly powerful artificial intelligence models. The November election will decide to what extent Georgia embraces the energy-hungry facilities in the future, with voters choosing a new governor, the lawmakers who shape the state's policies on data centers and other state leaders who play a role in carrying out those policies. At the top of the ballot, Keisha Lance Bottoms, the Democratic nominee for governor, has criticized Republican nominee Rick Jackson, a wealthy healthcare executive, for his investment in a data center in Texas through a company Jackson was the head of until recently. Though his campaign has tried to distance itself from that development, in his campaign financial disclosure, Jackson is listed as the CEO and president of Datahub Developers, the company that is advancing the data center in Texas that the local community is fighting. Bottoms and Jackson had a fiery exchange at a recent debate where they swapped accusations of being involved in advancing data centers. "There is a community asking him to not build a data center, a massive data center in their community, and he is moving forward. So, if he is an investor in data centers, if he builds data centers, he cannot be trusted on this," Bottoms said in the debate organized by Atlanta News First and Gray Media. Jackson fired back, accusing Bottoms of approving three data centers during her time as mayor of Atlanta, but Bottoms said that she was "not sure what data centers he's referencing," saying there was only one at Georgia Tech that wasn't one of the hyperscale data centers that cause concerns today. Attorney general candidate says family has 'moved on' from data center project once planned for their farmland At least one other candidate, Georgia state Sen. Brian Strickland, a McDonough Republican running for state attorney general, held a personal financial stake in a proposed data center as recently as the summer of 2025. But the proposal has since been shelved, according to public records and interviews. The Georgia Recorder examined financial disclosure documents for all candidates running for statewide office in November. The Recorder also reviewed other public records and reached out to all of the candidates and their campaigns to ask whether the candidate has a direct financial stake in a data center. In phone calls, text messages and emails with candidates and their campaign staff, all except those described in the story reported having no financial interest in data center projects. Public records show that Strickland, a lawyer who represents a suburban district southeast of Atlanta, was involved in advancing a $1.2 billion data center on his family's farmland in Henry County. On May 15, 2024, he authorized a real estate development firm focused on technology to pursue rezoning for the project. Strickland's personal financial disclosure statement shows that the state senator holds a greater-than-5% stake in Strickland Road Farms, which was a co-applicant in the rezoning application for the proposed 1.25 million-square-feet data center. The project came close to being finalized mid-2025 – about the same time Strickland launched his bid for higher office – but Strickland told reporters last week that his family backed out over concerns about the noise that would come from the data center and now says the project is "dead." A public hearing before the Henry County Board of Commissioners was scheduled to consider rezoning part of the farmland on June 17, 2025, but Carlotta Harrell, the commission's chair, said at the top of the meeting that the agenda item, along with other rezoning public hearings, "have all been removed at the request of the applicant and we will hear these items at a later time." County and local development officials confirmed the project is now inactive. The Democratic nominee for attorney general, state Rep. Tanya Miller, pressed Strickland on the project at last week's Atlanta Press Club debate. "It wasn't until days – and mind you, we're talking days – after he announced his run for attorney general, did he remove the agenda item from the public hearing. He didn't remove the data center application. He's playing with words. He's shape shifting," Miller said to reporters after the debate. Opponents of the data center project, like Connie Snow, a member of Conserve Henry County, a local advocacy group focused on zoning issues, say they're worried the project will be revived after the November election. "They've all told us that he's withdrawn and all this other stuff, but I don't think that it's going to go away," Snow said in an interview. "You have to also remember that all this happened coincidentally enough as it was getting close to election time." Snow also participated in a press call organized by the Democratic Party of Georgia. But Strickland said the decision to halt the project was not related to his decision to run for office and says the family now plans to add to an existing residence on the property and that his "parents decided to keep the entire farm intact." artigo.texto: City commission candidates split on data center restrictions at forum Incumbents and challengers divide over moratorium ahead of election What This Story Is About - City commission candidates at a forum discussed their positions on data center restrictions and a proposed moratorium. Why It Matters - The city’s handling of data center regulations has become a key dividing line between incumbents and challengers ahead of the election. For Context - Two city commission candidates, Don Langley and Sue Parrigan, did not attend the forum, though Parrigan provided a written statement defending the city’s existing data center ordinance. BOWLING GREEN, Ky. (WBKO) - Voters packed State Street Baptist Church Monday, Oct.19 for a candidate forum focused on city commission and contested magistrate races. Doors opened at 5:30 p.m. for a meet and greet. The forum started at 6:30 p.m., giving voters a chance to hear directly from candidates seeking to represent them on city issues and in county government. City commission candidates address data centers A central topic heading into the election is the ongoing debate over data centers. Candidates at the forum responded to questions on the issue. Incumbent Melinda Hill, who is running for re-election, voted against a proposed moratorium in June. She said restrictions already in place protect the community. “City commission voted five to zero with the strictest restrictions for data centers,” Hill said. “We’ve already put those in place. So yes, I know you’re mad there wasn’t a moratorium, or some of you are. But be thankful we put very strict restrictions for our community regarding data centers.” Fellow incumbent Carlos Bailey voted for the moratorium. He said he wanted a pause so outside experts could be brought in. “The reason why we wanted to have that is because we wanted to bring in the experts, because none of us on here were experts, to see how it is doing in other communities,” Bailey said. “We wanted to bring in people who actually are living with data centers, like Memphis and Gallatin, Tennessee. They could tell us how it affects their everyday life.” Thomas Morris said the data center debate is the main reason he is running. He said he supported a moratorium. “I went to Gallatin, Tennessee, talked to a city commissioner there,” Morris said. “I asked him what piece of advice do you have. He said, ‘take your time.’ In my opinion, we did not take our time. We rushed it through, and this is an issue that could come back to bite us.” Incumbent Dana Beasley Brown said she backed a moratorium because of transparency and unanswered questions about impact. “We haven’t done the research, like Commissioner Bailey said, about our unique karst topography and what a data center of that size, the impact it could have on it,” Beasley Brown said. “The fact that we have had a real long drought this summer, and thinking about our water usage, how we make sure we have enough for our kids and grandkids. It’s these concerns I have in mind, and the need to stop and make sure our whole community gets to give input about whether we want a data center in our future or not.” Two candidates absent from forum Two city commission candidates were not at the forum: Don Langley and Sue Parrigan. WBKO reached out to Langley for comment but has not yet heard back. Parrigan responded with a statement: “A pause does not stop a data center. A rule does! The city commission proactively voted unanimously to approve an ordinance to set rules to keep data centers off your street.” Voters react after forum Michael Trapasso was among those in attendance. He said data centers were his top concern heading into the forum. “My main issue was the data centers, of which I’m very much against,” Trapasso said. “I enjoyed hearing what people had to say, getting an idea about who these people are and how they feel about various issues. I thought it was quite enlightening.” Resident Sheila Downs said the forum was helpful for meeting the candidates, but it was difficult to draw lines between each candidate’s views. “I thought the forum was very nice. It was very informative,” Downs said. “One of the things that I noticed, and a couple of people did stand out to me, but they seemed to collaborate with each other and not a lot of them took the initiative to say, ‘this is what I’m going to do.’ So, I wasn’t able to differentiate between who was going to do what.” Both Downs and Trapasso say they’ll be heading to the polls Nov. 3. artigo.texto: Rising demand for energy storage systems driven by the spread of artificial intelligence data centers, coupled with expectations for the commercialization of next-generation batteries, has pushed a Shinhan Asset Management exchange-traded fund investing in solid-state battery companies to the top of three-month return rankings. The SOL Solid-State Battery & Silicon Anode ETF posted a 22.76% return over the three months through Oct. 16, according to the Korea Exchange on the 19th. That was the highest return among domestically listed equity ETFs, excluding leveraged and inverse products. It also exceeded the KOSPI's return of minus 16.90% over the same period by 39.66 percentage points. The fund's main holdings include next-generation battery companies such as Samsung SDI, LG Energy Solution, EcoPro BM, Isu Specialty Chemical, Lotte Energy Materials and Daejoo Electronic Materials. The product focuses on competitiveness in next-generation technologies such as solid-state batteries and silicon anode materials, rather than short-term shifts in demand in the existing electric vehicle market. With the recent rally in domestic semiconductor shares losing momentum, secondary battery ETFs have moved into the top tier of returns. Analysts attribute the shift to improved investor sentiment as the battery industry, long weighed down by slowing EV demand, secures a new growth driver centered on ESS. Growing electricity demand from AI data centers and the expansion of renewable power generation are cited as the main drivers of ESS market growth. LG Energy Solution posted preliminary third-quarter operating profit of 756 billion won ($528 million), beating market expectations. The expansion of its North American ESS business and the conversion of production facilities are seen as supporting the earnings recovery. "The secondary battery industry is securing a new demand base through ESS, and growth drivers are diversifying as the commercialization of next-generation technologies such as solid-state batteries and silicon anode materials comes into view," said Kim Jung-hyun, head of the ETF business group at Shinhan Asset Management. "Going forward, the earnings recovery through ESS and competitiveness in next-generation technologies such as solid-state batteries will be key factors determining corporate value."

artigo.texto: In China, new-energy heavy truck sales have overtaken diesel truck sales. Just three years ago, new-energy heavy trucks accounted for only around 5% of sales, but electrification is spreading on the back of Chinese government support and lower transport costs. That contrasts with the United States and Europe, where heavy truck electrification remains in the single digits. Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Limited (CATL; 宁德时代), the world's largest battery maker, unveiled a new battery system aimed at long-haul heavy electric trucks as it moves to tap the long-distance transport market. On the 21st, according to China First Commercial Vehicle Network, about 65,800 heavy trucks were newly registered for insurance in China's domestic market in September, of which about 33,100 were new-energy vehicles. That was 50.3% of the total, a majority. While total heavy truck registrations fell 21% from a year earlier, registrations of new-energy vehicles rose 37%. Electrification of China's heavy truck market has accelerated rapidly in recent years. According to China First Commercial Vehicle Network, the sales share of new-energy heavy trucks surged from the 5% range in 2022–2023 to 13.6% in 2024 and 28.9% in 2025, then reached 38.1% in January–September this year. New energy includes not only pure electric vehicles but also Hydrogen Fuel Cell vehicles. CATL said, "In the heavy truck electrification market, the competition between internal combustion and electric vehicles is already over; from now on, the competition will be between EV technologies and business models." Compared with major global markets, China's pace of electrification stands out even more. According to the International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT), in the first half of this year, zero-emission vehicles accounted for only 2.3% of new registrations of heavy trucks over 12 tons in the European Union (EU). In the United States, the figure was 0.34% last year. However, collection standards and periods differ by country. ◇ Chinese government to provide support in the 4 trillion won range for replacing old cargo trucks China's rapid electrification appears to reflect a combination of government support and improved economics. According to CATL, the Chinese government is building more than 3,000 heavy truck-dedicated charging and battery exchange facilities, centered on major metropolitan areas and expressways, to reach a 40% electrification rate for heavy trucks. It is also pushing plans to create a "carbon zero (0)" road transport network spanning a total of 30,000 kilometers. In particular, it allocated 22 billion yuan (about 4.3688 trillion won) from ultra-long-term special government bonds to support scrapping and replacing old commercial cargo trucks, and in some regions, the combined central and local government subsidies reportedly reach up to 220,000 yuan (about 43.68 million won). Electric trucks cost more upfront than diesel trucks, but their maintenance expense is relatively lower, so the longer the driving distance and the higher the utilization rate, the greater the potential cost savings. Adoption is said to be especially fast on short-haul, fixed routes such as mines, ports, steel mills, and construction sites. That is because fixed routes make it easier to secure charging infrastructure, and repeated vehicle operation can yield fuel cost savings. ◇ CATL unveils new "battery swap + auxiliary battery" system Against this backdrop, CATL has introduced a battery solution to improve long-haul efficiency for heavy electric trucks. On the 20th (local time), CATL held a product launch at the Shoudu International Exhibition and Convention Center in Shunyi District, Beijing, unveiling four new rechargeable batteries for heavy electric trucks and a new battery swap system. The new system combines a fixed auxiliary battery with the existing battery swap system. First, a main battery with up to 513 kWh capacity is mounted under the truck, and it can be replaced at a swap station in about five minutes without lengthy charging. CATL is operating battery swap systems on five major transport corridors: Guangdong–Shanghai, Chengdu–Wuhan, Changzhou–Yulin, Ningde–Xiamen, and the Hainan Island ring road. The fixed auxiliary battery is mounted behind the driver's seat. With a capacity of 77 kWh, it assists vehicle operation when the main battery's power is low. Because electric truck drivers, concerned about running out of charge, typically left about 30% remaining and then exchanged the battery, an auxiliary battery was added separately to improve this. CATL said this would allow the main battery to be used down to under 5% remaining, improving efficiency. CATL began mass production the same day as the product launch and signed cooperation agreements totaling 13,000 vehicles with logistics and transport companies including China Post, SF Express, STO Express, and YTO Express. It plans to expand battery exchange stations to 900 by the end of this year and 2,000 next year. In the long run, it aims to build 10,000 nationwide. ◇ The key is the economics of charging infrastructure Still, it is uncertain whether CATL's battery swap method will become mainstream for heavy electric trucks. Building battery exchange stations requires significant upfront investment expense, and if sufficient vehicle utilization is not secured, operating profitability risks falling. For vehicles from multiple manufacturers to use the same exchange facilities, battery specifications and vehicle designs must be standardized in cooperation with automakers. It will also face unavoidable competition from ultra-fast charging technology. In Europe and the United States, megawatt-class ultra-fast charging technology and infrastructure for heavy electric trucks are being developed. artigo.texto: Gentari and BYD Malaysia have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to explore the deployment of BYD’s Flash Charging technology in Malaysia. The collaboration aims to expand ultra-fast EV charging infrastructure beyond showrooms, including along major intercity routes connecting key population centres. BYD’s Flash Charging technology is capable of delivering up to 1.5MW which would provide approximately 400km of driving range in just five minutes for compatible EVs under optimal conditions. The MoU was signed in Shenzhen, China, on 21 October 2026, between Gentari Group CEO Sushil Purohit and BYD Malaysia Managing Director Jacob Ma. The ceremony was witnessed by BYD Chairman Wang Chuanfu and BYD Vice President Liu Xueliang. Gentari and BYD to explore Flash Charging along major highways Under the agreement, Gentari and BYD Malaysia will jointly identify suitable locations for BYD Flash Charging stations, especially along key intercity corridors. Both companies will also assess power infrastructure requirements, battery energy storage systems (BESS), technical and commercial feasibility and potential operating models to support future deployment. The collaboration combines Gentari’s experience in developing and operating EV charging networks with BYD’s battery and high-power charging technology. Gentari Group CEO Sushil Purohit said, “Malaysia’s EV market is growing, but the next phase of adoption will depend on the quality, convenience and reliability of the charging experience.” He added, “Speed is one part of that equation. Drivers also need chargers in the right places, backed by reliable power and dependable operations. BYD’s leadership in EV, battery and high-power charging technology, combined with Gentari’s experience in developing and operating EV charging networks, gives us a strong foundation to strengthen Malaysia’s EV charging ecosystem and support wider adoption.” Gentari currently operates more than 600 EV charging points in Malaysia. Through its Gentari Go Roaming Hub, it also provides access to approximately 18,000 charging points across Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and India. BYD Vice President and General Manager of BYD Asia Pacific Auto Sales Division Liu Xueliang said, “Malaysia is an important market for BYD, and we are pleased to bring BYD Flash Charging here as part of our continued efforts to support the country’s growing EV adoption. Through our collaboration with Gentari, we look forward to exploring how this technology can contribute to a faster, more convenient and more connected charging experience for Malaysian EV users.” Meanwhile, BYD Malaysia Managing Director Jacob Ma said, “We are very excited to see this collaboration come together. As an EV leader, we believe our responsibility goes beyond delivering great vehicles. We want to give our customers the confidence to make the switch to electric and enjoy a truly seamless EV ownership experience. This is an important step for BYD in Malaysia, and we are proud to be part of the journey to build a stronger and more complete EV ecosystem for Malaysians.” Besides EV charging infrastructure, Gentari and BYD will also explore collaboration in renewable energy generation and energy storage. BYD Flash Charging stations already spotted in Malaysia As reported previously, BYD Malaysia had confirmed plans to introduce its Flash Charging technology in Malaysia, starting with Denza showrooms before expanding to other locations. The Flash Charging stations can deliver up to 1,500kW (1.5MW) of DC charging output. When paired with compatible EVs equipped with BYD’s second-generation Blade Battery technology, it can charge the battery from 10% to 70% in five minutes, or from 10% to 97% in just nine minutes. The chargers are also supported by BESS to manage the massive power demands without requiring the same level of power directly from the grid. Earlier this week, we spotted what appears to be BYD Flash Charging BESS equipment at Denza Glenmarie in Shah Alam. This was followed by another sighting at Denza Balakong, where the distinctive T-shaped overhead Flash charging structure and battery storage cabinets have already been installed. While the Flash Charging technology supports a maximum DC output of 1,500kW, compatible vehicles are required to achieve the highest charging speeds. The Denza Z9 GT is currently the only model available in Malaysia that supports BYD’s full Flash Charging capability. As shared by BYD Malaysia earlier, the Flash Charger will also be open to other BYD models and non-BYD EVs, up to their respective supported DC charging rates. BYD Malaysia has yet to reveal the official opening dates for the Flash Charging stations in Malaysia.

artigo.texto: Global Silicon-carbon Anode Materials for Solid State Battery Market Projected to Reach US$111 Million by 2032, at 18.0% CAGR 1.1 Silicon-carbon Anode Materials for Solid State Battery Market Summary Silicon-carbon anode materials for solid state batteries are high-capacity anode materials developed for solid-state and semi-solid lithium battery systems. They are typically based on nano-silicon, silicon oxide, graphite, and porous carbon, and are improved through composite structure design, surface coating, and interface stabilization. The materials are mainly used in automotive power batteries, high-end consumer electronics batteries, and next-generation high-safety energy storage batteries. The market is still in an early commercialization stage as solid state batteries move from sample validation and pilot projects toward small-scale production. Demand for silicon-carbon anode materials is increasing as automakers, battery manufacturers, and material companies accelerate joint development programs. Compared with conventional graphite anodes, silicon-carbon systems offer much higher theoretical capacity, but they also face challenges such as volume expansion, interfacial side reactions, initial efficiency loss, and batch-to-batch consistency. According to the new market research report "Global Silicon-carbon Anode Materials for Solid State Battery Market Growth 2026-2032", published by LP Information, the global Silicon-carbon Anode Materials for Solid State Battery market size is projected to reach US$111 million by 2032, at a CAGR of 18.0% during the forecast period. According to LP Information, the global key manufacturers of Silicon-carbon Anode Materials for Solid State Battery include Group14 Technologies, Sila Nanotechnologies, Amprius, etc. In 2025, the global top three players had a share of approximately 31.65% in terms of revenue. To read the full report or request a free sample report, please use the link: https://www.lpinformationdata.com/reports/1866822/silicon---carbon-anode-materials-for-solid-state-battery 1.2 Industrial Chain The upstream segment mainly includes metallurgical-grade silicon, silane, graphite, and porous carbon, with representative suppliers such as Elkem, Hemlock, and East Hope Group. Raw material purity, particle size distribution, carbon structure, and supply stability directly affect capacity performance, swelling control, cycle life, and batch consistency, while also forming the basis for cost control and mass production. The midstream segment focuses on silicon-carbon composite structure engineering, interface stabilization, swelling suppression, surface coating modification, and particle morphology optimization. The main challenge is to balance high capacity with long cycle life while controlling initial efficiency, tap density, and processing compatibility. Stable mixing, heat treatment, coating, and classification processes directly affect yield, customer qualification time, and unit manufacturing cost. Downstream demand mainly comes from automotive power batteries and consumer electronics lithium batteries. Power battery customers focus on longer driving range, fast charging capability, safety, and long-term cycling performance, while consumer electronics customers emphasize volumetric energy density and thinner product design. Silicon-carbon anodes help battery makers improve energy density and create differentiated performance for solid state batteries, premium vehicles, and high-end devices. 1.3 Influencing Factors Drivers: The core growth driver is rising demand for high-energy-density batteries. Longer-range electric vehicles, fast-charging platforms, and thinner high-end consumer electronics are pushing anode materials from conventional graphite toward silicon-carbon systems. As solid state battery development and demonstration projects accelerate, battery makers are increasing validation demand for high-capacity, low-swelling, and long-life anode materials, supporting order growth and market expansion. Challenges: The main barrier is process stability and cost pressure. Silicon materials tend to expand and trigger interfacial side reactions during charge and discharge, which raises requirements for coating, structure design, and battery system matching. If batch consistency, initial efficiency, and cycle life cannot meet customer requirements steadily, qualification cycles will be extended and production expansion and profitability will be constrained. Trend: Future development will focus on higher capacity, lower swelling, and better adaptation to solid state battery systems. Material suppliers will use nano-structure design, porous carbon frameworks, elastic coating layers, and interface modification to improve cycling stability, while developing customized products for different solid electrolytes and cell processes. Firm’s experience and meeting format The firm said it only works with local governments and has 40 years of experience with large industrial projects. Firm representatives only took questions from county leaders. There was no public comment for this portion of the meeting. Copyright 2026 WTOC. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: O recuo na infraestrutura da Nscale em Loughton deve-se a atrasos na ligação à rede elétrica britânica. A Microsoft confirmou o cancelamento do acordo celebrado com a startup britânica Nscale para o aluguer de capacidade de computação num novo centro de dados dedicado à inteligência artificial (IA) em Loughton, a nordeste de Londres. A decisão assenta em constrangimentos infraestruturais na rede elétrica do Reino Unido. Segundo a imprensa britânica, a distribuidora UK Power Networks informou a Nscale de que o complexo de Loughton não teria acesso à energia elétrica necessária antes da década de 2030. Em declarações oficiais, um porta-voz da multinacional norte-americana esclareceu que a “decisão dizia respeito a um único local” e sublinhou que a empresa “continua empenhada na sua parceria com a Nscale”. Por seu turno, a Nscale confirmou que está a procurar fontes alternativas de energia elétrica para o local e que o percalço não afeta os restantes contratos da empresa. Impacto nas Ambições Britânicas e no Mercado de IA O projeto de Loughton tinha sido classificado pelo ex-primeiro-ministro britânico Keir Starmer como “o maior centro de dados de IA soberano do Reino Unido”. O anúncio do cancelamento surge numa altura em que a Nscale prepara a sua Oferta Pública Inicial (IPO) em Nova Iorque, com uma valorização estimada em 35 mil milhões de dólares. A desistência da Microsoft junta-se a outro recuo recente no mercado britânico de supercomputação: no início do ano, a OpenAI retirou-se de uma parceria com a Nscale e a Nvidia que visava implementar uma versão britânica do projeto de infraestruturas Stargate.

artigo.texto: Proposal to pause new data centers in Michigan City sparks protests over Google exemption MICHIGAN CITY, Ind. (WSBT) — Michigan City's Common Council took the first step toward pressing pause on future data center developments. But one major project would be exempt. Protesters outside Tuesday's meeting said the proposed moratorium does not go far enough because Google's data center project is already under construction and would not be affected. A proposal to pause new data center developments is back before the Michigan City Common Council, but opponents say the ordinance leaves out a major piece — Google's data center project that is already underway. They want the council to remove that exemption before moving forward. Protesters gathered outside City Hall before Tuesday's council meeting, chanting and holding signs. They say they are concerned about future data center projects and the rules governing the Google project that is already underway. "It totally exempts Google and all of its future phases and build out for a moratorium and effectively pause on data center development here," said protester Ashley Williams. The ordinance would pause future data center development, but it would not apply to current projects like Google's, which has already broken ground. Councilman Bryant Dabney (D), one of the ordinance's sponsors, says the city has no plans to stop the project. "Some people want us to stop what's going on now, but we have millions of dollars that have already been given to Michigan City with permitting fees, building fees that are happening over there," said Dabney. Tuesday was only a first reading of the ordinance. The council will be able to make amendments during its second reading at their next meeting on November 4.

artigo.texto: Ecobiz.asia – The Philippines will develop a national carbon market policy framework to regulate carbon credit projects and transactions, as the government seeks to attract climate investment and strengthen implementation of its emissions-reduction commitments under the Paris Agreement. President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. ordered the development of the framework through Executive Order No. 127, signed on Oct. 13, directing the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) to establish rules for the country’s participation in domestic and international carbon markets. The order, announced by the Presidential Communications Office on Saturday (Oct. 17), designates the DENR as the Philippines’ national authority for carbon markets and establishes an Inter-Agency Committee on Carbon Markets to coordinate government policy and oversee implementation. The proposed Philippine Carbon Market Policy Framework will set requirements for carbon credit projects, project approvals, transaction monitoring and benefit-sharing arrangements. It will also establish safeguards to ensure that carbon market activities comply with national policies and international standards. The government aims to use carbon markets to expand access to climate finance, technology and investment while supporting projects that reduce or remove greenhouse gas emissions. “There is a need to formulate a national carbon market framework aligned with international standards, through a whole-of-government approach, to support the achievement of the country’s NDCs,” the executive order states. The Philippines’ nationally determined contribution (NDC) sets out its climate commitments under the Paris Agreement. Carbon markets can help finance emissions-reduction activities by allowing eligible projects to generate credits that can be traded, subject to applicable rules and safeguards. Under the order, the Inter-Agency Committee on Carbon Markets will be chaired by the Climate Change Commission, with the Department of Finance as vice chair. Other members include the DENR, Department of Energy, Department of Agriculture, Department of Transportation, Department of Trade and Industry, and Securities and Exchange Commission. The committee will coordinate policies across government agencies, review implementation of the framework and approve reasonable processing fees for carbon market applications and certifications. The DENR will also establish and maintain the Philippine National Carbon Registry, a digital system intended to track carbon credits and related transactions. The agency is required to submit the proposed framework to the inter-agency committee for review and approval within 30 days of the executive order taking effect. The order will take effect upon publication in the Official Gazette or a newspaper of general circulation. The framework is expected to provide a coordinated basis for the Philippines’ participation in carbon markets, including mechanisms for international cooperation under the Paris Agreement and voluntary carbon markets. Its detailed rules, however, remain to be developed. ***

artigo.texto: Trontek to Unveil 5-MWh BESS, Targets 12 GWh Capacity by 2028 Trontek Electronics will unveil its 5-MWh EKOM battery energy storage system at The Battery Show India 2026 as it plans to scale manufacturing capacity from 3 GWh to 12 GWh by 2028. October 19, 2026. By News Bureau Trontek Electronics, an Indian battery and energy technology company advancing the future of energy storage, will unveil its 5-MWh EKOM containerised Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) at The Battery Show India 2026, marking a step in its evolution from mobility batteries to large-scale energy storage. With active manufacturing capacity of 3 GWh and plans to scale to 12 GWh by 2028, the company is building capabilities to address India’s expanding energy storage needs. Trontek will showcase EKOM at Stall C16, Hall 18, from October 22–24, 2026, at India Expo Mart & Centre, Greater Noida. The launch expands Trontek’s presence into large-scale energy storage, bringing its battery expertise to applications beyond electric mobility. Designed for industrial and utility-scale requirements, the EKOM platform addresses the growing role of energy storage in renewable energy integration, power management and the evolving needs of India’s energy infrastructure. The unveiling comes as energy storage gains strategic importance in India’s energy transition. As renewable energy capacity expands and electricity demand evolves, BESS is emerging as a critical enabler of greater flexibility in how power is stored, managed and deployed. Trontek’s move into this segment reflects its ambition to participate in this expanding market through locally developed and manufactured solutions. Building on more than two decades of experience in battery technology and manufacturing, Trontek is extending its capabilities across a broader range of energy applications. The company is targeting 12 GWh of manufacturing capacity by 2028. Speaking ahead of the unveiling, Samrath S. Kochar, Founder & CEO, Trontek, said, “Energy storage is becoming central to how India powers its next phase of growth. With EKOM, we are taking Trontek’s two-decade battery expertise into large-scale energy storage, building capabilities in India for the country’s evolving industrial and energy needs. Our ambition is to contribute to a globally competitive Indian energy storage ecosystem.” The unveiling of Trontek’s 5-MWh EKOM containerised Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) marks the company’s expansion into large-scale energy storage, extending its battery technology expertise to industrial and utility-scale applications. At The Battery Show India 2026, Trontek will showcase its portfolio across electric mobility, energy storage, and power and critical infrastructure solutions. Its electric mobility segment includes battery solutions for two-wheelers, three-wheelers and other mobility applications. Under energy storage, the company offers POWERCUBE for residential applications, NOVARA for commercial facilities and EKOM for industrial and utility-scale storage, including the newly unveiled 5-MWh system. Its power and critical infrastructure portfolio includes inverters and solar solutions for distributed energy applications, along with battery systems for telecom infrastructure and backup power requirements. The portfolio reflects Trontek’s expansion from a mobility-focused battery business into a broader energy technology company, with Made-in-India solutions spanning mobility, distributed energy and large-scale energy storage. A key pillar of Trontek’s expansion is the development of energy storage solutions suited to Indian market requirements, supported by local engineering and manufacturing capabilities. As demand grows across residential, commercial, industrial and utility applications, the company sees an opportunity to build scale while contributing to the development of India’s domestic energy storage ecosystem. please contact: contact@energetica-india.net.

artigo.texto: Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos, Jr has ordered the creation of a national carbon market policy framework to attract climate investments and support domestic emissions cuts, the Presidential Communications Office announced on 17 October. To continue reading, subscribe to Eco‑Business. Access all our exclusive content and archive — with a 7-day free trial. Then just US$5/month. Cancel anytime. - Exclusive access to training across business and policy topics - Direct access to industry leaders at Eco-Business events - A seat among the decision makers shaping the region's sustainable development The executive order, signed on 13 October, directs the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) to develop rules governing participation in domestic and international carbon markets, which enable trading in credits generated by projects that reduce or remove greenhouse gas emissions. The framework will cover voluntary carbon credits, bought by choice rather than legal obligation, as well as credits under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, which sets government approval and accounting rules for international carbon trading. The categories can overlap, but voluntary credits do not automatically meet Article 6 requirements. Under the order, the DENR will provide technical, policy and regulatory inputs for nature-based solutions, forestry and waste, while the Department of Energy will cover the energy sector. The Department of Agriculture and Philippine Statistics Authority will handle agriculture-related inputs, and the Department of Transportation will cover transport-related carbon credit projects. The Department of Finance will address fiscal policy, investment promotion, climate finance and the fiscal implications of carbon market transactions. “There is a need to formulate a national carbon market framework aligned with international standards, through a whole-of-government approach, to support the achievement of the country’s NDCs,” the order stated, referring to the Nationally Determined Contribution, a country’s climate action plan under the Paris Agreement. The Philippines submitted its updated pledge in September, seeking to strengthen its net sink status but without committing to a fossil fuel phase-out or net zero. John Leo Algo, national coordinator of the 40-member civil society network Aksyon Klima Pilipinas, said the order signals that the framework could be completed by COP31 or early 2027, potentially attracting investors awaiting clearer rules. But its contribution to stronger climate ambition remains uncertain, he told Eco-Business. “While the 2026 NDC has been finalised, it is missing a 1.5°C-aligned decarbonisation pathway and, subsequently, how much of its conditional target is planned to be achieved through carbon markets.” Algo urged meaningful consultations in the coming weeks, including with communities whose lands are being considered for carbon projects, rather than only prospective market participants. Jonathan Joson, Philippine operations head at Singapore-based carbon solutions firm Kennemer Eco Solutions, welcomed the order’s multi-agency approach. “I am more confident that this executive order resolves the fragmentation. There is higher regulatory certainty leading to investor confidence,” he told Eco-Business. Joson previously warned that carbon credit rules released last year, covering only clean energy projects, could divert investment from nature-based solutions, agriculture and blue carbon without an overarching framework. The order follows a Philippine-Singapore Article 6 agreement signed in May, establishing a legal framework for transferring emissions reductions between the countries. Observers cautioned that credible benefits would depend on robust rules for measuring and approving those reductions. Other Southeast Asian countries have also pursued such agreements before establishing comprehensive domestic carbon markets. Vietnam, which plans to make its carbon market fully operational around 2028, signed an agreement with Singapore last year allowing credits generated by Vietnamese projects to be transferred to the city-state. Thailand also signed an Article 6 agreement with Singapore last year. It operates voluntary crediting schemes and is exploring an emissions trading system, but has yet to introduce a nationwide compliance carbon market.

artigo.texto: For once, I have to agree with Cooper Freeman regarding putting a data center in the middle of Cook Inlet. One has to wonder why Louis Wolfson, representing Deep Green, would come to Alaska from Massachusetts and think building a massive data center in Cook Inlet was a good idea. The 32-foot tide alone would be a serious engineering concern! Why would one want to try and permit such a beast? One would have to do a huge number of studies in a very inhospitable environment to be able to convince scientists, permitting experts and the public that your submarine heat pump wouldn’t harm the environment. This will likely be a long process, cost millions of dollars and may or may not be successful in the end (assuming the engineers could design such a thing). Why build at the bottom of Cook Inlet when we have so much land in Alaska? Wolfson should have looked out the window while flying into the Anchorage International Airport and seen all that open land. Here’s a suggestion — why not build a data center on land, far enough away from neighborhoods (since many people aren’t that thrilled about having a data center nearby), but close enough to use the waste heat from the data center to either heat homes or, better yet, grow fresh, hydroponically grown produce? Having a large land-based anchor customer should lower everyone’s power bill if structured properly (much like the Kinross Fort Knox mine’s large baseload power consumption lowers everyone’s monthly electric bill in Fairbanks). If approached this way, a data center would bring real benefits to the general public — Alaskans would certainly welcome lower energy bills and more farm-to-table fresh produce! — Rick Van Nieuwenhuyse, GeoMetallica Inc., Fairbanks Have something on your mind? artigo.texto: Spartanburg County weighs new rules for data center development Officials discuss changes to zoning ordinance as residents push back on Pine Street project SPARTANBURG COUNTY, S.C. (FOX Carolina) - Spartanburg County officials are considering new standards for data center development as they work to establish rules for future projects. The county’s Land Use Committee discussed potential amendments to the Performance Zoning Ordinance, known as the PZO, during a meeting Tuesday at Cleveland Park’s event space. The discussion followed months of research and visits to other parts of the country to examine how other jurisdictions regulate data centers. The county’s planning and development director led a discussion comparing data center regulations in nearby counties and other states. Potential new standards Proposed changes could address the size and type of data centers, their equipment and their proximity to existing homes. Other potential standards include setbacks and buffers, noise mitigation, and measures to manage the effects of electricity and water use. Land Use Committee Chair Grant DeShields said regulating data centers requires balancing competing interests. “The complication of trying to regulate data centers in a proper way that we don’t alienate new data centers from coming here, but at the same time protect our legacy landowners that live here and the people and the citizens that we already have that enjoy peaceful neighborhoods,” DeShields said. DeShields said the county’s current moratorium on data center development is temporary and that establishing permanent regulations is a priority. “There are not data center specific regulations at all. That was the reason for the moratorium to begin with,” DeShields said. County staff also are considering whether to restrict where larger data centers can be built. One option is an overlay district that would designate specific areas for the facilities. The PZO governs development in the county’s Southwest Planning Area, an unincorporated area near Duncan, Lyman, Reidville, Greer and Woodruff. The rest of the county, including the Pine Street corridor, is governed by a separate ordinance, the Unified Land Management Ordinance, or ULMO. DeShields said any changes to the PZO would apply to the entire county, including areas governed by the ULMO. The Valara data center site along South Pine Street falls under the ULMO. The project has faced legal challenges over its classification as a “minor development.” DeShields said the county is working to address potential environmental impacts at the Valara site through a community development agreement. He said the agreement includes environmental studies and monitoring requirements, separate from the broader zoning changes under consideration. Resident reaction Spartanburg County resident Lisa Weir attended Tuesday’s meeting and said she was encouraged by the discussion. “I feel like they are understanding the necessity to put guardrails around or fences around what’s happening with the data centers,” Weir said. Weir said she appreciated hearing about standards used in other areas, including a jurisdiction in Pennsylvania that she said requires buffers of 500 to 1,000 feet between data centers and other properties. She described the county’s current land-use ordinance as “very complicated” compared with those in other communities. But she questioned why the discussion had not happened sooner. “This meeting could have taken place about a year ago,” Weir said. Weir cited the Pine Street site’s proximity to schools, including E.P. Todd, Pine Street School and the South Carolina School for the Deaf and the Blind, as a primary concern. She urged more residents to join opposition to data center development without additional regulations. “I would appreciate if many more people of Spartanburg would mobilize and get involved in it. Because it is imperative that we do this,” Weir said. “It won’t be an immediate thing that we see. But it will have long-term health effects down the line. For everyone.” What’s next Tuesday’s discussion was not a final vote on new data center regulations. County staff must continue developing the proposed amendments before they can proceed through the formal review and approval process. City staff said they plan to discuss recommendations to the planning commission sometime in November. Feel more informed, prepared, and connected with FOX Carolina. artigo.texto: Optical PCIe Extends the Reach of AI Rack Design Lumentum, Astera Labs, and Corning demoed optical PCIe, which extends reach beyond copper and enables more flexible, disaggregated AI rack designs, though it’s still an early-stage proof of concept. As AI racks become denser and PCIe data rates continue to rise, traditional electrical interconnects face familiar constraints in reach, signal integrity, power, thermal management, and cable density. Optical PCIe is emerging as one possible way to ease some of those pressures. PCIe, or Peripheral Component Interconnect Express, is a widely used architecture that links accelerators, switches, memory, storage, and other devices. Optical PCIe preserves that architecture but carries the signals as light over fiber rather than as electrical signals over copper. At the 2026 OCP Global Summit in San Jose, Lumentum, Astera Labs, and Corning used a rack-level demonstration to show how that approach could work in practice. The setup combined Astera Labs’ Scorpio Smart Fabric Switch, Lumentum’s optical interconnect, and Corning multimode fiber. The links used VCSELs (vertical-cavity surface-emitting lasers), which are semiconductor lasers that emit light from the chip surface. Lumentum described the system as a proof of concept, not a product announcement. “Optical PCIe does not eliminate every system constraint, but it can relax several of them by moving data over lightweight, low-loss optical links across longer distances,” Christian Urricariet, senior director of product and strategic marketing at Lumentum, told Data Center Knowledge. Copper’s Limits Become More Apparent as AI Systems Scale One of the clearest pressure points for electrical interconnects is distance. “Given today’s high data rates as well as future even higher data rates, optical connections can span tens to hundreds of meters within a data center,” Joshua Fennimore, commercial technology manager at Corning Optical Communications, told Data Center Knowledge. “Passive copper connections are generally limited to only a few meters, while active copper can extend somewhat farther.” Those constraints become harder to manage as PCIe speeds increase. Urricariet said that higher PCIe data rates make electrical links more sensitive to loss, crosstalk, and equalization requirements over the distances that operators want to support. “Designers may need to add retimers or place connected devices closer together, while high-speed copper cables can become bulky and difficult to route and manage,” Urricariet noted. More Reach Could Reshape Rack and Row Design The practical appeal of optical PCIe is not simply replacing copper with fiber. It is the ability to change where infrastructure can be placed within a rack, or even across multiple racks. Fennimore said copper’s limited reach tends to keep switches and compute hardware physically close together. Fiber, by contrast, gives designers more room to separate those systems while still maintaining high-speed connectivity. “Fiber allows those systems to be separated across racks or rows inside a data center, giving operators greater flexibility to optimize rack layouts around compute density, power, cooling, serviceability, and cable management,” Fennimore said. That added reach could support broader architectural changes as well. Jignesh Shah, senior director of product marketing for the Signal Connectivity Group at Astera Labs, said optical PCIe could enable scale-up designs that span multiple racks rather than being confined to a single enclosure or a short electrical path. “With optical PCIe, reach can be tens of meters, which allows for large scale-up architectures across multiple racks and disaggregated scale-up architectures, with dedicated racks for GPUs, switches, and memory,” Shah told Data Center Knowledge. “Optical PCIe also enables high-density solutions, which are needed for high-radix switches and GPU applications.” In practical terms, the promise of optical PCIe is greater flexibility for system architects. By easing the constraints imposed by the electrical channel budget, Urricariet said, optical PCIe could make it easier to build more modular and composable rack-scale designs, particularly in AI environments where power delivery, thermal limits, and serviceability are becoming just as important as raw performance. Copper Still Has a Strong Role Even as vendors push optical PCIe forward, copper is not going away. For short distances, copper remains the more established and cost-effective choice. According to Shah, once designs move beyond about 3 meters of reach, operators are at a point where it makes sense to evaluate both copper and optical options. “Ultimately, the variables that customers care about come down to power, density, and latency requirements, which can influence a decision between copper and optical,” Shah said. “Optical can support higher density and lower latency, but given copper’s maturity, copper currently offers the best TCO for anything within a few meters.” A Working Demo, Not Yet a Broad Deployment Story For now, the technology remains in its early stages. Urricariet said the OCP demonstration showed fully operational optical links using multiple 32 GB/s channels and an error-free PCIe 5 link in a rack-representative system. But moving from a controlled demonstration to broad deployment will require more than a successful show-floor proof of concept. “Moving from a demonstration to broad deployment requires further work across system integration, reliability, manufacturing, and customer qualification,” Urricariet said. Copper still has a place, and that’s not going to change, but as the demands of AI data centers grow, optical PCIe provides another option. “The goal is not to suggest that every PCIe connection will become optical, but to expand the set of practical system architectures as AI racks grow in scale and complexity,” Urricariet said.

artigo.texto: FracTracker e Public Citizen identificaram 35 ações de permissão tomadas pelos reguladores no Texas nas semanas após o governador Greg Abbott ordenar uma moratória. Os reguladores do Texas não pararam de processar licenças para projetos de data centers quando o governador Greg Abbott ordenou uma pausa no mês passado, de acordo com uma análise de registros públicos divulgada na segunda-feira pelo grupo de vigilância de petróleo e gás FracTracker. Em meio a uma onda de oposição pública à crescente construção de infraestrutura digital no Texas, a Abbott instruiu a Comissão de Qualidade Ambiental do Texas, em uma carta de 21 de setembro, “para suspender todas as licenças solicitadas pelos data centers”. Mas o FracTracker, em colaboração com o Public Citizen, identificou 35 ações de autorização tomadas pelo TCEQ para projetos de data centers nas semanas subsequentes. “A TCEQ continuou analisando os pedidos e emitindo aprovações que permitem o prosseguimento do desenvolvimento do data center”, disseram os grupos em um comunicado à imprensa na segunda-feira. “Essas ações não sinalizam uma agência tentando fazer uma pausa.” O escritório da Abbott e o TCEQ não responderam imediatamente a um pedido de comentário. Abbott descreveu a sua moratória sobre projectos de centros de dados como uma oportunidade para as agências estatais avaliarem o impacto das instalações nos recursos hídricos e na estabilidade da rede. “Nenhuma outra agência estadual deverá avançar com aprovações regulatórias relacionadas a data centers até que esta informação seja adquirida”, escreveu Abbott em sua carta de 21 de setembro ao diretor executivo da TCEQ, Kelly Keel. Desde essa carta, o TCEQ acelerou ou designou engenheiros para 14 licenças, aprovou a cobertura de águas pluviais para 11, certificou estimativas de emissões para sete e emitiu edital público para três, de acordo com documentos de licenciamento coletados pela FracTracker e Public Citizen. As licenças referem-se à construção de instalações de geração de energia a gás para instalações que necessitam de muita energia. Todos os maiores projetos de energia a gás atualmente propostos no Texas destinam-se especificamente a servir centros de dados, que são planejados principalmente para operar inteligência artificial. Os projectos libertariam dezenas de milhares de toneladas de poluentes regulamentados, de acordo com documentos de licenciamento, bem como mais de 100 milhões de toneladas por ano de gases com efeito de estufa – uma quantidade enorme, aproximadamente igual às emissões anuais de um país industrializado de média dimensão. No dia seguinte à pausa da Abbott nas licenças de data center, em 22 de setembro, FracTracker e Public Citizen descobriram que a TCEQ enviou avisos de aprovação preliminar para três grandes projetos: NRG Prairie Energy Center, a usina de energia ABI-1 da VoltaGrid e o data center autoalimentado da Nexus em Hubbard. A agência abriu períodos de comentários públicos sobre dois desses projetos nos dias seguintes. FracTracker e Public Citizen encontraram aprovações de licenças de gerenciamento de águas pluviais para construção de data centers emitidas após 21 de setembro, inclusive para o Caldwell Valley Technology Park no condado de Caldwell, campus Abilene de Crusoe e campus Cedar Creek da EdgeConneX. O relatório identificou vários outros projetos que continuam a avançar através de licenciamento. Por exemplo, os registros mostram que o TCEQ recebeu um pedido de licença para geradores na Edged Energy em Dallas em 6 de outubro, e um engenheiro concluiu uma revisão inicial em 9 de outubro. “Nossa pesquisa descobriu inconsistências gritantes entre as ações regulatórias e as diretrizes do Governador Abbott”, disse Sam Law, gerente de comunicações da FracTracker Alliance e autor do relatório. “Precisamos de uma pausa real para estudar as ameaças que representam à terra, à água e aos meios de subsistência dos texanos.” Sobre esta história Talvez você tenha notado: esta história, como todas as notícias que publicamos, é de leitura gratuita. artigo.texto: - Riot Platforms is contending with sector pressure as Bitcoin miners shift toward AI data centers, a move that brings high capital needs, rising competition and heavier depreciation tied to new infrastructure. - The push to repurpose secured power and mining facilities into AI and high performance computing contracts is changing how Riot Platforms earns revenue, shifting the focus from Bitcoin prices to long term data center agreements. - This development raises questions about how Riot Platforms' investment narrative could be affected by rising AI data center costs and execution risks. Compare how Riot Platforms stacks up against other high capital intensity plays in the AI build out by focusing on 55 AI infrastructure stocks before the next sentiment swing affects this theme. Riot Platforms Investment Narrative Recap To own Riot Platforms, you need to believe the pivot from Bitcoin mining to AI and high performance computing can turn secured power and long leases into a durable cash engine. The recent share price drop and rising short interest underline how sensitive that story is to sentiment around AI infrastructure and Bitcoin at the same time. In the near term, the key swing factor is execution on AI data center build outs and financing, especially replacing the US$573m interim facility before major rent starts. The biggest risk is that high build costs, heavy depreciation and any Bitcoin price weakness keep reported earnings under pressure while liquidity remains tight. The most relevant context for this selloff is the earlier commitment to a 20 year, 191 MW lease with a frontier AI lab and the expanded 50 MW AMD agreement. Together they underpin about US$9.8b of contracted data center revenue and are intended to shift Riot Platforms away from pure Bitcoin price exposure toward long dated leases. Those contracts now meet a tougher market mood on AI infrastructure and financing. For you, the task is weighing whether current sector pressure and concerns about depreciation, cash runway and refinancing risk outweigh the potential from secured power, vertical integration through ESS Metron and E4A, and the large Corsicana campus opportunity. Riot Platforms Forecasts And What Has To Go Right Riot Platforms' narrative projects US$1.8b of revenue and US$208.0 million of earnings by 2029. That path assumes revenue expands at 37.9% a year and earnings move from a loss of about US$1.3b today to positive territory, which is a very large swing in profit expectations that depends on AI data center leases turning contracted revenue into actual cash generation.

artigo.texto: EverWind, a Nova Scotia-based energy infrastructure company, has announced plans for over CA$ 10 billion (US$ 7.09 billion) in private investment for a data center campus at its Point Tupper industrial site while Anthropic has confirmed it has entered into a lease agreement at the campus. As outlined in a press release, the planned investment includes more than CA$ 8 billion (US$ 5.68 billion) to develop, construct, own, and finance the campus. The remaining CA$ 2 billion (US$ 1.42 billion) will be used to expand EverWind’s onshore wind portfolio in Nova Scotia. “Point Tupper has supported industry in the Strait Region for more than 50 years. Today’s announcement represents major new investment in Nova Scotia’s digital and energy infrastructure and highlights the role Nova Scotians can play in driving Canada’s renewed economic ambitions, marking a new chapter for the site and creating opportunities for rural Nova Scotia,” said Trent Vichie, EverWind founder and Chief Executive Officer. The campus plans to have an initial capacity of 95 MW in late 2027 but by 2028, total capacity will balloon to 420 MW. The company also said that the CA$ 2 billion will support its four renewable energy generation projects in Bear Lake, Windy Ridge, Kmtnuk, and Upper Afton. The data center is said to complement EverWind’s plans for green hydrogen and ammonia at Point Tupper. Following EverWind’s announcement, Jacob Glick, Anthropic Head of Public Policy, Canada, announced on LinkedIn that the Claude developer had signed its first data center lease in Canada with EverWind. “Canada and Nova Scotia have both set a high bar for how data centres get built. We’ve signed the federal Responsible Data Centre Development Principles, and we’re committed to meeting Premier Houston’s conditions: protecting ratepayers, safeguarding water and making sure Nova Scotians benefit,” wrote Glick. While not its first lease agreement, the deal is part of a growing trend for the company as it pushes to meet demand for its AI products. As w.media reported in July, Anthropic signed a 20-year lease agreement with US digital infrastructure company TeraWulf. That lease covers 401 MW of critical IT load at a facility in Kentucky and is expected to generate US$ 19 billion in contracted revenue over the initial term. The company also entered into its first data center lease in Australia in September. The AI company has made a long-term commitment at the Western Downs Digital Park in Queensland which is expected to have a peak capacity of 2.16 GW.

artigo.texto: There are now 170 megapacks in place alongside the onshore converter station for Ørsted’s Hornsea 3 Offshore Wind Farm, near Norwich, Norfolk. Each is the length of a classic Routemaster London bus but weighs the same as five buses. The system, known as Iceni after the Norfolk-based warrior tribe of the Roman era, will have a capacity of 600 MWh (and a 300 MW power rating). This is equivalent to the daily power consumption of 80,000 UK homes. The Iceni team comprises specialists from Ørsted, Hitachi Energy, Knights Brown & Tesla working together on this first-of-its-kind project. What makes this BESS unique is the split layout of the site with the two areas, separated by the Hornsea 3 Onshore Converter station, linked by 18 x 33 kV cables, each over 600 meters in length. In addition, the shared grid connection point with Hornsea 3 has added additional technical complexity over a stand-alone connection point to the National Grid. The project is now in the final stages of the mechanical and electrical installation, with the 33 kV cross-site cables currently being installed and terminated. The first stage of commissioning and testing is well underway, and preparations are being made for energization of the BESS Transformer. When completed, the battery energy storage system will be one of the largest in Europe. Beatrice d’Eufemia, Project Manager for Iceni BESS at Ørsted, said: “It’s a milestone moment for Ørsted that construction is now complete on our first large-scale battery energy storage system in the UK. “The system will make the best use of renewable energy produced in the UK as when electricity generation exceeds demand, the excess can be stored and then used when demand is greater, helping balance the grid, and lower electricity costs for everyone.” Richard Swann, Construction Manager for Iceni BESS at Ørsted, said: “It’s a real testament to the hard work, dedication and cooperation of the team from many different organizations that the construction has been completed successfully.” David Shillabeer, Head of Transmission & Distribution, at Knights Brown, said: “Reaching this milestone is a significant achievement for everyone involved in the Iceni project. Delivering a battery energy storage system of this scale has required close collaboration between Ørsted, Knights Brown and the many other organizations that have contributed to its success. “Beyond the engineering, the scheme has enabled us to invest in local people, develop skills and create opportunities across Norfolk and the wider region. We are proud to have played our part in an important project that will support the UK’s transition to a more resilient, low-carbon energy system, while leaving a positive legacy for the communities in which we work.”

artigo.texto: A Microsoft vai-se retirar do projeto de desenvolvimento de um data center de inteligência artificial (IA) no Reino Unido por preocupações com o fornecimento de energia, segundo avança o jornal “The Guardian”. O empreendimento, que é liderado pela britânica Nscale, previa a criação do maior data center de IA do país, com inauguração prevista para o próximo ano em Essex. Já tinham surgido dúvidas sobre o local escolhido para o projeto, mas a Microsoft, um dos maiores clientes previstos para o projeto, informou à empresa que vai sair do acordo. A decisão ocorreu um mês depois de serem conhecidos problemas no fornecimento de energia, o que iria afetar o início das operações deste projeto. O governo de Keir Starmer destacou este projeto como o “maior data center soberano de IA do Reino Unido”. Com a saída da Microsoft a Nscale perdeu o único cliente anunciado publicamente para o data center. Contudo, um porta-voz da empresa britânica revelou que continuam comprometidos com o projeto e com o Reino Unido e estão a explorar novas fontes de energia para o projeto. artigo.texto: A Microsoft desistiu de um acordo para a utilização de um centro de dados da fornecedora britânica de infraestruturas Nscale. A decisão afeta as instalações planeadas para Loughton, em Essex, e surge na sequência de atrasos significativos na garantia de fornecimento de energia elétrica. Segundo a Reuters, que cita um relatório original do jornal Telegraph, os responsáveis pela rede elétrica nacional britânica alertaram a Nscale de que não existiria capacidade de fornecimento para o centro de dados antes da década de 2030. A gigante norte-americana era considerada um dos dois maiores clientes desta empresa de serviços na nuvem. Impacto e resposta da Nscale Apesar do revés no projeto de Essex, um porta-voz da Nscale desvalorizou a quebra do contrato e garantiu que a relação com a Microsoft se mantém forte e com perspetivas de longo prazo. A fornecedora sublinha que o problema elétrico em redor da região de Londres não afeta os restantes compromissos estabelecidos. A empresa reafirmou ainda a sua dedicação ao mercado do Reino Unido e explicou que está a explorar fontes de energia alternativas para o local, além de procurar outras áreas de expansão no país. A Microsoft recusou comentar o caso de forma oficial. Crescimento e entrada na bolsa A Nscale, que conta com o apoio financeiro da Nvidia, fornece infraestruturas de computação, energia e software para o treino e execução de modelos de inteligência artificial. A empresa concorre no mesmo segmento que a CoreWeave, Nebius, Crusoe e Lambda, e registou um crescimento acentuado desde o seu lançamento. Num período de apenas dois anos e meio, o valor total dos seus contratos saltou de 100 milhões de dólares para mais de 103 mil milhões de dólares (cerca de 94 mil milhões de euros). No mês passado, a Nscale formalizou o pedido para uma oferta pública inicial nos Estados Unidos. O prospeto da operação apontava precisamente a Microsoft e a Anthropic como os seus principais clientes futuros.
