artigo.texto: EXCLUSIVE: As massive data centers rise across the country to power America's artificial intelligence boom, one of the industry's biggest builders is making the case that the benefits extend far beyond the technology inside. During an exclusive tour of Compass Datacenters' sprawling campus in Red Oak, Texas, Fox News Digital got a rare look inside the infrastructure behind the nation's growing appetite for computing. Getting inside took roughly three months' of approvals. Once on site, Fox News Digital passed through six layers of security and suited up in personal protective equipment before entering the facility, where photos and recording devices were prohibited. Beyond the checkpoints, the interior was remarkably clean and surprisingly quiet, with little of the industrial noise one might expect from an operation running around the clock. Inside, rows of towering server racks stretched across the spotless floor, surrounded by the electrical and cooling systems needed to keep the equipment operating. At Red Oak, Compass uses a closed-loop cooling system that recirculates coolant rather than continuously drawing water to cool the equipment. DATA CENTER CEO SHARES THE POWERFUL WAY AMERICAN COMMUNITIES CAN BENEFIT FROM THE NEW TECH BOOM Compass CEO Chris Crosby, a North Texas native, said the Red Oak campus has not used water for cooling since it began operating. "We haven't used water since inception," Crosby said, noting the importance of conserving the region's resources. "Water is precious in North Texas." Beyond cooling, security is another major consideration for facilities housing vast amounts of computing infrastructure. Crosby the extensive security is not about keeping the facilities secret, but rather protecting the sensitive information and critical infrastructure housed inside. "Hacking is real, attacks on infrastructure are real," Crosby said. "If people knew that a bank or a government was operating at a particular facility, they could infiltrate that facility. So that's why the levels of security are so high at our campuses." The campus, roughly 20 miles south of Dallas, will eventually include 10 data center buildings spanning roughly 2.6 million square feet. A Schneider Electric manufacturing facility and a workforce training center operated in partnership with Texas State Technical College are also located on the campus. AMERICA’S NEW BLUE-COLLAR JOB BOOM IS ONE NOBODY SAW COMING — AND IT’S JUST GETTING STARTED Crosby says the development offers a glimpse at an often-overlooked side of America's data center boom: blue-collar jobs. "Data centers are where the economic engine is going to be going forward," Crosby told Fox News Digital, pointing to the jobs, economic activity and tax revenue generated by the industry. Roughly 600 people work for Compass at the campus, while Schneider Electric employs about 300 more, according to Crosby. Thousands of construction workers have also cycled through the development since work began in 2019. And the company says it needs more. "We can't get enough people into this career," Crosby said. That demand helped spur the creation of MEI Pathways, a workforce development program built in partnership with Texas State Technical College. The $12.6 million training facility offers a 12-week program aimed at preparing electricians, mechanics and technicians for jobs in the industry. Building data centers also requires an array of skilled trades, including carpenters, welders and concrete workers. A SOUTHERN STATE JUST TOOK THE TOP SPOT IN ONE OF THE WORLD’S FASTEST-GROWING INDUSTRIES "There was a war on blue-collar jobs for a long time — everybody had to get a four-year degree," Crosby said. "I'm so glad that's over with." Compass has worked with local officials on roads, sewer and other infrastructure and donated $15 million toward a new animal shelter after Ellis County's previous shelter arrangement ended. The investments come as Texas grapples with how to accommodate the enormous electricity demands accompanying the industry's growth while protecting the reliability of its power grid. "I am tired of the elitism that this doesn't create jobs," he said.

artigo.texto: Algeria, Tunisia and Egypt are stepping up investment in renewable energy and battery storage, with new wind and solar tenders alongside plans to expand local energy storage manufacturing across North Africa. Algeria’s state-owned electricity utility Sonelgaz has issued a tender for the development of two wind farms with a combined capacity of 200 MW. The projects will be located in the provinces of Laghouat and Djelfa, with each facility expected to contribute 100 MW of wind power. The contract covers engineering, civil construction, equipment procurement, installation and commissioning. The scope offers opportunities for renewable energy developers and engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) companies capable of delivering large-scale wind infrastructure, including the electrical systems required to connect the projects to the national grid. In Tunisia, the state-owned electricity and gas company STEG has launched a procurement process for a 50 MW solar power plant in the Tataouine Governorate. The facility will be equipped with a battery energy storage system (BESS) rated at 10 MW/20 MWh, enabling electricity generated during periods of strong sunlight to be stored for later use. The project is supported by financing from the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD). READ: Uganda targets commercial oil production by June 2027 Energy flexibility The inclusion of battery storage is expected to improve the management of intermittent solar generation and provide greater flexibility in electricity supply. The tender could attract companies specialising in photovoltaic technology, energy storage equipment and integrated power management systems. Egypt is pursuing a different approach by developing domestic capacity to assemble battery storage systems. Rosatom’s energy storage division has entered into a partnership with Telecom and Technology to establish an assembly facility with an annual production capacity of 500 MWh. The facility will target industrial and telecommunications customers, sectors that require dependable electricity supplies and backup power solutions. In Israel, Doral Group is expanding its Hadarey Shean project with an additional 150 MW of solar generation capacity and 800 MWh of battery storage. The expansion is valued at approximately US $260.89M, according to the reported investment figure. The projects demonstrate the region’s growing focus on combining renewable electricity generation with storage technologies to improve power system reliability. Algeria’s wind tender and Tunisia’s solar-plus-storage development are creating procurement opportunities, while Egypt’s planned assembly facility could strengthen the regional supply chain for battery systems. For international developers and EPC contractors, the latest initiatives provide potential opportunities across project design, construction, equipment supply and storage integration. Companies seeking contracts in the region will need to assess technical specifications, grid connection requirements, financing conditions and local procurement rules. As renewable energy deployment expands across North Africa and neighbouring markets, the ability to deliver projects that combine generation capacity with effective storage solutions is likely to become increasingly important for developers seeking to compete in the region.

artigo.texto: VW ID. Cross ganha versão com bateria menor por R$ 158 mil na Europa Com bateria menor de 37 kWh e autonomia de até 324 km, nova opção de entrada do SUV elétrico busca atrair motoristas urbanos e trabalhadores que dependem do deslocamento diário A Volkswagen deu início à pré-venda de uma nova opção de entrada para o ID. Cross, menor SUV 100% elétrico da alemã. A novidade adota um pacote de baterias menor, de 37 kWh, mirando consumidores que buscam menor preço de aquisição para trajetos urbanos ou de deslocamento diário. Na Alemanha, a versão parte de 27.995 euros (cerca de R$ 158 mil), valor que torna o utilitário esportivo o elétrico de entrada da marca. A nova configuração expande o portfólio apresentado globalmente em meados de julho, que estreou com a versão topo de linha Style por 36,5 mil euros (cerca de R$ 222 mil). Baterias, autonomia e recarga A nova bateria de 37 kWh de capacidade líquida oferece autonomia de até 324 km (WLTP). Ela pode ser combinada a dois níveis de potência: 85 kW (116 cv) e 99 kW (135 cv), ambas atingindo velocidade máxima de 160 km/h. Para os motoristas que buscam maior alcance, a gama do ID. Cross contempla ainda o conjunto com bateria de 52 kWh e motor de 155 kW (211 cv), capaz de rodar até 427 km com uma única carga. Em estações de carregamento rápido em corrente contínua (DC) de até 105 kW, as baterias recuperam de 10% a 80% da carga em cerca de 24 minutos. Versões, espaço e tecnologia a bordo O ID. Cross com bateria de 37 kWh é oferecido nas linhas de acabamento Trend, Life e Style. Mesmo na opção de entrada Trend, o SUV compacto inclui itens de série como assistente de estacionamento dianteiro e traseiro (Park Distance Control) e integração com smartphones sem fio (App Connect). Construído sobre a nova plataforma MEB+, o modelo tem dimensões externas similares às do T-Cross convencional que conhecemos aqui pelo mercado brasileiro (4,15 metros de comprimento), mas aproveita a arquitetura elétrica para ampliar o espaço interno: - Porta-malas principal: 475 litros (20 litros a mais que o T-Cross a combustão), além de um compartimento sob o piso. - Porta-malas dianteiro (frunk): 25 litros sob o capô, ideal para acomodar os cabos de recarga. - Cabine digital e nostálgica: traz tela central de 12,9 polegadas e painel digital de 10,25 polegadas, que conta com um modo clássico capaz de reproduzir o layout analógico dos mostradores do Golf de primeira geração. - Assistências avançadas: opcionais e versões superiores contam com o sistema Connected Travel Assist (que reconhece semáforos e para o carro automaticamente no sinal vermelho), função Vehicle-to-Load (V2L, para alimentar eletrônicos externos de até 3,6 kW), som Harman Kardon e bancos elétricos com massagem. Mira no mercado brasileiro Embora a chegada do ID. Cross ao Brasil ainda não tenha sido confirmada oficialmente pela matriz, o SUV compacto é considerado um dos fortes candidatos da ofensiva elétrica no país. Por compartilhar o apelo de nome e porte do T-Cross, um dos maiores acertos da marca e líder de vendas no mercado nacional, a novidade surge como o produto de volume ideal para acelerar a estratégia de eletrificação da fabricante alemã na América Latina.

artigo.texto: Coloque a eixos nas suas fontes preferidas do Google Veja nossas notícias com mais destaque nas suas buscas. Coloque a eixos nas suas fontes preferidas do Google Veja nossas notícias com mais destaque nas suas buscas. O Brasil acaba de transformar em lei uma política de incentivos para ampliar a instalação de data centers no país. O Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata) chega em um momento de forte crescimento da demanda por capacidade computacional, impulsionada pela inteligência artificial, e encontra um país com atributos importantes para disputar esses investimentos, entre eles uma matriz elétrica predominantemente renovável com possibilidade de expansão a custos competitivos. A oportunidade é evidente, mas empreendimentos que concentram centenas de megawatts de demanda contínua também exigem pensar em como o sistema elétrico brasileiro será capaz de absorver essa nova carga sem comprometer a expansão do sistema nem implicar custos aos demais consumidores. Um dos pontos de atenção do Redata está na exigência de energia renovável ou de baixa emissão. A regulamentação dirá o que cabe nessa segunda categoria, mas a possibilidade de incluir o gás natural traz uma contradição importante. O gás natural entra nessa discussão por uma questão de operação. Data centers funcionam 24 horas por dia, sete dias por semana, com uma carga praticamente constante e exigências elevadas de continuidade do fornecimento. Ao mesmo tempo, a expansão do parque elétrico instalado no país tem se dado principalmente por meio de fontes variáveis, como solar e eólica. Essa combinação de demanda firme e oferta variável aumenta a necessidade de flexibilidade do sistema elétrico, hoje atendida em parte justamente pela geração térmica despachável a gás. O processo depende ainda da expansão das redes de transmissão. Tais reforços podem levar de cinco a dez anos, enquanto um data center pode ser implantado em prazo muito menor, da ordem de um ano e meio. A discussão sobre flexibilidade, portanto, não pode ser separada das condições da rede e do planejamento de sua expansão. O estudo do Instituto E+ Metodologia Integrada para Transição Energética e Desenvolvimento Industrial no Brasil, prestes a ser concluído, simula a entrada de data centers, projetos de aço de baixa emissão e processamento de terras raras no sistema elétrico entre 2029 e 2039. O estudo mostra que a capacidade da rede é determinante para a localização e a escala desses investimentos. Além de geração disponível, é preciso que a infraestrutura elétrica tenha capacidade para atender a nova carga no ponto em que ela será conectada. Nas simulações, Campinas apresenta melhores condições para grandes data centers em conexões à rede de 500 kV, enquanto, em Fortaleza, a estrutura de 230 kV oferece as condições mais favoráveis analisadas. Em níveis inferiores de tensão, a capacidade para receber grandes cargas diminui. No Pecém, a concentração de projetos eletrointensivos pode levar diferentes empreendimentos a disputar capacidade de conexão antes da entrada em operação das obras de expansão previstas para a rede. A expansão da transmissão, por sua vez, pode demorar muito além do prazo de implantação de um data center, o que torna a capacidade de conexão uma variável cada vez mais relevante para a localização e o cronograma desses investimentos. A contratação de energia deve assegurar adicionalidade, contribuindo para ampliar a oferta de energia limpa e competitiva necessária ao atendimento da nova demanda. A entrada da dessas cargas requer expansão da oferta de baixa emissão e dos recursos de flexibilidade, sem que os custos sistêmicos associados a esses empreendimentos recaiam sobre os demais consumidores. Por fim, o Redata acerta ao associar incentivos à instalação de data centers no país a contrapartidas em pesquisa e desenvolvimento, capacidade computacional para o mercado brasileiro e eficiência no uso de recursos. Mas a escala do consumo elétrico exige que a política pública olhe também para a produtividade energética. Afinal, a atração de data centers precisa caminhar junto com o planejamento elétrico de uma maneira favorável à sociedade brasileira como um todo. Os incentivos devem contribuir para ampliar a oferta de energia limpa e competitiva, assegurar capacidade de rede e gerar valor para o país, preservando as vantagens energéticas que tornam o Brasil atraente para esses investimentos. Clauber Leite é diretor de Energia Sustentável e Bioeconomia do Instituto E+ Transição Energética.

artigo.texto: Saft inaugurates its first solid-state battery production lines in Bordeaux TotalEnergies' subsidiary opens lines in Bordeaux combining sulfide and polymer electrolytes. It targets aerospace and space, with energy densities stated to be up to 50% higher than lithium-ion. Saft, a subsidiary of TotalEnergies, is inaugurating new production lines for solid-electrolyte batteries, known as "all-solid-state" or "Solid-State" batteries, at its Bordeaux site. According to the company, it becomes the first French manufacturer with development and production capabilities combining sulfide and polymer technologies at room temperature. The announcement comes in a market where manufacturers are stepping up investment, such as the 12 GWh joint venture formalised by Premier Energies and RCT Nexor. Separately, according to Wood Mackenzie, four-hour storage beats gas peaking on cost. A solid electrolyte replacing the liquid one All-solid-state batteries replace the traditional liquid electrolyte with a solid one. Saft says this architecture provides a higher level of safety. It would also allow energy densities of up to 50% higher than those of conventional lithium-ion batteries, according to the group. The manufacturer also highlights more environmentally responsible manufacturing processes. Dry electrode production would cut the CO2 emissions associated with that step by up to 40%, according to Saft. The company specifies that the solid electrolyte combines sulfide and polymer technologies at room temperature, which, it says, offers a wide range of applications. Aerospace and space in focus Saft is targeting the electrification and decarbonisation of aeronautics and space, two sectors where gains in safety, performance and energy density are particularly strategic, according to the company. In aviation, it says it has already delivered semi-solid cells to assess future electric and hybrid aircraft architectures. The group identifies all-solid-state batteries as a key technology for the gradual electrification of aviation. It also points to strong interest from the space sector in these cells. Cedric Duclos, Chief Executive Officer of Saft, states that the new line turns several years of research into concrete industrial capabilities and confirms the ambition to make France and Europe leading players in this technology. Saft, which claims more than 100 years of experience in high-performance batteries, is 100% owned by TotalEnergies. The company did not disclose, in this announcement, a production capacity or an investment amount for the new lines. artigo.texto: Burgess emphasizes transparency, data center oversight ahead of election Georgia House District 164 candidate discusses priorities if elected You can view Burgess’ full interview with WTOC above. SAVANNAH, Ga. (WTOC) - Voters in Georgia’s 164th State House District will decide next month who will represent them. Stephanie Burgess will represent the Democratic party on November’s ticket. “When I thought about what we’re facing right now in the state and even in the nation, I’m like, why not me?” Burgess said. Burgess works as an attorney and said her law experience would be helpful when it comes to public safety policy. She said when looking at current public safety issues, like Flock cameras, she thinks voters are looking at them as larger transparency issues. “I can say that transparency and accountability may not be listed on the ballot, but that’s what’s on the ballot this year,” Burgess said. Data center transparency Burgess said one of her main focuses would be bringing transparency to development, specifically data centers. “If I’m elected, the voters of 164 would have voted me in. And so I would need to promote what their issues are. And if they don’t want a data center, then I’m not voting for a data center,” Burgess said. Balancing growth and cost of living Burgess said balancing development with quality of life and rising costs of living is another priority. “Growth should not harm the people. It should help the people,” Burgess said. If elected, Burgess would be the first Democrat to represent the district in the 29 years Republican Ron Stephens has held it. “We have big issues. I’m a big fighter, and we need big change,” Burgess said. Early voting is underway. Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3. Copyright 2026 WTOC. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Boone City Council approves guidelines for potential data center The Boone City Council approved a Memorandum of Understanding with Lightedge on Monday, moving the city one step closer to potentially hosting a data center. The agreement includes stipulations such as capping the data center's monthly water use at 75,000 gallons, which is roughly equal to the usage of five five-person households. Lightedge would not qualify for city property tax incentives and would be required to pay for any necessary utility upgrades. Mayor Dave Casotti said the city is carefully considering the potential impact of the project. "We would not do something for Boone that would harm the economy, the infrastructure, the environment," he said. Not everyone supported the council's decision. Nearly 50 people attended Monday's meeting, but approximately a dozen left after learning public comments on the data center would not be heard. Some attendees stayed and expressed their concerns. "You're elected officials listening to your constituents — they overwhelmingly don't want a data center. You are failing your constituents," one said. Ultimately, no final decision has been made, and Boone is just one of several locations being considered for the project. If the data center does come to Boone, Casotti said the council has taken steps to ensure the process is well-prepared. "We didn't do this by the seat of our pants," Casotti said.

artigo.texto: A questão, que mal foi recebida pelos candidatos no ano passado, tem grande importância numa corrida que poderá determinar o controlo do Congresso. SUNBURY, Ohio — Uma proposta para um grande data center revolucionou a política neste subúrbio de Columbus, de tendência republicana. Isso pode significar problemas para o senador norte-americano Jon Husted, uma figura de longa data na política republicana estadual que foi nomeado para seu cargo em 2025, depois que o ex-senador JD Vance se tornou vice-presidente. Husted está concorrendo contra Sherrod Brown, um democrata que cumpriu três mandatos no Senado antes de perder sua cadeira há dois anos. Em Sunbury, a disputa pelo Senado está na mesma votação que um referendo que proibiria grandes centros de dados. Os defensores da medida dizem que não confiam em nenhum dos partidos para enfrentar a influência das empresas de tecnologia, mas têm menos fé nos republicanos. Esse sentimento estende-se a grande parte do estado e pode ter consequências numa eleição que pode determinar se os democratas assumirão o controlo da Câmara. “Estou muito decepcionado com a abordagem de ambas as partes ao meu problema”, disse Larry Thode, um residente da área de Sunbury que votou nos republicanos durante a maior parte de sua vida e cuja propriedade fica próxima a um data center planejado da Amazon Web Services. Thode culpa mais os republicanos do que os democratas porque são eles que estão no poder, disse ele. O partido controla o governo de Ohio há mais de uma década, com Husted servindo como vice-governador de 2019 a 2025. Os republicanos também controlam o governo federal, com o presidente Donald Trump apoiando o desenvolvimento de data centers de IA. Alicia Doty, vizinha de Thode, compartilha dessa frustração. Ela votou principalmente nos democratas no passado, mas sente que o partido precisa ser mais claro na oposição aos grandes data centers. Dito isto, as suas preocupações com os Democratas são pequenas comparadas com a sua decepção pelo facto de os Republicanos acolherem favoravelmente o desenvolvimento. A campanha de Husted disse que ele apoia o planejamento cuidadoso dos data centers, com proteção aos consumidores e respeito às comunidades locais, mas Doty ainda não está convencido. “Não acredito em Jon Husted nem por um segundo”, disse ela. Sunbury, uma cidade de cerca de 9.000 habitantes, fica perto do extremo nordeste dos subúrbios de Columbus, onde subdivisões habitacionais se transformam em terras agrícolas e florestas. A cidade fica no condado de Delaware, que tem a renda familiar média mais alta de Ohio e um histórico de apoio aos republicanos. A Amazon Web Services está propondo construir um data center com demanda de eletricidade de várias centenas de megawatts em um campo agrícola entre as propriedades de Thode e Doty. De acordo com o plano, Sunbury anexaria o terreno da AWS e permitiria seu desenvolvimento. Os oponentes reuniram assinaturas suficientes para colocar em votação local uma medida que proibiria data centers com demanda de eletricidade de pelo menos 25 megawatts. A reação foi intensa, em parte porque os moradores de Sunbury observaram como os data centers transformaram as terras agrícolas de New Albany, uma cidade a cerca de 24 quilômetros de distância. New Albany agora tem uma das concentrações mais densas de data centers do país. “Dizimada” é como Doty descreve a cidade próxima, e ela quer evitar o mesmo destino. Ela observou que a proposta de Sunbury começa com um data center, mas os planejadores discutiram a construção de um parque industrial ao sul de sua propriedade que pode atrair data centers adicionais. “Orelha de Lata” Muitas comunidades em Ohio estão resistindo aos data centers e essa oposição muitas vezes se sobrepõe à desconfiança nos políticos. “Existe esse tipo de populismo forcado em relação aos data centers que realmente emergiu”, disse Kyle Kondik, editor-chefe do Crystal Ball de Sabato, do Centro de Política da Universidade da Virgínia. Brown aproveitou a questão, enquanto Husted concorre num partido liderado por Trump, que apoia empresas de centros de dados e critica os oponentes do desenvolvimento. Trump interpretou mal a opinião pública sobre os data centers, respondendo à raiva dos eleitores com o que Kondik chamou de “ouvido de lata”. A resposta marca um afastamento do talento passado de Trump para explorar tendências políticas subjacentes, disse Kondik. A oposição aos data centers é mais forte em Ohio do que em outros lugares. Por exemplo, 3 por cento dos eleitores de Ohio, numa sondagem recente do New York Times/Siena, afirmaram que a inteligência artificial e os centros de dados foram a sua principal questão nas eleições, o maior número de qualquer estado com uma corrida competitiva ao Senado dos EUA. Na mesma pesquisa, os eleitores de Ohio disseram confiar nos democratas nesta questão por 11 pontos, mais uma vez o maior número de qualquer estado com uma disputa competitiva pelo Senado. artigo.texto: Almost nobody wakes up thinking about a data center. But by the time you’ve checked the weather, paid a bill and answered a few emails, you’ve probably used several. Your bank runs on them, your hospital, your streaming account, every AI tool you’ve tried, and increasingly, more of the public services you rely on. You just never see them. That’s becoming a problem for my industry. In August, supervisors in Pinal County, Arizona, voted down a large data center campus after so many residents turned up to object that the county opened five overflow rooms across three buildings. Some said they hadn’t even heard about the project until several meetings in. Developers have lost similar votes this year in Florida, Virginia and North Carolina. I work on the power systems inside these buildings, in Britain and increasingly in the US. A lot of the backlash is aimed at the wrong target. Some of it is our own fault, and we should own that. Start with water, because that’s what most people worry about. Agriculture accounts for around 72% of the world’s freshwater withdrawals, according to the UN Food and Agriculture Organization. Data centers barely show up in that picture. That’s no comfort if you live next to a new campus in a dry county, and I get that. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimates US data centers used about 17 billion gallons of water for cooling in 2023, and that could double or even quadruple by 2028. The water used to generate their electricity is roughly 12 times that again, and companies rarely report it. In Britain the picture looks very different. Research for England’s water market operator puts data centers at about 0.2% of non-household water use, a figure the government quoted in Parliament last month. A cooler climate helps, and so do cooling systems that barely use water for most of the year. So national figures don’t tell you much either way. What matters is the specific site, where it is, and how it’s cooled. Why the anger, then? Part of it is simple. The benefits of cloud services and AI are spread across millions of people. The costs, real or imagined, land on one town. Residents see the construction trucks, the new power lines and the backup generators. They don’t see the hospital or the bank that relies on what’s inside. These are also big, windowless, heavily secured buildings. When people can’t easily find out how much water and power a site will use, or who actually benefits, politicians fill the gap with rhetoric. And a data center is an easy stand-in for bigger fears about AI, climate change, jobs and big tech. A planning meeting turns into a vote on the future. I don’t blame people for that. Using AI or watching Netflix doesn’t mean you give up the right to ask how it’s made. So, here’s what I think my industry needs to do. Publish the numbers. Water and energy use, how they’re measured, and how they’ll change as a site grows. That should include the water behind the electricity, not just what goes through the cooling system. Build for the place. A cooling design that works in a cool, wet climate can be the wrong choice in the desert. Water, grid capacity and what the community actually wants should decide where and how we build. Take power seriously. In my experience it’s often a harder problem than water. A large campus can draw as much electricity as a small city. When the grid connection isn’t ready, the fallback is usually on-site gas or diesel generators, and “temporary” tends to last a lot longer than anyone said. Communities are right to ask for a proper connection plan and firm limits on how long those generators run. Treat residents as partners. Tell them early and give them a real say. If we promise jobs, tax revenue or better infrastructure, put numbers on it, not just headlines. The good news is the technology is moving the right way. Newer sites increasingly use air cooling or sealed liquid loops that keep reusing the same water instead of evaporating it. That isn’t universal yet, which is why planning standards matter. Efficiency is also just good business. Power and water drive our costs, our resilience and our ability to grow, so we have every reason to use less of both. But we should prove it with measured results, not targets and press releases. The quickest way to win back trust is site-by-site public reporting, so communities can check what was promised against what was delivered: water, energy, cooling method, backup generation. That lets planners do their jobs properly. They can steer projects away from water-stressed areas, test whether grid plans are realistic, and hear local concerns while designs can still change, instead of telling the community after everything’s been decided. Judge data centers on how well they’re designed, powered, sited and run. Scrutiny on those terms is fair, and we should welcome it. Blanket opposition isn’t. It ignores the services everyone depends on and the improvements that are already here. artigo.texto: SAN ANTONIO – In August, several San Antonio councilmembers, including District 6’s Ric Galvan, proposed a possible moratorium on the city accepting applications for new data centers. “My council colleagues do not fully support that,” Galvan said. “We had a couple of folks who did, and it was four or five of us that supported it fully, but not enough to move forward.” He said 19 of the city’s 28 data centers are in his district alone and more applications to build new ones have been filed. Galvan said the district’s appeal, combined with an outdated city land use code, allows data centers to be built near housing developments and hospitals. “As the energy [production infrastructures] are built, the fiber optic cables are built, as well as the land is available, right, it’s been easy for a lot of data centers to come in and say, well, we’ll set up here,” Galvan said. Among the proposed regulation items is updating the land use code, restricting new data centers to areas already zoned for industrial or heavy commercial use and requiring city council approval before a data center can be built. Galvan laid out, “We’re asking for specific use authorization. A very technical term, but just means that any kind of development in this category needs a specific form of authorization from the City Council. We do this for bars. We do for amusement parks. We do it for carnivals. We do all kinds of different developments in our city every two weeks of city council.” The councilman said this type of authorization is something the city can utilize when it comes to developments including data centers. He said the push for regulations on new data centers is out of concern of possible oversaturation of data centers in certain areas of the city, not just in the district he represents. “We are going to see them as they’ve been applied to, or been applying for, placed in District 7, 8, 4, 3, 2, and even District 1.” Tuesday, the city’s Zoning Commission will convene to discuss the same proposed regulations pertaining to zoning issues that were presented to the city council on October 15. During the commission’s meeting, the board will hear public comment on the proposed regulations, and Galvan is encouraging San Antonians to speak up. “It’s really critical that our residents are able to always give thought to development without the consideration on any kind of policy development we have here, particularly on data centers,” he said. Galvan said the public comment portion of the meeting is scheduled for 1:00 p.m. at the Cliff Morton Development and Business Services Center (One Stop) located at 1901 S. Alamo Street. Residents can go in person and give public comment at1:00 p.m. The City Council’s official vote on the proposed regulations is set for next Thursday, October 29. READ MORE:

artigo.texto: On Monday, the Pittsburg City Council agreed to a future agenda item request to discuss a 45-day moratorium on data centers. The item was approved in a 4-0 vote with mayor Dionne Adams recusing herself. The moratorium will return either later this week or at the earliest date possible. According to other cities (such as the City of Oakley), and the law, a city can only impose a moratorium for 45-days. However, this is the first step of a 2-year moratorium as long as the city is working on policy. Including two 1-year extensions. Councilmember Juan Antonio Banales laid out a 45-day plan for a moratorium. Banales explained that phase 1 of the project has already been entitled and approved. That decision has been made and they would honor their legal obligations, but any future data center developments in Pittsburg have not decided. He said that is where the community staff has an opportunity to influence future developments. He provided a plan for which the community can participate over the next 45-days and beyond: A formal pause: proposing this week during a special meeting that the council consider a 45-day moratorium on future data center development in the city of Pittsburg. (Covering phase 2 & 3 and other future developments, but does not impact Phase 1) “The moratorium does two things, first it gives our community clarity. There is a lot of confusion out there about what is the status of data center projects and developments,” explained Banales. “This makes it clear. Second, it allows our advisory committee on data centers to finish its work.” He also said Pittsburg Power and AVAIO are currently negotiating the power agreement for Phase 1. If a deal is reached, it will come before the council for approval. Next Steps: Advisory Committee Recommendations. Banales said he expected the recommendations to come back to the city council. Policy Framework: once recommendations are in, council will give clear policy framework for data centers in Pittsburg. “That means, where should data centers not be allowed. Where are they appropriate and what standards should they have to meet before it can be considered – including design, noise, water and energy use,” said Banales. “The goal is future decisions are made under rules set in advance rather than one project at a time.” He again proposed the 45-day pause for a formal moratorium, consider power agreements, let committee finish its work and set a policy. “Many of you have engaged on this issue with passion, research and with real care for this city and this is what exactly what civic participation should look like and it has made the process better. Disagreement is welcome here, strong opinions are welcome here,” said Banales. “But some of what we have seen in recent weeks has crossed a line. Personal attacks, threats, behavior meant to intimidate rather than persuade are not acceptable.” A five-minute recess was called due to audience interference, however, Banales wanted to continue. “Pittsburg is better than that, Pittsburg has always been a city Councilmember Jelani Killings confirmed this moratorium would not impact Phase 1 and there are now responsibilities they cannot renege on. He noted a lot of the information provided by the public has not been factual and the city wants to put out information that is pertinent to project adopted. He also said they have worked to improve community engagement and to share factual information. “The process is still unfolding and the engagement is still happening,” said Killings who added he supported the 45-day moratorium and allow the advisory committee to finish their work. Baneles then made the motion for a 45-day moratorium to be discussed at a special council meeting later this week or earliest date possible. It was approved in a 4-0 vote with Mayor Dionne Adams recusing herself. Back in June 2018, the council began the process for a 100-acre Technology Park and by December 2024, AvAIO partnerd with the city of Pittsburg. The 300,000 square-foot data center is set to be located on the old Delta View Golf Course site which has been labeled a “technology center” after the golf course closed in 2018. artigo.texto: New certification program supports flexible system configurations and helps reduce complexity when modular installations undergo certification and code authority review. - The certification addresses modular DC energy storage systems that connect evaluated subsystems, including power conversion systems. - Compatible subsystem models are documented in the UL Product iQ® certification database for verification by code authorities. - Evaluations address electrical safety, communication and interoperability between the system and identified subsystems. NORTHBROOK, Ill., October 20, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--UL Solutions (NYSE: ULS), a global leader in applied safety science, today announced a new certification pathway designed to help manufacturers of modular direct current (DC) energy storage systems, used for backup power for critical infrastructure and grid-scale energy storage, bring systems to market with greater flexibility and clearer documentation for installation reviews. An energy storage system captures energy so it can be stored for later use and provides electricity to the grid or to a building's wiring system. A battery energy storage system can help save energy by reducing the number of times electricity must be converted from one form to another, including conversion between alternating current (AC) and DC. It can also simplify the connection to solar panels, backup generators and other equipment. Many of these systems use a modular design, allowing manufacturers to combine different components for a project. However, confirming that those components work safely together can make certification and installation reviews more complex. The new certification program offers manufacturers an alternative to seeking a full matched-assembly system listing at the outset. When a compatible subsystem is identified, the resulting certification documentation can provide manufacturers, developers and code authorities with information about the evaluated configuration. "Modular energy storage designs require a clear way to demonstrate how the system and its critical subsystems work together," said Wesley Kwok, vice president and general manager of the Energy and Industrial Automation group at UL Solutions. "This certification program gives manufacturers, developers and code authorities documented information about evaluated system combinations while supporting a more flexible approach to DC energy storage system design." Through the new certification program, UL Solutions evaluates the DC energy storage system with each identified subsystem to applicable requirements of UL 9540, the Standard for Energy Storage Systems and Equipment. The evaluation addresses electrical, communication and interoperability between the system and its evaluated subsystems. Compatible subsystem models are documented in the UL Product iQ® certification database under the DC energy storage system certification category, allowing code authorities to verify evaluated combinations.

artigo.texto: A Ucrânia lançou um ataque massivo contra um porto petrolífero e um centro de dados em São Petersburgo, na Rússia. Um ataque em larga escala com drones, realizado pela Ucrânia nas primeiras horas de 18 de outubro, teve como alvo um porto petrolífero, um centro de dados e uma ponte em São Petersburgo. A Rússia informou que um grande incêndio deflagrou no porto petrolífero e que as forças locais abateram 127 drones. Segundo o Kyiv Independent, num ataque em grande escala ocorrido na noite de 17 de outubro e na madrugada de 18 de outubro, as forças ucranianas alvejaram uma instalação petrolífera, um centro de dados e uma ponte na cidade de São Petersburgo, no noroeste da Rússia. Segundo a mídia estatal russa, drones ucranianos atacaram o porto petrolífero de São Petersburgo e um centro de dados pertencente ao VKontakte (VK), uma das principais redes sociais da Rússia. Segundo o governador de São Petersburgo, Aleksandr Beglov, incêndios deflagraram no porto petrolífero de São Petersburgo e em diversas instalações de infraestrutura civil em outros quatro distritos da cidade. Equipes de resgate foram mobilizadas para combater os incêndios; não há relatos de vítimas. O tráfego aéreo no Aeroporto Internacional de Pulkovo também foi afetado pelo ataque. Entretanto, o governador da região de Leningrado (que circunda São Petersburgo), Aleksandr Drozdenko, anunciou que as defesas aéreas abateram 127 drones ucranianos na área. Detritos de drones danificaram quatro carros em um estacionamento. Também foram relatados incêndios, mas as autoridades ainda não divulgaram a extensão total dos danos. Os canais que monitoram a situação na Ucrânia e na Rússia, Exilenova+ e Supernova+, informaram que o ataque começou por volta das 2h50 da manhã, horário local. Vídeos gravados por moradores de São Petersburgo parecem mostrar drones sobrevoando a cidade, juntamente com sistemas de defesa aérea em operação. Outras imagens mostram explosões iluminando o céu noturno sobre a cidade de cerca de 5,6 milhões de habitantes, localizada a aproximadamente 856 km ao norte da fronteira com a Ucrânia. Alguns vídeos parecem mostrar um drone ucraniano atingindo uma ponte de oito faixas. Outras imagens mostram chamas irrompendo no porto petrolífero de São Petersburgo. Localizado na zona portuária da cidade, o porto petrolífero de São Petersburgo é uma das principais instalações de armazenamento e exportação de combustíveis da Rússia. A instalação movimenta e transporta produtos petrolíferos por via marítima, ferroviária e rodoviária, com uma capacidade de produção estimada em cerca de 12,5 milhões de toneladas por ano. A fabricante ucraniana de drones Fire Point afirma ter usado drones de ataque FP-1 no ataque que teve como alvo o porto petrolífero. O ataque ocorreu depois que o acordo de cessar-fogo sobre instalações de energia entre a Rússia e a Ucrânia, que o presidente dos EUA , Donald Trump, havia anunciado que promoveria, não produziu os resultados esperados. A agência de notícias russa Astra informou que uma subestação elétrica também foi atingida. Houve relatos de falta de energia e baixa pressão da água em algumas áreas, além de danos a um prédio residencial. Essas informações não foram verificadas de forma independente. O jornal Kyiv Independent observou que ainda não era possível verificar de forma independente os alvos atingidos ou a extensão dos danos causados pelo ataque. O ataque em São Petersburgo fez parte da campanha da Ucrânia que utiliza drones de longo alcance para atingir instalações petrolíferas, logística militar e infraestrutura tecnológica em território russo. Nas últimas semanas, Kiev expandiu seus alvos para incluir centros de dados, após dois centros pertencentes à empresa russa de tecnologia Yandex terem sido atacados por drones nos dias 8 e 9 de outubro, interrompendo diversos serviços. Os ataques também ocorreram em um momento em que a Rússia continuava a intensificar seus ataques à infraestrutura energética e tecnológica da Ucrânia, às vésperas do inverno. Em 12 de outubro, Kiev acusou a Rússia de continuar atacando alvos do setor energético, apesar do anúncio do presidente dos EUA, Donald Trump, de um acordo de cessar-fogo no setor. De acordo com a Ucrânia, atacar instalações petrolíferas poderia pressionar a capacidade de fornecimento de combustível da Rússia, enquanto ataques a centros de dados correm o risco de interromper o funcionamento dos serviços digitais.

artigo.texto: BMW inicia produção em massa de baterias de 6ª geração na China Para promover a industrialização em larga escala, a empresa trabalha em colaboração com fabricantes chineses de baterias O BMW Group deu início oficial à produção em massa de suas baterias de alta voltagem de 6ª geração na 5ª feira (15.out.2026) em Shenyang, capital da Província de Liaoning, no nordeste da China, estabelecendo um marco que destaca um passo fundamental em sua estratégia de eletrificação e localização no país. “O início da produção de baterias é um passo fundamental para trazer os modelos Neue Klasse (Nova Classe) para a China, aproveitando as capacidades sistêmicas da BMW em pesquisa e desenvolvimento, engenharia, compras e produção em Shenyang”, disse Birgit Boehm, presidente e CEO da BMW Brilliance Automotive Ltd. Com um investimento de 10 bilhões de yuans (US$ 1,49 bilhão), o projeto de baterias apresenta um design avançado de células cilíndricas de grande porte. Para promover a industrialização em larga escala dessas células, a BMW tem trabalhado em estreita colaboração com fabricantes chineses de baterias, incluindo a CATL e a EVE Energy. Shenyang é a maior base de produção do BMW Group em todo o mundo. Desde 2010, a BMW investiu mais de 120 bilhões de yuans na cidade, e o veículo de número 7 milhões saiu da linha de produção em maio deste ano. Milan Nedeljković, presidente do conselho de administração da BMW AG, afirmou que as fortes vantagens geográficas de Shenyang, as sólidas bases industriais e o ambiente de negócios favorável incentivaram a BMW a continuar aumentando os investimentos e transformar a base de Shenyang em uma referência para a cooperação industrial mutuamente benéfica entre a China e parceiros estrangeiros. A BMW também anunciou na 5ª feira (15.out) que seu novo BMW i3, desenvolvido especificamente para o mercado chinês, conseguiu fazer um percurso de 1.213 km sem recarga. De acordo com os planos da empresa, cerca de 20 modelos novos e atualizados, equipados com a tecnologia Neue Klasse, chegarão ao mercado chinês até 2027. Até 2030, a BMW pretende elevar a participação dos veículos produzidos localmente e vendidos na China para mais de 95%. A empresa também está avaliando a expansão das exportações de modelos produzidos na China, em Shenyang, para mercados internacionais, incluindo o Sudeste Asiático. Nedeljković disse que a China é o mercado mais dinâmico e competitivo do mundo e que a BMW está comprometida em aprofundar a cooperação mutuamente benéfica e abrir um futuro para a eletrificação junto com a China. Este texto foi publicado originalmente pela Agência Xinhua, em 16 de outubro de 2026. O conteúdo é livre para republicação, citada a fonte, e foi adaptado para o padrão do Poder360.

artigo.texto: The Hayward City Council is scheduled to vote Tuesday on a temporary moratorium on consideration and approval of new data centers in the City. The moratorium is being recommended to give City staff time to thoroughly evaluate the economic, environmental, public health, cost-of-living and other effects of data center development in Hayward. Data centers are buildings designed and equipped for high-density computing and require dedicated uninterrupted power supplies and cooling systems. The advent and expansion of artificial intelligence is driving development of larger-scale and hyperscale data centers with ever increasing energy demands. In Hayward, there are four existing and approved data centers near Pacific Gas and Electric Company’s Eastern Substation in the southwestern portion of Hayward’s industrial crescent on the City of Hayward’s westside: - A 24-megawatt (MW) facility called SF09 operating on a 10.9-acre site along Corporate Avenue. - A 35-MW facility called SF11 operating on a 4.24-acre site also on Corporate Avenue. - A 49-MW facility called Hayward Exchange @92 operating on 6.57 acres of a larger industrial campus along Clawiter Road near Breakwater Court. - A 76.6-MW facility called Stack Data Center (SVY03A) under construction on an 11.3-acre site on Eden Landing Road. Additionally, the City has been approached by a developer planning to submit applications for two new data centers that would operate at 99 megawatts each within a half mile of Hayward’s existing data centers in the vicinity of Arden Road and Corporate Avenue. The moratorium, if adopted, could remain in place for up to two years. Effectively, it is intended to call a time-out and provide time to monitor and analyze the cumulative impacts of current and potential future data center development on energy and water supplies, air quality, industrial noise levels, City emergency response capacity and City economic development priorities. For more information, you can read the staff report to the City Council and related materials on the City of Hayward’s legislative website and a Frequently Asked Questions page on data center development in Hayward on the City of Hayward’s main informational website, www.hayward-ca.gov.

artigo.texto: Trending LORDSTOWN – In a unanimous opinion, the Ohio Supreme Court ruled Tuesday that Lordstown officials were within their rights to stop processing the site-plan review requested by a Bristolville 25 developer, which was the first step toward obtaining a permit to construct four three-story data centers and ancillary structures in an area of the Trumbull County village zoned for industrial use. Last year, village officials imposed a moratorium after Bristolville 25 had issued a permit request with the village planning/ zoning office. Mayor Jackie Woodward said she learned of the court’s decision Tuesday. “This is a pretty significant victory not only for Lordstown but all the municipalities in Ohio who want to maintain the ability to decide and do what is best for their local communities. This sets a precedent for other communities dealing with the same situation with data centers. It allows each community to decide what they want and what is best for their local area.” The court’s decision indicates that Lordstown does not have to complete a site-plan review for a proposed data center that was submitted days before the village imposed a moratorium on data centers. In November 2025, Lordstown passed an ordinance banning data centers within the corporate boundaries. In January 2026, the village repealed the total ban and replaced it with a six-month moratorium on data center construction, which was set to expire July 4. Before its expiration, the council extended the moratorium through the remainder of 2026. Bristolville 25 initiated the first step in October 2025 under Lordstown's codified ordinances to construct the data centers and was notified the next day by the village planning and zoning administrator that a ban on data centers was pending before the village council. Two weeks later, the village council adopted the ban, which it later converted to a moratorium on data centers. Bristolville sought a writ of mandamus from the Supreme Court to compel the village to follow its site plan review process and act upon it under the village's pre-moratorium ordinances. The company argued the village must follow the zoning law in effect on the day the company submitted its plan, which at that time did not prohibit data centers. The court ruling stated that Bristolville's arguments may have prompted a duty for the village to act on the request had the company completed all the steps required to apply for a zoning permit. Because the company had not completed the required preliminary steps to apply for a permit, the village was under no obligation to consider its proposal. Bristolville purchased land from BHGH Properties in February 2025 to construct the data center complex. Under village law, an applicant for a zoning permit for new construction must undergo a site plan review overseen by the village zoning and planning office. Village officials submit a final site plan review for approval by the village's planning and zoning commission. If the commission approves the site plan, then a developer can file for a zoning permit. No construction can begin until a zoning permit is issued. Bristolville delivered its draft site plan to begin the permitting process in October 2025. The village planning and zoning administrator responded, notifying Bristolville about the pending ban, and stated the office could not begin the site plan review until the village council decided on the ban. Bristolville responded by asking the planning and zoning office to proceed because, at that time, data centers were still permitted under village law. Village Solicitor Matt Ries, who reviewed the draft site plan, notified Bristolville that the village officials were proceeding with the site plan, but indicated that, based on the newly enacted ban, the proposal would likely be prohibited. Once the ban was transformed into a moratorium, the village suspended any further review of Bristolville's plan. While the moratorium was in effect, the village's obligations to conduct site-plan reviews or to act on any application for a permit for data-center construction were suspended. Bristolville said the company then asked the Supreme Court to order the village to move forward with the review. Because it submitted its site plan for review before the moratorium, Bristolville argued that the village had a legal duty to proceed with the review. The court stated that Lordstown does not have a duty to act on the request, "unless the moratorium is unenforceable as to Bristolville's submission." Late last year, village council pulled back on its ban on data centers and in January approved temporary moratorium instead. Solicitor Matt Ries has said the originally ban was scheduled to take place in December 2025 but the 180-day moratorium was approved in January, which would give the village or any municipality an opportunity to study the environmental pollution concerns. Ries has said under a Lordstown ordinance, a company has to operate within the permit with what was approved as a site plan review. He said courts favor moratoriums over bans because they are temporary. Village residents have expressed concerns that any large-scale data center would strain Lordstown's energy and water systems, drive up utility bills and bring other complications. At the time company officials said the proposed facility by Bristolville 25 Developers LLC was to be built on 133 acres in both Trumbull and Mahoning counties, employing 120 full-time employees with an average wage of over $84 an hour. Bristolville cited two Supreme Court decisions to argue it had a legal right to proceed with the permitting process. artigo.texto: ‘Not off the table’: East Lansing weighs data center rules amid AI discussion Michigan State University hosts discussion on responsible AI use and data centers EAST LANSING, Mich. (News 10) - Michigan State University brought students face to face with two topics on artificial intelligence Monday during a public discussion on how to use AI responsibly and how East Lansing is preparing to accommodate the data centers that power it. The discussion was part of East Lansing’s “Data Week,” a series of talks on AI and data centers leading up to a community forum on a proposed data center ordinance later this week. Professor compares AI to a tool Teagan Dixon, a professor at the Broad College of Business, compared AI to a tool in a workshop. “It’s not just something that’s a corporate thing anymore. It’s on our phones. It’s in our smart apps. It’s in our smart devices,” Dixon said. “A hammer can be used very irresponsibly in a multitude of ways... but you give a woodworker a hammer and they’re going to build something... I think that there’s so much fear about it that the bad things are what’s talked about more than the good things,” Dixon said. City says data center not off the table The discussion also touched on the issue of bringing a data center to East Lansing. Principal Planner Landon Bartley said it’s not off the table. “We don’t have any current applications, but we’ve received a lot of interest,” Bartley said. That’s part of why the city has a moratorium in place until March 2027, giving planners time to write an ordinance addressing noise and other environmental concerns. “Can it be on-site or off-site, renewable or not? Water, can it be evaporative cooling or something else that won’t use as much water?” Bartley said. Bartley said it’s important for residents to weigh in before any ordinance is final. “I think the big concern that I’ve heard from people is not those small ones. It’s the big ones, the hyperscale ones that we’ve seen elsewhere in the country... if they have specific concerns, show up to a meeting and air those concerns,” Bartley said. Bartley said the city of East Lansing has some smaller scale data centers in the area already, and there is not enough land available for a hyperscale data center like the ones that have drawn concerns in other communities. Community forum set for Thursday Residents will have a chance to weigh in later this week. The city’s planning and zoning staff will hold a community forum on a data center ordinance to guide future proposals. The forum will begin at 6:30 p.m. Thursday at the Hannah Community Center. artigo.texto: Battery banks are (rightfully) getting a bit of a reputation on planes these days, so safer, more stable options are needed. LASER has been at the forefront of powerbanks, even introducing the newer LiFePO4 batteries to their battery banks last year, and are now introducing semi-solid state batteries with a focus on safety and peace of mind. Chris Lau, Managing Director of LASER said “We’ve been closely following semi solid state battery development for some time, since first visiting an EV factory several years ago, and advancements since that time mean that it can now move into smaller, more compact options. Simply put, I believe that Semi Solid State chemistry makes this the safest powerbank technology available in Australia today. We are focused on safety and peace of mind, and we know that it is a huge concern for Australian consumers these days when buying powerbanks.” The new ChargeCore PowerBanks come in three capacities, 10,000mAh, 20,000mAh and 27,000mAh offering a USB Type-C and two USB-A ports giving you versatile charging for your phones, tablets and more. The 10k and 20kmAh PowerBanks are able to deliver 20W of power across the three ports, while the 27,000mAh option can charge devices at up to 35W. All three models include an easy-to-read digital battery display showing how much is left, as well as including integrated protection against overcharging, overcurrent, short circuits and overheating. The new ChargeCore PowerBanks are available now in Black, with LASER also announcing Galactica, Grey, and Dark Cherry colour options are coming soon for their 10K and 20K ChargeCore PowerBanks. While the ChargeCore range is arriving now, LASER is also looking ahead, with Magnetic Charging and Waterproof options also using the semi-solid state battery tech coming soon. artigo.texto: The Northern Virginia locality with the most data centers in the commonwealth is set to consider a plan to pause new data center and substation applications for one year. At its meeting Tuesday, Loudoun County’s Board of Supervisors is scheduled to vote on a resolution being referred to as a “Legislative Pause on Data Center and Substation Applications.” The proposal would prevent the Board of Supervisors from acting on any legislative application that proposes or would allow for a data center or substation, retroactively effective Sept. 15, 2026. It includes exceptions for projects aimed at improving grid reliability. The step comes after elected officials approved a plan directing county staff to draft a resolution for the pause during a meeting last month. The idea isn’t considered a moratorium, which Loudoun’s lawyers said wouldn’t be legal. Instead, it’s a push to slow data center growth in the suburb with over 200 of them. “If it brings them to the table to renegotiate some of what’s going on, then that’s fine,” Loudoun resident Edward Facundo told WTOP. “It’s not that we don’t want data centers. I think that needs to be done in a way that makes sense for the county and makes sense for the people that live here.” Supporters of the data center industry argue the tech hubs bring jobs and generate tax revenue for communities. Loudoun’s elected officials said the pause is necessary so the county can finish creating rules overseeing the industry and ensuring surrounding neighborhoods are protected. “Just driving through Ashburn and some of these places, they’re an eyesore,” Loudoun resident Stephanie Fulbright said in Sterling on Monday afternoon. “They add no beauty or anything to our community, and fortunately, I don’t have to live with it in my backyard. But a lot of people do.” Related stories - Fauquier County restricts future data center development with new zoning rules - Close to home or across the state, Marylanders don’t want data centers, poll finds - ‘The people are fed up’: Md. governor signs executive order targeting data centers The proposal would pause consideration of an application for a year from the time it’s filed. There are currently 33 active legislative applications for data centers or substations, according to county documents. One is solely a grid-reliability substation. Under the draft plan, projects considered “grid reliability” substations can still advance through the process. Those are defined in the resolution as electrical substations that meet a specific set of criteria. Kathy Kadane, who said she’s lived in Loudoun since 1990, said she supports the yearlong pause, because “if the federal government right now is too dysfunctional to regulate Big Tech in all its various forms, then I think the counties and states have to step up.” Jareer Elass, meanwhile, said the pause is necessary because data centers are “taking up valuable land. It’s a drain on our resources, and it’s AI, and I’m anti-AI.” Get breaking news and daily headlines delivered to your email inbox by signing up here. © 2026 WTOP. All Rights Reserved. artigo.texto: UL Solutions Introduces Certification Pathway for DC Energy Storage Systems, Simplifying Reviews of Modular Installations New certification program supports flexible system configurations and helps reduce complexity when modular installations undergo certification and code authority review. - The certification addresses modular DC energy storage systems that connect evaluated subsystems, including power conversion systems. - Compatible subsystem models are documented in the UL Product iQ® certification database for verification by code authorities. - Evaluations address electrical safety, communication and interoperability between the system and identified subsystems. NORTHBROOK, Ill.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 20, 2026-- UL Solutions (NYSE: ULS), a global leader in applied safety science, today announced a new certification pathway designed to help manufacturers of modular direct current (DC) energy storage systems, used for backup power for critical infrastructure and grid-scale energy storage, bring systems to market with greater flexibility and clearer documentation for installation reviews. This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261020793648/en/ Modular DC battery energy storage systems can be configured with different components to meet project needs. The new UL Solutions certification pathway evaluates identified system combinations for electrical safety, communication and interoperability. An energy storage system captures energy so it can be stored for later use and provides electricity to the grid or to a building’s wiring system. A battery energy storage system can help save energy by reducing the number of times electricity must be converted from one form to another, including conversion between alternating current (AC) and DC. It can also simplify the connection to solar panels, backup generators and other equipment. Many of these systems use a modular design, allowing manufacturers to combine different components for a project. However, confirming that those components work safely together can make certification and installation reviews more complex. The new certification program offers manufacturers an alternative to seeking a full matched-assembly system listing at the outset. When a compatible subsystem is identified, the resulting certification documentation can provide manufacturers, developers and code authorities with information about the evaluated configuration. “Modular energy storage designs require a clear way to demonstrate how the system and its critical subsystems work together,” said Wesley Kwok, vice president and general manager of the Energy and Industrial Automation group at UL Solutions. “This certification program gives manufacturers, developers and code authorities documented information about evaluated system combinations while supporting a more flexible approach to DC energy storage system design.” Through the new certification program, UL Solutions evaluates the DC energy storage system with each identified subsystem to applicable requirements of UL 9540, the Standard for Energy Storage Systems and Equipment. The evaluation addresses electrical, communication and interoperability between the system and its evaluated subsystems. Compatible subsystem models are documented in the UL Product iQ® certification database under the DC energy storage system certification category, allowing code authorities to verify evaluated combinations. UL 9540 testing covers electrical, electrochemical, mechanical and other types of energy storage technologies used in systems intended to supply electrical energy. Its evaluation framework includes charging and discharging, protection, controls, communication between devices and other system-level considerations. Learn more about UL Solutions energy storage system testing and certification services at UL.com/services/energy-storage-system-testing-and-certification. About UL Solutions A global leader in applied safety science, UL Solutions Inc. (NYSE: ULS) transforms safety, security and sustainability challenges into opportunities for customers in more than 110 countries. UL Solutions delivers testing, inspection and certification services, advisory offerings and software solutions that support our customers’ product innovation and business growth. The UL Mark serves as a recognized symbol of trust in our customers’ products and reflects an unwavering commitment to advancing our safety mission. We help our customers innovate, launch new products and services, navigate global markets and complex supply chains, and grow sustainably and responsibly into the future. Our science is your advantage. artigo.texto: BMX launched the SolidSafe Duo on Oct. 19 for the iPhone Duo, pairing a custom 5,000mAh semi-solid-state cell with a 360-degree rotating stand and integrated USB-C lanyard. BMX launched the SolidSafe Duo on Oct. 19 for the iPhone Duo. The new phone shape demands accessories that match its proportions, and this pack avoids overhang by using a custom 5,000mAh semi-solid-state cell instead of a standard lithium-ion design. A conventional cell would force the battery past the edges or cut capacity. The semi-solid-state format gives BMX the flexibility to shape the pack around the iPhone Duo's dimensions. The cell contains less liquid electrolyte than standard lithium-ion batteries. Less liquid means less flammable material inside the cell, which lowers fire risk from heat, physical damage, or internal short circuits. Battery recalls have made that trade-off visible. The integrated rotating ring stand handles portrait reading, landscape video, and partially folded hands-free calls. It rotates 360 degrees and stays attached when you shift position, so you never remove the pack to change angles. Charging reaches up to 15 watts through MagSafe or 20 watts via the attached USB-C lanyard cable. The cable stays with the battery, eliminating a separate cord to pack or lose. The same cable accepts up to 15 watts to recharge the pack. A full-color LCD shows remaining capacity and live charging wattage at the same time, so you can track both how much power you have left and how fast it is charging. The SolidSafe Duo costs more than generic MagSafe packs. For iPhone Duo owners, the tailored fit and semi-solid-state safety profile justify the premium. Less expensive options will likely arrive in coming months, but this is a solid launch option. This is part of the MagSafe Monday series, which examines the latest MagSafe and wireless charging gear for Apple devices. Source:9to5mac.com

artigo.texto: (Photo courtesy of PCO) President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has directed the development of a national carbon market policy framework aimed at attracting investments in climate-related projects and strengthening the Philippines’ efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Under Executive Order (EO) No. 127, signed on October 13, the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) was tasked with crafting the Philippine Carbon Market Policy Framework to regulate the country’s participation in domestic and international carbon markets. Carbon markets enable governments and businesses to trade carbon credits earned through projects that reduce or remove greenhouse gas emissions. The order emphasized the need for a coordinated government approach aligned with international standards to help the Philippines meet its nationally determined contributions (NDCs) under the Paris Agreement. NDCs outline each country’s commitments to reducing emissions and addressing climate change. The framework seeks to expand access to climate financing, technology, and investments while encouraging projects eligible to generate carbon credits. It will establish regulations covering carbon credit trading, project approvals, participant qualifications, transaction monitoring, and benefit-sharing mechanisms. Safeguards will also be introduced to ensure compliance with domestic environmental policies and international standards. To supervise implementation, Marcos established the Inter-Agency Committee on Carbon Markets (IACCM), chaired by the Climate Change Commission (CCC), with the Department of Finance (DOF) serving as vice chair. The committee will coordinate government policies, assess the framework’s implementation, and approve reasonable processing fees for carbon market applications and certifications. Its members include the DENR, Department of Energy (DOE), Department of Agriculture (DA), Department of Transportation (DOTr), Department of Trade and Industry (DTI), and Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). The DENR was also designated as the national authority for carbon markets, responsible for authorizing emission reduction projects and ensuring their compliance with environmental regulations. Additionally, the agency will establish and manage the Philippine National Carbon Registry, a digital platform designed to record carbon credits and monitor related transactions. The DENR must submit the proposed framework to the inter-agency committee for review and approval within 30 days of the order’s effectivity. EO 127 takes effect immediately upon publication in the Official Gazette or a newspaper of general circulation.

artigo.texto: A Nscale informou que a Microsoft desistiu do contrato para operar seu data center em Loughton, no condado britânico de Essex. O recuo ocorre enquanto a companhia de neocloud sediada no Reino Unido prepara uma oferta pública inicial com meta de captar até US$ 3 bilhões, possivelmente antes do fim deste mês. A instalação vinha enfrentando atrasos por restrições no fornecimento de eletricidade. A Nscale não detalhou os motivos da saída da Microsoft. Em nota, a empresa afirmou que mantém o compromisso com a unidade de Loughton e com o mercado britânico e que procura outras opções de energia para o local e novas frentes de expansão no país. A Microsoft não se manifestou sobre o ocorrido. Apesar do recuo, a Nscale classificou a relação com a Microsoft como forte e de longo prazo. Segundo a empresa, a falha de abastecimento elétrico na área londrina não atinge os outros acordos. Nos documentos da oferta, Microsoft e Anthropic aparecem como responsáveis por cerca de 85% da carteira de contratos da Nscale. A unidade norueguesa mais relevante da companhia acumula atraso de seis meses e trabalha com 6,4 megawatts, diante de uma previsão de 30 megawatts. O momento é delicado para os investimentos em infraestrutura de IA. A CoreWeave, outra neocloud, sofreu queda de 25% na semana, a pior desde novembro, em meio a temores sobre dívidas e financiamento de data centers. A australiana Firmus abandonou a ideia de listar ações depois de não obter investidores dispostos a bancar o valor almejado.

artigo.texto: Dive Brief: - Central Georgia Electric Membership Corp. will deploy up to 50 MW of small-scale, customer-sited energy storage in partnership with Base Power, the organizations said last week. - Set to begin in 2027, the deployment marks Base Power’s first utility partnership outside its home state of Texas, Base and CGEMC said. CGEMC will charge the batteries when wholesale power prices and members’ energy demand are low and discharge during periods of peak demand, helping to stabilize the grid across its 14-county territory southeast of Atlanta. - The batteries will add capacity to a CGEMC system that could see substantial large-load growth in the coming years. Multiple data center projects are proposed or under development in its territory, including a 240-MW Equinix campus near Hampton. Dive Insight: Base Power operates as a retail energy choice provider in Texas and the Illinois zone of the PJM Interconnection, and as a direct partner for public power entities in parts of Texas. The company says its fleet has more than 750 MWh of capacity spread over 30,000-plus homes. Base is one of several companies that provide deeply discounted home battery subscriptions via energy choice retail frameworks in restructured markets or utility partnerships in regulated markets. In both scenarios, Base installs and maintains relatively large residential backup batteries at little or no direct cost to the homeowner. When the grid is up and running, Base or its utility partners charge and discharge the batteries to shave demand peaks, mitigate price spikes and tap energy arbitrage value. During outages, Base says each 39.2-kWh battery can provide up to 36 hours of backup power. Base’s partnership with CGEMC marks its first outside Texas and one of its first in a regulated utility market. Base is also partnering with El Paso Electric, a vertically integrated utility serving parts of far west Texas outside the deregulated Electric Reliability Council of Texas market, on a resilience-focused pilot program. While that means the company and its utility partners target different value streams, the core business proposition — using distributed batteries to reduce power supply costs — remains the same, company spokesperson Gabriel Federman said in an email. “In Texas, that means addressing transmission and energy costs through peak-shaving and arbitrage. In Georgia, the main value is in transmission and reducing capacity obligations,” Federman said. “However, the core principles and the value of distributed storage [are] consistent across markets.” Both transmission-scale energy storage and customer-sited distributed batteries deliver benefits at the wholesale level, according to an analysis published in September by the consultancy ICF. Distributed BESS offers additional value in alleviating distribution grid congestion, boosting local resilience and allowing utilities to defer grid upgrades, ICF said. Unlike vertically integrated utilities that earn a regulated rate of return on infrastructure spending, member-owned rural electric cooperatives like CGEMC and not-for-profit municipal power utilities like Base Power partner Austin Energy have strong incentives to minimize wholesale power costs and avoid expensive system investments. Regardless of local market structure, they’re tapping distribution-connected energy storage for help — from networked residential batteries to multi-megawatt installations at substations or industrial sites. George Weaver, CGEMC president and CEO, framed the utility’s partnership with Base Power as a win for members themselves and the grid they pay to support. The 50-MW deployment will “add flexible local capacity to support our electric system while giving participating members greater peace of mind through dependable backup battery power,” Weaver said in a statement.
