artigo.texto: Nscale Loses Microsoft Deal as Power Delays Threaten AI The cancellation highlights the financial risks developers face when grid connections fall behind project schedules and customers cannot wait for capacity. Microsoft has terminated its contract for Nscale’s planned AI data center in Loughton, England, after delays to the site’s expected power connection. The cancellation highlights a growing challenge for data center developers: customer demand and financing commitments do not guarantee that electricity will be supplied in time to meet commercial schedules. For developers, delayed power can leave construction and financing costs running while revenue remains out of reach. For cloud operators, it can mean scrambling for replacement capacity when a planned facility misses its delivery schedule. The risk can be especially acute for neocloud providers, which often depend on a small number of large customers and finance GPU deployments against specific contracts. Nscale announced the Loughton project in 2025 as a 50 MW campus that could scale to 90 MW, with plans to deploy 23,040 Nvidia GB300 GPUs for Microsoft Azure. A company spokesperson confirmed that Microsoft terminated the contract. Nscale remains committed to the site and is exploring alternative power sources as well as other UK expansion opportunities, according to the spokesperson. The company also said the issue does not affect its other contracts with Microsoft and that the broader relationship between the companies remains strong. The Guardian reported that UK Power Networks told Nscale it could not supply enough electricity for the site until the early to mid-2030s, well after the project’s planned opening. The companies have not disclosed any financial consequences tied to the termination. “Capacity that isn’t energized generates no revenue, but the costs keep running,” said Alex Cordovil, research director at Dell’Oro Group. Power Timing Remains a Core Risk AI infrastructure projects depend on three elements aligning at the same time: a creditworthy customer, financing supported by that customer commitment, and available electricity, Cordovil said. Developers generally have more control over winning customers and arranging financing than they do over the timing of utility power delivery. Grid operators can revise connection commitments by six months or a year, and in some cases longer, Cordovil said. Permitting processes that depend on third parties can also push projects off schedule. “The problem isn’t necessarily that AI demand disappears,” said Neil Osnato, founder of Persistence Analytics Group. “It’s that capital can become committed long before the physical and financial assumptions supporting its recovery are proven.” How severe those consequences become depends on the underlying contracts, including missed-milestone provisions, termination rights, and equipment commitments. Nscale has not publicly detailed how much it spent on the Loughton project, whether any termination payments apply, or what contractual protections were in place. Neocloud May Be More Exposed Than Hyperscalers A delayed site can create a larger financial shock for neoclouds than for hyperscalers, Cordovil said. Neoclouds often operate with more concentrated customer bases, higher capital costs, and GPU financing tied to specific deployments. “A hyperscaler can absorb one delayed site across a large, diversified fleet and balance sheet,” Cordovil said. “A neocloud typically has more concentrated customers and a higher cost of capital.” If an anchor customer walks away, the provider can be left with equipment and financing structures built around a deployment that no longer has a buyer. A replacement customer may recover part of the investment, but not necessarily the original economics. “The issue with neoclouds is that the debt and financing is colossal, and the demand they’re betting on is not assured,” said Owen Rogers, senior research director of cloud computing at Uptime Institute Intelligence. Nscale’s September IPO filing reported $103.4 billion in active and contracted total contract value as of Aug. 31, 2026, compared with $2.6 billion in active contract value. The filing said Microsoft’s agreements with the company provided for payments of up to $43.8 billion through December 2033, subject to delivery and service-availability requirements. Separate agreements with Anthropic provided for up to $44.6 billion. Nscale also said in the filing that, as of the prospectus date, it had not secured binding financing commitments for the GPU equipment and infrastructure needed to fulfill the Anthropic agreements. The filing does not specify how much financing or equipment spending, if any, was tied specifically to Loughton. artigo.texto: Portland, Westbrook look to tighten regulations on potential data centers The two Cumberland County cities held meetings on Monday where the city councils voted to advance restrictions on data center construction. Portland, Westbrook look to tighten regulations on potential data centers The two Cumberland County cities held meetings on Monday where the city councils voted to advance restrictions on data center construction. On Monday, Portland and Westbrook held separate city council meetings to discuss restrictions on data centers. Right now, no data centers have been proposed, but each council took actions to change land use codes. PORTLAND: The city council voted to ask Planning and Urban Development to develop recommendations to present to the city council. Those recommendations will center around land use as it relates to data center noise, placement and environmental concerns. The city council is also worried about the placement of potential data centers and the proximity to neighboring buildings in Maine's largest city. This was not a ban or moratorium on data centers in Portland. WESTBROOK: In June, the city council proposed a moratorium on data centers, with an exception for "server rooms" as part of businesses. Under it, no data centers can be built on land in the city. Monday's comments also focused on land near Rock Row where the city does not want data center construction. No proposals have been submitted, according to Mayor David Morse. The city council is expected to vote to finalize that moratorium at its next meeting after public comment. "Westbrook welcomes thoughtful investment, always. Part of thoughtful planning includes determining which uses are appropriate for our community and ensuring development serves the people who live here. The prospect of investment must be weighed against the use of our resources and the effects on residents' quality of life," Morse said. Back in April, Gov. Janet Mills vetoed a moratorium on data centers in Maine.

artigo.texto: Cincinnati launches zoning study to guide data center growth, seeks public input CINCINNATI (WKRC) - Cincinnati is taking steps to get ahead of the growing demand for data centers, and it held a public meeting about its zoning study aimed at understanding their potential impacts and how the city should regulate them. The city began its data center zoning study in February at the direction of the city manager. City research presented at Monday's meeting said there are 240 data centers in Ohio, giving the state the sixth-most data centers in the country. Cincinnati officials also said the city currently has eight data centers. Sophia Ferries-Rowe, a city planner with the Department of City Planning and Engagement, said the study is intended to give the city time to determine long-term rules for data centers. “The purpose of the IDC [Interim Development Control Overlay #89 "Data Centers" and Zoning Study] is to give us, as a city, time to study data centers and figure out how we want to regulate them permanently in our zoning code,” Ferries-Rowe said. A primary goal of the study is to define what a “data center” is for zoning and regulatory purposes. The study is also examining what regulations other cities across the country are putting in place. During the meeting, the Metropolitan Sewer District of Greater Cincinnati and Greater Cincinnati Water Works discussed how data centers use water and addressed common concerns. Scott Bessler, superintendent of the Metropolitan Sewer District of Greater Cincinnati, said the city has a lot of high-water-use customers, and generally, data centers are under the same regulations as other high-use customers. “Our primary concern is protecting our treatment plant performance and public infrastructure,” Bessler said. "So, construction and start-up activities of data centers have been known to create wastewater containing chemicals, metals, or other elevated nutrient levels." The meeting also included information about the energy data centers use. One slide in the presentation compared the energy a certain size of data center uses with a city that uses the same amount of energy. It showed that a medium-sized data center uses between 43.8 and 438 gigawatts annually, which is equivalent to a city with a population between 3,500 and 34,000. The slide used Mason as an example of a city, residences and businesses, that would use the same amount of power a medium-sized data center uses. "It requires a lot of energy," Rob McCracken from the city's Office of Environment & Sustainability said. "Electric utilities are allowed to recoup their investment. So, any investment in infrastructure they make, all the ratepayers pay." That is one concern Manny Addo had, who attended the meeting. "If we can find a way where we could shave that cost and let it go where it belongs, it would be a great idea," said Addo. Attendees were able to ask questions. One attendee raised concerns that data centers vary widely, particularly those used for artificial intelligence, and asked whether zoning should consider not only size but also reusability, citing a lack of plans for reuse for some facilities. Addo said he found the presentations helpful, and is happy the city is trying to get ahead of things. “The rapid growth of data centers may pose a challenge, because we may not be able to grapple with the growth and to anticipate or cover all the disadvantages that it might come with,” Addo said. The team working on the study hopes to have zoning recommendations by February, though the study could be extended if necessary. City officials said Cincinnati currently has no building permit applications for data centers. If an application is submitted before zoning code changes are adopted, it would have to be approved by the Planning Commission.

Mesa Grande Band Tribe completes first public clean energy installation Solar and batteries power three tribal facilities Systems cut costs and ride out grid outages Stock video by Los Muertos Crew via Pexels Oct 20, 2026 Mesa Grande Band Completes First Public Clean Energy Installation on Reservation The Mesa Grande Band of Diegueno Mission Indians, working with the Solar Electric Light Fund, has finished installing solar and battery storage systems at three Tribal facilities on the Mesa Grande Reservation in San Diego County, California, according to the Tribe. The project represents the first public clean energy installation on the reservation and advances the Tribe's long-term effort to strengthen energy sovereignty. Solar panels and batteries now serve the Tekamuk, Hallyeyaaw and Golden Eagle administration buildings. The three structures function as civic and community hubs, supporting Tribal government, housing services, cultural and educational programming, food distribution and emergency response. The solar systems are sized to cover the three facilities' present electricity needs while leaving room for future growth. Combined, they are expected to produce roughly 60 MWh of solar electricity each year and to reduce the Tribe's electricity costs by at least $16,780 annually. The battery storage allows the administration buildings to keep running independently of the electric grid during outages, which the Tribe describes as common in the rural community. Curtis La Chusa, chairman of the Mesa Grande Tribal Council, commented that electricity is often taken for granted and tends to go unnoticed until service is lost, while noting that power interruptions are a regular reality at Mesa Grande. He said outages there can last for days at a time, disrupting the services the Tribe provides to its members. The installation builds on more than two decades of Tribal efforts to expand access to reliable, affordable clean energy. Grid electricity did not reach the reservation until the 1950s, and some homes remain off the grid today, relying on small generators for basic household needs. Over the years Mesa Grande has pursued residential solar, renewable energy planning and workforce development. Four Tribal members with prior solar installation training were employed on the project. Bob Freling, executive director of the Solar Electric Light Fund, the nonprofit that facilitated the project, said reliable and affordable energy gives communities room to invest in future priorities. He indicated that lower energy costs and stronger resilience can free up resources while providing a sustainable foundation for growth, and that the organization looks forward to seeing how clean energy helps Mesa Grande meet its goals. The clean energy work coincides with the Tribe's start on a long-term plan for new housing and community infrastructure. The plan calls for 1,500 new homes to address housing affordability and supply shortages that have historically limited how many members can live on Tribal land. The development would include the first new housing built on the reservation since 2005. La Chusa said Mesa Grande has a bright future ahead, describing the effort as beginning with enabling Tribal members to return home and providing the spaces and services needed for them to thrive. Funding for the project came from the William, Jeff and Jennifer Gross Family Foundation and others, according to the Tribe. Interactive table based on the Store Companies dataset for this report. 1. Será o primerio nó de uma rede descentralizada que deverá estender-se a Espanha e ao sul de França. Um grupo de investidores pretende construir no Parque Empresarial do Sorraia, em Coruche, o primeiro de vários centros de dados "compactos" para treino e inferência de inteligência artificial (IA). Neste empreendimento inicial, pretendem investir 220 milhões de euros para construir uma infraestrutura com 6,4 MW, capacidade quase equiparável à do data center da Covilhã. Deverá entrar em operação no final de 2027 e empregar cerca de 30 pessoas. O promotor é o fundo Aura Capital, mais especificamente a Aura Technologies, que se assume como "uma plataforma europeia de investimento e desenvolvimento focada em infraestrutura digital". artigo.texto: (KNSI) — The St. Cloud City Council voted 5-0 Monday night to set a November 16th public hearing on proposed data center rules. Council Member Tami Calhoun pulled the item from the consent agenda for discussion, mainly to thank city staff for their work preparing the proposal. “I was so appreciative that [Community Development] Director [Matt] Glaesman had given us all this background information because that’s what we need. We need the information going forward.” No developer has brought a specific project to the city. Calhoun told KNSI data centers are relatively new and the city’s planning rules haven’t caught up. “So we need to be sure, be proactive, and be sure that we get exactly what we want in there before we’re ever approached to ask if we want a data center.” Calhoun says energy use, noise and what happens to a building if a data center operator leaves are among the concerns she’ll be weighing before the hearing. In a memo to the council and Planning Commission, Glaesman says adopting standards ahead of a site-specific proposal is the best practice. The city’s code currently has no data center category and allows a broad “communication facility” use by right in the I3 planned industrial district, with no design standards. The proposal has two parts. A comprehensive plan amendment would call data centers a valuable part of the city’s economy and tax base, while saying the city must limit effects on residential areas and address noise, public resources and the environment. A land development code amendment would create two categories. Smaller enterprise data centers, with 2,000 servers or fewer, 10,000 square feet or less of building area and 50 megawatts or less of peak electrical use, would be allowed by right in the C3 Central Business and C5 Highway Commercial districts. Larger hyperscale facilities would need a conditional use permit in the I3 district and would have to stay a quarter mile from residential zoning. All data centers would have to submit studies on noise, environmental impacts, community impact, backup power, sustainability and decommissioning. Projects of 450,000 square feet or more also require a state environmental review, and the memo says findings from that review could be grounds to deny a permit. The Planning Commission recommended approval of both items on a 4-2 vote October 13th. In a September 8th letter to the city, Pipefitters Local 539 voiced support for responsible data center development and asked for clear, objective standards with no arbitrary geographic restrictions. ___ Copyright © 2026 Leighton Media. artigo.texto: Premier Energies Limited’s wholly owned subsidiary, Premier Battery Technologies Private Limited (PBTPL), has executed a share allotment cum shareholders agreement with RCT Nexor Energy Private Limited, part of Germany’s RCT Group, to formalise Premier Energies Storage Solutions Private Limited (PESSPL) as a joint venture (JV) company of PBTPL and RCT Nexor Energy. The agreement formalised the joint venture announced in September 2026 between PBTPL and RCT Nexor Energy. PESSPL will establish a 12 GWh battery energy storage system (BESS) manufacturing facility at Seetharampur in Telangana, with the first 6 GWh phase expected to be set up in FY 2027-28. The facility will manufacture and assemble BESS products for residential, small business, commercial, industrial and utility-scale applications. PESSPL is currently a wholly owned subsidiary of PBTPL. Under the agreement, RCT Nexor Energy will receive a 15 per cent equity interest in PESSPL through four milestone-linked allotments and will have the option to acquire an additional 5 per cent stake after completion of Phase I.

artigo.texto: Plataformas Broadcast Soluções de Dados e Conteúdos Soluções de Tecnologia 19 de outubro de 2026, às 04:12 SHENZHEN, China, Oct. 19, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) — BYD Energy Storage has built a comprehensive after-sales service network in a multitier framework: station O&M, project centers, regional centers and global headquarters. BYD Energy Storage operates nine O&M centers globally, each spanning 2,500 square meters. Its after-sales service network covers China, Chile, South Africa, the UK, the US, Australia, Japan, Poland, and the Middle East. New service centers will open in South Africa and Bulgaria in 2027 to further expand its global service footprint. The centers deliver core functions including spare parts storage and management, batteries repair and maintenance, regional spare parts allocation, batteries recycling, and training for locally hired engineers. BYD Energy Storages regional centers fully comply with local regulatory requirements, deliver structured workforce training and enable rapid on-site response. The professional service team comprises over 200 field engineers and more than 100 R&D specialists. The company enforces standardized service SLAs: response within 24 hours, on-site arrival within 48 hours, and fault troubleshooting within 7 days. The company’s global service network has achieved widespread coverage. It forms a multi-point supply network that ensures rapid spare parts delivery worldwide. Furthermore, leveraging localized production lines, its O&M teams integrate regional resources to deliver local battery repair services, providing global customers with fast, convenient, and localized after-sales support. Our global service footprint is tailored to our fastgrowing BESS deployments. Trustworthy aftersales support underpins the longterm stable operation of energy storage assets, commented Mr. He Dehong, Head of Global After-sales Service at BYD Energy Storage. Guided by its vision, empower global energy storage industry with digital and intelligent service, BYD Energy Storages mature global O&M system strongly supports its expanding battery energy storage footprint. The company topped global BESS shipments at over 60 GWh in 2025, and has delivered more than 650 energy storage projects in total, supported by standardized, localized after-sales services for reliable asset operation. artigo.texto: Offshore Data Center e Kalypso miram gás encalhado para computação offshore A Offshore Data Center LLC firmou uma parceria com a Kalypso Offshore Energy com o objetivo de ajudar proprietários de gás offshore a monetizar reservas encalhadas, subutilizadas e subvalorizadas por meio da geração de energia para computação de IA no mar, segundo o World Oil. As duas empresas avaliarão instalações recém-construídas, bem como a reutilização de infraestrutura offshore existente, incluindo estruturas ociosas selecionadas, para computação modular de borda e de inferência. Art Schroeder, fundador e diretor-presidente da Offshore Data Center, observou que muitas plataformas no Golfo da América estão programadas para descomissionamento, embora algumas possam ainda manter vida estrutural útil. Ele afirmou que as empresas pretendem colaborar com operadores e reguladores, junto com a Kalypso, para explorar a instalação de data centers modulares em ativos existentes adequados, gerando nova receita a partir de recursos offshore e potencialmente adiando determinados gastos com a Obrigação de Aposentadoria de Ativos. A instalação da geração de energia e da computação próximas aos recursos de gás offshore tem como objetivo encurtar a cadeia tradicional, na qual o gás é convertido em energia e depois enviado a um data center em terra. A Offshore Data Center está reunindo parceiros como a Horton do Brasil, cujos projetos de casco semissubmersível, segundo as empresas, poderiam ser até 50% mais leves, com estabilidade aprimorada. De acordo com as empresas, isso permitiria que a construção na costa do Golfo dos Estados Unidos competisse com estaleiros na Coreia, na China e em Singapura. Parceiros da Offshore Data Center também fornecem sistemas de resfriamento em circuito fechado destinados a reduzir substancialmente as cargas de resfriamento dos data centers. A Kalypso liderará o trabalho de cabos submarinos que ligam as instalações à rede elétrica, às redes de comunicação e à costa. Isso abrange o desenvolvimento de rotas, a engenharia, a instalação e a conexão de cabos de fibra óptica, de energia e umbilicais, além de suporte de reparo, operações e manutenção. Owen Rataj, diretor da Kalypso Offshore Energy, afirmou que um data center offshore é tão bom quanto os cabos que o conectam, e que fibra de baixa latência até a costa, conexões de energia confiáveis e capacidade de reparo e manutenção próximas aos ativos são o que transformam uma plataforma offshore em capacidade de computação utilizável.

artigo.texto: New PCE Metric Could Recover Stranded Data Center Power PCE measures how much provisioned power is available for compute rather than support systems, helping operators free up capacity for AI demand without new grid power. As AI-driven demand strains data center power availability, operators are under pressure to do more within fixed electrical envelopes. In many cases, importing more power from the grid is not immediately possible, and adding new on-site capacity is expensive or slow. That is why a proposed metric, called power compute effectiveness (PCE), is attracting interest. PCE is designed to show how much of a facility’s provisioned power is structurally available for compute and how much is tied up in cooling, electrical losses, and other support systems. The proposed metric is not positioned as a replacement for power usage effectiveness (PUE), the industry-standard metric that compares total facility energy to the energy used by IT equipment. Instead, proponents say it answers a different question, one that is becoming more urgent in retrofit and expansion projects: within a fixed power envelope, how much capacity is really available for servers? “I see value in PCE beyond the initial design phase, particularly for operators evaluating retrofits and figuring out how much provisioned power can actually support IT equipment,” said Bill Kleyman, executive chair of Data Center Programs at AFCOM. “The right framing is to consider PCE as a complement to PUE.” PUE vs. PCE PUE has been one of the data center industry’s most widely adopted metrics for more than two decades. It helped focus attention on facility overhead and pushed operators to improve energy performance. According to Uptime Institute, average PUE has improved from roughly 2.5 to about 1.6 over the last 20 years, while some facilities now report 1.1 or better. Even so, PUE has limits. It reflects operational efficiency once a facility is running and can leave room for interpretation about what counts as IT load versus facility load. Fan power, for example, may be classified differently from one site to another, and shared utility metering can further complicate the picture. PCE, by contrast, looks upstream. In a paper published by the Open Compute Project, Airsys Cooling Technologies defines the metric as the share of a data center’s provisioned power allocated to compute rather than to supporting infrastructure. “PCE asks a very simple question: Of all the power provisioned for a data center, how much is actually provisioned for compute?” said Paul Quigley, Chief Strategic Relations Officer at Airsys and one of the paper’s co-authors. If a facility has 100 MW of provisioned power and 70 MW is structurally available for compute, its PCE is 0.70. The remaining 30 MW might be allocated to cooling and heat rejection, electrical conversion, distribution losses, and auxiliary systems such as lighting, controls, and security. That distinction is central. PUE asks how efficiently a running data center uses energy. PCE asks how a data center’s provisioned power has been allocated before the servers are even turned on. Why the Metric Matters The appeal of PCE becomes clearer when operators are trying to add more compute without expanding their total power envelope. If a 100 MW facility initially reserves 30 MW for cooling, losses, and auxiliary loads, it has a PCE of 0.70. If an infrastructure redesign cuts those support requirements to 20 MW, the same facility can support 80 MW of compute and raise its PCE to 0.80, all without increasing total provisioned power. “The infrastructure changes needed to achieve this gain may require significant capital investment,” Quigley said. “What PCE uncovers is whether investment in cooling, electrical architecture, or other infrastructure can reallocate a larger portion of the existing power envelope to compute.” That is particularly relevant today, when utility constraints are making new capacity harder to secure in many markets. PCE does not tell operators that every non-compute megawatt can or should be recovered. What it does is make the existing allocation visible, giving designers and operators a way to evaluate whether changes to the infrastructure could free up more power for IT. Quigley offered an example: a facility may have 20 MW provisioned for an older cooling architecture, 7 MW associated with electrical conversion and distribution losses, and 3 MW dedicated to auxiliary loads. An engineering study might show that a cooling retrofit could reduce the cooling allocation from 20 MW to 12 MW. If that change is technically and financially justified, the facility could make another 8 MW structurally available for compute, subject to its remaining constraints. Because the metric is new, there is no validated industry average yet. In the Airsys/OCP paper, two real-world examples produced PCE scores of 0.705 for a 20 MW colocation site and 0.79 for a 100 MW hyperscale campus. Quigley said many older, air-cooled facilities may land between 0.50 and 0.65, while well-designed liquid-cooled sites could reach the high 0.80s. For now, those ranges should be viewed as directional rather than as established benchmarks. Where PCE May Be Most Useful PCE appears to have its greatest near-term value in design work, retrofits, and capital planning. In retrofits, PCE can highlight where infrastructure overhead is consuming an outsized share of provisioned capacity and help operators identify which upgrades are most likely to recover stranded power. A 30 MW site built 15 years ago, for example, might have a PCE of 0.60, leaving 18 MW for compute and 12 MW for support systems. If most of that support load is tied to cooling rather than to UPS losses or building loads, the analysis may point toward cooling upgrades as the better use of capital. O Piauí avançou na implantação da política estadual de crédito de carbono com a realização da primeira reunião do Conselho Gestor do REDD+, nesta terça-feira (20), no Centro de Educação Ambiental (CEA), em Teresina. A iniciativa busca reduzir as emissões de gases de efeito estufa provocadas pelo desmatamento e pela degradação florestal, além de criar mecanismos para beneficiar comunidades que contribuem para a preservação ambiental. O encontro foi aberto pelo secretário de Estado do Meio Ambiente e Recursos Hídricos, Feliphe Araújo. O conselho reúne representantes do poder público, da sociedade civil, da academia, dos povos indígenas, das comunidades quilombolas e tradicionais, da agricultura familiar e do setor produtivo. A proposta é garantir participação social, transparência e segurança na construção da política, que poderá gerar recursos para a conservação das florestas e beneficiar populações envolvidas na proteção dos biomas piauienses. Política prevê benefícios para comunidades Feliphe Araújo destacou que a implantação do projeto é uma das prioridades da gestão estadual. Segundo o secretário, a política precisa ser construída com regulamentação, diálogo e participação dos diferentes setores da sociedade. “Queremos proteger nossas florestas e, ao mesmo tempo, gerar recursos para beneficiar as pessoas que ajudam a preservar o meio ambiente. Por isso, é fundamental que esse processo seja construído com diálogo, transparência e participação de todos os setores”, afirmou. De acordo com o secretário, o Estado já avançou na elaboração de normas, na regulamentação da iniciativa e na busca por parceiros para viabilizar o projeto. A experiência de outros estados, como o Tocantins, também é utilizada como referência para orientar as próximas etapas. REDD+ busca reduzir emissões e preservar florestas O REDD+ é um mecanismo voltado à redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa associadas ao desmatamento e à degradação florestal. A iniciativa também pode viabilizar pagamentos por serviços ambientais, com benefícios para povos indígenas, comunidades quilombolas, populações tradicionais e agricultores familiares. Além da política de crédito de carbono, o secretário ressaltou a importância de associar a preservação ambiental ao desenvolvimento econômico. Entre as ações complementares citadas estão a recuperação de áreas degradadas, a educação ambiental, a fiscalização e a prevenção e o combate aos incêndios florestais. A primeira reunião do Conselho Gestor representa uma etapa na organização da governança do projeto. A estrutura busca assegurar que as decisões sejam debatidas coletivamente e que a política estadual seja desenvolvida com responsabilidade ambiental e participação social.

artigo.texto: Chery pairs 12C liquid battery cells with 400 Wh/kg solid-state technology Chery outlined its Rhinoceros Battery roadmap at the 2026 Chery Global Innovation Conference on October 20, including a dedicated Rhinoceros S solid-state battery pilot line scheduled to enter operation in 2027, reports IT-Home. The schedule adds a manufacturing milestone to Chery’s existing development plan. The company previously targeted solid-state battery applications in vehicles as early as 2026, while chairman Yin Tongyue said in September that vehicle-level testing would begin in 2027. Pilot-line operation and vehicle validation are separate stages, and neither establishes a date for customer deliveries. The manufacturing timeline also needs context. Chery completed construction of a 0.5 GWh pilot line for 60 Ah-class solid-state cells in February 2026 and issued equipment procurement tenders in early October. Chery has not clarified whether the line scheduled to enter operation in 2027 is that facility, a separate installation, or a further stage of commissioning. Rhinoceros S specifications and development challenges Chery lists the Rhinoceros S solid-state battery at 400 Wh/kg, with an operating temperature range of -40°C to 100°C. The company also reported an internal thermal-box test at 200°C. Still, it did not disclose the test duration, state of charge, or sample configuration needed to compare the result with standardised battery-safety tests. The 400 Wh/kg figure is not new in itself. Chery previously presented solid-state technology targeting 600 Wh/kg. Its development programs use different electrolyte and cathode formulations: earlier reporting identifies a sulfide-based electrolyte and high-nickel ternary cathode for the 400 Wh/kg cell, compared with an in-situ polymerised electrolyte and lithium-rich manganese cathode for the 600 Wh/kg route. The figures therefore describe different technical approaches and should not be treated as directly comparable versions of the same cell. Chery identified material-interface contact, battery-pack integration, and its proprietary Dedicated Management System (DMS) as engineering priorities. In solid-state cells, maintaining stable contact between the solid electrolyte and electrodes during repeated charging and discharging remains a key technical challenge. The timing places Chery among several Chinese automakers and battery manufacturers targeting solid-state battery trial production or vehicle validation around 2027. CATL and BYD have both targeted small-scale solid-state battery production for that year. Their plans are at different development stages and do not indicate that any of the companies will reach mass production in 2027. Liquid cells, sodium-ion storage and ammonia-fueled SOFC The Rhinoceros portfolio also covers liquid-electrolyte cells and sodium-ion batteries for energy storage. Chery lists a peak charging rate of 12C and a sustained average above 8C for its liquid cells; these figures do not apply to the Rhinoceros S solid-state battery. Its sodium-ion storage cells are rated for up to 15,000 cycles in commercial, industrial, and residential applications. For vehicles, Chery has outlined a long-term solid-state battery range target of up to 1,500 km. This remains a development target, not a confirmed range for a production vehicle. Chery also presented an ammonia-fueled solid oxide fuel cell (SOFC) system for stationary power generation. The conference slides identify ammonia as the fuel and describe green ammonia produced using wind and solar power. They list electrical efficiency of 60%, combined heat and power (CHP) efficiency of 90%, adjustable output from 30% to 100%, and a 90-day deployment window. Ammonia can serve as a hydrogen carrier for fuel-cell systems, but fuel processing and ammonia production affect overall efficiency and emissions. Using renewable electricity to produce ammonia does not, by itself, establish zero lifecycle emissions. An independent assessment of the stated efficiency figures would require more operating details. Proposed applications include decentralised power generation and remote charging infrastructure. Their viability would depend on fuel supply and transport, installation requirements, electricity demand, and operating costs.

artigo.texto: On his terrace overlooking the forest in eastern Pennsylvania, Ed Negra lays out four letters. All are from a developer promising a $10,000 check to each household once its data center is running. “I call it a bribe,” says the American retiree. The scene is picture-perfect. Autumn leaves are turning russet, and there is a stunning mountain view in this corner of Pennsylvania, a key state in America’s upcoming midterm elections. “We thought it was a beautiful place to retire,” says the septuagenarian, who used to manage a large building-supply store in neighboring New Jersey. He and his wife settled in a sprawling gated community with round-the-clock security. Eagle Rock Resort, in Hazle Township, has hundreds of comfortable homes scattered through the woods, two golf courses, swimming pools, an equestrian center and even a few ski slopes for the winter. “We didn’t know until we heard all the noise” of chainsaws in late 2024, Negra recalls. More than 1,200 acres (500 hectares) of land below the resort were cleared to build the future server complex. Residents quickly mobilized. They were furious that no one had warned them, and they worried about noise and pollution. Their fight echoes many conflicts across the United States over data centers, which have become an issue in the November 3 vote. Local opposition blocked or delayed at least 75 data center projects in the first three months of 2026, according to Data Center Watch, which tracks resistance to the industry. And polls show that the hostility crosses party lines. But Republican President Donald Trump fervently backs these projects in the name of US dominance in artificial intelligence, and he chastises those who oppose them. – ‘Drop in the bucket’ – In Hazle Township, residents won a court-ordered halt to construction as well as a municipal moratorium. A few pieces of heavy equipment sit idle on the vast cleared tract. The logs have already been hauled away. But developer NorthPoint Development has not given up. Its letters now flood local mailboxes, saying “there is a lot of misinformation and fear that has circulated about data centers and our project.” The letters also lay out a $165 million fund for the township and its residents. The money would pay for a new police station, lower trash fees and more. Part of it, $45 million, is to be paid directly to the 4,500 households once the data center’s first building goes into service. In the former mining town, one in six residents lives below the poverty line, according to official data. “For a young, struggling couple… living from paycheck to paycheck, $10,000 is a lot of money,” says Jeff Fasnacht, a retired high school teacher who lives in the gated community. Like Negra, he sees the offer as a bribe. He also calls it “a drop in the bucket” compared with how much value his home could lose if the project goes ahead. “This was supposed to be pristine forest forever,” sighs the golf enthusiast. Neither the developer nor township officials responded to AFP’s requests for comment. – ‘David and Goliath’ – Across the valley, residents of rural Sugarloaf Township are fighting a high-voltage power line that is likely intended to supply the data center. They are not eligible for the possible $10,000 check. “There’s no amount of money that can replace or take away the beauty, the tranquility that we live in,” says Annie Vinatieri. She shares a house with her in-laws, her husband and their young son. She has been fighting the power line for almost two years. “This fight feels akin to a David and Goliath fight,” she says. She takes heart in how many residents have rallied against tech interests: “The empowerment is unbelievable.” Erika Cook, 42, lives nearby and works remotely for an insurance company. She and her husband raise a few chickens and keep a vegetable garden. They also tap maple trees for syrup in the woods on their property. Part of that land is now the target of an eminent domain proceeding to make room for a huge transmission tower. Republicans dominate at the ballot box in this region. Cook says opposition to data centers has one virtue here: “It’s bringing people together… across party lines.”

artigo.texto: SHENZHEN, China, Oct. 20, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- A BYD Energy Storage desenvolveu uma rede abrangente de serviços pós-venda em uma estrutura de vários níveis: operação e manutenção de estações, centros de projetos, centros regionais e sede global. A BYD Energy Storage opera nove centros de O&M de 2.500 metros quadrados em todo o mundo. Ela conta com uma rede de serviços de pós-venda em diversos países como China, Chile, África do Sul, Reino Unido, Estados Unidos, Austrália, Japão, Polônia e Oriente Médio. Novos centros de serviços serão inaugurados na África do Sul e na Bulgária em 2027 para expandir ainda mais sua presença global de serviços. Os centros desempenham funções essenciais, como armazenamento e gestão de peças de reposição, reparo e manutenção de baterias, alocação regional de peças de reposição, reciclagem de baterias e treinamento de engenheiros contratados localmente. Os centros regionais da BYD Energy Storage estão em total conformidade com os requisitos regulamentares locais, oferecem treinamento estruturado para a força de trabalho e viabilizam uma resposta local rápida. A equipe de serviços profissionais é composta por mais de 200 engenheiros de campo e mais de 100 especialistas em P&D. A empresa aplica SLAs de serviço padronizados: resposta em até 24 horas, chegada ao local em até 48 horas e solução de problemas em até 7 dias. A rede global de serviços da empresa alcança uma ampla cobertura. Ela forma uma rede de suprimentos multiponto que garante a entrega rápida de peças de reposição em todo o mundo. Além disso, com suas linhas de produção locais, as equipes de operação e manutenção integram recursos regionais para oferecer serviços locais de reparo de baterias, fornecendo aos clientes globais um suporte pós-venda rápido, conveniente e localizado. "Nossa presença global de serviços é adaptada às nossas implementações de BESS em rápido crescimento. "O suporte pós-venda confiável sustenta a operação estável de longo prazo dos ativos de armazenamento de energia", comentou He Dehong, Chefe de Serviço Pós-Venda Global da BYD Energy Storage. Guiado por sua visão de capacitar o setor global de armazenamento de energia com serviços digitais e inteligentes, o sistema global maduro de O&M da BYD Energy Storage apoia fortemente sua crescente presença no armazenamento de energia em baterias. A empresa liderou as remessas globais de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS), superando 60 GWh em 2025, e entregou, ao todo, mais de 650 projetos de armazenamento de energia, contando com serviços pós-venda padronizados e localizados que garantem a operação confiável dos ativos. artigo.texto: Martin city leaders discuss regulations to get ahead of any potential data centers MARTIN, Tenn. (WBBJ) - The city of martin is getting ahead of a possible data center. City leaders held a meeting to set regulations before any project involving the construction of a data center is even proposed. They recommended capping noise at 60 decibels day and night, requiring 30 foot setbacks for small data centers, and 75 to 100 feet for hyperscale centers, keeping buildings mostly hidden from view, and limiting driveway access. The ordinance passed unanimously. “The regulations I’ve been working on for communities would define what a data center is and then would set up additional requirements, additional buffer from the nearest residential structure,” explained Donny Bunton, Martin city planner. If no regulation was put in before the proposal, it falls under general industrial use requirements, which are not as restrictive and do not include a buffer for the nearest residential structures. artigo.texto: Trending WHEELING - A preliminary draft of proposed amendments to the city of Wheeling’s Planning and Zoning code to include rules and regulations specifically for data centers was reviewed by city leaders on Tuesday night. Members of the Rules Committee of Wheeling City Council met at length prior to Tuesday night’s regular council meeting to discuss the proposed draft. Officials stressed the comprehensive document, currently 15 pages in length, is still a work in progress. However, several language tweaks and suggestions for changes were offered during Tuesday night’s session, and city leaders proposed the latest version of the draft be posted on the city’s website today in order to give the public the opportunity to review it and provide input to council members as the proposed amendment moves forward. "Put it out to the public with the understanding that this is a working draft," Councilman Dave Palmer noted. "That way, we can be contacted with suggestions from the public, listen more to ideas that are out there, and see if we thought we missed anything. It’s going to change. But I think we do have to get it out there to the public." The discussion comes in the wake of concerns by city leaders and the public over the past several months about the looming development of a new data center in the Wheeling neighborhood of Warwood. The former Centre Foundry & Machine Company property was acquired last year by the Silicon Foundation, an energy and artificial intelligence compute infrastructure company with international roots which plans to develop a new data center and energy technology campus at the Warwood location. Mayor Denny Magruder and other city leaders thanked Wheeling City Solicitor Rosemary Humway-Warmuth for working to put together the proposed zoning amendments, along with help from Building and Planning Director Brenda J. Delbert, City Clerk Jessica Holloway and others. This included research stemming from within the city’s own existing codes to municipalities around the country that have addressed similar situations. "I know some folks thought that we weren’t working on this, but those folks who have been working on it I think have been doing so for more than three months," Magruder said. "I think it’s a good move in the right direction." The city has already developed a memorandum of understanding with Silicon Foundation in which the company agrees not to apply with the state to expand and become what is considered a high-impact data center. Vice Mayor Jerry Skavounakis, chairman of the Rules Committee, said there was no previous example in the state of West Virginia on which legislation specific to municipal planning and zoning for data centers could be based. "There’s not a template that she was able to use," the vice mayor said. "There isn’t one. This is something she had to do from scratch. "I know you put a lot of time and effort into this, and I appreciate it," he told the city solicitor. The planning and zoning amendments to include language pertaining to data centers would first require a permitting process. A special use permit application would have to be submitted and approved, and the application process alone would involve a considerable list of requirements. Permitting requirements address a checklist of issues related to the site plan, a utility impact review, anticipated electrical demand and expected peak demands, adequate electrical service without unreasonable burden to city services and public utilities, daily maximum water demands and consumption, wastewater discharges, description of proposed cooling and water conservation measures, location and specifications of backup generators, anticipated air emissions, anticipated noise-producing equipment, proposed storm water management, noise levels and other issues. "There’s a list of things that they have to provide the city," Councilman Ty Thorngate said. "I think that is, to me, the most important thing in this." The application fee alone is currently set at $5,000, according to the proposed language. A surety bond must be provided by the applicant, as well. Currently, the surety bond is set at $75,000, but Humway-Warmuth noted this can be increased. "This is in case that applicant does not fulfill what they are required to fulfill," she said. "We’re not wed to that amount. It may be something you may want to modify - that’s at your discretion." The applicant must also cover the cost for industry experts the city will hire as consultants to review their application to make sure the company is meeting the requirements, to make any recommendations and to assure that industry standards are being met. "This allows us to use experts within this field, rely upon them, and then pass the cost off to the application - which would be the proposed data center, not the citizens," Sklavounakis said. Proposed language also includes potential fines for violations, but city officials noted that financial punishment would not likely have much of an impact on a company involved in data center development. "The big issue isn’t just the fines, we want to make sure that if they are doing stuff that they’re not supposed to be doing, we can revoke their permit in addition to the fines," Sklavounakis said. "If this data center wants to come here, the first thing they’re going to have to do is they have to get a permit. They’re not going to be able to operate without a permit." Humway-Warmuth noted the basic framework of the draft was based in part by language developed more than two decades ago when wireless communication boomed across the country and cell phone towers and infrastructure came to the city. The city created wireless telecommunication-specific ordinances to address issues related to these developments and several tweaks have been implemented in the city over the years, as well. artigo.texto: VP da WEG defende novas receitas para ampliar mercado de baterias no Brasil Companhia propõe combinar remuneração por capacidade e serviços à rede para sustentar crescimento do armazenamento além do primeiro leilão A WEG defende avanços na regulação para permitir que os sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias, conhecidos como BESS, sejam remunerados pelos diferentes serviços que prestam ao setor elétrico. Segundo Manfred Peter Johann, vice-presidente de Automação e Sistemas da companhia, combinar fontes de receita é necessário para desenvolver o mercado, além do primeiro leilão previsto para dezembro. “O primeiro leilão é fundamental para criar escala, mas o mercado não pode depender exclusivamente dele”, afirmou em entrevista à CNN. Entre as atividades citadas pelo executivo estão a disponibilidade de capacidade, a arbitragem de energia, o controle de frequência e tensão, os serviços ancilares e o suporte à rede. “Quando conseguirmos combinar essas diferentes fontes de receita, o BESS passa a ter uma lógica econômica própria e tende a ser considerado naturalmente em projetos de geração, transmissão, distribuição e também por consumidores industriais”, disse. Para os projetos que serão contratados nos leilões de dezembro, as diretrizes do Ministério de Minas e Energia preveem remuneração por disponibilidade de potência, com contratos de 15 anos e início de suprimento em 1º de agosto de 2028. Nesse modelo, a Portaria Normativa MME nº 136 determina que a receita fixa deve remunerar integralmente os usos que o Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico fizer dos empreendimentos vencedores, observados os compromissos contratados, sem receitas adicionais fora do Contrato de Potência de Reserva de Capacidade. A energia utilizada na recarga e a injetada pelos sistemas serão liquidadas no mercado de curto prazo. Os resultados positivos e negativos dessa liquidação serão destinados à Conta de Potência para Reserva de Capacidade, conforme os limites estabelecidos na portaria. Johann projeta que, em 2030, o armazenamento será uma parte habitual dos investimentos do setor elétrico brasileiro. Ele relaciona essa perspectiva ao crescimento da geração solar e eólica, à necessidade de flexibilidade, às restrições de transmissão e à demanda por confiabilidade e qualidade de energia. Além do leilão, a WEG identifica oportunidades em aplicações comerciais e industriais, data centers, microrredes e serviços para a rede, tanto no Brasil quanto no exterior. A companhia ampliou em setembro o projeto de sua fábrica de sistemas de armazenamento em Itajaí, em Santa Catarina. Com investimento total estimado de R$ 330 milhões, a unidade terá capacidade de produção de 4 GWh por ano. O início das operações está previsto para o segundo semestre de 2027. “Estamos fazendo um investimento de longo prazo porque entendemos que o armazenamento será uma parte cada vez mais relevante do sistema elétrico”, afirmou.

artigo.texto: From Pilot to Production: Mastering Liquid Cooling Deployment Moving liquid cooling from pilot to production brings new challenges. Explore eight critical considerations for deploying DLC at scale. October 19, 2026 Sponsored by Schneider Electric The reality of AI infrastructure has arrived: the power-hungry chips of today, such as the NVIDIA Blackwell, have rendered traditional air cooling obsolete. With rack densities soaring from 20 kW to over 140 kW, and the 1 MW milestone looming, the industry is transitioning from speculative planning to an urgent, high-stakes deployment phase. Direct liquid cooling (DLC) has become the IT industry’s preferred cooling method for extreme chip power densities, but the jump from a small-scale pilot to a full production environment is fraught with technical traps. Here we detail 8 common DLC deployment challenges and tips for overcoming them. Specification Challenges 1. Material incompatibility between the CDU and connected components increases the risk of galvanic corrosion, which can create debris that clogs cold plates and damages servers. Operators must minimize the difference in the anodic index between the materials used for all wetted surfaces. Strictly follow IT manufacturer guidelines for compatible materials. 2. Opposing liquid and air-cooling requirements force a tradeoff between operating energy savings and the capital costs of chilled water plants. When you cool your IT equipment with water, you can set your chilled water temperature higher compared to air. For every 0.6°C (1°F) increase in chilled water temperature, the chiller efficiency increases 1%-2%. The best path forward is to perform a total cost of ownership (TCO) analysis over a 10-year period or more to decide whether to share an existing low-temperature chiller or build a dedicated high-temperature chiller. 3. Direct coupling between servers and DLC infrastructure complicates specification because the cooling pipes are physically connected to the IT equipment, introducing new variables related to space, leak risks, and specific coolant flow needs. Collaborate closely with IT and infrastructure vendors to specify compatible quick-connect couplings and dedicate a single cooling loop to a single server model to avoid uneven cooling. 4. A lack of CDU system efficiency standards makes it very difficult to compare the capacity and efficiency ratings of different CDUs. Variables including fluid types, flow rates, fluid temperatures, and ambient temperature influence a CDU’s efficiency or capacity rating. The standards exist for air cooling, but not liquid cooling. Until official ASHRAE testing standards are finalized, request vendors to provide performance ratings based on draft test points. 5. Provisioning IT space for unknown liquid-cooled IT creates the risk of overpaying for oversized piping or stranding cooling capacity, as the system must be prepared for unknown maximum and minimum rack densities. To mitigate these variations, size the main loop piping diameter for the bulk CDU capacity, ensuring the piping is long enough to accommodate the maximum number of racks (lowest density). However, size the branch piping and manifolds for the highest potential rack density. Installation Challenge 6. The complexity of preventing TCS contamination drastically increases the risk of server damage through fouling, microbial growth, corrosion, or scaling. Combat these risks by taking proactive steps in the design and installation process. Limiting the size of individual cooling loops will help to contain any contamination. During installation, assemble components in clean environments, add biocide before the initial system fill, and thoroughly flush the loop while purging all air before connecting any IT equipment. Operational Challenges 7. A lack of clarity between cooling and server vendor warranties creates undue stress, often leading to finger-pointing if a leak or component failure occurs. You can help set boundaries by getting your IT vendors on the same page by having agreement on a common TCS supply temperature, flow rate and pressure. Clarify operations and maintenance responsibilities between installers, cooling vendors, and IT vendors early in the specification process. Review all warranties to ensure that required maintenance steps (like filter replacements) do not void another vendor’s warranty. 8. Slow DLC system response to GPU power transients poses a risk of expensive GPUs overheating during sudden power spikes common in AI training workloads. You can use software to power cap the GPUs, although this negatively impacts AI training times. A better operational approach is to implement a strict test plan, starting servers at a low utilization percentage and monitoring GPU temperatures as workloads increase. If temperatures approach dangerous levels (e.g., 90°C), decrease the chilled water supply temperature (e.g., by 5°C) to increase the rate of heat transfer, or increase the coolant flow rate. Where the Liquid Meets the Chip Moving from a conceptual pilot to a robust, production-ready liquid cooling environment requires a fundamental shift in how data center life cycles around specification, installation and operation are managed. The complexity of AI-ready infrastructure leaves no room for silos. With the right technical framework, it becomes the foundation for sustainable, high-performance AI growth. Want to learn more? His passion lies in innovation and sustainability, and he is known for challenging traditional mindsets to accelerate conservation and drive meaningful progress. artigo.texto: Gerando resumo Paolla Oliveira, de 44 anos, foi coroada rainha de bateria da Imperatriz Leopoldinense neste sábado (17), no Rio de Janeiro. A cantora Iza, que deixou o posto, foi responsável pela coroação. Ela entregou a faixa à atriz e as duas deram um beijo. Para a ocasião, a atriz apostou em um figurino com pedrarias verdes, em referência às cores da escola. Paolla anunciou seu retorno ao carnaval no fim de setembro, em uma publicação nas redes sociais. “Voltar não estava nos meus planos. Mas foi olhando o carnaval de um pouco mais longe que percebi o tamanho do meu amor por ele. O carnaval tá no meu corpo, nas minhas lembranças, no jeito que eu sinto alegria. Como é que a gente se despede completamente de uma coisa que faz parte da gente?”, escreveu a atriz no Instagram. Antes de assumir o posto na Imperatriz, Paolla foi rainha de bateria da Grande Rio até 2025, escola pela qual desfilou por cinco anos. Na ocasião, Paolla Oliveira afirmou que precisava se dedicar às gravações de Vale Tudo, novela da TV Globo em que interpretou Heleninha Roitman, e aos cuidados com o pai, diagnosticado com demência frontotemporal. Ela foi substituída por Virginia Fonseca, que permaneceu apenas um ano no posto. Atualmente, Anitta é a rainha de bateria da Grande Rio.

artigo.texto: Milton Cunha detona Virginia como Rainha de Bateria: "Catastrófico" Em entrevista a Blogueirinha, carnavalesco criticou desempenho da influenciadora e comentou a relação dela com a comunidade da Grande Rio O carnavalesco e comentarista Milton Cunha, 64, criticou o desempenho de Virginia Fonseca, 27, como Rainha de Bateria da Grande Rio durante participação no "Blogueirinha Entrevista", exibido pelo Multishow na última segunda-feira (19). Ao avaliar o samba da influenciadora, ele usou palavras como “catastrófico” e “terrível”. Durante a conversa, Milton também comentou a presença de celebridades em postos de destaque no Carnaval e afirmou que quem chega a uma escola de samba precisa respeitar a comunidade. “Qualquer pessoa que chegar na escola de samba tem que chegar na humildade, no sapatinho, por ali ser um território de comunidade”, declarou. Ao falar sobre Virginia, Milton relembrou a apresentação da influenciadora na quadra da Grande Rio, quando David Brazil teria pedido que ela mostrasse o samba no pé. “Os problemas da Virginia começaram no dia da apresentação dela na quadra. Quando o David Brazil disse: ‘Samba, Virginia’... Aí ela faz aquele passo dela e o queixo de todo mundo [foi para o chão], ‘o que é isso?’, e tal. Ali a gente já viu que não tinha samba no pé”, afirmou. Questionado por Blogueirinha sobre a possibilidade de Virginia aprender a sambar, o carnavalesco disse que também esperava que ela se aproximasse das pessoas que representaria na escola. “Além de esperança de aprender, esperança de que ela virasse íntima daquela gente que ela iria representar. Isso não vem. Aí chegam os ensaios técnicos, aí loucura em cima de loucura porque ela não consegue compreender qual é a estrutura do desfile”, avaliou. Em seguida, um integrante da plateia pediu que Milton definisse o samba da influenciadora. “Catastrófico, terrível, absurdo, impossível ritmicamente, é melhor não”, respondeu ele. O comentarista também comparou a experiência de Virginia com a de outras personalidades que ocuparam o posto de rainha de bateria. Ao citar Paolla Oliveira, ele afirmou que a atriz demonstrou envolvimento com a escola desde o início da trajetória na Grande Rio. “Ser rica e famosa não funciona na quadra da escola de samba”, disse Milton, ao comentar a relação entre celebridades e as comunidades das agremiações. Ele também afirmou que a responsabilidade pela escolha de personalidades para esses cargos não é apenas de quem os ocupa. “A responsabilidade é de quem a convida”, declarou. Virginia Fonseca deixou o posto na Grande Rio Virginia anunciou que deixaria o posto de rainha de bateria da Grande Rio em uma publicação nas redes sociais feita em agosto deste ano. No texto, a influenciadora agradeceu à escola pela oportunidade e afirmou que procurou se dedicar à função. “Não poupei esforços para entregar o meu melhor. Então, venho com o coração apertado e cheio de verdade, me despedir do posto de rainha de bateria da Grande Rio. E antes de qualquer palavra, quero agradecer ao Carnaval e à Grande Rio por me permitirem sentir essa magia de perto. É uma experiência única viver o maior espetáculo da terra”, escreveu. Ela também destacou o acolhimento recebido na agremiação e reconheceu as exigências do cargo. “A Grande Rio sempre me tratou como uma verdadeira rainha. Ali, me senti em casa, amada, protegida e, acima de tudo feliz. Entre vaias e aplausos, a gente caminhou junto, de mãos dadas e com muita coragem dos dois lados”, afirmou.

artigo.texto: California has always hidden the true price of progress somewhere beyond the horizon. The water arrives from a distant river. The electricity crosses a mountain range. By the time the benefits reach us, the damage has been assigned elsewhere. Now the future is arriving in windowless buildings. Data centers are rising from industrial corridors and farmland with the appetite of cities. They pull electricity by the hundreds of megawatts. Inside, servers build fortunes. Outside, residents open their utility bills and wonder what will remain. Before California approves another facility, every host community deserves an answer: What will this project make better here? Gov. Gavin Newsom recently signed seven laws that begin to make the hidden costs visible. Until those are in effect, a company could arrive with the appetite of a city and quietly leave its bill for wires and water with people who never asked for it. Now utility regulators must reckon with what it takes to serve that appetite. The rates and connection terms are meant to make new users shoulder their share of the grid and the electricity it must supply, instead of loading those costs onto a family studying its bill. Regulators must now make that promise real. The water, too, must come into the open. Data centers are water guzzlers, using huge volumes for cooling. Before construction, a developer must show where that water will come from, how the facility will fare in drought and who will pay for the new pipes. After the servers begin to hum, estimates must give way to actual water use. State planners will gain an account of energy consumption and efficiency. A town needs numbers it can see. And the project can no longer pass under a blanket environmental exemption. A quicker path through court is reserved for facilities that meet demanding conditions on clean power, water and protection of ratepayers. In California, speed must be earned. These laws draw a floor beneath the bargain. They do not guarantee that a neighborhood gains something lasting from the land, power and water it commits. California should establish a “community benefit standard” for every new data center and major expansion. Protect the resources of the place. Pay every cost the project creates. Then deliver a public benefit that residents can see, measure and enforce. The first requirements are obligations, not generosity. Developers must disclose projected electricity demand, water consumption, emissions, noise and infrastructure needs. That includes drought, extreme heat and nearby projects. Households cannot pay for capacity reserved by a corporation that may never use it. No company should receive applause for obeying environmental law. Efficient cooling is not a community gift when the machinery is necessary to run the servers. A research grant cannot excuse an unacceptable water plan. Public benefits cannot purchase permission to pollute a neighborhood or drain an aquifer. Only after those tests are met does the additional bargain begin. Each major project should fund at least one substantial technology program tied to an identified public need. Residents and public agencies would help choose the priority. California should measure what changes, not what gets announced. One developer might finance advanced water reuse with a local district beyond what is required to address its own demand. The compact would state how much freshwater demand must be eliminated, how savings will be verified and who will operate the system. Buying equipment would not count. Producing verified water savings would. Another facility might guarantee computing capacity to California hospitals and universities studying rare diseases, cancer or wildfire behavior. The agreement would specify secure access, support and computing hours, and bind the tenant. Researchers would receive usable capacity, not whatever remains after commercial customers finish. A third project could finance batteries and controls that keep a clinic, cooling center or water system operating during an outage. The equipment must serve the public in an emergency. Backup power reserved for company servers would not qualify. Every project must still provide a direct local benefit. A statewide research program may supplement that commitment, but it cannot replace it. The compact would name beneficiaries, funding, responsible parties, milestones and penalties for failure. Its duties would survive a sale or tenant change. Independent verification would report delivery, not spending. If one method underperforms, the agreements between data centers and communities should permit another. The obligation itself remains. Contribution levels should reflect project size. Small facilities could pool resources. Large campuses could not divide themselves into smaller applications to escape responsibility. Broader innovation contributions should be legally sound and separate from required mitigation. Projects with unacceptable impacts should be rejected or relocated. Those meeting environmental standards and securing credible, enforceable benefits deserve coordinated reviews and clear timelines. The Legislature has drawn the line against making families pay for the servers that power someone else’s fortune. The industry can meet that line by showing, in public and before construction, how it will protect the grid and water system. Then it can show what it will build for the people living outside its walls. For too long, California has sent the rewards of progress in one direction and the damage in another. If our communities are asked to power the future, that future must also power them.

artigo.texto: By Paul Williamson, Director of Development, Key Capture Energy Key Capture Energy has two battery energy storage systems (BESS) under development in Ulster County, KCE NY 34 in Saugerties and KCE NY 5 in New Paltz. Local officials and residents often ask us a simple question why here? The answer is just as simple: battery energy storage is needed in the Hudson Valley to ensure residents and businesses have a stable and reliable electric grid today and in the future. New York’s grid operator says the state has hit an inflection point. The Hudson Valley won’t have enough power to meet peak summer demand starting in 2032, and the gap could grow significantly by the middle of the 2030s if planned projects are delayed. Right now the region depends heavily on older plants like Danskammer in Newburgh, which filed for bankruptcy in June, but the grid operator did not let it close because there was nothing to replace it. Keeping old, inefficient plants like this available forces ratepayers to cover costs the plant owner can’t recover from New York’s power markets. Statewide, that has cost ratepayers tens of millions of dollars a year. The alternative of building new transmission lines to import power from upstate is also expensive and can take many years. The cheaper option for Hudson Valley residents is to permit and build new power resources close to where they are needed. Battery energy storage can help with these problems. Batteries charge when the grid has extra power and send it back when demand spikes, which cuts into the most expensive hours of the year. That’s why New York set a goal of 6 gigawatts of storage by 2030, a buildout state regulators have said could save nearly $2 billion in overall system costs. KCE NY 5 was recently awarded a contract that will help make those savings a reality. Battery storage placed where the lines are most crowded does the most to help keep costs off Ulster County bills. Both of KCE’s projects are intentionally located near existing substations. BESS works where a project can connect to the grid and send power back to the community and surrounding region when the electric grid needs energy. In addition to helping keep the lights on for households and businesses, both projects will provide millions of dollars in local economic benefits including taxes, wages for local union jobs during construction and other community benefits. We know residents have questions as these are some of the first BESS projects proposed in the Hudson Valley. While new in the region, battery energy storage systems have been built in virtually every state in the country with roughly 1,000 similarly sized projects operating safely today and saving customers money in states like Texas and California. Key Capture Energy currently operates 14 projects nationwide, including several of comparable size to the ones proposed in New Paltz and Saugerties. Simply put, battery energy storage is safe. To address concerns around fire safety after three battery storage fires in New York in the summer of 2023, the state convened a fire safety working group and over two years developed one of the strictest fire and safety codes in the country, which went into effect in January of 2026. The FDNY and fire safety experts nationally have repeatedly analyzed and said again and again that battery storage built to this updated code is safe. The fire code requires that any system installed today must pass national and international fire safety testing, every project has to undergo an independent third-party safety review during permitting to ensure these codes are met, and an Emergency Response Plan must be created with coordination from the local fire department before operations. Developers are also required to train local first responders prior to a facility starting operations and offer training annually afterwards. Earlier this month, Ulster County community leaders and local first responders heard directly from state officials and fire safety leaders on why storage is needed regionally and the safety standards BESS must comply with in New York. The Hudson Valley’s grid congestion problem gets more expensive for everyone each year that nothing is built. These projects are key to reducing the threat of blackouts in the region and are strategically sited next to existing electrical infrastructure. As a leading battery energy storage company in New York, KCE’s team takes pride in being valued members of our host communities and we hope to earn your support along the way. If you have questions, don’t hesitate to reach out to our team or come by a local Town or Planning Board meeting. Paul Williamson is Director of Development of Key Capture Energy. artigo.texto: A Nscale, empresa de computação em nuvem voltada a inteligência artificial, negocia um novo contrato com a Anthropic, dona do chatbot Claude, que pode valer cerca de US$ 45 bilhões. A informação é da Bloomberg, confirmada por fonte da Reuters nesta segunda-feira (19). O acordo seria para um segundo prédio no complexo de data centers Monarch, na Virgínia Ocidental (EUA), com capacidade de 460 megawatts, usando os chips de IA Vera Rubin, da Nvidia. Quanto a Anthropic já investiu em infraestrutura Em agosto, a empresa, que vem de um trimestre com receita 45% maior às vésperas de seu IPO, já havia fechado outro contrato de US$ 45 bilhões com a Nscale. Somando outros fornecedores, a Anthropic acumula cerca de US$ 150 bilhões em contratos. São US$ 50 bilhões com a Fluidstack, US$ 10 bilhões com a startup Volta e US$ 45 bilhões com a SpaceX, de Elon Musk. A Anthropic também tem direito de preferência sobre um terceiro prédio planejado para o complexo Monarch. As negociações seguem em andamento, e nem a empresa nem a Nscale comentaram o assunto. No Brasil, a brasileira Zup já disputa se tornar parceira local da Anthropic, sinal de como a empresa também mira expansão fora dos Estados Unidos. A pressão por cautela Um grupo de investidores pressiona a Nscale a reduzir a meta de avaliação do IPO, hoje em cerca de US$ 30 bilhões. Na semana passada, ações da CoreWeave, rival da Nscale, caíram com o mercado preocupado com a dívida de US$ 50 bilhões da companhia. Publicidade A queda gerou venda generalizada de papéis de IA. O episódio reacende a dúvida sobre até quando o apetite por contratos gigantescos resiste a um mercado cético com dívida, preocupação que já levava empresas a reavaliar gastos com IA. A Microsoft, aliás, desistiu de ser a principal cliente de outro projeto de data center da Nscale, depois que atrasos na conexão de energia empurraram a entrega para a década de 2030. O que acontece agora Segundo o Valor, a Nscale elevou o valor de contratos de US$ 100 milhões para mais de US$ 103 bilhões em dois anos e meio. O acordo com a Anthropic pode fechar em dias, mas não há decisão definitiva até a publicação desta matéria.

artigo.texto: Vídeo: minas de carvão de Criciúma podem abrigar data centers; empresa italiana visitará a região Prefeito afirma que empresário do setor de mineração conhecerá o potencial das estruturas Por Rafaela Custódio Atualizada 2 min de leitura As minas de carvão desativadas de Criciúma e da região carbonífera poderão ganhar novas utilidades, incluindo o armazenamento de data centers. Uma empresa italiana demonstrou interesse nas estruturas subterrâneas e enviará uma missão ao Sul de Santa Catarina no fim de novembro para conhecer as instalações e avaliar possibilidades de investimento. A informação foi divulgada pelo prefeito de Criciúma, Vagner Espindola, ao Portal Engeplus. Segundo o prefeito, a iniciativa faz parte de uma estratégia para diversificar a economia do município, com foco em tecnologia e inovação, aproveitando áreas que hoje enfrentam restrições para novos empreendimentos em razão do passivo ambiental deixado pela mineração. “Porque a grande virada de chave, na realidade, da cidade de Criciúma, ela está voltada para a tecnologia, para a inovação”, afirmou. Espindola destacou que as áreas afetadas pela atividade carbonífera representam um desafio para o desenvolvimento urbano e econômico, principalmente em razão das restrições impostas pela Ação Civil Pública (ACP) do Carvão. “O que nós temos é a herança de um passivo ambiental. E é este passivo ambiental que hoje, ele praticamente sentencia grandes glebas de terras da nossa cidade e que estão impedidas, por conta da ação civil pública do carvão, de edificar qualquer construção. Então, nós ficamos muito amarrados por conta dessa ação civil pública”, declarou. O prefeito relatou que conheceu uma experiência semelhante durante uma viagem ao norte da Itália, neste ano. Na ocasião, a comitiva conheceu uma empresa de mineração de calcário que, conforme Espindola, encontrou novas possibilidades de uso para antigas áreas subterrâneas de extração mineral. “Mas, quando a gente ergue um pouquinho a cabeça e sai de Criciúma, a gente consegue encontrar ali ferramentas para a gente fazer essa inversão das matrizes econômicas. A prova disso, quando nós fomos agora, este ano, para o norte da Itália, e lá nós conhecemos uma empresa de mineração de calcário, que, quando esvaiu-se toda a extração daquele mineral, deu-se para as cavas subterrâneas, as minas, uma nova utilidade. Hoje, essas cavas subterrâneas, elas servem de armazenamento de data centers, armazenamento de champanhes, vinhos e até maçãs”, contou. A partir da apresentação das características das áreas da região carbonífera, o empresário responsável pela empresa demonstrou interesse em conhecer as estruturas locais.
