artigo.texto: The Gujarat Electricity Regulatory Commission (GERC) has finalized the Gujarat Electricity Regulatory Commission (Grid Interactive Battery Energy Storage System) Regulations, 2026, establishing a regulatory framework for integrating Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) into Gujarat’s electricity grid. The regulations aim to improve grid stability, enhance operational flexibility, and support the growing integration of renewable energy sources, particularly solar and wind power, whose generation depends on weather conditions. The new framework aligns with guidelines issued by the Ministry of Power, Government of India, which recognize energy storage as an important component of electricity generation, transmission, distribution, and ancillary services. Battery energy storage systems can help balance electricity supply and demand by storing surplus power and releasing it when required, thereby supporting reliable grid operations. GERC initiated the regulatory process by publishing the draft regulations on May 12, 2026. The Commission subsequently conducted a public consultation process to gather feedback from stakeholders. Written comments and objections were received from 20 stakeholders, followed by a public hearing on June 15, 2026. The finalized regulations incorporate the Commission’s decisions on key aspects of BESS procurement, project registration, operating models, charging arrangements, and grid control. Under the finalized framework, electricity distribution licensees and other applicable licensees are primarily required to procure BESS capacity through competitive bidding under Section 63 of the Electricity Act, 2003. This approach is intended to promote transparent procurement and cost-effective tariff discovery. Procurement under Section 62 will be permitted only in exceptional circumstances, subject to prior approval from the Commission and the submission of adequate techno-commercial justification. The regulations also establish registration and minimum project-size requirements for grid-connected battery storage installations in Gujarat. All grid-connected BESS projects must register with the Gujarat Energy Development Agency (GEDA). For standalone installations, the minimum individual project size has been specified as above 1 MW in power capacity, with an energy storage duration of at least two hours. Such projects must connect to the electricity network at 11 kV or higher. The framework allows battery storage systems to operate under different business models, including co-located projects alongside renewable energy plants, standalone installations, systems embedded within transmission or distribution networks, and consumer or prosumer arrangements. These provisions are intended to accommodate different applications of energy storage across the power sector. For co-located BESS installations, the Commission has specified that charging must take place exclusively from the associated renewable energy plant. This restriction is designed to avoid complications in energy accounting and Renewable Purchase Obligation (RPO) compliance. Grid charging without the appropriate contract demand will attract temporary supply tariffs, discouraging unauthorized electricity consumption through the grid. The regulations also clarify the role of the State Load Despatch Centre (SLDC) in maintaining grid security. The SLDC will retain overriding authority to issue dispatch instructions to all grid-connected BESS during grid disturbances, helping safeguard system reliability. With these regulations, Gujarat has established a framework for the controlled deployment and operation of battery energy storage systems. The measures are expected to support renewable energy integration, improve grid flexibility, and strengthen the state’s ability to manage changing electricity demand and generation patterns. artigo.texto: The Converter as the Control Point for AI Data Center Power With AI workloads driving unprecedented growth in data center power demand, projected by some analysts to reach as much as 70% annually through 2027, the industry's first AI power debate centered on capacity: where will the next hundreds of megawatts come from? AI factories introduce concentrated, fast-changing loads that can create steep ramps in demand and power consumption. At the same time, utilities and grid operators are scrutinizing how very large loads behave during disturbances, not simply whether enough generation exists to serve them. This creates a new design requirement. The data center must remain highly available while presenting the grid, on-site generators, and internal distribution system with a manageable load profile. The solution is a coordinated power architecture in which converters, storage, controls, protection, medium-voltage equipment, and digital systems work as one. Within that architecture, PCS has become increasingly important. As AI facilities grow in scale and complexity, they are evolving from simple power electronics components into key control layers that help coordinate how energy moves through the site. No longer just a conversion device In a conventional description, a converter does what it says: converts direct current from a battery or renewable source into alternating current for the facility or grid and reverses that flow when charging storage. In an AI data center, a modern PCS functions as a high-speed, controllable electrical interface, regulating active and reactive power, limiting current, shaping ramp rates, supporting voltage and frequency stability, and responding through grid-connected and islanded operating modes. That distinction matters because AI power problems happen on several timescales. Fast converter controls can respond to sharp electrical changes, battery energy storage systems (BESS) can buffer sustained ramps or temporary capacity limits, and Power Plant Controllers (PPC) can coordinate the PCS with generators, utility signals, switchgear, facility-management systems, and state-of-charge constraints. Together, these layers help make volatile loads more predictable. Four roles for power conversion in the AI power architecture 1. Load smoothing and generator protection AI workload changes can push on-site generation and utility connections beyond comfortable ramp-rate or power-quality envelopes. A bidirectional PCS paired with BESS can absorb excess power or inject power rapidly, reducing sudden changes seen by the rest of the system. 2. Voltage support and disturbance ride-through Converters can supply or absorb reactive power and follow a defined ride-through behavior. The objective is to prevent a short grid event from becoming a large, coordinated loss of data center load or a site-wide transfer event. 3. Grid-connected, islanded, and restoration modes With appropriate system design, controls, and protection, storage and PCS can support transitions between grid-connected and islanded operation, stabilize an islanded bus, and contribute to restoration or black-start pathways. These are system functions and must be validated at the site level. 4. Capacity shaping and flexible interconnection When a grid connection is constrained, storage can reduce peaks, manage import limits, and help the facility operate within an agreed envelope. This does not eliminate the need for interconnection studies or network upgrades, but it can create additional design options. A practical architecture For large campuses, PCS should be evaluated as part of a repeatable medium-voltage building block rather than as an isolated converter. A typical architecture can combine battery blocks, medium-voltage transformers, switchgear, power plant controllers, protection, telemetry, and supervisory controls. Modular, factory-tested blocks reduce the number of site interfaces and create a platform that can be repeated as the campus expands, reducing integration risks and streamlining deployment. The control hierarchy is equally important. Converter-level controls provide the fastest response. Plant controls coordinate multiple converters and enforce site-level active-power, reactive-power, voltage, frequency, and import or export objectives. Higher-level energy management can optimize state of charge, demand response, market participation, and on-site generation use. Clear ownership of each control loop is essential to avoid conflicting commands or unstable interactions. Model first, then prove the response AI data centers require a validation process that connects product capability to site behavior. The work should begin with the actual load profile, grid strength, fault levels, generator characteristics, protection philosophy, and intended operating modes. Steady-state studies alone are not enough for the most dynamic use cases. Electromagnetic-transient models, hardware-in-the-loop testing and staged commissioning can be used to test ramp events, voltage disturbances, current limits, control handoffs, and islanding sequences before the full site is energized. This model-to-test-to-commission approach also changes procurement. Instead of buying an inverter only against a nameplate rating, owners can define measurable performance at the point of interconnection: response time, ramp-rate control, reactive capability, recovery after a fault, operating envelopes, and telemetry. The commercial specification becomes a performance specification. From passive load to grid-interacting energy system The power challenge facing AI data centers is not solved by adding capacity alone. It is solved by coordinating capacity with controllability. As campuses combine utility connections, on-site generation, batteries, renewables, and increasingly power-dense compute, the converter becomes one of the few assets capable of acting fast enough to keep those elements working together. artigo.texto: For most of the past decade, the question about energy storage was whether it would ever be affordable. That question has been answered. Stationary battery packs fell to around $70/kWh in 2025, down 45% year on year, according to BloombergNEF. Africa installed an estimated 17GW of solar in 2026, a 45% rise on the year before, according to energy think tank Ember. And in South Africa, more than 90% of residential solar systems now sold include a battery system. Yet of the $13.84 billion in energy transition investment Africa attracted in 2025, as tracked by Electron Intelligence, just $666 million, under 5%, went to storage and flexibility. That gap, between how cheap storage has become and how slowly it is being financed, protected and integrated into grid planning, runs through the latest ESI Africa Industry Insights Volume into Energy & Storage. According to Nicolette Pombo-van Zyl, Editor-in-Chief of ESI Africa, storage has stopped being the add-on that gets bolted onto a renewable project at the end. “It is now the part that decides whether a project gets financed, whether a grid stays stable after sunset and whether the clean energy already being generated is actually used. The industry’s challenge is that capital, regulation and data have not yet caught up with that reality,” says Pombo-van Zyl. The cheapest battery is not always the cheapest system Comparative modelling in South Africa puts lithium iron phosphate (LFP) ahead of every rival chemistry for stationary storage, with a levelised cost of storage of about R4.05 to R4.25 per kilowatt-hour (kWh). Paired with solar PV, it delivers electricity at around R1.92/kWh, undercutting gas turbine peaking at R7.07/kWh. But the ESI Africa volume shows that battery chemistry is only the start of the pricing. Deployment scale, physical degradation in hot climates and the cost of capital decide whether that advantage survives a real project. Import tariffs and freight can inflate storage capital costs by 15 to 35% across emerging markets. A companion feature maps the chemistry landscape beyond LFP, from sodium-ion, which removes lithium from the equation and is now entering utility tenders in India, to LMFP, lithium manganese-rich and solid-state batteries. Its takeaway for a minerals-rich continent points to a threat that the cheapest battery chemistry may use less of the minerals Africa wants to move up the value chain. artigo.texto: Publicidade O avanço da inteligência artificial (IA) está aumentando a demanda por infraestrutura física e abrindo novas possibilidades de investimento no mercado imobiliário. Nesse cenário, mostra a XP, os data centers, instalações responsáveis pelo armazenamento, processamento e circulação de dados, podem ganhar relevância e representar uma nova frente de atuação para os fundos imobiliários (FIIs). Embora a IA seja frequentemente associada ao desenvolvimento de software, sua operação depende de uma estrutura física robusta, que envolve semicondutores, energia elétrica, redes de transmissão, sistemas de resfriamento e data centers. Essa cadeia pode ser dividida em três grandes frentes: semicondutores, infraestrutura e otimização de negócios. Enquanto a primeira reúne os componentes necessários ao processamento de dados, a segunda abrange os recursos físicos que sustentam a tecnologia. A terceira envolve a aplicação da IA para transformar operações e modelos de negócios em diferentes setores da economia. Leia Mais: Dupla taxa, falta de transparência e emissões: as maiores dores dos cotistas de FIIs Como os FIIs podem investir em data centers Segundo a XP, os fundos imobiliários podem acessar esse mercado por meio da aquisição de data centers operacionais, do financiamento de projetos em desenvolvimento e do investimento em infraestruturas associadas, como subestações elétricas. Nesse modelo, a exposição do cotista é imobiliária. O fundo adquire o imóvel e recebe os aluguéis pagos pelo operador responsável pelo data center ou pela infraestrutura locada. Continua depois da publicidade As receitas provenientes de serviços de computação em nuvem, processamento de dados ou outras atividades tecnológicas permanecem com o operador, e não são diretamente apropriadas pelo fundo. A distinção é importante porque o crescimento da demanda por inteligência artificial não garante, por si só, retornos elevados para os FIIs expostos ao segmento. O desempenho do investimento continua condicionado ao preço de aquisição do imóvel, às condições contratuais, à qualidade técnica da estrutura, à disponibilidade de energia e à capacidade financeira do inquilino. A perspectiva de expansão dos serviços digitais pode favorecer a ocupação dos empreendimentos e a capacidade de pagamento dos locatários. Continua depois da publicidade Ainda assim, diz a XP, o resultado depende de como cada ativo foi adquirido, da estrutura de financiamento e das necessidades futuras de investimento para manter a infraestrutura competitiva. Além disso, a exposição a data centers pode oferecer aos fundos acesso a um segmento com características distintas de outros mercados imobiliários. A demanda por infraestrutura digital está ligada à expansão dos serviços tecnológicos, embora isso não elimine riscos de crédito, vacância ou obsolescência dos imóveis. Leia Mais: Data centers ganham espaço nos FIIs após Redata? Fundos miram renda de longo prazo Continua depois da publicidade Sale and leaseback, built to suit e desenvolvimento de novos projetos Os FIIs podem acessar o segmento por diferentes estruturas de investimento, com níveis variados de risco e previsibilidade de receitas. Entre as possibilidades estão a compra de ativos estabilizados, as operações de sale and leaseback (SLB), os contratos built to suit (BTS), o financiamento de obras por meio de certificados de recebíveis imobiliários (CRIs) e o desenvolvimento de novos empreendimentos. Na aquisição de um ativo estabilizado, o fundo compra um data center já construído, conectado à rede elétrica e ocupado por um inquilino. Essa estrutura reduz a exposição aos riscos de construção, energização e comercialização, embora permaneçam os riscos relacionados ao contrato, ao locatário e à necessidade de modernização do imóvel. No sale and leaseback, o operador vende o imóvel ao fundo e permanece no local como locatário, mediante um contrato de aluguel. A operação permite que a empresa libere capital anteriormente imobilizado no empreendimento para direcioná-lo à expansão das atividades, à compra de equipamentos ou ao desenvolvimento de novos projetos. Continua depois da publicidade Já no modelo built to suit, o imóvel é construído ou adaptado de acordo com as necessidades específicas do futuro ocupante. Em contrapartida, o locatário firma um contrato de longo prazo, que deve remunerar adequadamente o capital investido pelo proprietário. Contratos longos ajudam a reduzir riscos, mas não eliminam problemas Para a XP, o elevado grau de especialização dos data centers reforça a importância de contratos de locação de longo prazo, especialmente quando o imóvel foi desenvolvido para atender às necessidades de um único operador. Essas estruturas podem ampliar a previsibilidade das receitas e reduzir a exposição a renegociações frequentes. Contratos atípicos podem prever prazos extensos, reajustes periódicos pela inflação e penalidades por rescisão antecipada. Quando essas penalidades são elevadas e vinculadas ao saldo de aluguéis até o vencimento, podem desestimular a saída antecipada do inquilino e favorecer o alinhamento entre o prazo contratual e o horizonte de retorno do investimento. A infraestrutura de data centers apresenta uma particularidade para o mercado imobiliário: as características técnicas que tornam um empreendimento adequado a determinado operador também podem limitar suas alternativas de uso. A disponibilidade de energia, os sistemas de resfriamento e as especificações construtivas influenciam tanto a operação quanto o potencial de reutilização do imóvel. artigo.texto: Residents in four Madison County townships will vote in November on an advisory measure asking whether data center development should be allowed in their communities. Ballot initiatives in Chouteau, Granite City, Nameoki and Venice townships will ask voters whether they support future data center development and construction. In Illinois, townships are subdivisions of local government that operate alongside cities and villages. The township’s elected board may oversee local infrastructure, such as water and sewer services. Each of the townships included in the advisory measure overlaps with Granite City. Because the measures are nonbinding, they would not ban data centers even if residents vote against the projects. Heather Groetecke, a lifelong Granite City resident, led the effort to collect signatures for the initiatives. She first became aware of potential data center development near her home in Nameoki Township when officials held community meetings this spring about proposals for two sites in Granite City and another in nearby Pontoon Beach. Groetecke said she began organizing when officials failed to answer her questions about environmental hazards and other concerns. “I (have) never really even been involved in politics in my whole life, and I don’t really like it either,” she said. “But I don’t want a data center.” Groetecke initially wanted to put a data center moratorium on the ballot. But she said political advisers close to the signature campaign recommended a nonbinding measure because it would be easier to pass. “They can still do what they want to do,” Groetecke said. “But if we win by the majority, I think that speaks volumes.” Data center proposals in the Granite City area Data center developers are eyeing the Granite City area for projects. City officials heard public comment about a proposal involving two sites along the Route 3 industrial corridor. Officials in nearby Pontoon Beach heard a similar proposal in May, the Alton Telegraph reported. The Belleville News-Democrat reported that the Granite City project received mixed reviews in a February forum. Trade union leaders voiced support for the potential economic development and property tax revenue, while other residents said they were concerned about utility rate hikes, environmental impacts and transparency. Developer Cloverleaf Infrastructure said in a public city council meeting in Granite City last November that it doesn’t sign nondisclosure agreements with local governments. The developer also promised not to use groundwater wells to cool its data centers and suggested “enforceable” zoning requirements to limit noise and light pollution. Cloverleaf officials have said the company works with big names in tech, including Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, Google and OpenAI. Some residents accused Granite City Mayor Mike Parkinson and other city officials of misleading the public when they said that they knew little about data center development in public meetings. Residents said in May that officials negotiated a possible land sale for a data center project with special governing district America’s Central Port before alerting the public. Parkinson told the Belleville News-Democrat that the documents cited by residents were taken out of context and that the city never collaborated with the port authority to bring in data center projects. Months before the community meetings, Parkinson, Madison County Executive Chris Slusser and Granite City’s economic development director, Cathy Hamilton, were among several St. Louis-area leaders who toured a Google data center on a trip financed by Greater St. Louis Inc. Officials were asked to sign nondisclosure agreements before touring the facility. Granite City officials say the data center project was tabled along with similar proposals in Edwardsville and Troy, Illinois. Granite City officials did not respond to requests for comment.

artigo.texto: Three roundtable groups weighed options Saturday during the first of three public discussions about data centers being held at different Statesboro venues. But if participants decided anything, it was only for themselves. Open to everyone, the next will be held 9 a.m. Thursday, Oct. 22, in the Statesboro Home Builders Association building, 1223 Merchants Way. Then the third and final installment in this "deliberative discussion series" is scheduled for 6 p.m. Tuesday, Oct. 27, in the Jones-Love Cultural Center at Luetta Moore Park, 121 Martin Luther King Jr. Drive. The Institute for Vibrant and Engaged Communities, or IVEC, from Georgia Southern University is hosting the series, "Weighing the Options: Data Centers in Our Community." The first session started at 5 p.m. Saturday, Oct. 17, in the Honey Bowen Building at Memorial Park on Fair Road. About 20 people or one or two more, including the organizers, showed up. "At the Institute for Vibrant and Engaged Communities, we believe community engagement is an important part of community governance, and so we have created these forums because this is an issue that is important to the community," said IVEC Director Candice Bodkin, Ph.D. "We're personally concerned that there's not good conversation or dialogue that's happening around concerns about data centers." As she noted, citizens speaking at formal hearings such as those of the Bulloch County Board of Commissioners or Statesboro City Council often are assigned three or five minutes each, with no back-and-forth dialogue. "So this is an opportunity for folks to sit down with their neighbors, talk about their concerns, talk through some options," Bodkin said. "It's not meant to be that we come to a conclusion, or decision, that this is what we recommend." However, the IVEC team is taking notes of participants' concerns and ideas, with the intent of delivering a report to city and county leaders. Jayce Sudweeks, Ph.D., who co-founded the institute with Bodkin four years ago but is now in a new position with the university — director of Interdisciplinary Clusters of University Excellence — helped lead the event. Four graduate students completed the IVEC team that hosted the Saturday conversation. Participants gathered around three tables for mostly separate, small-group discussions. Basic rule: 'Be kind' Sudweeks emphasized a couple of points at the outset. "Number one, the university has not taken a stance for or against data centers," he said. "So we're trying to be as neutral and unbiased as we can, and so for this report we want (to hear from) everybody. It will reflect people who are for it, people who are against it, all of those types of things." Then he asked participants "to be kind and polite to your neighbors" in the room and across the table. Guidebook's facts IVEC has produced a 26-page deliberation guide entitled "Data Centers in Our Backyard: How should our community decide?" and gave copies to participants at the check-in table. According to the introductory pages, 73 data centers were operating in Georgia as of December 2025. Around that time, Georgia Power was approved by the state Public Service Commission for approximately 10 gigawatts of new capacity, mostly for data centers. The average residential monthly power bill had increased by $43 since 2022. Meanwhile, Georgia since 2018 has exempted data center equipment from state and local sales tax, with state estimates placing the revenue loss at about $2.5 billion in fiscal year 2026. The IVEC guide lists its sources for these facts, and some local ones. One of those local facts is that about three out of four voters in Bulloch County's primary election in May, in ballot questions asked by both parties, opposed data centers locating here. Another factoid highlighted in the guide is that the maximum size allowed for a data center under Statesboro's 2026 data center ordinance is 50 acres. "The term 'data center' covers a wide range of facilities," notes one section of the guide. It mentions that a small data center, "about the size of a large room" is already located in Statesboro, reportedly helping speed internet service for businesses. But Project Camellia, the data center OpenAI announced in July it plans to build in neighboring Effingham County, would occupy a nearly 1,400-acre campus and use 3.2 gigawatts of electricity. So, 4AM Development LLC's proposed two-story, total 230,000-square-foot building on an almost 27-acre site on Burkhalter Road in the edge of Statesboro is between those extremes. With a set of high-voltage transmission lines already running parallel to one side of the triangular tract, the developers applied to Georgia Power for an up to 99-megawatt supply. Timelines of events The guidebook carries a detailed timeline for that project and the city's actions. On Aug. 18, the tract was rezoned from R-4 high-density residential to "O" for office by a 3-2 vote of City Council, including the mayor's tiebreaker. But the project also needs a special use permit, also requiring council approval, and that process is now being held up by a legal challenge filed by a group of citizens in Superior Court. A parallel timeline traces the Bulloch County Board of Commissioners' actions in regard to data center policy. This includes a moratorium on data centers in the county unincorporated area, in effect most of the year and now extended until Dec. 31. An outright ban was defeated by commissioners' 4-3 vote, including the chairman's tiebreaker, Sept. 1, and the commissioners are now naming an up to 21-citizen "working group" to study the issue. The county working group will be a completely different thing from the IVEC sessions. artigo.texto: Data center stocks remain under pressure after Korea IPO plunges 30% - Shares of cloud provider Elice Group dropped 30% during their market debut in South Korea. - Elice Group has been compared to CoreWeave, the U.S. neocloud at the center of last week's sell-off. - Concerns about overcapacity in computing power amid lackluster AI revenues are persisting. Data center stocks are being squeezed on Tuesday following a lackluster initial public offering overnight from a South Korean cloud company that has been compared to U.S. neocloud CoreWeave. Shares of Elice dropped 30% during their market debut overnight, as investors grow increasingly wary of artificial intelligence-dedicated computing power providers amid concerns about overcapacity. The bearish sentiment spilled into U.S. tech equities before some names clambered back into the green. CoreWeave shares are up 1.6% after dropping 4% just after market open Tuesday; Nebius shed about 1% while Iren was down about 4% in late morning trading. HSBC said in a Monday note that the troubles for the heavily levered CoreWeave are not going away. "Debt market woes and moderating LLM revenues are exacerbating structural concerns for neoclouds," HSBC analyst Abhishek Shukla wrote. Shukla has a reduce rating on CoreWeave with a price target of $39, implying 36.5% downside. Elice's IPO was small, having raised just $150 million, according to Reuters. Its market cap also equates to roughly $1.3 billion. The company provides a range of AI-related services, including cloud computing equipment, training libraries and application interfaces for businesses. Despite its size, investors are likely looking at it as a a signal of investor sentiment toward the AI build-out. Trouble for neoclouds, which some investors see as the weakest link in the emerging AI value chain, started earlier this month with less-than-stellar revenues reported by the private AI algorithm companies and pressure from higher interest rates. Frontier model Anthropic showed a deceleration in quarterly revenues, with sales dropping from 140% growth in the second quarter to 45% in the third. OpenAI also disappointed, reporting revenue that was $20 billion shy of what analysts expected, analyst Stephanie Roth at Wolfe said in a Sunday note. Profitability concerns for AI algorithm companies were the focus of a report last week from advisory firm Gartner predicting that 80% of neoclouds could cease independent operations by 2030. "Our research indicates that enterprise and consumer AI revenue will be insufficient to support profitable returns on all planned AI capital expenditures" between 2027 and 2030, Will Sommer, senior director analyst at Gartner, said. Gartner stood by its analysis in a Monday interview with CNBC. "At the moment, we have more compute capacity than we have demand, and we have a lot of the tokens and processing power being given away in freemium solutions," Gartner chief forecaster John Lovelock told CNBC. "Everyone in the AI race is running for a last-man standing position. Pretty much every market that Gartner is tracking in our AI race is likely to collapse down to a duopoly."

artigo.texto: Transmission grid fees in Belgium could increase by 92% for battery energy storage systems (BESS) and by 150% for offshore wind projects by 2035, according to a study by Aurora Energy Research examining the evolution of network tariffs and their economic implications for energy projects. The report, titled Transmission Grid Fees in Belgium: Outlook & Impact Assessment, was commissioned by Adaptogen Capital, BayWa r.e., Norther, Otary and Storm, amid regulatory changes affecting the costs of accessing and using Belgium's electricity transmission infrastructure. The analysis follows the publication of the tariff methodology for the 2028–2031 regulatory period by Belgium's energy regulator, CREG, ahead of transmission system operator Elia's expected publication of updated grid tariffs in 2027. Grid fees for batteries could reach €112/kW by 2035 One of the main changes examined in the study is the planned phase-out of the 10-year grid fee exemption for battery energy storage systems, a mechanism that has helped limit network costs for eligible storage projects. According to Aurora's central scenario, the combined effect of removing this exemption and rising overall network costs could result in a 92% increase in the total grid fee burden for a typical battery, reaching €112/kW by 2035. The study estimates that, without mitigation measures, average annual margins for battery storage projects could fall to €47/kW. Björn Hofman, Senior Associate, Advisory, at Aurora Energy Research, warned that rising grid fees could place additional pressure on the economics of battery storage projects and other grid-connected assets in Belgium. He noted that discount mechanisms are available, including incentives to avoid charging during peak hours and the potential introduction of voluntary flexible connection agreements. However, these measures are unlikely to fully offset the projected increase in network costs. Offshore wind faces a potential 150% increase The second major regulatory change identified by Aurora is the introduction of a capacity-based feed-in fee for electricity injected into the grid, which would add another cost component for renewable electricity generators. According to the analysis, Belgium's projected feed-in fees could reach €11/kW, exceeding the levels expected in neighbouring markets. Germany is preparing similar charges in the range of €4–7/kW, while Belgium has yet to announce comparable protections for existing projects or developments that have already committed investment. Aurora notes that Germany has announced a 20-year exemption for assets that reach a final investment decision (FID) before the new fee enters into force. The Netherlands is also expected to introduce an equivalent exemption to maintain comparable investment conditions across European markets. Belgium, by contrast, has not yet made a similar commitment to protect projects from changes to the tariff framework after investment decisions have been taken. This regulatory difference could affect the competitiveness of Belgian renewable energy projects relative to those in neighbouring countries. Industry representatives call for protection of existing investments Mathias Verkest, CEO of Otary, warned that allocating grid costs between electricity consumers and producers could have implications for final electricity prices and the financing conditions of new projects. He explained that developers may seek to pass additional costs on to consumers. Where this is not possible, higher network charges could instead translate into increased risk premiums, potentially raising the cost of financing new developments. Verkest therefore supported the introduction of grandfathering provisions to protect existing and upcoming projects, following the approach adopted in Germany and the Netherlands. Similarly, Christophe De Schryver, Executive Manager at Norther, stressed that investment in renewable electricity generation depends on a stable and predictable regulatory framework over long periods. He warned that introducing substantial new injection charges without protecting previously committed investments could undermine investor confidence and weaken Belgium's attractiveness for future energy investment. Aurora identifies measures to limit rising network costs The study outlines several measures that could help contain the increase in transmission charges, including alternative financing arrangements for part of the required grid investment, stimulating electricity demand to expand the tariff billing base, and stricter cost controls. For the remaining costs, Aurora recommends implementing grandfathering exemptions for existing and upcoming projects, maintaining discounts for avoiding consumption during peak periods, and extending flexible connection discounts to both voluntary and imposed agreements. The consultancy warns that, without regulatory action, higher network charges could delay investment decisions in storage and renewable electricity generation while increasing costs for electricity consumers. The report therefore identifies the evolution of transmission tariffs as a factor that could influence the profitability of BESS and offshore wind projects, financing conditions and the deployment of renewable energy capacity in Belgium over the coming decade.

artigo.texto: Expansão da inteligência artificial impulsiona investimentos em sistemas privados de energia, mas escassez de equipamentos e atrasos nas entregas desafiam o setor INFRAESTRUTURA DIGITAL Data centers apostam em energia própria e 38% devem ter geração independente até 2030 Por Redação A expansão da inteligência artificial e dos serviços de computação em nuvem está levando empresas de tecnologia a investir na produção própria de energia para abastecer seus data centers. A estratégia busca reduzir a dependência das redes elétricas convencionais e acelerar a implantação de novos empreendimentos. Segundo projeções da Bloom Energy, 38% dessas instalações deverão utilizar sistemas próprios de geração como principal fonte de energia até 2030. A mudança ocorre diante do aumento dos prazos para conexão à rede pública. Desde 2017, o intervalo entre a solicitação de acesso à energia e o início das operações comerciais cresceu aproximadamente 60%. Atualmente, a espera média supera 2.100 dias, o equivalente a quase seis anos, considerando projetos que pretendiam iniciar o fornecimento em 2025. Para contornar as limitações da infraestrutura elétrica, empresas responsáveis pela construção e operação de data centers estão adotando sistemas conhecidos como behind-the-meter (BTM), que permitem gerar energia diretamente no local de consumo, reduzindo a necessidade de conexão à rede pública. A Bloom Energy estima que aproximadamente 27% dos data centers poderão ser abastecidos integralmente por energia produzida em suas próprias instalações até 2030. A alternativa oferece maior autonomia energética e pode reduzir os riscos de atrasos na entrada em operação dos empreendimentos. Entretanto, o crescimento da demanda por esses sistemas criou novos desafios para o setor. Entrega de equipamentos pode levar seis anos A procura por turbinas a gás, transformadores e outros componentes necessários à geração de energia tem superado a capacidade de fornecimento dos fabricantes. De acordo com a consultoria Wood Mackenzie, os prazos de entrega de turbinas a gás já chegam a seis anos, ultrapassando as estimativas anteriores, que variavam entre dois e quatro anos. Com isso, a disponibilidade de equipamentos passou a influenciar diretamente o planejamento dos projetos. Além dos custos de produção, as empresas precisam considerar o tempo necessário para adquirir, instalar e colocar os sistemas em funcionamento. Outro desafio está na integração de diferentes tecnologias de geração em uma única estrutura, especialmente quando os equipamentos chegam em etapas distintas. Operação exige novas soluções tecnológicas A complexidade dos sistemas privados também está ampliando a demanda por empresas especializadas em operação e manutenção de infraestrutura energética. Entre as companhias que atuam nesse mercado estão a Kyuden Energy Partners, a Consolidated Asset Management Services (CAMS) e a Ethos Energy. A CAMS possui experiência em projetos que somam 70 gigawatts (GW) de capacidade de geração e concentra parte de sua atuação em soluções que utilizam gás natural e fontes renováveis. Já a Ethos Energy, com experiência na gestão de mais de 100 instalações e 40 GW de capacidade de geração, desenvolveu um centro de monitoramento remoto que utiliza inteligência artificial para acompanhar simultaneamente diferentes unidades produtoras de energia. A tecnologia permite identificar falhas, acompanhar o desempenho dos equipamentos e apoiar a manutenção das operações. Expansão dos data centers depende de planejamento A busca por independência energética representa uma mudança no modelo de implantação dos data centers. Em vez de aguardar exclusivamente a disponibilidade da rede pública, as empresas passam a incorporar a geração própria desde as etapas iniciais dos projetos. Essa transformação, entretanto, exige investimentos adicionais, equipes técnicas especializadas e maior coordenação entre fornecedores de equipamentos e operadores. Com o crescimento da demanda por processamento de dados e inteligência artificial, a capacidade de garantir fornecimento contínuo de energia deverá permanecer entre os principais fatores de competitividade do setor. Embora a geração própria ajude a superar as restrições de conexão elétrica, a disponibilidade de equipamentos e a complexidade operacional continuam condicionando o ritmo de expansão da infraestrutura digital.

artigo.texto: Datagroup data center in Kyiv ceases operations after Russian attack Ukrinform A missile strike disabled equipment at Datagroup’s data center in Kyiv, making restoration impossible. According to Ukrinform, the company’s press service announced the shutdown in a post on Facebook. “As a result of the overnight ballistic attack, the equipment and infrastructure of the Datagroup data center were completely disabled. Unfortunately, its restoration and further operation are impossible,” the statement said. The company reported that none of its employees were injured. Client services are currently being provided from backup sites. As reported, one person was killed and eight were injured in Kyiv following the overnight attack by Russian forces.

artigo.texto: Crédito de carbono de alta qualidade sobe 75%, diz MSCI AGÊNCIA DE COMUNICAÇÃO Conteúdo de responsabilidade da empresa 7 de outubro de 2026 Os créditos de carbono classificados como de alta qualidade pela MSCI tiveram valorização de 75% em 12 meses e chegaram a US$ 14 por tonelada, enquanto os de menor qualidade são negociados abaixo de US$ 2. Os dados foram apresentados por Guy Turner, diretor-geral da área de mercados de carbono da companhia, durante a Climate Week NYC, realizada em Nova York em setembro de 2026, e indicam avanços em três frentes: ampliação dos sistemas regulados, diferenciação de preços por qualidade e mobilização de capital. Segundo a apresentação, foram registrados US$ 5,5 bilhões em investimentos em contratos futuros e projetos, distribuídos em mais de 200 transações, com um quarto dos recursos destinado a iniciativas de remoção de carbono. Os contratos de compra antecipada de créditos de restauração da natureza monitorados pela MSCI, com entrega prevista para 2035, alcançaram US$ 45 por tonelada, alta de 10% em relação ao primeiro semestre de 2025. Sistemas regulados ganham escala No período analisado, a União Europeia passou a incluir integralmente as emissões do transporte marítimo no comércio de emissões do bloco, o EU ETS. A Indonésia avançou em normas para dar clareza e amplitude às negociações de carbono, e o México se comprometeu a lançar um sistema nacional em 2027, com cobertura de 40% de suas emissões. Na Ásia, a Índia colocou em operação um portal para administrar registros e transações do período de conformidade de 2025 a 2027, que abrange 740 entidades e mais de 700 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono equivalente (CO₂e). O Vietnã contabilizou as primeiras operações de seu sistema, referentes ao ciclo 2025 a 2026, e o Japão tornou obrigatório o GX-ETS, que cobre 40% das emissões nacionais de gases de efeito estufa e reúne entre 300 e 400 empresas. Para Laura Albuquerque, co-CEO da Future Climate e membra do Comitê da Ambição Net Zero da Rede Brasileira do Pacto Global da ONU, durante cerca de duas décadas a defesa desses mercados se apoiou em estudos sobre seu potencial para reduzir o custo de cumprimento das metas climáticas. “A lógica econômica permanece: direcionar recursos para oportunidades de redução e remoção de emissões que permitam alcançar essas metas com maior eficiência. A diferença é que, hoje, a experiência acumulada oferece dados concretos para orientar decisões de política pública e investimento”, afirma. Demanda corporativa e integridade No segmento de créditos, os números da MSCI mostram atividade consistente. Cerca de 4 mil empresas definiram metas pela Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi), o equivalente a 4 bilhões de toneladas de emissões, e um quarto delas assumiu compromissos de emissões líquidas zero (net zero). Em 12 meses, mil novos projetos foram registrados, outros 1.150 entraram na carteira em preparação e empresas aposentaram créditos provenientes de 2.850 projetos. A projeção da MSCI indica que as aposentadorias globais de 2026 devem ficar próximas do volume de 2025, em torno de 200 milhões de toneladas. Na leitura da co-CEO, o sinal mais relevante está na distância de valor entre projetos, que torna a avaliação de qualidade parte central da decisão de alocação de recursos para compradores e investidores. A executiva observa ainda que a convergência em torno dos Core Carbon Principles, definidos pelo Conselho de Integridade para o Mercado Voluntário de Carbono (ICVCM, na sigla em inglês), cria uma linguagem comum sobre integridade, mas exige que preços e financiamento reconheçam os custos de desenvolvimento. Capital antes da receita Para as desenvolvedoras, o cenário evidencia a necessidade de recursos antes da geração de receita. “Projetos exigem recursos para estruturação, implantação, monitoramento, ratings para a verificação ao longo de anos. A valorização dos créditos de qualidade precisa se traduzir em condições de financiamento que permitam produzir essa oferta”, diz Laura. Segundo ela, os contratos futuros podem contribuir nesse processo ao conectar a demanda dos compradores ao ciclo de investimento dos projetos. O Brasil tem diferentes vias de demanda em construção: o mercado voluntário; o Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões (SBCE), instituído pela Lei nº 15.042, de 11 de dezembro de 2024, com os Certificados de Redução ou Remoção Verificada de Emissões (CRVEs); os mecanismos do Artigo 6 do Acordo de Paris; o programa de combustível sustentável de aviação (SAF, na sigla em inglês) previsto na Lei nº 14.993; e o Esquema de Compensação e Redução de Carbono para a Aviação Internacional (Corsia). Na avaliação da executiva, são caminhos com regras e escalas distintas, que precisam ser considerados na estruturação dos investimentos. Laura pondera que preços, investimentos e aposentadorias não substituem a mensuração dos resultados climáticos, embora demonstrem uma base observável de atividade econômica, demanda e alocação de capital. “Para o país, a oportunidade está em usar essa experiência para desenvolver um mercado capaz de financiar projetos de qualidade, e o próximo avanço dependerá de transformar os sinais de demanda em capital disponível para quem entrega reduções e remoções verificáveis”, conclui a executiva. artigo.texto: Trending For over an hour, Rachel Wallace, Democrat candidate for the 9th congressional seat, answered questions from the audience at a town hall held this week at Lycoming College. Although she admitted that not everyone might not agree with what she was saying, her goal was not to over promise and then not be able to deliver results on those promises. Right out of the gate, Wallace got down in the weeds about what are some of the key issues in the election where she is facing off against Republican Congressman Dan Mueser, who has been in office since 2019. Although she was critical of Mueser for not being a resident of the district he represents-which is legal in Pennsylvania-in her opening remarks, Wallace particularly criticized the fact that her opponent voted for last year's budget bill, which Republicans have called the "One Big Beautiful Bill", and how it has affected residents of the district. "Dan Meuser voted for a budget bill that is an absolute disaster for our part of Pennsylvania. It cut food assistance for more than 8,000 people in our communities here. It cut health insurance for nearly 30,000 people in our district, essentially defunding our hospitals and our nursing homes. It tried to take away local control on AI data centers, and it gave an $80 billion tax break to AI data center developers," Wallace said. Seeing his vote spurred her on to run for his seat in the House of Representatives. She continued by outlining the three things she is focusing on in her campaign. The first, she said, is lowering costs. "Will you raise your hand if you feel good about how much everything costs right now? You're not that blessed. Me neither. At the grocery store, at the gas pump, on our utility bills, at the pharmacy, looking at our healthcare premiums and deductibles going up next year, everything costs too much, and Dan Meuser has voted in support of all of those policies, from the budget bill...through the war in Iran, which has been a disaster...to tariffs that are hurting us and our farmers and our local employers. So there is a lot to be done in Congress next year to lower costs, and that needs to be at the top of priority list because people here are struggling," Wallace said. "The one thing I want to underline here is home heating oil, since last year, has gone up 75 percent, and one-third of our district heats their homes with home heating oil. So this is not an election about national politics. This is not an election about how we're feeling about the country. This is an election about how we're feeling about heating our own homes, and it is going to be a crisis. It is going to be scary here in Pennsylvania, and we're going to need to take fast, short-term action because it is not going to be pretty if we don't. So we need to lower costs," she said. Citing stories that Mueser has doubled his wealth since he got in office, Wallace stated that her second priority if elected would be to root out corruption and fraud in Washington. "Don't you think it's long past time that we ban congressional stock trading," she asked the audience who responded by applauding loudly. Her third and final priority, she said, would be to bring people to solve local problems. She highlighted the problems volunteer fire companies are having with the cost of equipment increasing. "They fight fires, they recruit other firefighters, and they sell chicken barbecues to try to raise a million dollars to buy a fire truck. And many of our fire departments do all of those things for free. It is a tremendous service. It says something about Pennsylvania and who we are that our communities do that for free," she said. She noted that the amount of funding available to help with buying firefighting equipment has not changed in the past 20 years. "Years ago, it cost 200, 300,000 to buy a truck. Now it's over a million dollars, but the pot hasn't changed. And so this is what I'm talking about when I talk about how do we solve our local problems. We've got to get that fund up so that it meets the needs of our firefighters," she said. Wallace also cited AI data centers as another huge issue, with seven of the 12 counties in the district she's seeking to represent "somewhere in the pipeline of at least one, if not more AI data centers." "I went to Muncy, (I) sat down in Lebanon, in Frackville. I've been with our farmers in central Pennsylvania who are fighting losing their land for power lines for a data center in Allenwood...We just need to take a pause here. We need a short pause so that our local and county ordinances can catch up, so that Harrisburg can catch up. They got some tax breaks they've got to repeal last time I checked, and so that Washington can catch up, and we can get everybody's house in order before we move forward here, because things are happening incredibly fast, and our communities are being asked to pay the cost. When big tech and AI developers, they're the ones who should pay the cost, not us," she said. She also feels the country needs to slow down in developing AI. "I think we are moving very fast to a world that we do not understand where we are going. We do not understand what AI is capable of. We do not understand what it means for our economy. We don't understand what these data centers are going to do to our water, to our quality of life. We need to slow down and make sure that we have answers," she said. Questions from the audience ran the gamut from the rising costs of healthcare to a critique of the administration to whether she would agree to abolishing ICE. artigo.texto: Trontek Electronics will unveil its 5 MWh EKOM containerised Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) at The Battery Show India 2026, marking the company’s entry into large-scale energy storage for industrial and utility applications. The company will showcase the system at Stall C16, Hall 18, at India Expo Mart & Centre in Greater Noida from October 22 to 24, 2026. The launch extends Trontek’s battery technology and manufacturing experience into applications beyond electric mobility. The EKOM platform is designed to address larger energy storage requirements as India expands its renewable energy capacity and seeks greater flexibility in power management. Battery energy storage systems can help manage variations in electricity supply and demand, support renewable energy integration and improve the use of stored power across industrial and utility operations. Trontek has more than two decades of experience in battery technology and manufacturing. The company currently has an active manufacturing capacity of 3 GWh and plans to increase this to 12 GWh by 2028. The proposed expansion is intended to support its growing presence across mobility, distributed energy and large-scale storage markets. Samrath S Kochar, Founder and CEO of Trontek, said energy storage would play an important role in meeting India’s future power requirements. He said the EKOM launch would extend the company’s battery expertise into large-scale applications while supporting the development of domestic energy storage capabilities. At the exhibition, Trontek will present its products across three business areas: electric mobility, energy storage, and power and critical infrastructure solutions. Its electric mobility portfolio includes battery solutions for two-wheelers, three-wheelers and other mobility applications. Under energy storage, the company offers POWERCUBE for residential applications, NOVARA for commercial facilities and EKOM for industrial and utility-scale requirements. The newly unveiled 5 MWh system will form part of the EKOM range. The company will also display inverter and solar solutions for distributed energy applications, along with battery systems for telecom infrastructure and backup power requirements. Trontek’s expanded portfolio reflects its move towards a broader energy technology business, supported by Indian engineering and manufacturing capabilities. The company aims to develop products for residential, commercial, industrial and utility customers as demand for energy storage increases. The EKOM unveiling marks a new phase in Trontek’s business development as it seeks to build manufacturing scale and expand its participation in India’s changing energy landscape. Its planned capacity increase to 12 GWh by 2028 forms a key part of this strategy.

artigo.texto: - Nigeria has commissioned a 1MW solar mini grid with 2.4MWh of battery energy storage in Tallasse, Balanga Local Government Area, Gombe State, serving 6,028 active connections. - The facility powers productive-use businesses, including electric groundnut oil processing, rice milling, flour grinding and electric tricycles, linking clean electricity directly to rural enterprise and job creation. - The project forms part of the US$750 million Distributed Access through Renewable Energy Scale-up programme, which targets 1,350 mini grids and electricity access for 17.5 million Nigerians. The Federal Government, through the Rural Electrification Agency, has commissioned the Tallasse solar mini grid in partnership with the Gombe State Government and a private sector developer. The facility combines 1MW of solar generation with a 2.4MWh battery energy storage system to improve supply reliability for households, commercial users and productive enterprises. The project serves 6,028 connections, comprising 5,929 residential customers, 84 commercial connections and 15 dedicated productive-use nodes. Its design moves beyond household electrification by supporting agricultural processing, local logistics and small business growth in a community that had lacked a national grid connection for more than 17 years. The Tallasse installation includes electric groundnut oil processing equipment, modular rice milling machinery, flour grinding facilities and electric tricycles. These assets are intended to help farmers process produce locally, reduce operating costs, create income opportunities and strengthen rural value chains. Officials said the battery storage component is central to the economic case for the project, because reliable power is required to sustain milling, processing and transport activities. The approach reflects a wider policy shift from measuring installed capacity alone to measuring the commercial and social value created by electricity access. The Tallasse project is being delivered under the Distributed Access through Renewable Energy Scale-up programme, a US$750 million World Bank funded initiative managed by the Rural Electrification Agency. DARES aims to provide new or improved electricity access to more than 17.5 million Nigerians through private sector led distributed renewable energy solutions. The programme targets the deployment of 1,350 mini grids, including 250 interconnected systems, alongside more than one million standalone solar home systems. It is also expected to support more than 237,000 micro, small and medium enterprises and replace more than 280,000 polluting petrol and diesel generator sets. DARES is designed to mobilise more than US$1 billion in private capital, with additional parallel financing from development partners, including US$100 million from the Global Energy Alliance for People and Planet and US$200 million from the Japan International Cooperation Agency. The commissioning of the Tallasse facility coincided with the flag-off of four interconnected mini grid projects in Dukku, Bajoga, Kumo and Kaltungo, with a combined planned capacity of 16MW. The wider Gombe programme is expected to deepen off-grid electricity penetration and support commercial activity across the state. The Rural Electrification Agency said the initiative forms part of a broader national strategy to expand mini grids, embedded generation, solar home systems and dedicated clean power solutions for universities, markets and agricultural clusters. The agency is also working to unlock domestic and international financing to accelerate private sector participation in Nigeria’s distributed energy market. artigo.texto: AI’s GPU Refresh Cycle Is Becoming a Stranded-Capital Problem Key Highlights - Proactive lifecycle planning involves designing infrastructure that accommodates hardware upgrades and facilitates easy disassembly and component reuse. - Effective disposition strategies include asset traceability, secure sanitization, and compliance with international trade and data security regulations. - Market timing and operational readiness are critical; continuous assessment of asset value ensures hardware is sold or repurposed at optimal moments. - Design-for-recycling principles should be integrated into hardware architecture, emphasizing modularity and material recoverability to extend equipment lifespan. - Organizational alignment at the executive level is essential to prevent stranded capital and maximize the return on AI hardware investments. The AI infrastructure buildout is measured in gigawatts and successive generations of accelerators. But as operators bring new compute capacity online, a less visible question is gaining financial urgency: What happens to GPU systems when their first production assignment ends? For hardware that remains functional but no longer meets the performance or efficiency requirements of a leading-edge AI cluster, retirement need not mean obsolescence. Equipment may be redeployed, resold, harvested for components or processed to recover materials. The outcome depends on decisions made long before a system leaves its rack. That was the central argument advanced by Linda Li, chief strategy officer of Re-Teck and its parent company, Li Tong Group, in the latest onsite installment of the DCF Show podcast, hosted by Data Center Frontier Contributing Editor Doug Black at the DCF Trends Summit 2026 in Northern Virginia. For Li, the acceleration of GPU refresh cycles is making lifecycle management a question of capital preservation, facilities design and executive governance—not merely IT asset disposition. Plan for the Exit Before the Equipment Arrives Li draws on more than two decades of her company’s work in reverse supply chains for consumer electronics and telecommunications equipment. Both sectors have managed rapid generational shifts without assuming that every displaced device had exhausted its useful life. “We are dealing with a totally different organism,” she said, describing the combination of rapid accelerator iterations, rising rack power density and increasingly sophisticated thermal requirements. The response, in her view, has two levels. The first is physical infrastructure: facilities designed to accommodate successive generations of servers without extensive reconstruction. Scalable power distribution, adaptable raceways, modular rack systems and high-capacity air and liquid cooling can create room for hardware transitions that may arrive sooner than originally expected. The second is the network of partners and contracts around the assets. Rather than recruiting an IT asset disposition (ITAD) provider when a refresh is imminent, operators should assess processing capacity, certification, geographic reach and compliance during procurement. Li pointed to the telecom industry's transition from 3G to 4G and 5G. In that environment, she explained, the contract to supply next-generation network equipment can also obligate the supplier to take back and decommission what is being replaced. She believes AI infrastructure purchasing should incorporate similar provisions. “What kind of planning needs to be done and when it needs to be done” are inseparable questions, Li said. “You can't answer one without the other.” Finding the Next Life of a GPU The appropriate disposition pathway cannot be fixed years in advance. Li described a framework established when equipment enters service, with final decisions made at retirement as its condition, market demand and operational needs become clearer. The first consideration is remaining capability. An accelerator that is no longer economical for frontier model training may still be useful for inference, enterprise AI or academic research. For large operators with multiple sites or classes of workload, moving the equipment internally can preserve more value than selling it—and can reduce the need for additional purchases. That requires identifying suitable destinations and approving transfers in advance. Otherwise, reusable systems can become stranded in the organizational handoff. The second consideration is component-level economics. Demand for an entire previous-generation server may soften even while individual GPUs, memory modules or specialized networking cards retain strong market value. Recovering those parts requires an engineering understanding of the equipment’s design and assembly, not just the ability to transport and recycle a chassis. Harvested components can also become internal service spares. That approach may help operators maintain installed systems while reducing lead times and dependence on replacement-parts supply chains. For Li, the relevant unit of value is not always a complete server; sometimes it is the individual component that can serve another application. Her third consideration—one she said should actually rank first—is risk. Data security, access controls, regulatory obligations and environmental rules can override an otherwise attractive commercial opportunity. The fourth is material recovery: recovering and refining valuable inputs when equipment or components cannot be economically reused. Together, the four factors place resale and recycling within a broader decision process. The aim is not simply to maximize the price of decommissioned hardware, but to retain value without compromising security or compliance. The Resale Market Won’t Wait Hardware value is also time-sensitive. During the conversation, Black relayed an anecdote heard earlier at the summit about H100 accelerators attracting unusually high prices in secondary markets. Li cautioned against assuming such conditions would last.

artigo.texto: 0 a 100% na bateria do iPhone 18 Pro: a pegadinha O iPhone 18 Pro finalmente carrega rápido de verdade, mas a Apple jogou bem baixo um detalhe na hora da compra. A fonte de energia do smartphone dobrável iPhone Duo, primeiro aparelho da Apple na categoria teve novos detalhes técnicos revelados. Um deles envolve a bateria do aparelho e uma comparação inevitável com dispositivos rivais. Ao todo, o conjunto de baterias do iPhone Duo tem 4.883 mAh. Outro dobrável com o mesmo formato de tela, chamado de passaporte, é o Galaxy Z Fold 8 da Samsung — que fica apenas logo atrás, com 4.800 mAh de bateria. Nesse quesito, a Maçã vence também o iPhone 18 Pro (4.288 mAh) e o dobrável Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold (4.806 mAh), mas fica atrás do Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra (5.000 mAh) e do Motorola Razr Fold (6.000 mAh). Porém, a quantidade de mAh não significa necessariamente que a bateria de um dispositivo dura mais em qualquer condição. Esse valor envolve a capacidade da fonte de bateria em armazenamento de energia (medido em mAh, ou miliamperes-hora), mas o consumo depende de outros componentes do hardware e otimização do sistema operacional. Mais detalhes do iPhone Duo A Apple não costuma detalhar todas as especificações dos seus celulares, incluindo a quantidade de RAM e o tamanho da bateria. Porém, desta vez ele acabou fazendo isso de forma acidental. Os valores foram revelados em documentos submetidos pela empresa no EPREL, um órgão regulador da União Europeia que obriga a divulgação desses dados para eletrônicos de consumo. Como aponta o Tom’s Guide ao analisar o documento, outros detalhes revelados pela submissão incluem detalhes como: - a certificação IP68 de resistência contra água e poeira; - a duração garantida de 1.000 ciclos de recarga para a bateria (ou seja, para manter ao menos 80% da capacidade total); - a durabilidade de 140 quedas em um teste de resistência até quebrar (quando fechado) e somente 35 quedas (no modo aberto); - uma resistência contra riscos na tela parecida com a do iPhone 18 Pro Max no display externo; - um grau de reparabilidade (facilidade e possibilidade de conserto) de 2.65, número inferior aos rivais da Samsung e ao iPhone 18 Pro Max. Por que o iPhone Duo só está com previsão de entrega de fevereiro de 2027 no Brasil? Entenda nesta matéria! /Com informações de Tom’s Guide.

artigo.texto: EPRI Research: Li-Ion Battery Storage Failure Risk Down 98% Since 2018 As battery storage deployment accelerates across the U.S., a new report by the Electric Power Research Institute highlights that safety performance is significantly improving in newer systems than in vintage lithium-ion battery energy storage system (BESS) designs. According to EPRI’s “Risk Factors and Failure Statistics of Lithium-Ion BESS” white paper within its Battery Energy Storage System Failure Incident Database, annual BESS failures per deployed GWh declined 98% between 2018 and 2025. The analysis found that BESS safety risk overall is comparable to oil-filled transformers, which reportedly maintain a 0.1% annual failure rate as a long-established power grid technology. EPRI attributes these lessons learned from early failures that caused destructive fires to having been incorporated into the latest designs and best practices. The institute explained that some of its incident research dates back to 2011. Still, drawing on more than a decade of cumulative incident data, the institute urges operators to conduct safety reviews and retrofits for early-vintage systems to mitigate fire risks. These concerns are underscored by previous incidents at high-profile facilities. The fires at Moss Landing, Morris and Surprise Vistra Corp.’s battery energy storage facility at the Moss Landing Power Plant in Monterey County, California, serves as an early example of these early-vintage risks. A major lithium-ion battery fire in January 2025 damaged over half of the site’s 300-MW system. The Moss Landing facility suffered a second fire in September 2026 due to leftover, damaged batteries that reignited during ongoing cleanup efforts. In 2021, another major fire incident took place at the Superior Battery Inc. warehouse in Morris, Illinois, which contained roughly 180,000 to 200,000 pounds of lithium batteries. While the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency conducted extensive air quality testing around the incident, investigators determined that the blaze was triggered by a water reaction from a severe roof leak. Rainwater reportedly dripped onto the batteries, sparking an initial reaction. Before those disasters, a thermal runaway event in Surprise, Arizona, severely injured eight firefighters in 2019. An internal cell defect within the utility-sized lithium batteries used on-site for storage and distribution of solar energy at the APS McMicken substation triggered the failure, according to an Arizona Public Service analysis. As these batteries fail, technical safety flaws, such as escaping gases, create intense and potentially devastating fire dangers to utility-scale BESS made up of lithium-ion chemistry. BESS advancements driving down failure rates All of these incidents occurred during the period of EPRI’s research, which highlights that while the rate of battery storage failures is becoming less frequent relative to massive-scale deployment, they can still be severe. EPRI noted that the 2019 BESS failure incident in Arizona was part of a wider BESS safety research effort, initiated to inform energy storage industry stakeholders and the public. Residential energy storage system failures were not tracked in this research. Managing these risks, however, remains a critical focus as BESS installations accelerate nationwide, driven by utilities dealing with grid constraints and the growing power demands of AI data centers. Currently in the U.S., installed capacity has passed 52 GW and has grown at an average rate of 70% per year over the last three years, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. Lakshmi Srinivasan, principal team lead of Energy Storage at EPRI, told EnergyTech that key aspects evaluated that weren’t known before include statistical analysis on the impact of indoor versus outdoor BESS architecture. Srinivasan noted that the data “demonstrates that modularization and spacing can limit the amount of a system that is damaged in an incident, also limiting first response needs and environmental and public health impacts.” These latest BESS advances have reportedly yielded major benefits in California, where utility-scale storage capacity grew to 13 GW by the end of 2024. According to EPRI, this has directly reduced the state's reliance on “Flex Alerts,” which are voluntary calls for residents to reduce consumption during peak demand periods, typically on hot summer days. “The number of Flex Alerts has dropped to zero (in 2023 and 2024) from 11 in 2022, due to the use of energy storage to reduce supply constraints,” said Srinivasan. Safely scaling future storage deployments EPRI aims to help power operators apply these standards to accelerate large-scale renewable integration. This guidance is particularly critical as operators navigate thermal risks for lithium-ion BESS across various project types, including behind-the-meter installations. To mitigate these risks, Srinivasan explained that conducting safety analyses of older systems can “help ensure the latest safety designs and practices are being implemented for all systems operating today.” While safety improvements are a continuous process, Srinivasan emphasized that dedicated research and development efforts are actively reducing risks in both existing and new BESS deployments. These advancements ultimately aim to deliver tangible benefits to the grid and local communities. “These benefits include supporting grid flexibility, reliability and resilience through applications such as renewable integration and peak demand reduction,” she added. Although lithium-ion remains a dominant mix for energy storage due to its high energy density and quick discharge, the industry is actively seeking alternatives to mitigate foreign supply chain risks and thermal safety concerns. artigo.texto: A China está a intensificar os investimentos no armazenamento de energia e na conservação dos ecossistemas, procurando conciliar a transição energética com a proteção ambiental. As duas prioridades foram destacadas em iniciativas divulgadas pela agência estatal Xinhua. Durante a Conferência Mundial de Armazenamento de Energia, realizada em Ningde, foram apresentados dados que atribuem à China 56% da expansão mundial da capacidade de armazenamento em baterias em 2025. No primeiro semestre de 2026, a produção chinesa de baterias destinadas a este setor ultrapassou 420 GWh, mais 110% do que no período homólogo. Paralelamente, o Presidente Xi Jinping defendeu o reforço da conservação ecológica durante uma visita à Mongólia Interior. Na reserva natural do lago Huangqihai, destacou a importância da recuperação das zonas húmidas, da proteção da biodiversidade e do cumprimento da legislação ambiental. A estratégia inclui ainda novas inspeções ambientais e a aplicação do Código Ecológico e Ambiental, em vigor desde agosto. Apesar dos progressos anunciados, persistem desafios relacionados com os custos das tecnologias, a fiscalização e a sustentabilidade dos resultados a longo prazo.

artigo.texto: Beyond Colossus: 5C Advances $575M Memphis AI Factory Expansion Key Highlights - 5C Data Centers is converting a former Fred's distribution complex in Memphis into a high-density AI computing facility, with a $575 million fourth-phase construction permit application. - 5C plans to expand available power at MEM01 from approximately 20 MW to 84 MW, using fuel cell technology to supply additional capacity rather than relying on a corresponding increase in utility power. - The project's announced AI architecture includes NVIDIA GB200 and newer GB300 NVL72 systems, liquid cooling, high-bandwidth networking and integrated storage to support large-scale AI training and inference. - Memphis is considering a data center moratorium and new zoning standards while conducting a 90-day policy review addressing electricity demand, water resources, air quality and community impacts. - 5C has secured more than $1.4 billion in financing for its North American AI infrastructure platform, supporting development in Memphis and other markets as questions remain about execution, infrastructure capacity and local economic benefits. Memphis has emerged as a major center of AI infrastructure development, driven largely by the extraordinary scale of xAI's Colossus supercomputing operations. But the city's growing AI computing market extends beyond Elon Musk's flagship project. At the former headquarters and distribution complex of discount retailer Fred's, 5C Data Centers is developing another substantial AI computing facility, combining industrial adaptive reuse with a phased expansion strategy and plans for behind-the-meter power generation. On October 6, 2026, a $575 million commercial alteration permit application was filed for the fourth phase of 5C's MEM01 data center at 4300 Getwell Road. The application covers approximately 504,000 square feet of the property's 1.1 million-square-foot building, representing the largest construction phase yet proposed at the site. MEM01 is already operating. According to September reporting from The Daily Memphian, 5C had established operations in approximately 200,000 square feet of the former Fred's property, leaving substantial additional space available for conversion. The latest permit application marks a significant escalation in the scope of the development. The expansion also introduces a major new element to 5C's power strategy. On October 11, 5C Group Chief Revenue Officer Brad Nimri told The Daily Memphian that the company plans to increase available power at MEM01 from approximately 20 MW to 84 MW over the next six months, using fuel cell technology to supply the additional capacity rather than relying on a corresponding increase in electricity from Memphis Light, Gas and Water (MLGW). Like Colossus, which began with the conversion of a former Electrolux manufacturing facility, 5C's development reflects the growing role of industrial adaptive reuse in AI infrastructure. The projects differ considerably in scale and their approaches to on-site power generation, but both illustrate the challenge of transforming existing industrial properties into high-density computing environments with substantial electrical requirements. As Memphis considers tighter oversight of data center development, 5C's expansion underscores a broader industry challenge: bringing new AI computing capacity online while navigating power constraints, regulatory scrutiny and mounting concerns over the environmental and community impacts of large-scale infrastructure. From Retail Distribution to AI Infrastructure The MEM01 development occupies a property with a long history in Memphis commerce. Fred's operated hundreds of discount retail and pharmacy locations across the southeastern United States before declaring bankruptcy in 2019. Its former headquarters and distribution complex on Getwell Road, near Memphis International Airport, served as a major logistics hub for the regional retail chain. In June 2026, 5C acquired the 1.1 million-square-foot complex and its approximately 58-acre property from Olymbec USA for $25 million, according to Shelby County property records, securing ownership of a site where data center construction and infrastructure modifications were already underway. The project's development history reflects a rapid escalation in scale. Plans submitted in late 2024 and reported in 2025 contemplated converting the property into a data center supporting an initial 15-MW IT load. An April 2025 construction permit, valued at $25 million, described a more limited initial deployment of 2.5 MW, together with infrastructure designed to support future expansion. Additional permits issued in early 2026 included $100 million for interior construction and $8 million for accessory structures. The October phase-four application, valued at $575 million, represents a substantial increase in the scope of planned construction, although permit valuations do not necessarily represent completed capital expenditures or the project's total investment. The expansion also illustrates the distinction between announced capacity and operational computing infrastructure. According to 5C's published data center portfolio, the Memphis facility's 20-MW capacity for 2026 is fully committed, with additional capacity listed for subsequent years. That commercial designation does not establish how much electrical capacity has been energized or how much IT load is currently supporting customer workloads. The company has not publicly disclosed a complete inventory of installed and operating AI accelerators at the site, leaving the precise scale of its commissioned computing infrastructure unclear.
