artigo.texto: From robotic gloves to safer batteries, CUHK puts research to work Summary CUHK researchers are developing technologies for use beyond the laboratory in Hong Kong. A robotic glove uses air-powered artificial muscles to help stroke survivors and people with spinal injuries open and close their hands for rehabilitation and daily tasks. Researchers also developed a sulfur-based flow battery with water-based electrolytes, while a startup is commercializing the technology for solar installations, electric vehicle charging and artificial intelligence data centers. Key Facts - The robotic glove was developed by a team led by Raymond Tong, a CUHK professor of biomedical engineering. - The glove can respond to signals associated with a patient’s intention to move, and clinical trials involve people with strokes and spinal injuries. - The sulfur-based flow battery was developed by a team led by CUHK professor Yi-Chun Lu, and Luquos Energy has installed a demonstration system on campus. - Luquos Energy estimates that the battery’s electrolyte could remain usable for more than 15 years, although that is not a verified real-world service life. - The company is building a production line in Shenzhen and has developed battery systems for projects including electric vehicle charging. Wearable device helps patients regain hand movement as university-developed battery technology targets energy storage HONG KONG — From helping stroke patients perform everyday tasks to developing safer ways to store electricity, researchers at The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) are developing technologies for use beyond the laboratory. During a visit to the university on Sept. 1, a reporter tried on a robotic glove that moved the fingers with noticeable force, but without jerking them. For stroke survivors who cannot move their hands, that movement could help them do something as ordinary as holding a spoon or picking up a phone. The device uses air-powered artificial muscles developed by a team led by Raymond Tong, a professor of biomedical engineering at CUHK. Unlike conventional motor-driven rehabilitation equipment, the lightweight system uses a small pump to help patients open and close their hands. “Nowadays, you can see those exoskeletons are very rigid. They are very heavy,” Tong said, inviting the reporter to try the device. Patients can use it both for rehabilitation exercises and everyday tasks, including gripping objects, writing and eating. Tong said the system can also respond to signals associated with a patient’s intention to move. “They can use the brain to control it,” he said. “I just imagine moving the hand and the hand moves.” Tong said the team was conducting clinical trials involving people with strokes and spinal injuries, with plans to expand use in hospitals. He also described work with children who have difficulty standing or walking. Elsewhere on campus, researchers showed a battery designed to reduce the fire risks associated with conventional lithium-ion batteries. Developed by a team led by CUHK professor Yi-Chun Lu, the sulfur-based flow battery uses water-based electrolytes. Luquos Energy, a startup founded to commercialize the research, has installed a demonstration system on campus. “This is a completely different technology compared to lithium,” said Luquos Energy CEO Simon Zengyue Wang. “We do not use lithium. We use sulfur.” “The battery electrolyte is water, so it never catches fire,” Wang said. The company estimates its electrolyte could remain usable for more than 15 years, although that is not a verified real-world service life. Wang said the technology could serve solar installations and power-hungry artificial intelligence data centers because it can discharge electricity for “over eight hours, even 12 hours, even longer.” He said Luquos Energy was building a production line in Shenzhen and had already developed battery systems for projects including electric vehicle charging. artigo.texto: The European Commission has selected 77 projects to receive funding under the Innovation Fund call for proposals announced in December 2025. The total amount of funding is €3.4 billion, drawn from revenues generated by the European Union Emissions Trading Scheme (EU ETS). These projects come from various EU countries and span a range of sectors – from energy-intensive industries and ‘green’ energy to reducing the use of fossil fuels in aviation and shipping. This was reported by the European Commission. The spectrum of decarbonisation The winning projects span 23 countries in the European Economic Area. The list includes technologies of various types and scales. These include projects in the following sectors: - energy-intensive sectors — steel, cement and chemicals, as well as the production of advanced decarbonised fuels; - manufacturing – this refers to equipment in the clean technology sector. Specifically, this includes heat pumps and electric vehicle batteries, as well as critical raw materials; - renewable energy – the use of wind, solar and hydro power; - mobility – reducing the use of fossil fuels in aviation, road transport and maritime transport. The cumulative environmental impact of implementing all 77 projects is a reduction in greenhouse gas emissions of 290 million tonnes over the first ten years. This is equivalent to a reduction in CO₂ emissions of approximately one tonne every second for a decade. "These projects demonstrate that European innovators are turning climate ambitions into industrial leadership. By reinvesting revenue from the EU Emissions Trading System into clean technologies, the Innovation Fund is helping companies enter the market, reduce emissions and strengthen Europe’s competitiveness,” emphasised Wopke Hoekstra, the European Commissioner for Climate Action. The winners of the competition were selected across five categories: Large-scale general decarbonisation – 12 projects totalling €1.58 billion. The funding will be directed towards low-carbon fuels and emissions management in industry, particularly in the ferrous metallurgy and chemical sectors. General medium-scale decarbonisation – 17 projects totalling €458 million. This group includes projects relating to chemical products, oil refineries, the maritime sector, glass, ceramics and building materials, cement and lime, bioenergy, cast iron and steel, as well as hydrogen. General small-scale decarbonisation – 20 projects totalling €124 million. The projects presented here are from the critical raw materials processing sector, the pulp and paper industry, the construction sector, oil refining, the chemical and hydrogen industries, and so on. Clean technology manufacturing – 12 projects worth €895 million aimed at the production of solar panels, batteries for electric cars, heat pumps, electrolysers and rare-earth magnets. Pilot projects – 16 initiatives totalling €394 million. In addition, 84 projects, although they did not receive funding, did pass the evaluation process. This may therefore help them to secure funding for their implementation from other sources – whether private or public. It should be noted that Ukraine’s National Emissions Trading System has not yet been approved. There is currently one ministerial bill and three parliamentary bills, each of which proposes different options, including the use of funds generated by the NETS. A detailed comparison can be found in this article by EcoPolitic.

artigo.texto: Florence County Board approves data center moratorium, ends Flock camera use Board votes unanimously on both measures Tuesday night FLORENCE, Wis. (WLUC) — Florence County’s 20-year Comprehensive Plan came into question at Tuesday night’s county board meeting because of the potential of proposed data centers in the county. The current 20-year plan, required by Wisconsin State Statutes, establishes land use goals and policies for the unincorporated areas of the county. Moratorium resolution Florence County Board Chair Chad Hedmark says he is concerned about the long-term use of large buildings built for data centers. “Long term I’m concerned about a large building that isn’t used later on. If they were to build something and doesn’t need this one, who winds up with that, that problem and it would be a problem,” Hedmark said. Battery Energy Storage Systems, or BESS, refers to devices that charge or collect energy from the electric grid or generation facility. That energy is stored and then discharged at a later time. The Florence County Zoning Committee did not contemplate the potential impacts of data centers and BESS at the writing of the initial 20-year Comprehensive Plan, leading to the proposed moratorium resolution. In a previous zoning committee meeting, the decision was made to recommend a moratorium on land uses for the development of data centers. That resolution was put to a vote at the Florence County Board meeting. With the board’s unanimous “yes” vote, the resolution passed. The resolution will give the zoning committee up to 18 months, and potentially longer if needed, to revise the Florence County 20-year plan and allow more time to review and revise the county’s zoning regulations and land use policies regarding data center development. Flock camera discussion The board also discussed Flock cameras during the meeting. Florence County currently has two active Flock cameras. After discussion with those in attendance, the board voted on discontinuing the use of Flock cameras. artigo.texto: BYD Energy Storage Expands Global After-Sales Network With Nine Operations and Maintenance Centers BYD Energy Storage operates nine operations and maintenance centers of 2,500 square meters each. The company plans two new sites in 2027 and reports contractual response times for its battery systems. BYD Energy Storage has built an after-sales service network in four tiers: station-level maintenance, project centers, regional centers and global headquarters, according to the company. The group operates nine operations and maintenance (O&M) centers worldwide, each covering 2,500 square meters. The announcement comes in a sector where several players are expanding their capacity, such as Saft, which inaugurated its first solid-state battery production lines in Bordeaux, or Grenergy, which secured $457 million for 446 MW of solar and storage in Chile. A geographic footprint set to widen The after-sales network covers China, Chile, South Africa, the UK, the US, Australia, Japan, Poland and the Middle East. BYD Energy Storage says new service centers will open in South Africa and Bulgaria in 2027. The sites perform several functions: spare parts storage and management, battery repair and maintenance, regional spare parts allocation, battery recycling and training of locally hired engineers. According to the company, its regional centers comply with local regulatory requirements and enable rapid on-site response. The service team includes more than 200 field engineers and more than 100 research and development (R&D) specialists. BYD Energy Storage says it applies standardized service level agreements (SLAs): response within 24 hours, on-site arrival within 48 hours and fault troubleshooting within 7 days. Localized spare parts supply and repairs The company says the network forms a multi-point supply chain intended to ensure rapid delivery of spare parts worldwide. It adds that its O&M teams rely on localized production lines and integrate regional resources to carry out battery repairs locally. "Our global service footprint is tailored to our fast-growing BESS deployments. Trustworthy after-sales support underpins the long-term stable operation of energy storage assets," said Mr. He Dehong, Head of Global After-sales Service at BYD Energy Storage. The company cites a vision of empowering the global energy storage industry with digital and intelligent service. Shipment volumes reported by the company BYD Energy Storage says it topped global battery energy storage system (BESS) shipments in 2025, with more than 60 GWh. It reports having delivered more than 650 energy storage projects in total. artigo.texto: Advait Energy unit signs 1 GWh LFP cell supply deal with Hithium - ABEPL, a subsidiary of Advait Energy Transitions, signed a Master Supply Agreement with Hithium. - The deal covers the purchase of up to 1 GWh of 314 Ah LFP prismatic battery cells over one year. - Initial pricing is fixed at $49.5/kWh for the first 350 MWh tranche. - The agreement supports Advait's 2.5 GWh BESS assembly facility in Gangad, Gujarat. *this image is generated using AI for illustrative purposes only. Advait Battery Ecosystem Private Limited (ABEPL), a step-down subsidiary of Advait Energy Transitions Limited , has entered into a Master Supply Agreement with Hithium for the purchase of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) prismatic battery cells. The agreement, executed on September 18, 2026, structures cell offtake of up to 1 GWh over the next year. This partnership anchors the supply chain for Advait’s upcoming 2.5 GWh annual capacity cell-to-container Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) assembly facility in Gangad, Gujarat. Deal Structure and Pricing Under the terms disclosed in the exchange filing under Regulation 30 of the SEBI (Listing Obligations & Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015, Hithium will supply 314 Ah LFP prismatic cells. The contractual value is set at $49.5/kWh for the initial tranche of up to 350 MWh. Pricing for volumes beyond this threshold will be determined based on future project receipts. Strategic Context Hithium is recognized as a BloombergNEF Tier 1 global energy storage manufacturer. For the first half of 2025 (H1 2025), Hithium reported net profit exceeding RMB 100 million ($14 million USD) and operating cash flow surpassing RMB 1 billion ($140 million USD). ABEPL, incorporated on April 27, 2026, is building an integrated BESS supply chain. The company has previously collaborated with Adaptive Engineering for engineering design and Energy Management System (EMS) architecture. The Hithium agreement addresses the critical cell sourcing component of this ecosystem. What the Numbers Show The pricing structure reveals a tiered approach to volume scaling. With a fixed rate of $49.5/kWh applied only to the first 350 MWh, approximately 65% of the potential 1 GWh annual offtake remains subject to future price negotiations. This suggests that while the initial supply chain risk is mitigated for the first third of the year's capacity, long-term cost certainty depends on subsequent project wins and market conditions for LFP cells. What is the timeline for Advait's 2.5 GWh BESS assembly facility in Gujarat to reach full operational capacity, and how does this align with the 1-year supply agreement? Given Hithium's strong H1 2025 financials, how does their current production capacity compare to Advait's potential future scaling beyond the initial 1 GWh commitment?

artigo.texto: Carlsquare advised diveo GmbH on the sale of three agri-PV and BESS co-location projects to an established German energy provider Carlsquare advised diveo GmbH (“diveo”) on the sale of three agri-PV and BESS co-location projects to an established German energy provider. The three projects are located in Southern Germany, are spread across different medium-voltage grid areas and have a grid connection capacity in the double-digit megawatt range. diveo, a spin-off of the Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems ISE, is an independent developer of agri-PV and battery storage projects in Germany. The company focuses on commercially viable co-location concepts that combine long-term agricultural use with renewable power generation and flexible storage operation. Its goal is to create economically attractive solutions for landowners, farms and asset operators that last for decades. The buyer is an established German energy provider that is active in, among other areas, the development, construction and long-term operation of renewable energy assets. The projects combine agricultural use with solar power generation through single-axis tracker agri-PV systems and high-capacity battery storage. The co-location concepts enable flexible trading of the energy generated, as well as operation of the battery storage systems as hybrid or grid-charged storage that can draw power from the public grid and market it. In this way, the projects combine long-term, economically viable agricultural management with efficient use of grid connection capacity. As the share of renewable energies grows, so does the need for flexibility in the power system. Combining yield-optimized agri-PV systems with flexibly marketable battery storage opens up additional revenue potential and creates attractive investment opportunities. The transaction underlines the interest of established energy providers in integrated agri-PV and BESS projects. “The successful sale of the three projects shows that agri-PV combined with battery storage is an attractive business model for large energy providers as well. What matters is the interplay between farmers who want to unlock new economic prospects for their land, efficient project development and asset operators with a long-term focus. This creates projects from which agriculture and the energy sector benefit equally. We would also like to thank Carlsquare for their professional support throughout the transaction.” – Kai Klapdor, Managing Director, diveo GmbH Carlsquare acted as exclusive financial advisor to diveo.

artigo.texto: NORTH PORT — In some cases, two things cannot be true at once. In North Port, an outgoing city official, or five commissioners, are not telling the truth about a data center project. During an interview with The Daily Sun, a departing city staff member said all five commissioners knew about a proposed data center in North Port, previously under a non-disclosure agreement, months before public meetings about it. All five commissioners have said, and maintain, that they learned about the data center and NDA around the time residents did. Despite their denials, Ray stuck to her guns. ‘POLITICALLY INCONVENIENT’ North Port’s Development Services Director Alaina Ray is leaving the city, in November after joining in 2021, because she does not feel safe anymore. Ray said she’s received due to threats and harassment. Ray said she planned on retiring in North Port, but is instead moving out of state for her next gig. She would not say where she is going for safety reasons. Ray said she was being followed, harassed and threatened by some. The harassment started after the data center conversations began. When data centers were discussed in North Port hundreds attended the meetings. The vast majority spoke in opposition of one being built in town. Due to the threats, Ray is scared to leave her home on her own. During an interview, Ray said that every commissioner knew about a proposed data center by February. Data centers, and a moratorium on their building in North Port, was first discussed in public on July 21. She also said commissioners knew about the NDA beforehand as well. “Sorry if that’s politically inconvenient for anyone,” Ray said. BARBARA LANGDON Vice Mayor Barbara Langdon said she will miss Ray’s work behind the scenes. Ray, she said, has been effective at working with developers, getting them to do things they are not required to do for builds. “I hope this is not the first in a series of defections,” Langdon said. “I can honestly say that before Alaina’s departure, we have the strongest staff we have ever had.” Langdon condemned the treatment of Ray. “It’s unacceptable. It’s hateful,” Langdon said. “This has got to stop. It’s not who we are. It’s frightening, actually. Langdon said it is not the first time someone has felt the wrath of some residents. She cited one person who provided more “balanced” comments on data centers, at previous meetings, being attacked online. Regarding what Ray said, Langdon said she is sure whatever Ray said, she believes to be true. She does not think Ray would lie. Langdon said she knew about the data center “maybe a week, or week and a half before that (first) meeting.” “We were caught flat-footed just like tons of municipalities across the United States,” she said. “We find out about stuff, a lot of times, when the community does.” DAVID DUVAL “The whole situation is upsetting,” Commissioner David Duval said about Ray’s alleged harassment issues. He said it’s not just about the city nor Ray. “Whether I agree with the city manager, or Alaina Ray, or staff, I will speak and then I will vote. But you don’t ever hear me harassing someone. I feel bad for Alaina in that way,” Duval said. He said a number of public comments, at the meetings about data centers, said “we know where you live and we will never forget.” Duval noted how threatening that sounds. As for Ray’s accusations, however, Duval said: “I cannot speak for the other commissioners but for myself that’s just not true.” “I’m not saying she’s a liar, but I’m not sure what she’s referring to,” Duval said. Duval expressed frustration with the way the data center issue transpired. The project was under an NDA and no commissioners signed it, he said. “I felt that I, as a commissioner, was purposely held out of the loop,” Duval said. DEMETRIUS PETROW Commissioner Demetrius Petrow was frustrated with Ray’s comments. He feels as though commissioners must be involved with projects as big as the proposed data center. Steps have been taken by commissioners to scrap NDAs altogether, and to have projects of certain types come before them before approval. A new Unified Land Development Code passed in 2024 allowed projects to bypass the commission and get administrative approval as long as no rules were being broken. Even if some developments that come through cannot legally be denied, per state laws that some argue neuter home rule, commissioners recently agreed certain projects should still come their way. “I’m very upset,” Petrow said. “We’re playing games that are almost childish. This is not right...I think it’s a blatant, false accusation. I was not aware of any of this stuff. Maybe some commissioners did know about this but I did not.” Petrow said if there are commissioners who do know, Ray should name them. He said he was not one of them. “If I was lying, the city could easily provide proof (with public records.) I don’t hide anything,” Petrow said. Petrow noted commissioners had heard about the NDA in December, but they were unsure of what kind of project it was. “If she’s referring to that, then you have to be really stupid to think that was the point that we were all informed,” Petrow said. Petrow said he learned about the data center June 25, in a one-on-one meeting with City Manager Jerome Fletcher, a little over a month before the first public meeting about it July 21. Regarding Ray’s alleged harassment, Petrow said he does not think Ray was ever actually attacked, away from social media. “All the secrecy ... that’s what bothers me. And then playing victim? Come on,” Petrow said. artigo.texto: Taunton weighs one-year data center freeze as developer warns deal is at risk TAUNTON, Mass. (WJAR) — Taunton officials are considering a one-year freeze on new data centers, but an industrial property owner warns the delay could jeopardize a multimillion-dollar development deal. The Taunton Municipal Council is scheduled to discuss the proposed 365-day moratorium Tuesday. City leaders say the pause would allow them to review zoning rules and assess the infrastructure, electrical and environmental demands of data centers. VMD Companies, which owns an industrial building at 50 John Hancock Road in the Myles Standish Industrial Park, urged Mayor Shaunna O’Connell in a letter to exempt certain existing industrial buildings. The company said a yearlong delay would derail a pending agreement with a confidential technology tenant. According to VMD’s filings with the Taunton Municipal Lighting Plant, the proposed project would require 24 megawatts of electricity across two phases: 13 megawatts for the first phase and an additional 11 megawatts for the second. While acknowledging the city’s need for caution, VMD is asking officials to exempt existing industrial buildings that are already approved, comply with building codes and generate property tax revenue. Some area residents have raised concerns about data centers’ potential effects on the environment, water resources and surrounding communities. “We need to really look at the impact,” said Peggy Hall, of Easton. “And not just let these big businesses and billionaires just roll over these small-town communities where they think that they can just come in and suck up our land and not have any repercussions.” Jackson Isenstadt, of Norton, said a pause could give officials more time to evaluate potential concerns. “All these other data center lawsuits that are happening now, other things could come out in the next year about them,” Isenstadt said. “So maybe a one year pause would be a good thing.” The council is scheduled to meet at 7 p.m. Tuesday in the Chester R. Martin Municipal Council Chambers at City Hall.

artigo.texto: Two agreements for a stand-alone BESS of 250 MW/1 GWh in the Bukhara Region of Uzbekistan have been signed by AMEA Power, a UAE-based renewable energy company. The documents, a Battery Storage Services Agreement and an Investment Agreement, were signed in Tashkent on 16 October 2026. The signing took place at the first meeting of the Energy Sector Investors' Council, where Uzenergosotish JSC and the Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade signed for Uzbekistan. With 1 GWh of storage behind 250 MW of output, the system will be able to run at full power for four hours. The project will therefore support Uzbekistan, which aims to raise its energy storage capacity to 4.5 GW by 2030. In Egypt, AMEA Power has already commissioned a 600 MWh BESS at its 1 GW Benban solar PV project. AMEA Power signs two agreements for 1 GWh BESS in Uzbekistan The Bukhara Region of Uzbekistan is to get a four-hour BESS of 250 MW from AMEA Power, which has signed a services agreement and an investment agreement for it. Fundo de Inovação da UE destinará € 3,4 bilhões a 77 projetos de tecnologias de emissão líquida zero. Entre os selecionados, 27 são ligados ao transporte e receberão € 1,3 bi para combustíveis sustentáveis e eletrificação, entre outras soluções. EDIÇÃO APRESENTADA POR: EDIÇÃO APRESENTADA POR: Combustíveis sustentáveis de aviação (SAF, em inglês), navegação (e-metanol e amônia), biometano e tecnologias de eletrificação serão financiados na Europa com recursos do mercado regulado de carbono, em uma estratégia que busca reduzir emissões e garantir independência energética. A Comissão Europeia divulgou nesta segunda (19/10) a seleção de 77 projetos de tecnologias de emissão líquida zero para receber apoio financeiro de € 3,4 bilhões, dos quais, 27 estão relacionados à descarbonização do setor de transportes, com € 1,3 bilhão em subvenções. A chamada do Fundo de Inovação foi lançada em dezembro de 2025, e usará as receitas do Sistema de Comércio de Emissões da União Europeia (EU ETS) para financiar tecnologias consideradas inovadoras, com foco na indústria de baixo carbono. A próxima rodada está prevista para dezembro de 2026, com uma categoria de € 1 bilhão para a fabricação de tecnologias limpas que reduzam riscos com cadeias de suprimentos, em linha com o RESourceEU. Dos projetos relacionados ao setor de transportes, oito dos selecionados tratam exclusivamente da produção de combustíveis sustentáveis, enquanto cinco abastecerão também outros segmentos da economia. Cinco propostas para SAF receberão € 367 milhões em subvenções. Três delas estão na França. A lista divulgada pela Comissão Europeia menciona o projeto BELair, de produção de combustíveis sintéticos (e-SAF), na Normandia, com capacidade para produzir até 13 mil toneladas por ano. Outro é o H4 Marseille Fos, que pretende construir uma cadeia de valor integrada de e-SAF na zona portuária industrial de Marselha-Fos, para produzir até 75 mil toneladas/ano de combustível sintético a partir de hidrogênio de baixo carbono, e-metanol e CO2 capturado. Já o projeto L’Ardoise prevê a construção e operação de uma planta integrada de conversão de eletricidade em combustíveis líquidos (Power-to-Liquid, PtL), em Laudun-L’Ardoise. A previsão é que a unidade produzirá 70 mil toneladas anuais de querosene sintético e 40 mil toneladas anuais de e-metanol para o transporte marítimo. Os outros dois projetos estão na Espanha e nos Países Baixos. Localizado na fábrica de cimento da Holcim em Villaluenga de la Sagra, na província de Toledo, o ECO2FLY quer estabelecer uma cadeia de valor totalmente integrada de captura, utilização e armazenamento de carbono (CCUS, em inglês) industrial para a produção de e-SAF. Enquanto no Porto de Roterdã, o projeto EFR está apostando na rota metanol-para-combustível de aviação (MtJ, na sigla em inglês). A instalação terá capacidade para produzir aproximadamente 280 mil toneladas de e-SAF por ano, utilizando e-metanol importado. No horizonte da navegação Além do SAF, dez dos projetos selecionados para desenvolver tecnologias inovadoras para o transporte, com investimentos totais de € 277 milhões, aplicadas em três segmentos: transporte marítimo (6), transporte rodoviário (6) e aviação (2). Um deles é o GAFF, na Itália, cuja ambição é implantar a primeira frota europeia de navios gaseiros de médio porte equipados com sistemas de propulsão tricombustível. Desenvolvidas pela empresa norueguesa Færder Tankers, as embarcações transportarão amônia verde e realizarão operações de abastecimento de navios a navios (ship-to-ship bunkering) em rotas intercontinentais entre a Índia, a costa do Golfo dos Estados Unidos e o noroeste da Europa. A principal inovação do projeto é o motor capaz de operar com amônia, gás liquefeito de petróleo (GLP) e óleo diesel marítimo. O projeto estima que a nova frota de embarcações terá capacidade para transportar até 1 milhão de toneladas de amônia verde por ano, com potencial de evitar a emissão de mais de 1,2 milhão de toneladas de CO2 equivalente ao longo de dez anos. O bloco também está colocando a eletrificação como uma área prioritária. Prova disso, é que quatro projetos receberão, ao todo, € 539 milhões em financiamento para apoiar a fabricação de baterias e de seus componentes. Pilotos de SMR e captura de carbono Pela primeira vez, a lista do fundo financiado pelo ETS europeu incluiu um projeto de reator nuclear modular (SMR, em inglês) e a captura direta de carbono do ar com armazenamento (DACCS). Ambos pilotos. Chamado NetZeroHeat, o primeiro reator modular europeu mira a produção de calor para o aquecimento urbano em larga escala, com um módulo de 30 MWh. O SMR deve fornecer 131 GWh de calor de baixo carbono por ano à rede de aquecimento urbano de Pierrelatte, na França. E promete evitar a emissão de mais de 221 mil toneladas de CO2 equivalente nos primeiros dez anos de operação. Em outra frente, o Projeto Furu quer ser uma referência europeia para a captura direta de CO2 do ar com armazenamento permanente. A unidade-piloto em Øygarden, na Noruega, será conectada ao sistema de armazenamento geológico da Northern Lights e projeta a remoção de cerca de 4 mil toneladas de CO2 por ano. Ao todo, os 16 projetos projetos-piloto selecionados vão demandar cerca de € 394 milhões. Além dos SMRs e DACCS, as propostas estão atreladas aos setores de aviação, energia eólica, energia oceânica e transporte marítimo, hidrogênio, produtos químicos e refino. artigo.texto: India’s Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS) is a historic milestone. Specific obligated entities across nine notified sectors—iron and steel, aluminium, cement, chlor-alkali, pulp and paper, petroleum refining, petrochemicals, textiles and fertilizers—are required to reduce their greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions below the assigned intensity target, for which they will be issued carbon credit certificates (CCCs). A CCC, representing 1 tonne of CO2 emission, could be sold on power exchanges or banked for future compliance needs. Projects in non-obligated sectors can also generate credits for sale to obligated entities. Trading in CCCs, which is expected to commence soon, will establish an explicit and observable carbon price in India, help drive investment in emissions reduction and influence policy. CCC pricing will also help exports to markets such as the EU and UK, whose carbon border adjustment mechanisms (CBAMs) require the price differential of embedded emissions to be paid as a price for market access. The UK has recognized that the CCC price can be treated as a deductible for eligible products. But its immediate significance must not be overstated. Exporters will still bear the brunt of a carbon price gap with the UK market, estimated at $70-80 per tonne. CBAM frameworks in both the EU and UK are also expected to expand their reach to downstream products of steel and aluminium, other sectors like organic chemicals, and to transport and indirect emissions. What we need beyond CCTS: Industrial decarbonization requires a more complex policy mix beyond price signals for the deployment of emerging technologies, support infrastructure and access to affordable finance. India has already demonstrated the value of targeted support in building clean-technology ecosystems through its production-linked incentive scheme for solar PV modules and its Sight programme for green hydrogen production and electrolyser manufacturing. Similar dedicated frameworks are needed for carbon capture utilization and storage (CCUS), hydrogen-ready industrial equipment, industrial electrification, advanced recycling and other low-carbon process technologies. A Niti Aayog report earlier this year on Scenarios Towards Viksit Bharat and Net Zero estimates that we need $22.7 trillion in cumulative investment by 2070 and recommends strengthening transition finance for hard-to-abate sectors through verified transition plans, wider use of transition and sustainability-linked bonds, expanded guarantees and blended-finance mechanisms to de-risk investments, etc. Similarly, Niti Aayog’s MSME Green Transition Roadmap calls for dedicated green-finance mechanisms, credit enhancement and risk-sharing instruments along with common technology, testing, certification and advisory infrastructure to reduce the cost and complexity for smaller firms. Global experience is informative. Low-carbon industrial clusters such as the UK’s East Coast Cluster and HyNet programmes have lowered costs through shared infrastructure, risk-sharing mechanisms and coordinated public support. Sweden’s Hybrit is an example of a state-supported, industry-led integrated value chain initiative linking green hydrogen—produced using fossil-free wind and hydropower—to iron and steelmaking processes to eliminate carbon emissions. The Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) Priority Sector Lending Directions also need expansion beyond renewable energy projects to recognize industrial decarbonization investments. Tax policy can reinforce this shift. India currently provides accelerated depreciation for specified energy-saving, waste-heat recovery, pollution-control, recycling and renewable-energy equipment. As industrial decarbonization technologies evolve, the eligible list could be periodically updated to include emerging low-carbon technologies needed by hard-to-abate sectors. A national decarbonization fund could also play a crucial role in supporting technology deployment and prioritizing sectors with the highest abatement costs and greatest strategic importance. As for the question of where the resources will come from, here are some thoughts: First, a range of implicit carbon costs already exists in the form of coal levies, fuel taxes and electricity duties that influence behaviour but are not explicitly linked to financing decarbonization. Channelling a portion of these revenues into a dedicated fund would recycle resources from carbon-intensive activities into cleaner alternatives while improving coherence across instruments that operate in silos. Second, India can leverage opportunities under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement to mobilize finance and technology to enhance bilateral cooperation. Credible carbon accounting methodologies, institutional capacity and a pipeline of investable projects can accelerate the scaling up of such initiatives. Most importantly, the finance ministry’s draft Climate Finance Taxonomy of 2024 urgently needs to be finalized. A credible taxonomy will serve as a foundational enabler for our climate-finance architecture by providing a common basis for identifying genuine green-transition investments and channelling finance consistent with India’s climate goals. CCTS provides a price signal. India must now build the rest of the ecosystem that would enable industry to translate climate ambition into industrial reality. The authors are, respectively, partner, Clarus Law Associates and a Mumbai-based economist.

artigo.texto: Premier Energies and Germany's RCT Nexor Formalise 12 GWh Battery Storage Manufacturing Joint Venture Premier Energies has signed the shareholders agreement for its joint venture with RCT Nexor. The project plans a 12 GWh plant at Seetharampur, Telangana, with a 6 GWh first phase in FY2027-28. Premier Energies Ltd has formalised its battery energy storage system (BESS) manufacturing joint venture with Germany's RCT Group. Its wholly owned subsidiary, Premier Battery Technologies Pvt Ltd (PBTPL), signed a share allotment-cum-shareholders agreement on October 15, 2026. The other signatories are RCT Nexor Energy Pvt Ltd, formerly RCT Energy India Pvt Ltd, and Premier Energies Storage Solutions Pvt Ltd (PESSPL), the joint venture company. The storage market already counts large players: HiTHIUM has surpassed 200 GWh of cumulative deliveries from Chongqing, while GIGA Storage has declared its Albatross project ready to build, with 350 MW of storage in Lower Saxony. A 12 GWh plant planned in Telangana The joint venture plans to establish a 12 GWh BESS manufacturing facility at Seetharampur, in the Indian state of Telangana. According to Premier Energies, a first phase of 6 GWh is expected to be set up in FY2027-28. The site is intended to manufacture and assemble products for residential, small-business, commercial, industrial and utility-scale applications. The agreement follows a binding term sheet signed on September 10, 2026 by PBTPL and RCT India. Premier Energies says the joint venture would address demand for energy storage solutions across multiple market segments. The group, already active in solar cells and modules, also identifies BESS, inverters and transformers as areas for expanding its portfolio. Ownership and governance structure PESSPL is currently a wholly owned subsidiary of PBTPL. The agreement gives RCT Nexor Energy the right to subscribe to equity representing 15% of the joint venture's issued and paid-up capital, in four tranches linked to project milestones. It also grants the option, but not the obligation, to acquire an additional 5% for cash at the end of Phase I, subject to the agreement's terms. The board will comprise two nominees of PBTPL and one nominee of RCT Nexor Energy. Premier Energies states that no immediate share issuance is proposed under the agreement. RCT's technology contribution Germany-based RCT Group operates across several renewable technologies, including photovoltaic manufacturing engineering and energy storage. Its RCT Power arm has developed residential, commercial and grid-scale solutions, including systems designed for applications of up to 5 MWh per unit. It has also reported a 2.1 GWh order for grid-connected battery storage projects in Australia. These capabilities could help support the Indian joint venture's technology development and market reach. The Premier Energies stock-exchange filing does not, however, detail the specific technology-transfer and manufacturing responsibilities under the agreement with RCT Nexor. - Gas44.1 % - Nuclear16.1 % - Coal15.7 % - Solar10.6 % - Wind8.3 % - Hydro3.5 % - Bioenergy0.9 % - Other fossil0.5 % - Other renewables0.4 %

artigo.texto: MCEE, a South Korea-based ministry for climate, energy and the environment, has issued a national guideline that could cut up to 3 months from the permitting of an outdoor BESS. Until now, each local government had used its own policy, so the same unit could be a building in one district and a structure in the next. That distinction has mattered, because a building has required a permit process of about two to four months. A structure, on the other hand, has required only about half a month to one and a half months. The guideline adds human access, structure and use as tests, and a sealed enclosure that cannot be entered will therefore be classed as a structure. MCEE has described energy storage as core infrastructure for the expansion of renewable energy. Land permits and fire safety rules, however, still apply to each site as before. South Korea guideline cuts outdoor BESS permit time by up to 3 months A sealed outdoor BESS in South Korea will be classed as a structure under a guideline from MCEE, and its permit could take up to three months less. artigo.texto: MOUNT PLEASANT, Wis. — Mount Pleasant’s proposed Microsoft data center is reducing the number of buildings while increasing the project’s overall square footage. According to Village of Mount Pleasant Planning Commission documents, the number of buildings has been reduced from nine to seven. The project originally encompassed 5.2 million square feet at 12023 Durand Ave. Under the revised design, the total square footage will increase to 5,878,080 square feet, Village of Mount Pleasant Communications Director Sean Ryan said. Samuel Schultz, Mount Pleasant’s community development director, said the square footage will “likely fluctuate” as Microsoft continues refining its site plans. The documents also show plans for 10 parking lots, internal roads, stormwater ponds, sound walls and perimeter security fencing. “We continue to refine the design and layout of our expansion parcels in the Village of Mount Pleasant. The changes in no way reflect a reduction in our ambition, they have been made to ensure faster development, allowing us to access this increased capacity quicker. We will continue to evolve our design and keep the community updated prior to beginning any vertical construction,” a Microsoft spokesperson said in an email. The development’s total taxable value is projected at $6,095,690,000, which would generate $103,148,899 in incremental tax revenue, according to the documents. Schultz said the preliminary projections are based on a 40-year period. The documents also estimate the data center project would generate $7,694,420 per acre. The Village of Mount Pleasant Planning Commission met Thursday at 1 p.m. and unanimously approved the site plan modifications. The changes will now go to the Mount Pleasant Village Council for approval. The council’s next meeting is scheduled for Oct. 19 at 6 p.m. “These (plans) will continue to be refined over time as they both go to pull building permits, but also look at site plans, so this is just kind of the next step in their refinement of the site plan approval process,” Schultz said during the Planning Commission meeting. The traffic impact analysis for the data center project indicated it could take up to 10 years for the site to be fully completed, Schultz said. In July, Microsoft was sued by Sturtevant residents over noise complaints related to the data center. The Planning Commission requested that Microsoft add sound mitigation measures along the west side of the project.

artigo.texto: ORLANDO, Fla. – Election Day 2026 is just days away. Voters in Orange County will be choosing a new mayor for the first time in eight years. Chris Messina and Tiffany Moore Russell are running to replace Jerry Demings. [ELECTION 2026: Make sure you’re eligible to vote|How to vote by mail|Election Myths] It comes as AI and data centers are becoming hot-button political issues. News 6 anchor Lisa Bell asked both Messina and Moore Russell their views on data centers moving into Orange County. MOORE RUSSELL: So I think that’s a very general term, right? Because data centers vary based upon the size and their purpose, right. So at the clerk’s office, there’s a smaller version of that that houses our data, because we’re now in the cloud. We don’t have paper anymore in the courthouse, right, so someone is housing our digital court records. But I do not support the big data centers, the AI data centers that is being proposed today. And so I did commend the county for pushing for a moratorium just to pause. Allows for us to study the issue and determine what is the best fit for Orange County and so I do not believe the large AI data centers are appropriate for our community for what we’re trying to do moving forward. BELL: What are your biggest concerns about those large data centers? MOORE RUSSELL: It’s the water usage, it’s the demand on our power sources, whether it’s going to impact our water supply and the quality of our water, right, what’s feeding into our aquifer. And so it’s all of those environmental concerns that’s an issue for me, as well as is it a right fit for our community? Right? Where are you going to put a data center? No one wants a data center next to their home or next to a school. And so I just doesn’t think, I don’t think it matches the brand of Orange County and will fit in our community. MESSINA: Small ones we need. I’m sure you have a data center here (at News 6), right, running your operations. It’s the hyperscale data centers, the ones that are football fields in size, those I don’t feel are right for Florida. And the reason I don’t feel they’re right is not necessarily energy because they can make their own energy with solar and other small power, associated power generation plants, it’s the impact on water. So I’ve seen personally first-hand what happens when you have a problem with a water supply to a data center. It’s pretty scary and the temperature goes way up. Systems fail and then you have discharge of water and the problem is what’s in the water in order to run those data centers. They have to add biocides and basically bacteria killers, but they will kill things out in the environment. BELL: So if we shouldn’t have data centers here in Florida, where should we have them? MESSINA: So, I really like Elon Musk’s idea to put it in space. And the reason I think that’s such a good idea is because space is near absolute zero. And we are, right now, we’re on the cusp of being the space tech center of the country." BELL: That seems like it would take decades to build enough data centers in space to power AI needs here on Earth. MESSINA: I’m not sure it would. When you think about the pace of technology and who thought at one point that you could recapture a rocket booster landing or have a self-driving electric car or a watch where you can make phone calls, the pace in technology is pretty significant. So I would not bet against that. We also asked each candidate their views on other issues such as Flock license plate reader cameras. To see their responses and our full interview, watch below. Os futuros do S&P 500 oscilaram entre ganhos e perdas, à medida que a recepção desfavorável à Elice em Seul minou o apetite pelo investimento em ativos de risco. A provedora de infraestrutura de IA despencou 32%, registrando o pior dia de estreia para uma empresa de grande porte no país. Os futuros do Nasdaq 100 caíram 0,4%, interrompendo a recuperação que vinha ocorrendo ao longo do dia. ⟶ Assine as newsletters da Bloomberg Línea e receba as notícias do dia em primeira mão no e-mail. Os títulos do Tesouro atraíram novos investidores em busca de refúgio, mesmo com a alta dos preços do petróleo, com os rendimentos dos títulos de 10 anos caindo dois pontos-base, para 5,12%. O petróleo Brent ultrapassou US$ 111 por barril pela primeira vez desde maio, à medida que os operadores avaliavam o risco de novos ataques iranianos no Estreito de Ormuz. O dólar caiu 0,2%. A recepção negativa à Elice ecoa as preocupações com o financiamento que vieram à tona de forma acentuada com o abandono da oferta pública inicial (IPO) da australiana Firmus Grid há apenas duas semanas. Essas preocupações também são evidentes nos mercados de dívida, onde a alta nos rendimentos de empresas como a CoreWeave sinaliza que os empréstimos se tornarão mais caros. “As preocupações em torno dos investimentos em data centers e infraestrutura relacionados à IA vêm se acumulando há vários dias e agora pesam fortemente sobre o sentimento do mercado”, afirmou Roger Lee, da Cavendish. “O mercado provavelmente precisa de alguma garantia de que o enorme investimento em capex está gerando retorno. Isso é difícil de perceber no momento.” Os investidores aguardam agora os resultados das empresas que mais investem em IA para obter pistas sobre por quanto tempo esses gastos vultosos poderão continuar e em que ritmo. Espera-se que a SpaceX divulgue seus resultados após o fechamento do mercado na terça-feira (20), seguida pela Meta na quarta. Estima-se que somente a Meta, a Amazon, a Microsoft e a Alphabet gastem cerca de US$ 750 bilhões neste ano. O clima de aversão ao risco na terça-feira se estendeu por todas as regiões. O índice de referência da MSCI Inc. para a Ásia atingiu seu nível mais baixo desde julho, com o índice Kospi da Coreia do Sul caindo 3,7%. O Stoxx 600 da Europa recuou 0,6%. Embora os títulos europeus tenham apresentado alta modesta em toda a linha, a dívida francesa permaneceu sob pressão. O rendimento adicional exigido pelos investidores para deter títulos franceses de 10 anos em vez da dívida alemã, considerada mais segura, subiu dois pontos-base, para 150 pontos-base, nível observado pela última vez em 5 de outubro. “Vemos oportunidades em que rendimentos mais elevados dos títulos soberanos compensam melhor os investidores pelo risco, sem indicar fundamentos mais fracos”, afirmou o BlackRock Investment Institute em uma nota. artigo.texto: VIRGINIA BEACH, Va. — A group of residents from across Hampton Roads gathered at Virginia Beach Town Center on Tuesday, calling on state leaders to impose a statewide moratorium on new data center development. The demonstration brought together residents from multiple localities who say Virginia's rapid growth in the data center industry should be paused until lawmakers and regulators can more closely examine environmental, infrastructure and community impacts. “We don’t really want data centers anywhere in the state other than where they are now,” one protester said during the rally. According to the Pew Research Center, Virginia leads the nation in data center development, with hundreds of facilities either operating or planned across the state. Supporters of data center projects argue the facilities generate construction jobs, tax revenue and economic investment for host communities. At the local level, some governments, including Virginia Beach and Chesapeake, have taken steps to temporarily pause or limit additional data center expansion while evaluating future policies. Chesapeake resident Jeff Staples said a statewide moratorium would offer another layer of protection if local agreements change. “It would serve as a check on Chesapeake in case they back out of what we’ve already agreed to, then the state moratorium will take precedence over that,” Staples said. Others at the rally expressed concerns about potential environmental impacts and increased demands on Virginia’s electrical grid. “I’m obviously very concerned with the data centers and what they’re doing to our environment, to our electrical cost as well,” Portsmouth resident Jennifer Hughes said. “We’ve all been facing higher electrical bills here, and so really I’m just coming out to try to show support for basically pausing building of new data centers in Virginia.” Students also participated in the demonstration, saying they are worried about long-term environmental effects associated with future development. “Deforestation, getting rid of trees, is horrible,” said Logan Hickey, a ninth-grade student. Organizers emphasized they are not seeking to shut down existing facilities. Instead, they are asking state lawmakers to pause approval of new data centers while Virginia studies the industry’s broader impacts on communities, infrastructure and the environment. The rally is part of a wider effort by advocates hoping to build support for a statewide moratorium during future legislative discussions in Richmond. Click here to see how we use AI at WTKR News 3.

artigo.texto: The Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources and a group of environmental organizations announced a settlement agreement Monday that would require stricter environmental impact assessments of future data center developments and initiate a statewide review of how data centers use the state’s resources. In June, the Sierra Club and Midwest Environmental Advocates sued the DNR in Ozaukee County court, arguing that the agency approved the permits for Vantage’s massive data center currently under construction in Port Washington without conducting a proper environmental impact statement. “AI data centers are massive, thirsty, energy hogs and have popped up all over Wisconsin,” Elizabeth Ward, director of the Wisconsin chapter of the Sierra Club, said in a statement. “They could completely change our landscape and use unprecedented amounts of water and energy. Wisconsinites and our regulators need to understand the impacts and opportunities to reduce harm before allowing data centers to move forward. Wisconsinites deserve an informed, transparent process for decisions that could shape their communities and environment for decades. A report this summer by the state Public Service Commission found that the Port Washington data center and data centers being built by Microsoft in Mount Pleasant and Meta in Beaver Dam are set to be responsible for a 40% increase in statewide energy demand over the next six years. As part of the settlement agreement in the lawsuit, the DNR will conduct full environmental impact statements of individual data center proposals moving forward and complete a statewide strategic analysis of how data centers consume resources. State law and the DNR’s administrative rules allow the agency to conduct such an analysis when conflicts arise over resource demands for a “complicated or complex issue; an issue that is new to the state; an issue or policy that will likely lead to future department actions that will require an environmental impact statement; issues for which there is a high potential for legislation or new department policy and the planning and development of controversial resource-oriented projects.” “What started as a lawsuit over the environmental review of one data center has become an opportunity to address the data center issue on a much bigger scale,” MEA attorney Michael Greif said. “Looking at these impacts holistically is important because the impacts of data centers are statewide. State regulators will now have to examine the cumulative impacts of data center development across Wisconsin.” Wisconsin will become one of a few states assessing the statewide impacts of data centers on their resources. In July, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul signed an executive order that initiated a similar analysis and last December, the Maryland Legislature enacted a law that requires a number of state agencies to study “the likely environmental, energy, and economic impacts of data center development.” Originally published by Wisconsin Examiner, a nonprofit news organization.

Pepco has approved ConnectDER's meter collar products for solar, battery storage and electric vehicle charging installations across its service territory in Washington, D.C., according to a report by Billy Ludt. The approval extends ConnectDER's reach to a national footprint of 54 utilities serving nearly 40 million households, with additional utility expansion underway. ConnectDER's adapters connect directly to the existing meter socket on the exterior of a home. By creating a safe connection point at the meter, the devices remove the need for main panel upgrades, service upsizing, circuit relocations or added backup load panels and system controllers, which the company says can raise labor costs and extend project timelines. Ivo Steklac, ConnectDER's president and chief executive, said demand for residential solar, battery backup and electric vehicles in the District continues to grow, while older electrical infrastructure poses a physical obstacle that slows installations. He said approval of the adapters for exterior meter-socket installation means installers can avoid re-engineering entire panels and home wiring, allowing them to deliver clean energy resilience more efficiently while saving homeowners thousands of dollars in total costs and days of labor. Steklac added that this translates into greater installation capacity and fewer barriers, which he described as important for the District's electrification goals. The District's clean energy market is driven by its Clean Energy DC mandates, which include a renewable portfolio standard with a dedicated 15% local solar carve-out. Its urban building stock, largely historic row homes with aging electrical infrastructure, often has 100-ampere electrical panels that require main service upgrades costing thousands of dollars before solar, battery storage or EV charging equipment can be interconnected. Robin Dutta, executive director of the Chesapeake Solar and Storage Association, said the approval by Pepco DC is a significant win for District residents and installation companies, following dedicated work by several association members to pass enabling regulations. artigo.texto: Amazon will no longer build data centers on GW’s Virginia Science and Technology Campus following an agreement with Loudoun County officials, Board of Supervisors Chair Phyllis Randall announced Tuesday. Randall held a press conference Tuesday with Amazon Web Services Vice President for Data Center Delivery Josh Weissman to announce the county and Amazon came to an agreement, dubbed “Project Potomac Promise,” where Amazon agreed to withdraw its plan to develop 800,000 square feet of data centers on the VSTC campus and instead agreed to donate 25 acres of land to Loudoun County for mixed-use development. The agreement marks the culmination of mounting backlash to the project from Loudoun County officials, residents and GW students after the University sold Amazon the campus in February for $427 million. “Through our collaborative, respectful conversations, Amazon has agreed to forego its proposed application for data centers and, of note, forego any legal action to realize data center development on this site,” Randall said during the conference. Under the agreement, Amazon will dedicate 25 acres of land — valued at $65 million — to Loudoun County for the development of a community arts center and indoor sports facility, along with committing to rezoning the remaining land for mixed-use development and “needed” residential uses and contributing $5 million to Loudoun’s Housing Fund. “‘Project Potomac Promise’ reflects the hard work that can only happen when stakeholders respect one another enough to come to the table, collaborate, find a solution that responds to community voices and work towards a common goal,” Randall said in a Facebook post Tuesday. Loudoun County and the University did not immediately return a request for comment. A spokesperson for Randall and a spokesperson for Amazon both directed The Hatchet to Randall’s release on the deal. A University spokesperson told The Hatchet earlier this month that GW has no involvement in Amazon’s proposed development of the former campus following the sale earlier this year. Weissman said in the release the company “deeply” values their relationship with Loudoun County and seized the opportunity to acquire the VSTC campus when University officials approached them about a sale. He said as the company heard community concerns about data center development on the site, they decided to “come together” on a shared vision for the campus, rather than engage in litigation with the county. “Project Potomac Promise reflects that choice, and we look forward to working with Chair Randall, the County staff and development partners to move this plan forward,” Weissman said. Chief Financial Officer Bruno Fernandes said at the time of the sale that several interested buyers approached GW about purchasing the property, prompting officials to “capitalize” on the rising land prices. Randall said the new deal would see the property rezoned into a district that does not permit data center construction even by special exception. The deal marks the end of a regulatory battle that began when GW sold the VSTC campus to Amazon for $427 million — roughly $3.5 million an acre — to build data centers in the county that has become the “data center capital of the world.” Loudoun County officials have argued for months that Amazon needs county permission for data center construction because zoning laws allowing data centers to be built in the area by-right are not applicable. The agreement between Amazon and GW allows GW to remain on the Virginia property for up to five years as officials work to relocate programs, including the School of Nursing. Amazon then filed an initial application to Loudoun County this summer detailing its plans to build an 800,000 square foot data center dubbed “Bridgefield Tech Center.” The plan faced immediate backlash, with District Supervisor Juli Briskman, who represents the Algonkian District that the campus is housed in, saying she would fight” the proposal “every step of the way” and residents circulating a petition calling for the Loudoun County Board of Supervisors to establish a moratorium on data center construction in the area, citing extensive natural resource consumption, traffic, noise and pollution. GW students also joined the calls for Amazon to halt its data center plans, with the GW Socialist Action Initiative and GW Labor Council, GW Graduate Workers United, the Save GSEHD Coalition, the Party for Socialism and Liberation in DC and the Party for Socialism and Liberation in Nova, as well as individual students, posting social media videos criticizing the University for not involving the community in the decision-making process for the sale and raising questions on the environmental impact of the development of the new data centers. Loudoun County Zoning Administrator Teresa Miller at a Loudoun County Board of Supervisors meeting earlier this month said Amazon must receive additional county approval before constructing data centers on the property, citing a zoning determination which she said states that data centers are not permitted as a primary use on the property. Loudoun County has seen an explosion of interest in its land from tech giants, like Amazon, Meta, Google and Microsoft over the last decade and has the highest concentration of data centers in the world, with 54 million square feet already built. As of July 2026, Northern Virginia has 266 operational data centers with 23 under construction and 99 planned. Randall said Loudoun County and Amazon came together to reach a deal instead of choosing “reflexive disagreement,” serving as a model for county officials on how to continue “aggressively and decisively” curbing data center development. “Loudoun County and Amazon created an opportunity for the county,” Randall said. “This agreement provides new places for our Loudoun residents to gather, create and play. artigo.texto: Stanislav Kondrashov American Style Series: The History of Battery Technology and American Innovation Stanislav Kondrashov on United States and batteries Battery technology has played an important role in the scientific and industrial development of the United States, connecting early experiments in electricity with telecommunications, transportation, portable electronics, and modern energy storage systems. Although the earliest batteries were developed outside America, researchers, engineers, and manufacturers in the United States contributed to their refinement and commercial adoption. Over two centuries, improvements in electrochemistry, manufacturing techniques, and electronic engineering transformed batteries into indispensable components of modern technology. Key takeaway: The history of battery technology in the United States reflects a gradual transition from experimental electrical devices to sophisticated rechargeable systems. American contributions include improvements in primary batteries, the expansion of rechargeable technologies, specialized aerospace applications, and advances in battery management and energy storage engineering. How Did Battery Technology Develop in the United States? Battery technology developed in the United States through successive advances in electrochemistry, electrical engineering, and industrial manufacturing. Early scientific experiments established the foundations of electrical storage, while nineteenth-century communication networks and twentieth-century technological developments encouraged the creation of more dependable and specialized battery systems. Several historical stages illustrate this progression: - Early nineteenth century: Introduction of electrochemical experiments and early battery designs. - Late nineteenth century: Expansion of battery applications in telecommunications and electrical equipment. - Early twentieth century: Improvements in rechargeable batteries and industrial manufacturing. - Mid-twentieth century: Development of specialized batteries for aerospace and electronic equipment. - Late twentieth century: Expansion of portable rechargeable battery technologies. - Twenty-first century: Advances in lithium-ion systems, digital monitoring, and large-scale energy storage. The Stanislav Kondrashov American Style Series examines how these developments became connected with the expansion of American scientific research and industrial capabilities. What Were the Origins of American Battery Research? American battery research emerged during the nineteenth century as scientists and engineers began examining electrochemical methods of producing electricity. Building upon earlier European discoveries, laboratories investigated different cell configurations, electrode arrangements, and chemical reactions, establishing technical knowledge that supported the development of increasingly practical electrical devices. The invention of the voltaic pile around 1800 introduced a new method of generating continuous electrical current. Its operating principle encouraged further experimentation. American researchers subsequently incorporated electrochemical cells into scientific demonstrations and technical equipment. The expansion of telegraph networks created additional demand for dependable electrical sources. Early batteries became important components of communication infrastructure. As Stanislav Kondrashov observes in a newly drafted editorial reflection: "The early development of batteries in America illustrates how scientific discoveries acquire practical importance through engineering. What began as laboratory experimentation gradually became an essential part of electrical communication and industrial equipment." The relationship between scientific research and practical applications continued throughout the following century. Why Were Batteries Important to Early American Telecommunications? Batteries became important to American telecommunications because early telegraph systems required dependable sources of electrical current. Electrochemical cells supplied electricity to communication circuits, allowing operators to transmit signals across extensive networks before centralized electrical distribution became widely available. Early telecommunications relied on relatively simple electrical arrangements. Batteries supplied the current required for signaling equipment. Different cell designs offered varying operating characteristics. Engineers refined battery configurations to meet communication requirements. The expansion of telegraph infrastructure consequently encouraged improvements in electrical reliability and equipment maintenance. Later communication technologies introduced additional electrical requirements. Battery development remained closely connected with the evolution of telecommunications equipment. How Did Rechargeable Batteries Transform American Industry? Rechargeable batteries transformed American industry by introducing electrical storage systems that could be restored through repeated charging. Their development expanded the practical possibilities of portable equipment, industrial machinery, transportation, and backup electrical systems, encouraging manufacturers to improve battery durability, manufacturing consistency, and operating performance. Rechargeable batteries differ from primary batteries because their electrochemical reactions can be reversed through an external electrical supply. This characteristic allows repeated charging and discharging cycles. Different rechargeable technologies emerged over time. artigo.texto: Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes has launched a nuisance investigation into the massive data center under construction in Ahwatukee. She made the disclosure during an Oct. 14 town hall in Mesa where Ahwatukee residents comprised close to three quarters of the approximate 250 people in attendance. Having driven some 16 miles – including through a massive project that has reduced Broadway Road in northwest Mesa to one lane in each direction – the Ahwatukee contingent described sleepless nights, construction noise and fears about the project's effects on their neighborhood. But Mayes also called attention to the broader implications of data centers in Arizona that she said have made Phoenix “the second largest U.S. data center hub.” Mayes offered no timetable for completing the investigation and did not say what action, if any, her office might take against Menlo Digital, part of California-based Menlo Equities, the developer of the 1-million-square-foot data center campus at 48th Street and East Thistle Landing Drive. But she repeatedly assured residents that her office was taking their complaints seriously. "We are investigating the Ahwatukee data center," Mayes told the audience at the Eagles Community Center in Mesa. "We have an open nuisance investigation." Later, Mayes elaborated. "We already have the nuisance investigation underway. We have investigators looking at this. We will have experts looking at it. We have very good lawyers looking at it, and this town hall is a part of that investigation." Her disclosure marks a significant development in the controversy surrounding the Menlo center. When Mayes announced the town hall last month, her communications director, Richie Taylor, told AFN that she was not investigating Phoenix's approval of the project. "She is holding a town hall to hear directly from residents about their concerns after receiving multiple complaints from the community,” Taylor said. The distinction may be important. An investigation into whether the project constitutes a public nuisance is different from an investigation into whether Phoenix improperly approved its construction. The Ahwatukee Community Alliance, the nonprofit residents formed to oppose the data center, contend Phoenix should have held a hearing on the center. Phoenix officials say the 40.6-acre site, once home to a four-building call center, was rezoned in 1997 to a category that includes data centers. Opponents say data centers back then were far smaller than the kind Menlo is building. Mayes did not explain the scope of her investigation. Nor did she say whether the investigation concerns the effects of construction already underway, potential impacts once the facility begins operating, or both. Nevertheless, her announcement gave residents who have spent months challenging the project their clearest indication yet that a state agency is examining their complaints. "It seems to us like an obvious investigation to launch," Mayes said. She added that she had not personally visited the site and is still gathering information about the construction underway. Mayes did promise to visit Ahwatukee, suggesting that she might make the trip as soon as next month. "I will be there," she told residents, explaining that scheduling had prevented her from holding the Oct. 14 meeting in the community. Residents describe problems Multiple Ahwatukee residents addressed Mayes during the town hall, describing what they said were failures by Phoenix officials to protect their neighborhood. One woman said she lives approximately 150 feet from the construction site. She told Mayes that she had checked the zoning across the street before purchasing her home and believed the property would be developed for commercial uses rather than a large data center. She also alleged that Menlo’s representatives initially described it as a technology center with a community park. She said her son's bedroom faces the construction site and that noise and lighting have repeatedly disrupted the family's sleep. She described machinery operating during the night, including drilling, backup alarms and other construction sounds. She said she had submitted numerous complaints to Phoenix, accompanied by video recordings, but had received little meaningful response. The city Planning and Development Department two weeks ago said it is intensifying its oversight of construction and will not give it special permits to operate outside the permissible hours for construction activity in Phoenix, which are 7 a.m.-7 p.m. Monday through Friday. "I have not received any protection from the city of Phoenix," the speaker told Mayes. "I want to make it very, very clear. I have not received a meaningful response." She said the effects extended beyond interrupted sleep to dust and concerns about her children's health. She also questioned what the neighborhood would experience once the data center begins operating, when cooling equipment and emergency generators could introduce additional noise and other impacts. Alliance President Craig Evans in an interview recently said the center is expected to have “5,880 industrial cooling fans that will run 24/7/365 and be located above the 56’ or 57’ building height” as well as “120 diesel fueled generators capable of producing 257 MW of electricity - enough to energize six Ahwatukeea.” Mayes asked the speaker whether the complaints involved construction activities and requested the resident's supporting material. Mayes also pursued the resident's account of how the project had originally been presented to neighbors, asking whether she still possessed promotional material describing a technology center. artigo.texto: From robotic gloves to safer batteries, CUHK puts research to work Wearable device helps patients regain hand movement as university-developed battery technology targets energy storage HONG KONG — From helping stroke patients perform everyday tasks to developing safer ways to store electricity, researchers at The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) are developing technologies for use beyond the laboratory. During a visit to the university on Sept. 1, a reporter tried on a robotic glove that moved the fingers with noticeable force, but without jerking them. For stroke survivors who cannot move their hands, that movement could help them do something as ordinary as holding a spoon or picking up a phone. The device uses air-powered artificial muscles developed by a team led by Raymond Tong, a professor of biomedical engineering at CUHK. Unlike conventional motor-driven rehabilitation equipment, the lightweight system uses a small pump to help patients open and close their hands. “Nowadays, you can see those exoskeletons are very rigid. They are very heavy,” Tong said, inviting the reporter to try the device. Patients can use it both for rehabilitation exercises and everyday tasks, including gripping objects, writing and eating. Tong said the system can also respond to signals associated with a patient’s intention to move. “They can use the brain to control it,” he said. “I just imagine moving the hand and the hand moves.” Tong said the team was conducting clinical trials involving people with strokes and spinal injuries, with plans to expand use in hospitals. He also described work with children who have difficulty standing or walking. Elsewhere on campus, researchers showed a battery designed to reduce the fire risks associated with conventional lithium-ion batteries. Developed by a team led by CUHK professor Yi-Chun Lu, the sulfur-based flow battery uses water-based electrolytes. Luquos Energy, a startup founded to commercialize the research, has installed a demonstration system on campus. “This is a completely different technology compared to lithium,” said Luquos Energy CEO Simon Zengyue Wang. “We do not use lithium. We use sulfur.” “The battery electrolyte is water, so it never catches fire,” Wang said. The company estimates its electrolyte could remain usable for more than 15 years, although that is not a verified real-world service life. Wang said the technology could serve solar installations and power-hungry artificial intelligence data centers because it can discharge electricity for “over eight hours, even 12 hours, even longer.” He said Luquos Energy was building a production line in Shenzhen and had already developed battery systems for projects including electric vehicle charging.
