artigo.texto: Fairfield leaders discuss C-PACE financing tool that could help businesses, proposed data center FAIRFIELD, Ala. (WBRC) - Fairfield city leaders are looking into a new financing tool that could help business and property owners pay for upgrades on commercial buildings, including the proposed Patmos data center. The tool is called C-PACE, or Commercial Property Assessed Clean Energy. Monday, the Fairfield City Council discussed considering the program, but tabled the issue for now. What is C-PACE? C-PACE lets businesses seek private financing for upgrades such as LED lighting, heating and cooling systems, and water-saving fixtures. A new state law allows cities to offer this kind of private financing locally. Mayor Herman Carnes Jr. said the city is not taking out a loan to build a data center. He said the program is about letting businesses and property owners tap into private money to fix up their buildings. Carnes called C-PACE a “help” mechanism and said it is not a financial liability for the city. “If we are saying we’re open for business, that means we need to do everything possible and legally tactical so that we can make sure that people be able to come in, purchase a building, not run out of money once they do the electrical system and then you have a building sitting,” Carnes said. Protest outside city hall Before the meeting, members of the Fairfield Environmental Justice Alliance protested outside city hall. They want more transparency around the Patmos data center project. Patmos wants to build a colocation data center and technology campus inside the former Walmart supercenter in Fairfield. Neighbors are asking city leaders to release all documents so they can see the potential impact. “A project with major effects on our community should be presented openly, examined carefully and discussed with the people who will live with the results,” said Gilda Walker of the Fairfield Environmental Justice Alliance. City says program not limited to Patmos The mayor said C-PACE is not just about Patmos and is available to businesses looking for financial help. A Patmos spokesperson sent WBRC this statement: “Fairfield taxpayers are not on the hook. Tonight (Monday) the City is only considering whether to adopt the C-PACE program; it is not issuing a loan, lending City money, or taking on any debt, guarantee or liability. Under Alabama law, C-PACE is private financing that a property owner voluntarily repays through an assessment on its own property, public funds cannot be used to fund or repay it, and billing, collection and enforcement are handled entirely by the private lender. Once adopted, the program is open to a wide range of property owners, including commercial properties such as office buildings and hotels, industrial, agricultural and multifamily properties. Patmos is one of several parties interested in using it, and others aren’t even in our industry.”- Patmos spokesperson, Kyler Schmitz City leaders discussed a possible work session on the issue and a town hall before any final vote. artigo.texto: Leilões de baterias abrem nova frente para a infraestrutura energética Previstos para dezembro, os primeiros certames do País vão contratar sistemas de armazenamento para atender à demanda e ampliar a flexibilidade da rede elétrica - Dois leilões estão previstos para 2 e 4 de dezembro, com regras distintas para a origem das baterias - Foram cadastrados 6.091 projetos, que somam 296,8 GW de potência; a participação depende de habilitação técnica - Contratos de 15 anos, com operação a partir de agosto de 2028, abrem oportunidades para fornecedores e financiadores Os dois primeiros leilões brasileiros dedicados à contratação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias de grande porte estão previstos para 2 e 4 de dezembro. Com contratos de 15 anos e início de operação em 1º de agosto de 2028, os certames abrem uma nova frente para desenvolvedores, fabricantes e financiadores de infraestrutura elétrica. O governo federal vai contratar a disponibilidade de potência desses sistemas: a capacidade de entregar energia à rede quando necessário. As baterias armazenam eletricidade e a devolvem conforme os comandos do Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS), contribuindo para atender aos horários de maior consumo e aproveitar excedentes de geração renovável. A expansão das usinas solares e eólicas tornou mais importante administrar as diferenças entre os horários de geração e consumo. Em determinados momentos, a oferta supera a demanda ou encontra limitações na rede. Nessas situações, o ONS pode determinar cortes de geração, conhecidos no setor como curtailment. Além do excesso de oferta, esses cortes podem decorrer de restrições elétricas e da necessidade de preservar a confiabilidade do sistema. Segundo o balanço de 2025 da Volt Robotics, cerca de 20% da energia que poderia ter sido gerada pelas usinas solares e eólicas deixou de ser aproveitada no País. Os cortes corresponderam a 4.021 megawatts médios, com perdas financeiras estimadas pela consultoria em R$ 6,5 bilhões. O impacto pressiona as receitas dos geradores e acrescenta desafios ao financiamento de novos projetos. Nesse cenário, as baterias funcionam como um reservatório de eletricidade. Podem ser carregadas nos períodos de maior disponibilidade de energia e descarregadas quando o sistema precisa de potência — por exemplo, após a redução da geração solar no fim do dia. O armazenamento pode ajudar a diminuir o descompasso entre oferta e demanda, embora não elimine todas as restrições que provocam cortes de geração. Como os leilões vão funcionar Os certames terão regras distintas. O primeiro, em 2 de dezembro, será destinado a sistemas que atendam aos requisitos de fabricação nacional das baterias, conforme os critérios de credenciamento do Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES). O segundo, em 4 de dezembro, não terá essa exigência, permitindo a participação de sistemas com equipamentos importados. O interesse do mercado aparece no volume de inscrições. A Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE), vinculada ao Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME), registrou 6.091 projetos, que somam 296,8 gigawatts (GW) de potência, um recorde de cadastramento para certames do setor elétrico brasileiro. Esse total representa a capacidade dos empreendimentos inscritos, e não o volume que será contratado. O cadastro também não garante participação nos leilões. Os projetos precisam passar pela análise e pela habilitação técnica da EPE para comprovar o atendimento aos requisitos estabelecidos. A quantidade de potência a contratar será definida pelo MME com apoio dos estudos de planejamento e operação do sistema. Em 30 de setembro, o ONS, a Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) e a EPE publicaram uma nota técnica com a capacidade remanescente da rede para conectar os novos sistemas de armazenamento. O documento ajuda a identificar os pontos nos quais há espaço para receber os empreendimentos. Entre os requisitos previstos estão potência mínima de 30 megawatts (MW), capacidade de operação contínua por pelo menos quatro horas e recarga completa em até seis horas. Os projetos vencedores serão remunerados pela disponibilidade da potência contratada e deverão seguir os comandos do ONS para carregar e descarregar as baterias. O que muda para a economia e para o consumidor Para o sistema elétrico, o armazenamento amplia as possibilidades de administrar a geração renovável e atender à demanda. Ao disponibilizar energia nos momentos necessários, as baterias podem reduzir o acionamento de fontes mais caras. O efeito final sobre os custos para o consumidor, porém, também dependerá do preço da potência contratada e das regras de custeio. Para as empresas, os leilões abrem oportunidades no desenvolvimento dos projetos, na fabricação e no fornecimento de equipamentos, na instalação e na manutenção dos sistemas. A modalidade com exigência de fabricação nacional também busca estimular a cadeia produtiva brasileira de armazenamento. Os contratos de 15 anos e a remuneração pela disponibilidade de potência oferecem uma base de receitas de longo prazo, que pode apoiar a estruturação de financiamentos com bancos e fundos de infraestrutura. A viabilidade de cada empreendimento dependerá também dos custos de implantação, operação e manutenção e do cumprimento das obrigações contratuais. Para a pessoa física, a exposição a esse mercado pode ocorrer indiretamente, em fundos, ações ou títulos de dívida de empresas que participem da cadeia de armazenamento. Essa relação precisa ser verificada em cada caso: um produto financeiro ligado ao setor elétrico não necessariamente financia ou reúne projetos de baterias.

artigo.texto: As preocupações com a localização, a procura de água e de electricidade levaram a apelos para uma maior supervisão da construção de centros de dados no estado de Cowboy, mas não para um alinhamento sobre como o conseguir. CODY, Wyoming. — Em uma noite quente de outubro, em um bar no centro de Cody, os habitantes de Wyoming se reuniram para refletir sobre o futuro do que alguns esperam que seja a próxima indústria em expansão do Estado Cowboy: os data centers. Neste verão, o governador cessante, Mark Gordon, assinou uma ordem executiva intitulada “Data Centers the Wyoming Way” que, segundo ele, “orientaria o desenvolvimento responsável no Wyoming”, ao mesmo tempo que manteria o estado um ponto de aterrissagem atraente para os enormes armazéns de servidores que alimentam a indústria de IA. Os potenciais impactos dos centros de dados no precioso abastecimento de água do Wyoming, nos já crescentes preços da electricidade e nas valiosas terras públicas têm irritado muitos cantos do estado. Gordon reconheceu essas preocupações numa declaração que acompanha a divulgação da ordem, que não é vinculativa. Grupos ambientalistas no Wyoming concordam que é necessário haver mais barreiras de proteção no desenvolvimento de data centers, mas não estão totalmente alinhados sobre como atingir esse objetivo. O capítulo do The Sierra Club do Wyoming acredita que uma moratória sobre data centers poderia ser útil em certas circunstâncias, mas o grupo não tomou posição sobre a utilidade de interromper o desenvolvimento em todo o estado. O Wyoming Outdoor Council vê uma oportunidade tangível para avançar em novas políticas de data center com a chegada de legisladores e um novo diretor do Departamento de Qualidade Ambiental. Mas uma moratória, na sua opinião, não garantiria essas barreiras de protecção e é, portanto, uma forma arriscada de gastar o capital político limitado dos grupos ambientalistas. “Por sua própria natureza, uma moratória é temporária, e um pedido de moratória sobre data centers seria realmente um paliativo”, disse Jocelyn Wulf, gerente de campanha de data center do Wyoming Outdoor Council, a algumas dezenas de residentes de Cody este mês na prefeitura do data center que a organização hospedava. Representantes de ambas as organizações disseram ao Naturlink que acreditam que a nova safra de legisladores tem apetite para mudar a forma como o Wyoming gerencia a construção de data centers. Nem todos em Cody pareciam convencidos de que os data centers seriam um resultado positivo para o Wyoming. “Qual é o benefício?” perguntou Anne Trosper, uma residente do Wyoming que trabalhou nas indústrias de petróleo e gás e de conservação. “Onde o Wyoming consegue dinheiro com isso?” Os data centers pagam impostos sobre a propriedade e impostos sobre vendas de eletricidade no Wyoming, além de hospedar trabalhos de construção na fase de construção das instalações e empregar um pequeno número de trabalhadores permanentes quando estiverem em funcionamento. Mas os data centers poderiam fornecer receitas fiscais ao Wyoming de outra forma familiar, embora indireta. Com os centros de dados a exigir enormes quantidades de energia – o Projecto Tembo da Google, anteriormente conhecido como Project Jade, poderia consumir até 10 gigawatts de electricidade, mais de cinco vezes o consumo de electricidade em todo o estado do Wyoming – muitas empresas estão a optar por satisfazer essa procura no Wyoming com combustíveis fósseis. Grande parte da base tributária do Wyoming provém de royalties pagos pelas indústrias do carvão, petróleo e gás, e o estado tem defendido o apoio da administração Trump aos combustíveis fósseis. Para alimentar o crescimento da indústria, alguns condados do Wyoming estão a zonear parcelas de terreno como parques industriais, isentando as empresas de centros de dados de obter licenças ao abrigo da Lei de Localização Industrial do Wyoming. O Wyoming Outdoor Council descreve este acordo como uma “brecha” que as empresas utilizam para construir mais rapidamente e evitar alguma supervisão pública. “Isso significa que não há um processo de revisão abrangente por parte das agências estatais”, disse Wulf na reunião de Cody, para que as comunidades não recebessem os pagamentos de assistência de impacto associados a alguns projectos que passam por esse processo. “Isto não quer dizer que ainda não estejam sujeitos às leis estaduais e federais, mas estamos a perder esse processo de revisão como um todo (porque) os governos locais devem então rever estes projectos da melhor forma possível. Apesar das suas melhores intenções, os governos locais têm uma capacidade mais limitada para uma revisão completa.” Cheyenne, capital do Wyoming, passou anos cortejando o desenvolvimento de data centers com sucesso misto. Embora a nova construção tenha criado muitos empregos temporários e alguns permanentes, a escala, a dimensão e os impactos dos novos projectos geraram controvérsia. Em 2025, WyoFile relatou que a Microsoft solicitou uma licença aérea para operar 128 geradores a diesel de backup para um complexo de data center ao sul da cidade. Em julho deste ano, o Conselho de Serviços Públicos de Cheyenne descobriu que um empreiteiro que trabalhava em um projeto de data center para a Meta, empresa-mãe do Facebook, introduziu acidentalmente uma bactéria rara no sistema de tratamento de águas residuais da cidade. Esse incidente ocorreu depois que os membros do conselho municipal de Cheyenne votaram contra uma proposta de moratória de 12 meses sobre o desenvolvimento de data centers em maio deste ano. “Guardrails são a direção que deveríamos seguir”, disse Emma Jones, organizadora associada da filial de Wyoming do Sierra Club, ao Naturlink. “Muitos membros da comunidade querem ver grupos defendendo moratórias porque (o desenvolvimento do data center) está avançando muito rápido.” Mas pedir uma moratória seria imprudente sem um plano sobre o que realizar durante a pausa, disse ela. artigo.texto: European independent power producer (IPP), R.Power, has energised its first standalone energy storage project in Poland and is now supporting grid stability. The 5 MW/10 MWh Herby battery energy storage system (BESS) is the IPP’s first standalone energy storage project to be energised and serves as a precursor to an extensive rollout of operations across the company’s European BESS pipeline. Herby BESS has secured an optimisation agreement with Entrix, a European leading energy trader. Entrix is now managing the trading and optimisation across all relevant electricity markets, while the qualification process for balancing services provision is ongoing. The partnership provides a blueprint for integrating innovative optimisation approaches across R.Power’s wider European BESS operations. Herby began construction in 4Q25, having secured its long-term contract in Poland’s capacity market auction in December 2024 and also a supplementary capacity market contract organised in September 2026. The project paves the way for R.Power’s advanced utility scale BESS projects – Jedwabno, Dziegielewo, Gdansk, Scornicesti, and Studina – to follow in suit as R.Power scales up its battery energy storage capacity across Europe. Rafał Hajduk, Chief Commercial Officer at R.Power, commented: “Herby is the first standalone BESS in R.Power’s portfolio to reach the market. We look forward to working together with Entrix on this interesting asset with capacity market contracts and asymmetrical battery design. With a combined capacity of 1.6 GW/5.8 GWh across several large BESS assets in the pipeline today – including Jedwabno, Dzięgielewo, Gdańsk, Scornicesti, and Studina – we’re taking the next step on the journey to deliver the storage capacity Poland and Europe needs.”

artigo.texto: China's CATL (3750) on Tuesday reported slower profit growth in the third quarter, hit by fierce competition in the electric vehicle battery market as China's auto sales growth cooled. Net profit at the world's largest EV battery maker rose 14.5 percent from a year earlier to 21.2 billion yuan (US$3.17 billion), according to a stock exchange filing, missing analysts' estimate of a 41.2 percent increase based on LSEG SmartEstimate data. The third-quarter net profit growth, which follows a 36.5 percent rise in the second quarter, is the slowest in nearly two years. Revenue climbed 58.6 percent year-on-year to 165.2 billion yuan, undershooting forecasts for a 60.2 percent increase, after growing 56.9 percent in the previous quarter. Reuters

artigo.texto: A área técnica da Aneel (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica) defende que a participação de transmissoras nos leilões de baterias depende da reversão de parte da receita da atividade para reduzir as tarifas. O entendimento consta de Ofício Conjunto obtido pela reportagem que também exige autorização prévia da agência para participação nos certames e separação contábil, financeira e contratual entre os negócios. A orientação se apoia em um parecer da Procuradoria Federal junto à Aneel. O documento corrobora o entendimento da procuradoria de que estaria sendo prestado um serviço de engenharia pelas Transmissoras. O ofício responde a uma consulta apresentada pela Taesa sobre a participação de concessionárias de transmissão no leilão de baterias, previsto para ocorrer em dezembro. (CNN Brasil) Pan American pede à Aneel ressarcimento de R$ 18 milhões por curtailment A empresa argentina PAE (Pan American Energy) pediu à Aneel (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica) o ressarcimento por cortes de geração no complexo eólico Novo Horizonte, com compensações estimadas pela companhia em R$ 18 milhões. (CNN Brasil) Terras raras e privatizações no debate presidencial Minerais críticos e privatizações foram os temas de energia do primeiro debate entre Lula (PT) e Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), no domingo (18/10), na Band. Houve embate só nas terras raras. As privatizações vieram nas considerações finais de Lula, sem direito a resposta. Terras raras. Lula perguntou se Flávio pretende “entregar” aos EUA as terras raras e os minerais críticos do país e disse que o adversário prometeu aderir ao Escudo das Américas. Flávio chamou a acusação de “mais uma fake news” e disse que foi aos EUA defender as empresas e os produtos brasileiros contra o tarifaço. Em março, numa conferência conservadora nos EUA, Flávio disse que o Brasil é a solução para os estadunidenses deixarem de depender da China em minerais críticos. O governo Lula descartou aderir à aliança de minerais proposta por Trump. (Agência Eixos) Aguila Energia financiará novos projetos com caixa própria A petroleira independente Águila Energia pretende financiar novos projetos de óleo e gás por meio da geração de caixa dos cinco campos terrestres que vão iniciar produção nos próximos meses. Com essa receita, a Águila pretende seguir com o plano de perfuração de novos poços nas cinco áreas, com investimentos de R$ 80 milhões, além de iniciar os estudos de 14 áreas em terra, arrematadas no leilão realizado pela Agência Nacional do Petróleo, Gás Natural e Biocombustíveis (ANP) em 7 de outubro. (Valor Econômico) Teles questionam obrigação de investir em data centers no leilão para expansão da telefonia móvel A Telefônica Brasil, dona da Vivo, e a Claro questionaram a proposta da Agência Nacional de Telecomunicações (Anatel) de incluir investimentos em data centers entre os compromissos previstos para as empresas vencedoras do futuro leilão de frequências destinadas à expansão da telefonia móvel, na porção superior da faixa de 6 Ghz. Em audiência pública realizada sexta-feira (16), as operadoras defenderam que os recursos sejam direcionados prioritariamente à ampliação da cobertura e à melhoria da qualidade dos serviços de telecomunicações. (Valor Econômico) China propõe controlar exportações de tecnologias para equipamentos solares A China propôs controles de exportação sobre 12 tecnologias utilizadas na fabricação de equipamentos solares, citando preocupações com a segurança nacional, como parte de uma revisão mais ampla que também abrange inteligência artificial e biotecnologia. O Ministério do Comércio do país propôs acrescentar as tecnologias fotovoltaicas à lista chinesa de controle de exportações, acrescentando que é necessária maior supervisão porque as tecnologias solares vêm sendo cada vez mais utilizadas em áreas sensíveis, como a aeroespacial e a de defesa nacional. O anúncio foi feito na útlima sexta-feira (16). (Folha de S. Paulo – com agência Reuters) PANORAMA DA MÍDIA O primeiro debate entre os dois principais concorrentes à Presidência da República, realizado ontem (18), pela TV Bandeirante, é destaque hoje na mídia, com reportagens, artigos e análises. O senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) e o presidente Lula (PT), adversários no segundo turno das eleições, trocaram acusações de corrupção, fizeram perguntas que deixaram o outro sem resposta, provocaram e envolveram familiares no primeiro debate entre os dois, na Band, na noite deste domingo (18). (Folha de S. Paulo) Com respostas curtas, ambos priorizaram manejar seu tempo de fala na tentativa de evitar que o adversário tivesse a palavra final, o que deixou o debate truncado e recheado de ofensas pessoais. (O Globo) “Decepcionante”, “triste”, “vergonhoso”, “infeliz”, “irresponsável”, “uma piada”. Foi assim que participantes de um grupo de pesquisa qualitativa descreveram o primeiro confronto entre os candidatos à Presidência Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) e Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), promovido neste domingo, 18, pelo Grupo Bandeirantes, Estadão, TV Gazeta, TV Cultura e Jovem Pan. Para esses eleitores, faltou qualidade e sobrou baixo nível nas discussões entre os dois nomes que querem governar o País pelos próximos quatro anos. (O Estado de S. Paulo) ** Valor Econômico: Criticado por especialistas em contas públicas e adversários pela série de medidas anunciadas pelo presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva às vésperas das eleições, como o aumento do Bolsa Família, o governo enviará ao Congresso Nacional uma proposta para alterar o Projeto de Lei Orçamentária Anual (PLOA) de 2027. artigo.texto: Salem does not have any undeveloped land that is currently zoned properly for a potential data center, but the city is involved in an upcoming data center in Roanoke County. Salem has just over an 11% ownership stake in the Wood Haven Technology Park property, at the junction of interstates 81 and 581, that the Western Virginia Regional Industrial Facility Authority voted last month to begin selling off to a data center developer. About a week before the Roanoke County site was announced, Google broke ground on another data center campus at Greenfield Industrial Center in Botetourt County. The two projects have caused a wealth of public opposition in the region, much of that coming from the Southwest Virginia Data Center Transparency Alliance, a group that has been requesting documents regarding data centers from key players and speaking out in opposition to the projects. The five candidates running for two seats on the Salem City Council have different things to say about data centers. The candidates include Republicans Hunter Holliday and J.D. Taylor and independents Mark Henrickson, A.J. Harpold and Jeffrey Hoeflich-Nickels. Holliday, completing his first term, is the only incumbent in the race. An Army veteran who grew up in Salem and returned to the city nine years ago, Holliday said his feelings on data centers and their growth in the region are “up in the air.” “For me to say I’m against it, I can’t say that,” Holliday said during a phone call Wednesday. “For me to say I’m for them, I also can’t say that.” He said he lived in Fairfax during the time when Northern Virginia was beginning to see a rapid growth of data centers and that he thinks data centers bring in good things for localities through an influx of tax revenue. He said he saw positive impacts on Northern Virginia’s schools and roads from that revenue while living there. Holliday said he feels that he needs to do more research on data centers and that, if re-elected, he would support chartering a bus to bring a group of residents to see firsthand a data center in Northern Virginia. He said he is not sure yet if this would be allowed — data centers don’t exactly have open-door policies for the public. Holliday declined to comment on what the Salem City Council’s involvement was in the Wood Haven project before the Sept. 11 vote by the regional authority to initiate the purchase agreement. Henrickson, a retired developer who now sits on the city’s planning commission, said recently in an interview that he looks at this as a regional issue, rather than a Salem-specific election matter. He said he feels people just don’t know enough yet about data centers, citing concerns with the amounts of energy and water they use. “Somewhere, technology is going to catch up,” he said. “We’re gonna figure this out. We’re not there yet.” Henrickson said he’d like to see the region integrate expertise from Virginia Tech’s engineering program in regional decisions involving data centers. Taylor, a pastor who has lived in Salem for a decade, said in a recent interview that it’s surprising that nobody has asked him about data centers yet during his campaign. He said as far as Salem is concerned, other “holes” need to be filled before managing data centers becomes a priority. He said the city needs to focus on replacing hundreds of jobs lost from the closures of two major plants in the city: General Electric in 2018 and Yokohama Tire earlier this year. He’d much rather see a semiconductor company or another manufacturer that makes parts that go into a data center, he said — arguing that such companies may bring more jobs to Salem than a data center would. He said “word doesn’t get around until it’s too late in many cases,” and that “you can’t fault” the Roanoke officials who put information out on social media about the Wood Haven project. He also said it’s hard to predict how much revenue will come directly into the locality in some cases. What he’s referring to are statements put on social media by Roanoke Vice Mayor Terry McGuire and city Councilman Phazhon Nash, stating their opposition to a data center in Wood Haven and explaining Roanoke City’s involvement in the project. This led to a statement from Mayor Joe Cobb, who said the two had violated the council’s code of conduct, and the establishment of a professional standards committee for the council. A.J. Harpold, who returned to Salem three years ago after growing up here, said the city can’t ignore data center growth. Harpold is opening a small business downtown and is a labor union organizer for dancers and choreographers. She said she hasn’t seen Salem residents react as negatively as Roanoke County and Roanoke city’s residents have reacted to the two data center developments. “I don’t think Salem has fully taken that in, fully absorbed what’s happening,” she said. “It still feels ‘over there.’ I also don’t think as many people knew about it in Salem … I don’t think anyone in Salem expected it to be on their door front.” She said she expects to see more reactions from the city’s residents as plans continue for Wood Haven, which she said Salem has a “fairly sizable” ownership in with its 11% stake. On data centers, Harpold said, “We have to be involved in some way. We can’t ignore it and pretend it doesn’t exist.” “If we can have a say in the direction of what this looks like with a data center, if we can have a say in doing the studies and finding out more about the long-term electricity and water usage, then obviously we should be involved,” she said. artigo.texto: A landmark permitting reform bill has united U.S. senators from both parties, but it is dividing the artificial intelligence data center sector. Some industry leaders say it would make data centers easier to build, while others worry it would make them substantially more expensive. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is being called “the most significant permitting reform bill in years” — intended to accelerate the build-out of major infrastructure and other large-scale projects across the U.S. The bill enjoys support on both sides of the aisle and is expected to clear the Senate during the lame-duck session following November's midterm elections. If it is signed into law, BAAJA would likely have significant implications for the data center industry, potentially rewriting the federal rulebook on how data centers purchase electricity and connect to regional grids. But industry insiders are split on whether the legislation would ultimately be a net positive for the sector or usher in disaster for at least some firms pursuing large-scale digital infrastructure projects. Some within the industry — and some critics of the sector — say BAAJA is poised to fuel further acceleration of the AI data center boom by flattening permitting hurdles and codifying a clear pathway to acquiring power. But others say consumer protection provisions in the bill will make acquiring power much more expensive, adding significant development costs early in projects that could push smaller operators to the sidelines. “Upfront capex, especially speculative, is a death knell,” said Harmol Samra, CEO of AI data center provider Host Digital. “This is just going to slow everyone down.” BAAJA is centered on measures intended to speed up the construction of energy assets, power transmission and other infrastructure, plus other major industrial projects for industries like manufacturing and mining. To do so, the bill would impose firm deadlines for permit approvals, exempt more projects from lengthy reviews, limit how long approvals can be challenged and give previously approved projects greater legal protection. Controversially, it would also make significant changes to the National Environmental Policy Act, the Clean Water Act and the Endangered Species Act. Those provisions have drawn vocal opposition from some environmental groups, with the Center for Biological Diversity calling it a “back-door deal” meant specifically to accelerate data center development. “This would be a golden ticket for huge AI data centers and tech billionaires. Gutting environmental safeguards means opening the floodgates for more gas-powered data centers fouling the air and draining communities’ water supplies,” said Camden Weber, senior climate and energy policy specialist at the Center for Biological Diversity. While other environmental groups have been more receptive — particularly to provisions aimed at accelerating transmission infrastructure that could bring more renewable generation onto the grid — there is truth in the notion that data centers will benefit from faster permitting. Large campuses can face federal delays when projects affect wetlands or trigger environmental or historic preservation reviews. More consequentially, faster approvals for new transmission and generation could shorten the wait for electricity in markets where developers can wait years for grid connections. Yet beyond its permitting reforms, BAAJA also contains a separate set of provisions aimed squarely at data centers, specifically at one of the sector’s most contentious issues: who ends up paying for the billions of dollars of new power infrastructure needed to provide them with electricity. The measures, which apply to data centers larger than 20 megawatts, are intended to ensure that regular electricity customers don’t get stuck with the bill for new power plants and infrastructure for electric transmission built specifically for data centers. Concerns that homeowners, businesses and other existing customers are effectively subsidizing grid improvements driven mainly by data center demand have become a central talking point in a rising wave of opposition to data center development. And lawmakers from both parties have been eager to show they are taking these concerns seriously. The Trump administration’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge, announced in March, aimed to address the same concern, with major tech firms committing to cover the full cost of power delivery and grid updates needed to serve them. But what constitutes “full cost” has remained a matter of interpretation. A report released this month by four Democratic senators found that tech giants generally accept responsibility for the cost of infrastructure built exclusively for them, such as a substation serving a single data center campus. But the answer is murkier when the new infrastructure also benefits other customers, such as a transmission line built primarily to deliver power to a new campus that also improves reliability elsewhere on the grid. Consumer advocates have argued that in such a case, the data center should bear all costs that would not have existed “but for” its arrival. Tech giants and other developers, according to the report, have generally only been willing to cover, at most, a portion of such shared costs and have fought with state regulators to shoulder as few of such shared grid costs as possible. “There is a significant gap between data center developers and the public regarding how much data centers should pay for shared infrastructure, and particularly for infrastructure built primarily, but not exclusively, for their benefit,” the report’s authors wrote. The standards for what constitutes a data center’s fair share of grid costs vary significantly across the balkanized U.S. grid system. artigo.texto: NTPC Renewable Energy Limited (NTPC REL) invites bids for an EPC package with land to develop up to 600 MW of solar capacity. The EPC project developer is required to arrange land for the solar project and the BESS project owner This comprises a (300 MW + 300 MW) ISTS-connected ground-mounted solar project near the Dhule Solar Project in Maharashtra. Bids have been invited until November 13, 2026. Brief Scope of Work Under the scope of work, the developer is require to handle design, engineering, manufacturing, supply, packing, forwarding, transportation, unloading, storage, and installation of the solar project. The bidders are expected to provide a 300 MW solar project under Block 1 for a minimum net worth / turnover threshold of Rs. 192 Crores. Under block 2, the bidder is expected to provide a 300 MW for a minimum financial requirement of Rs. 192 Crores, bringing the combined (Block 1 + Block 2) requirement to Rs. 384 Crores. The scope also requires the commissioning as well as the operation and maintenance (O&M) of the grid-connected solar PV project located near NTPC REL’s Dhule Solar Project. This includes the power evacuation system from the solar project to NTPC REL’s Dhule Solar Project PSS / ISTS substation, as well as the development of a terminal bay at NTPC REL’s Dhule Project PSS. Additionally, the scope includes identifying, acquiring, and completing the total transfer of ownership or lease of encumbrance-free land (including land for BESS) in favor of NTPC Renewable Energy Limited. The developer is required to supply, erect, and commission new 220 kV terminal line bays at NTPC REL’s Dhule Solar Project PSS. The EPC developer must develop a dedicated 220 kV transmission line, including Right of Way (ROW), from the solar plant to NTPC REL’s Dhule Solar Project PSS. The project comprises two blocks of 300 MW each. The evacuation scheme may involve either a single common PSS or two separate PSSs.

artigo.texto: Industrial Manufacturing U.S. Data Center Construction Starts Still Soaring Despite Some Bumps in the Road News reports about data centers being delayed or cancelled, or states and municipalities enacting or considering moratoria on data-center construction, are real, but are not the whole story, according to Industrial Info Resources data tracking. Released Tuesday, October 20, 2026 Reports related to this article: Written by John Egan for IIR News Intelligence (Sugar Land, Texas) Summary News reports about data centers being delayed or cancelled, or states and municipalities enacting or considering moratoria on data-center construction, are real, but are not the whole story, according to Industrial Info Resources data tracking. In fact, the pace of data-center construction starts in the U.S. is growing much faster than the pace of cancellations, delays, or moratoria being considered or enacted, meaning the drive to build data centers in the U.S. is still growing robustly. High Profile Announcements Obscure More Complex Picture Recent high-profile announcements that Big Tech firms or data-center developers have delayed or abandoned planned data centers, or that a growing number of communities are considering or enacting pauses on new data-center construction, may give a casual observer the idea that the drive to build data-centers in the U.S. is slowing, perhaps significantly. But data tracked by Industrial Info Resources tell a different story. While project abandonments and moratoria efforts are real, they constitute only a small part of the overall picture, the proverbial tail of the dog. The bigger picture is that U.S. data-center construction starts are continuing to grow far more rapidly. Project Activity Continues to Surge "Delays are real, but they are not the story that some headlines suggest," said Shane Mullins, IIR senior vice president for energy market solutions. "What we are seeing is developers prioritizing sites that already have power, or that can be powered with less risk of a delay--for example, at a location where a permit that is already in hand, or land that is not under a local or state moratorium. The pie is still growing fast. Even a sharp rise in moratoria is small next to the volume of projects moving into construction." "Weak, grid-dependent, early-stage projects are falling out and the projects that can get power are moving," he continued. "Construction activity still is ramping." New U.S. data-center project value entering Industrial Info Resources coverage has risen every half-year since late 2023, from about US$27 billion a month to about US$350 billion a month since April 2026. Monthly construction kickoffs have roughly doubled over the past year, though they have leveled off since an April 2026 peak of US$48.5 billion. The value of delayed projects was near zero until late 2025 and reached US$29.9 billion in July 2026 and US$27.6 billion in August 2026, he noted. In Industrial Info Resources' U.S. Behind the Meter Data-Center Power Development platform, monthly project activity has gone from US$10 billion to US$30 billion through 2023, to US$100 billion to US$250 billion in 2025, and US$220 billion to US$360 billion so far in 2026. Through early October, about $2.9 trillion has been added to that dataset this year. IIR's data showed that about $425 billion of data-center projects are under active construction in the U.S. now (part of roughly $643 billion globally), with substantially more value in earlier stages of development. By the Numbers - 5.1: Total investment value (TIV), in trillions, of U.S. data-center projects that have been proposed or under construction in the U.S. - 48.5: The US dollar value of data-center projects that began construction in April 2026 - 220-360: The monthly average value, in US billions, of data projects that have entered Industrial Info Resources coverage in 2026 - 27.6: The dollar value, in US billions, of data-center projects that were delayed in August 2026 What Factors Affect Data-Center Construction Decisions? "I'm not going to say moratoria aren't real, because they are," Mullins continued. For more on the data-center moratoria, see June 8, 2026, article - New York Lawmakers Pass One-Year Permitting Ban for New Data Centers. But, he said, "the data-center pie is growing so fast that even a surge of delays and moratoria this year is relatively small potatoes compared to projects that are moving into construction." For more on that, see September 22, 2026, article -- As Data-Center Construction Plans Soar, U.S. Electric Utilities Race to Serve Once-in-a-Lifetime Load Growth. Non-moratoria factors, including rising interest rates, can affect a developer's decision to begin constructing a data center. The interest rate on 10-year and 30-year U.S. Treasury securities is higher now than it has been in nearly two decades. And that's for bonds guaranteed by the U.S. government, which carry a AA+ rating by the major rating agencies. For issuers with lower credit rating, interest rates would be higher, potentially significantly higher, depending on their credit rating. Other factors affecting data-center construction decisions are the local conditions, including: - What is the cost of land? - Is a proposed location close to major fiber-optic routes, internet-exchange points and cloud-provider networks? - Are tax credits available, or are they in the process of being limited or withdrawn? - Is there a surplus, or a shortfall, of electric generation? - Is there an adequate supply of affordable skilled craft labor locally? Regarding the Electric Power situation, a growing number of electric utilities and regional grid managers have enacted a "bring your own generation" policy In which developers and Big Tech firms need to supply their own generation. artigo.texto: Australian consumer electronics company Laser says it next generation of ChargeCore powerbanks with next-generation semi-solid-state battery technology are the safest you can buy today. The new Laser ChargeCore battery range include models with three capacities and deliver safety and stability thanks to the onboard semi-solid-state technology. They are available in 10,000mAh, 20,000mAh, and 27,000mAh capacities with progressively more powerful 20W and 35W USB-C PD (Power Delivery) fast charging options. Semi-solid-state battery technology is an evolution in battery chemistry and the biggest advantage is improved thermal stability while still offering stronger and faster charging performance. The advancements in the battery technology can now be implemented in consumer products, including power banks that store and deliver more power in a compact design while remaining stable even under demanding conditions. The batteries have a gel-like core, which helps reduce overheating and fire risk. Its enhanced safety reduces heat, which means the battery has a longer life and can last through more charges and will not catch fire. Laser put the new ChargeCore semi-solid state batteries through rigorous testing and even when the battery was pierced, hammered, and sliced, it still worked and didn’t catch fire. Laser is celebrating its 40th anniversary 2027 and has made a name for itself as delivering affordable yet high-quality tech to Australian customers. Has sold power banks to Australians for the last 15 years and it prides itself as being on the cutting edge of battery technology. Laser launched Australia’s first range of LiFePO4 battery technology in 2025 and is now among the first to move to semi-solid-state technology with this latest range. “We’ve been closely following semi solid state battery development for some time, since first visiting an EV factory several years ago, and advancements since that time mean that it can now move into smaller, more compact options,” says Chris Lau, Laser Managing Director. “Simply put, I believe that semi-solid state chemistry makes this the safest powerbank technology available in Australia today. “We are focused on safety and peace of mind, and we know that it is a huge concern for Australian consumers these days when buying powerbanks,” “I’ve personally had the opportunity to see first-hand the testing that goes into the manufacturing of these semi solid state powerbanks, including the stress testing placed on the battery technology. “It gives you an appreciation for just how much engineering, testing and development sits behind something consumers simply put in their bag and use every day.” The Laser ChargeCore semi-solid state batteries include easy-to-read digital displays which the battery’s remaining capacity. And they also have built-in protection against overcharging, overcurrent, short circuits and overheating. Each battery has three ports: two USB-A and one USB-C while the 27,000mAh battery has two USB-Cs and one USB-A – so you can charge three devices at the same time. Each battery also comes with a 60W-rated cable and a built-in heat sensor. The batteries will be able to charge an iPhone 17 to 50% in about 30 minutes. The batteries will be able to charge smartphones, tablets, portable gaming devices, earphones, cameras, drones and much more. The ChargeCore 27,000mAh semi-solid-state power bank has a higher capacity output and can charge laptops, including the MacBook Air, Chromebooks and Surface devices. The new series is available in Black, Galactica, Grey, and Dark Cherry. Pricing and availability ChargeCore Everyday Semi Solid State Series at Harvey Norman and Laser Online – 10,000mAh with 20W USB-C PD – $49.95 (Black available now, Galactica, Grey, and Dark Cherry coming soon) – 20,000mAh with 20W USB-C PD – $69.95 (Black available now, Galactica, and Dark Cherry coming soon) – 27,000mAh with 35W USB-C PD – $99.95 (Black, available now)

artigo.texto: Coral Energía, an Argentine renewable energy developer and power marketer, is entering a key phase of operational growth driven by solar projects under construction, new battery energy storage systems (BESS) and the exploration of new commercial opportunities in the country"s evolving electricity market. The company expects to finish 2026 with around 260 MW of renewable capacity built within its contracted portfolio, while advancing several parallel developments that will define its position among Argentina"s renewable energy suppliers. "This is a year of growth and consolidation for Coral. Our goal is to strengthen our position among the key players in renewable electricity sales. Once all projects are operational, we will evaluate where the market is heading and where we should position ourselves," said Marcelo Álvarez, Director of Planning and Institutional Relations at Coral Energía, during an interview at Future Energy Summit (FES) Argentina. Coral Energía currently operates four solar parks built under the Generfe program in Santa Fe province, totalling 20 MW of installed capacity. At the same time, the company is advancing projects awarded under RenMDI, a national renewable energy auction designed to promote distributed and regional generation across Argentina. In addition, Coral Energía will soon begin construction of two battery energy storage systems (BESS) awarded through the AlmaGBA program, which aims to improve power system reliability in the Buenos Aires metropolitan area. The projects include: Project Capacity Grid connection Payment BESS Pilar 50 MW Edenor distribution grid USD 11,461 per MW/month BESS Parque 50 MW Edenor distribution grid USD 11,979 per MW/month Overall, the company currently accumulates around 400 MW between contracted renewable capacity and projects under development. Coral Energía"s strategic roadmap targets 1 GW of renewable energy contracts by 2030, reflecting the growing diversification of contracting mechanisms and business models in Argentina"s electricity market. The company"s strategy includes expanding its participation in several segments of Argentina"s energy market, including: - Standalone battery storage projects are expected under the upcoming AlmaSADI tender, which could allocate around 700 MW of BESS capacity across the country. - Renewable projects connected to distribution networks, where available grid capacity may allow new developments. - Corporate power purchase agreements (PPAs) within Argentina"s Mercado a Término de Energías Renovables (MATER). - New demand segments, such as mining operations and data centres, are increasingly seeking a renewable electricity supply. SIn storage, we are evaluating projects between 100 MW and 200 MW, although smaller systems could also emerge," Álvarez explained. Regarding renewable projects connected to distribution networks, the executive highlighted that grid node capacity determines the feasible project size. "We want to build the largest projects possible within each node"s technical limits. Today we have many developments between 10 MW and 20 MW, and the next step is increasing that range to 3050 MW projects, he said. This approach reflects growing congestion in Argentina"s high-voltage transmission system, which is encouraging developers to pursue generation projects connected directly to distribution networks. Álvarez also noted that mergers and acquisitions (M&A) could become part of the company"s growth strategy. "There may also be opportunities to acquire renewable parks already developed for the MATER market, particularly those with dispatch priority, he added. Potential role in transmission infrastructure projects Beyond renewable generation and storage, Coral Energía is also evaluating participation in electric transmission expansion projects in Argentina. The government is expected to launch tender documents this year for AMBA I, a major transmission project aimed at reinforcing the Buenos Aires metropolitan grid. Two additional high-voltage transmission projects could follow in late 2026 or 2027: Project Voltage Route Río Diamante Charlone O"Higgins 500 kV Central-west Argentina Puerto Madryn Choele Choel Bahía Blanca 500 kV Patagonia to the Buenos Aires region SCoral Energía could participate as part of a consortium. Our parent group, Corven, is actively evaluating involvement in some of these projects, Álvarez said. However, he noted that from a generator"s perspective, the economic participation in transmission projects is often relatively limited. As a result, developing new transmission infrastructure typically requires multi-stakeholder consortia involving different actors in the power system with aligned interests.

artigo.texto: ACCURE AI-based platform to provide analytics for Fidra's 1.4GW Thorpe Marsh BESS Germany-headquartered ACCURE will use its AI-driven software to provide independent analytics from factory testing through to commercial operations. Fidra Energy has selected ACCURE Battery Intelligence to provide battery analytics for its 1.4GW/3.1GWh Thorpe Marsh battery energy storage system (BESS). Germany-headquartered ACCURE will use its AI-driven software to provide independent analytics from factory testing through to commercial operations. At factory testing and commissioning, it will support the verification of battery performance against project requirements. Once the Thorpe Marsh project in Doncaster comes online, ACCURE’s predictive analysis will track battery health, state of charge (SOC) and rack availability. Construction at the project began in July this year, and it is due to enter commercial operations in 2027. Approved in early 2025, the 1.4GW project is the largest of its kind in the UK and represents over £1 billion in funding, including finance from the state-owned National Wealth Fund. In September last year, EDF was selected to provide long-term optimisation for 560MW of the project’s capacity, providing route-to-market (RtM) services. Statkraft has a power purchase agreement (PPA) with Fidra to optimise 280MW. ACCURE, for its part, is already onboarded at several Gore Street Energy Storage Fund’s UK sites, including the 80MW Stony project, which was energised last summer and is also optimised in the market by EDF; and Lower Road, a 10MW project that went online in 2020 and is optimised by Arenko. Notably, Gore Street’s collaboration with ACCURE at the time was a UK-first agreement that improved the insurance terms for projects in its portfolio. Read more about:

artigo.texto: Portland City Council considers putting new limits, regulations on data centers PORTLAND (WGME) -- Portland leaders discussed possible new restrictions on data centers Monday. It comes after the city's Housing and Economic Development Committee wrote a memo outlining potential holes in the existing ordinances. It says the ordinances “do not adequately address” the infrastructure demands as well as environmental and neighborhood impacts of data centers. Some of their concerns include land and water usage, noise pollution, and potentially higher electricity costs. "I'm opposed to data centers and want them to be regulated completely out of Portland, Maine," one Portland resident said. Scarborough, Gorham, Saco, Sanford, Westbrook, and other towns have approved temporary moratoriums on these centers to allow more time to address community concerns and update local zoning ordinances. Portland is considering doing the same, but no final decisions have been made.

artigo.texto: Norway's sovereign wealth fund is still avoiding battery storage, fearing a decline in returns Norway's sovereign wealth fund, the largest of its kind in the world, is not yet investing in battery storage. The reasons are the insufficient scale of available projects and the risk of so-called market cannibalization, in which a growing number of batteries gradually narrows the price spreads on which their operators make money. The fund nevertheless considers energy storage a potentially suitable complement to its investments in wind and solar power. “We see significant risk of market cannibalization from batteries,” said Borge Rygh Sivertsen, portfolio manager for new energy at Norway's sovereign wealth fund, at the Energirike conference in Haugesund, Norway. According to him, the economics of battery storage are based primarily on the differences between high and low electricity prices. Batteries buy electricity when prices are low and then sell it when electricity is more expensive. However, as the number of storage facilities grows, more operators compete for the same opportunities. If many batteries buy electricity during cheap hours and feed it into the grid when prices are high, the price spreads gradually narrow. This reduces the potential returns of individual projects and makes their future revenues less predictable. According to Sivertsen, this uncertainty is a significant obstacle to investment. The fund is therefore waiting for now, even though it considers storage a technology that could complement its portfolio of wind and solar power plants. Available projects are not large enough Another obstacle is the size of the investments. The Norwegian fund typically considers projects worth around 500 million euros, or approximately 5 billion Norwegian kroner. According to Sivertsen, it cannot invest in smaller projects on sufficiently competitive terms. The fund already invests in renewable energy in Europe. Through partnerships with RWE, Ørsted, Iberdrola and EnBW, it has acquired stakes in projects with a total installed capacity of 3.3 GW. The fund's investment mandate allows it to invest in renewable energy in Europe and North America, across the energy value chain from generation to electricity distribution. Energy storage is also covered, but its economic attractiveness must meet the fund's requirements. Investment environment clouded by uncertainty According to Sivertsen, geopolitical uncertainty, fluctuations in natural gas prices and higher inflation are also making energy projects harder to finance. These factors increase the cost of capital and make it harder for buyers and sellers to agree on project prices. The fund representative also noted that investors have recently been placing greater emphasis on energy security, while some have partially scaled back their financing of renewable energy. Uncertainty about future electricity supply and demand is therefore another risk that must be taken into account in investment decisions. Renewables currently account for approximately 1% of the value of Norway's sovereign wealth fund. According to Sivertsen, this share could rise to 2% under its investment mandate. artigo.texto: Artigo traduzido automaticamente por IA, ler original Dinâmicas em transformação: o que observar na construção de data centers nos EUA. 21 outubro 2026 O ambiente que envolve a construção de centros de dados continua a mudar. Com uma ordem executiva de 18 de agosto que torna juridicamente vinculativas as normas do seu Programa de Desenvolvimento Responsável de Infraestrutura (GRID, na sigla em inglês), a Pensilvânia, EUA, tornou-se recentemente o estado mais recente a introduzir novos requisitos que regem o desenvolvimento de centros de dados, acrescentando mais um exemplo de uma mudança mais ampla que está ocorrendo em todo o país. Depois de anos de competição acirrada entre os estados para atrair esses projetos, os legisladores e as comunidades estão cada vez mais fazendo perguntas diferentes; em particular, quem deve pagar pela infraestrutura necessária para suportá-los. Para os membros da Specialized Carriers & Rigging Association (SC&RA), essa é uma tendência que vale a pena acompanhar. Os novos requisitos da Pensilvânia incorporam a acessibilidade energética, a proteção ambiental, o uso da água, a contratação local e os benefícios para a comunidade de forma mais direta no processo de desenvolvimento. Os centros de dados também estão sendo removidos do programa de licenciamento acelerado do estado, e espera-se que os desenvolvedores cubram o custo da nova infraestrutura elétrica necessária para atender às suas instalações, em vez de repassar esses custos para outros clientes. As implicações vão além da Pensilvânia. Nova York suspendeu a emissão de licenças para grandes centros de dados, enquanto o Texas analisou minuciosamente projetos que aguardam conexão à sua rede elétrica. Em julho, legisladores em 15 estados haviam considerado algum tipo de restrição à construção de centros de dados. A discussão agora não se limita mais a discutir onde os centros de dados podem ser construídos . Cada vez mais, o foco é se a energia, a água, o transporte e outras infraestruturas necessárias para suportá-los conseguirão acompanhar o ritmo, e como os custos e impactos desse desenvolvimento devem ser distribuídos. Último exemplo A Pensilvânia oferece um exemplo útil. Segundo autoridades estaduais, mais de 100 centros de dados foram propostos no estado no ano anterior. No entanto, apenas uma fração deles avançou significativamente na fase de licenciamento, e somente cinco receberam todas as licenças necessárias para a primeira fase de desenvolvimento. Projetos já avançados podem absorver requisitos adicionais e continuar avançando, enquanto empreendimentos em estágio inicial ou especulativos têm mais flexibilidade. Essa distinção é importante para empresas que planejam equipamentos, pessoal e recursos em função da atividade de construção prevista. Além disso, o mercado de data centers evoluiu tão rapidamente que uma enorme carteira de projetos pode gerar uma compreensível sensação de certeza. Mas um projeto proposto não é um projeto aprovado, e um projeto aprovado não é necessariamente um projeto em construção. Os membros da SC&RA devem entender em que pé estão os projetos que acompanham. As principais licenças foram obtidas? Há energia suficiente disponível? Quem é responsável pelas melhorias necessárias na rede elétrica? As necessidades de água estão se tornando um problema? A oposição local está aumentando? As políticas estaduais ou municipais mudaram desde o anúncio do projeto? Essas não são questões que as empresas de guindastes e transporte sejam responsáveis por resolver. Mas as respostas delas podem influenciar quando — ou mesmo se — o equipamento chegará ao local. Também podem existir efeitos subsequentes para os projetos que prosseguem. Requisitos ambientais adicionais, compromissos de contratação local , acordos de benefícios comunitários e obrigações de infraestrutura podem aumentar os custos de desenvolvimento. Mais trabalho de engenharia, consultoria e regulamentação pode prolongar o tempo até o início da construção. Mudanças na viabilidade econômica do projeto podem, eventualmente, influenciar cronogramas, aquisições e contratos em toda a cadeia de suprimentos. Enorme oportunidade Nada disso diminui a enorme oportunidade que os data centers continuam a representar para o nosso setor. Isso, no entanto, reforça a importância de compreendermos o mercado para além do trabalho que temos imediatamente em mãos. Empresas de sucesso sempre acompanharam de perto o desenvolvimento da demanda futura. No mercado atual de data centers, elas deveriam estar atentas a outro fator igualmente importante: as condições que determinarão se essa demanda se transformará em trabalho concreto. A Pensilvânia pode ser o exemplo mais recente. Provavelmente não será o último. Este artigo foi publicado originalmente na edição de outubro da revista American Cranes & Transport. artigo.texto: ‘No data centers’: Fairfield residents question possible Patmos data center, C-PACE financing Chants of “No data centers” echoed outside Fairfield City Hall as residents protested a proposed Patmos data center and demanded more transparency from city leaders. The project has been under consideration for months, even though the Fairfield City Council passed a moratorium on future data centers. Questions surrounding a potential $150 million C-PACE financing arrangement are now adding to residents’ concerns. Some residents fear the financing could be used to help construct the Patmos facility and leave the city responsible for the debt. Mayor Herman Carnes strongly disputes that claim and said C-PACE is a financing option available to eligible businesses — not money the city would borrow to build the data center. Gilda Walker, with the Fairfield Environmental Justice Alliance, said residents have not received clear information about the project’s status or what actions city officials may have taken. “People should not have to rely on rumors or to piece together answers on their own,” Walker said. “We also need clear information about the financial side. The city is considering a resolution of intent that could help the project secure financing before the city takes that step. Residents deserve to understand what the resolution does, what commitments it could involve, and whether public resources or incentives are part of the proposal.” Carnes said residents are misunderstanding the purpose of the C-PACE program and insisted it is separate from the Patmos project. C-PACE, which stands for Commercial Property Assessed Clean Energy, is generally used to finance eligible energy, water and property-resilience improvements. Carnes described it as one tool in Fairfield’s effort to attract investment and revitalize the city. “Fairfield has a lot of buildings that are in real need of a lot of things roofs, electrical planning — you name it — before they can move in,” Carnes said. “The city is not tied to whatever amount the citizens are thinking. Those are accusations that are not factual. It's just to try to help bring business to the city of Fairfield. The citizens elected us to revitalize and try to find out ways to be creative. We're doing our job. Huntsville, [Texas] — as a matter of fact — they're using C-Pace. Instead of being behind, we are progressively finding new ways to bring business here in the city of Fairfield.” Questions about transparency intensified during Monday’s protest when Carnes handed reporters a document explaining how C-PACE financing works. A resident called out, “Mayor! Mayor! May I have one of those?” but her request went unanswered. Protesters said the exchange strengthened their concerns about access to information. Carnes, however, maintained that the city has been open with the public and that its actions are documented. “It's a good fit is what's needed,” Carnes said. “The city has been idle for two decades. That’s too long for nothing. City funds will not be used at all. Period. The city has nothing to do with that. That's a that's misleading for the citizens that don't know — putting this out. That's not true.” Walker said residents want information before any decisions are made, not after the fact. “A project with major effects on our community should be presented openly, examined carefully, and discussed with the people who will live with the results,” Walker said. “Today, we're asking city leaders to release the relevant documents and studies, explain the project's cost and expected benefits, and whole accessible public meetings where residents can ask questions and get direct answers.” A public town hall is expected to be part of the process before the C-PACE program can move forward. During its latest meeting, the Fairfield City Council voted to first hold a dedicated work session to discuss the program in its entirety. No date has been announced for either the work session or town hall.

artigo.texto: Stellenbosch solar and battery storage: Wine harvest shows why timing counts Stellenbosch’s procurement of up to 41.9 MW of solar photovoltaic capacity and 14.8 MWh of battery storage, awarded, 22 May 2026, comes as new data from Vergenoegd Löw shows how sharply electricity demand can rise during the wine harvest. The two developments point to a broader local energy issue: whether new solar and storage can help meet the needs of Stellenbosch’s commercial customers when demand is highest, beyond adding lower-cost power over the course of a year. At Vergenoegd Löw, an August 2026 PV-monitoring report provided to Cape Business News earlier this month shows what that seasonal demand looks like at an individual commercial operation. Harvest drives the electricity surge In February, the estate used more than twice as much electricity as it did in June. Its solar system generated the equivalent of 63% of that demand, so its grid electricity was only about a third higher. Compared with June, the estate’s reported load was 40 318 kWh higher in February. Grid electricity was only 6 603 kWh higher. Of interest is the coinciding timing of peak solar potential and the harvest season. February falls within the Cape wine harvest, when electricity demand rises sharply, while solar production is also strong. March followed the same pattern, with solar again covering more than half of the estate’s demand. January, the estate’s heaviest month for electricity, relied more on the grid and also drew on a generator. The estate still draws on the grid every month. What changes is the balance between on-site generation and grid electricity as demand and solar output rise and fall. For a seasonal commercial operation, generating more electricity on site during its busiest period can limit the increase in power that has to be bought from the grid. That matters as tariffs climb. Eskom’s tariff increases this year were close to 9%, from April for its direct customers and from July for municipalities. Almost half the load from PV Between January and August, the estate’s solar system generated the equivalent of almost half its electricity use. The monitoring report records 183.17 tonnes of CO₂ avoided over the same period. The harvest figures are more revealing than that average. In every other month, solar covered less than half of the estate’s demand. For a seasonal business, that timing is the central feature of the data: the harvest months, when demand climbs, are also the months in which solar covers the largest share of it. Stellenbosch is adding generation and storage The municipal project is on a very different scale, but its combination of solar and battery storage points to a wider change in Stellenbosch’s electricity system. The municipality’s tender, BSM 89/25, called for 41.9 MW of solar PV and 14.8 MWh of battery storage, procured through an independent power producer model. The RFP was issued in 2025, and the project was awarded in May 2026. For commercial electricity users, storage can address the gap between when solar is generated and when power is needed. At Vergenoegd Löw, the harvest provides a favourable match because its demand rises during a period of strong solar generation. The municipal buildout is also being accompanied by network investment. Stellenbosch has tendered for two 20 MVA, 66/11 kV transformers to replace three existing 7.5 MVA units at its main substation.

artigo.texto: LITTLETON, Colo. - The City of Littleton is considering a six-month moratorium on any future data center projects. Denver7 confirmed there are no current data center proposals within Littleton city limits that have been filed; the proactive move follows several communities across Colorado considering similar moratoriums. WATCH: City of Littleton considers six month moratorium on data centers The proposed ordinance acknowledges that demand for data centers has grown across the country, and the data centers require large amounts of electricity, water-intensive cooling systems and may create continuous noise and emissions. The moratorium directs City staff to study the land use, energy, water, noise, air quality, infrastructure, fiscal and economic impacts of data centers and proposed changes to the land use code for any potential future projects. Denver7's South Metro Reporter Danielle Kreutter heard from Littleton neighbors about their thoughts on data centers. "What would you like to see as far as restrictions or things that City Council should consider before they allow those kind of projects?" Kreutter asked long time Littleton resident, Paul Bingham. "Well, I can't think of anything beyond: simply not having any," said Bingham. Bingham has lived in Littleton for more than 60 years and has seen his fair share of changes and is hopeful data centers stay out of the city. "[They're] 10-15 football fields in size, a gigantic amount of water and electricity, it all sounds pretty bleak as far as I'm concerned," he said. He believes the space required for a data center will be a logistical challenge in Littleton regardless. "We don't have any land available for a data center. Not a great amount of it. It's all being taken up with, well, right now, a gigantic Costco," Bingham said of construction of the 159,000-square foot Costco project at the Mineral Place mixed-use development. Another Littleton resident, Billy Gooch, also noted how built out Littleton already is. "You need a lot of land, a lot of power, a lot of water. I'm not sure Littleton has any, much less all of those," said Gooch. Gooch worked in telecommunications for 14 years. "I've worked in and around data centers. There are ways to do it responsibly," he said. He's hopeful, if passed, the moratorium requires any possible future projects to follow that requirement. "What would you like to see, generally, included in those considerations?" asked Denver7's South Metro Reporter Danielle Kreutter. "At the very least, they need to pay their own way. No public subsidies. We need to make sure rate payers' electricity is not being impacted and that water is not being impacted," he said. The first hearing on the ordinance is Tuesday night, with a public hearing currently scheduled for November 3. A final vote will happen after the public hearing, however a date has not been set. artigo.texto: The increasingly contentious national debate over data centers moved into Mesa last week as Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes told a town hall that their explosive growth threatens to leave communities with higher utility bills, a range of health and environmental problems and inadequate government oversight. Addressing over 250 people at a Mesa community center Oct. 14, Mayes questioned whether Arizona has done enough to protect residents as developers rush to build the enormous facilities needed to support artificial intelligence, cloud computing and other digital services. The setting was particularly appropriate. Mesa has become a major data center hub, with over 7.5 million square feet of existing and proposed facilities. Yet roughly three-quarters of those attending the meeting had traveled from Ahwatukee, where residents have organized against a 1-million-square-foot facility currently being constructed amid neighborhoods with thousands of homes. Phoenix officials contend California-based Menlo Equities was allowed to build the five-building data campus because the site had been rezoned since the mid-1990s. Critics contend that when data centers were included in that zoning category 30 years ago, no one could envision the mammoth facilities that have torn apart communities across the country. Like Mesa, Phoenix last year adopted a more targeted set of guidelines for data centers, but projects like Menlo’s were not covered because they had already been approved under the older zoning standards. Mayes, a Democrat seeking reelection, has called for a moratorium on data center construction “to get our house in order to determine the principles that should guide this build-up, if it happens, and to decide what’s needed to protect our communities in Arizona. “This issue is too important to let data center developers themselves decide what is right for our state and our communities,” Mayes told the audience. She then put data centers’ explosive growth into perspective for Arizonans: “The Phoenix area is now the second largest U.S. data center hub. … My office has identified more than 180 operating or planned data centers across Arizona.” Of those, 110 are operating, 10 are under construction and almost 40 more are planned, according to Mayes. The Legislature and Gov. Katie Hobbs agreed in June to impose a three-year moratorium starting July 1 on millions of dollars in tax incentives that data centers have been getting from the state. The state Commerce Authority reportedly received 113 applications for those incentives in the second half of June before the moratorium took effect. In the last 10 years, 123 applications were filed. Mayes said her office’s research has found that data center growth in Arizona poses especially dire circumstances amid the state’s unfolding water crisis. “If all planned data centers in the Phoenix area are built,” she said, “stress on our local water supplies will increase by 32%. That would occur at the same time that Arizona loses 30% of our Colorado River water supplies.” She also asserted that data centers’ demand for electricity would drive up customers’ utility bills. Ironically, just hours before her town hall, Chris Bauer, vice president and treasurer for Pinnacle West Capital Corporation and its primary subsidiary, Arizona Public Service Company (APS), told the audience at the East Valley Partnership’s Statespersons’ Luncheon his company intends to “make growth pay for growth. The attorney general currently is suing APS’ proposed 14% rate hike. Mayes also cited noise and even temperature impacts of data centers. She said data centers “regularly generate 94 decibels of noise.” Mesa’s noise ordinance has a 24-hour average sound limit of 60 decibels for residential zones and 65 for commercial zones. She also cited a recent Arizona State University study that says data centers can add 4 degrees to a neighborhood’s temperature downwind from a facility. Mayes outlined a series of demands she wants Arizona to develop for data centers, starting with transparency. She said some data center companies have required municipalities to enter nondisclosure agreements “which limit the ability of local governments … to discuss the project with their constituents.” She said she is currently suing unidentified municipalities over such agreements. She also said data centers should be forbidden from creating nuisances, that natural resources must be protected, that developers be required to pay fully for their power, and that the facilities “must give back.” “In Arizona, it is a tradition that any large development project gives back to the community it inevitably impacts, whether this is through taxes, fees, assessments, or even water storage credits,” she said. “We must ensure that communities that host data centers and that choose to host data centers indeed all Arizonans benefit from their development.” Mayes conceded her office is studying a major issue that has developed when municipalities in Arizona try to deny a data center from being built. Proposition 207, passed by an overwhelming majority of voters in 2006, requires any government level in Arizona to compensate a property owner if zoning or other restrictions lower the fair market value of the property. Earlier this year, Phoenix City Council reversed a denial of a permit for a data center after the property owner filed a claim for over $50 million. “We’re hearing a lot about Prop 207 from cities,” Mayes told the audience – well, mainly from the city of Phoenix, and we are analyzing that issue. So I’m not going to opine yet on Prop 207. But what I will say very clearly is that Prop 207 does not prevent me as your attorney general from filing a nuisance lawsuit against the AI data center.” She added, “I am certain that there are data centers that are being plopped in the middle of new neighborhoods that would meet the classical definition of a nuisance.” Mayes’ Republican opponent, Senate President Warren Pe
